title: Zen and the Art of AI Research
text:
Image from Token for Token.
Jack Morris, writing on his Substack Token for Token, lays out what becoming an AI researcher actually takes, and argues temperament matters more than talent. The piece is structured as a set of Zen koans, and its most useful advice is about how to treat your own experiments:
What the essay argues:

title: Zen and the Art of AI Research
text:
My Notes

The same temperament running teaches: if you remove the AI specifics, this post sounds almost like advice for training for endurance-sport: show up even on bad days, treat a good result and a bad one as equally informative, distrust anything that looks too good, and accept that most of the work is grunt work. I have learned much from running as well as from research!

title: Zen and the Art of AI Research
text:
Related Posts

Proof Generation vs Digestion: Tao’s warning that AI races through proof generation and verification while leaving understanding behind, the same gap this essay names for research code.
Journey into Coding with AI [2/4]: Shifting Gears: on how much control to cede to coding AI and what judgment stays human, the tension the essay’s last sections work through.
NLP Benchmark Saturation: why benchmark-chasing has diminishing returns, the structural backdrop to the essay’s “don’t chase benchmarks.”
“Skills” Are Not Software Engineering: keeping engineering rigor rather than outsourcing it wholesale, a parallel to refusing to outsource understanding.
Terence Tao’s ChatGPT Research Buddy: Tao using ChatGPT as a research aid while keeping control of the math, the productive counterpart to the essay’s caution about not outsourcing understanding.

title: Harness Engineering
text:
Layered domain architecture with explicit cross-cutting boundaries, the rigid layering OpenAI enforces mechanically so agents can move fast without drift. Image from OpenAI.
Ryan Lopopolo, writing for OpenAI, reports on an experiment in Harness Engineering: Leveraging Codex in an Agent-First World: over five months a small team shipped an internal product of roughly a million lines of code with zero manually-written lines, every line produced by Codex while humans steered.
What the article reports:

title: Harness Engineering
text:
My Notes

Two views of the same problem: this report and a source-level read of Anthropic’s Claude Code, Dive into Claude Code: The Design Space of Today’s and Future AI Agent Systems, emphasize different halves of the same system. OpenAI’s account is mostly about the environment the agent works in (the repository as system of record, enforced layering, agent-to-agent review), and the Claude Code read is mostly about the agent program itself (a single agent loop, the permission system, the tools it exposes). Where they meet is the bet that the real engineering lives in the structure around the model rather than the model itself, which is also why the Claude Code analysis finds the loop nearly trivial and almost all the code in the systems wrapped around it.
The scarce resource is human attention: the entire design treats human time and attention as the fixed constraint and reorganizes everything else around it. Legible logs, progressive-disclosure docs, a map instead of a manual: these are all ways to spend less human attention per unit of agent work. It’s the same context-engineering discipline the field has been converging on, here applied at repository scale, and it generalizes past coding to any agentic pipeline. The move from a retrieval flow to a navigable repository the agent investigates on its own is the same reframing as Filesystems vs. RAG.
The engineers moved up a layer: the headline (a million lines, zero hand-written, a tenth of the time) is the part everyone repeats, but the report is careful that the end-to-end autonomy “depends heavily on the specific structure and tooling of this repository and should not be assumed to generalize without similar investment.” Humans went from writing code to specifying intent, encoding invariants, and validating outcomes, which is the same division of labor argued in “Skills” Are Not Software Engineering: the model proposes, and a deterministic layer of linters and structural tests enforces correctness.
Constraints enable the speed: the team front-loaded the kind of rigid architecture you normally postpone until you have hundreds of engineers, because for agents the constraints are what allow speed without decay. The operational detail worth stealing is that the custom lint error messages are written to inject remediation instructions into the agent’s context, so the guardrail doubles as a teaching signal. In a human workflow these rules would feel pedantic. With agents, once encoded they apply everywhere at once.
Autonomous generation produces entropy: Codex replicates whatever patterns already exist, including the bad ones, so the codebase drifts. The team spent a fifth of every week hand-cleaning “AI slop” until that obviously didn’t scale, then replaced it with encoded “golden principles” and recurring cleanup agents. A million lines in five months is also a million lines no human has read line by line, and the bet is that agent-legibility plus tests substitute for that reading. Whether that holds over years is exactly what the report says it doesn’t yet know, the same gap between production and understanding that Proof Generation vs Digestion names for mathematics.

title: Harness Engineering
text:
Related Posts

Dive into Claude Code: The Design Space of Today’s and Future AI Agent Systems: a source-level read of how a coding agent is actually architected, the design-space view this report’s practices fit into.
“Skills” Are Not Software Engineering: the model-proposes, runtime-ensures-correctness split that the enforced invariants and linters here implement.
Filesystems vs. RAG: repository-as-context and “give Codex a map,” the same reframing the report’s knowledge base makes.
Proof Generation vs Digestion: production outrunning understanding, the open question behind a million unread lines.

title: Automated Design of Agentic Systems
text:
The Meta Agent Search loop. A meta agent reads an ever-growing archive of previously discovered agents, proposes the code of a new one, evaluates it on held-out tasks, and appends it to the archive. The bottom strip shows three discovered designs: a multi-step peer-review agent, a verified multimodal agent, and a divide-and-conquer agent. Figure 1 from the paper [1].
In Automated Design of Agentic Systems [1] (ICLR 2025), Shengran Hu, Cong Lu, and Jeff Clune at the University of British Columbia and the Vector Institute argue that the design of LLM-powered agents should itself be automated, and introduce Meta Agent Search as a first instance.

title: Automated Design of Agentic Systems
text:
Methods
The authors cast Automated Design of Agentic Systems (ADAS) as an optimization problem with three components (Figure 2):

Search space: the set of agent designs the method can represent. Meta Agent Search makes this Python code: an agent is a forward(task) function that may call foundation-model APIs, use tools, keep internal state, and compose sub-agents. Because the language is Turing-complete, the space in principle covers any prompt, tool-use pattern, or workflow, not just variations on a fixed template.
Search algorithm: how the space is explored. A meta agent (a frontier LLM, GPT-4 in the experiments) reads an archive of previously discovered agents and programs a new one.
Evaluation function: how a candidate is scored. Each new agent runs on a held-out validation split of the target task, and its accuracy or F1 is the signal the meta agent maximizes.




Figure 2 from the paper [1].


The search loop is short. The meta agent works against a roughly 100-line framework that supplies basic primitives like foundation-model queries and prompt formatting, so it only writes the forward function, the same trick FunSearch [2] used to evolve programs from a small set of given building blocks. Each iteration runs four steps:

The archive is optionally seeded with baseline agents such as Chain-of-Thought and Self-Refine.
Conditioned on the whole archive, the meta agent writes a high-level description of a new agent (the prompt asks for one that is “interestingly new”) and then its code, with two self-reflection passes meant to keep the design novel.
The candidate runs on validation data. If it errors, the meta agent revises the code, repeating up to five times.
The working agent and its score are appended to the archive, and the next iteration conditions on the larger archive.

The archive is the memory that lets each iteration build on the last. Because it stores each agent’s full source code, not just a description, a new agent can copy and recombine code from earlier ones rather than start from scratch. The paper shows several designs discovered on the Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus (ARC) reusing earlier “stepping stones”: a multi-chain-of-thought-then-ensemble pattern that first appeared at iteration 3, and expert-critic ideas from iterations 5, 11, and 12 that the best agent later combined.

title: Automated Design of Agentic Systems
text:
Results
The experiments span three settings, all run with the same algorithm and only task-specific prompt text changed. The ARC abstraction benchmark is the case study. Four benchmarks covering reading, math, science, and multi-task reasoning (DROP, MGSM, MMLU, GPQA) are the main comparison. Held-out tasks and swapped base models test transfer. In every setting the meta agent is GPT-4, while the discovered agents and all baselines are scored with the cheaper GPT-3.5 over five runs each, reporting median accuracy or F1 with a 95% bootstrap confidence interval. The baselines are the standard hand-designed scaffolds (Chain-of-Thought, self-consistency, Self-Refine, LLM-Debate, Quality-Diversity, Step-back Abstraction, Role Assignment) plus the prompt-optimization method OPRO [3] , so the comparison isolates what searching over code buys beyond searching over prompts.
The ARC case study shows the search dynamic most clearly. Over 25 iterations, held-out test accuracy climbs from about 6% to 14%, above every hand-designed baseline. The left panel of Figure 3 tracks that climb and marks the iterations where key ideas first appeared. The right panel shows the best agent found, a “Structured Feedback and Ensemble” design that generates five chains of thought, routes them through three expert critics (efficiency, readability, simplicity) plus a human-like critic, and ensembles three refinement passes.



Figure 3 from the paper [1].


Across the four reasoning benchmarks the same ranking holds, and the margins are largest exactly where the base model already has the knowledge but makes avoidable errors:

Reading comprehension (DROP): 79.4 F1 against 65.8 for the best hand-designed agent, a 13.6-point gain.
Math (MGSM): 53.4% against 39.0% for LLM-Debate, the best baseline, a 14.4-point gain.
Multi-task (MMLU) and science (GPQA): smaller margins (69.6% vs. 67.6%, 34.6% vs. 32.9%), which the authors attribute to the base model lacking the underlying knowledge rather than the scaffold failing.
Cross-domain transfer: the top-3 agents found on MGSM, moved to held-out GSM8K and GSM-Hard, add 25.9% and 13.2% over the baselines. Moved to non-math MMLU and DROP they still beat the hand-designed scaffolds.
Cross-model transfer: the top-3 ARC agents found with GPT-3.5 keep their lead when run on Claude Haiku, GPT-4, and Claude Sonnet, with Sonnet reaching nearly 50% on ARC.

Meta Agent Search wins every column of the head-to-head, and it beats OPRO in all four domains, the result the authors lean on to argue that searching over whole agents, not just prompts, is what pays off.



Table 1 from the paper [1].

title: Automated Design of Agentic Systems
text:
My Notes

Transfer is the result that matters, and it comes from the scaffolds being domain-agnostic: it outweighs the ARC gain, a large relative jump on small absolute numbers (human-level is around 80% [4]). Scaffolds discovered on one task keep working on different tasks and on different base models, because the designs are reasoning-and-control patterns that manipulate model calls without encoding the task itself, with the task-specific content kept in the prompt the agent receives rather than in its code, so they behave less like solvers tuned to one benchmark. This parallels Promptbreeder [5], where evolved prompts transferred, but here the unit that transfers is executable code, a broader portability claim. The search optimized accuracy on a single domain with no cross-domain objective, yet the agents transfer anyway, which is good held-out evidence that the generality is real rather than fit to one benchmark. Optimizing for it directly is still untried.
Code as the search space: earlier automated-prompting work (OPRO [3], APE [6], Promptbreeder) searches over strings fed to a fixed scaffold, and DSPy [7] compiles a human-written module graph, optimizing the prompts and demonstrations inside it rather than the graph itself. ADAS widens the space to code, so the meta agent can invent new control flow (loops, early-exit, ensembles, self-critique), not just better prompts inside an existing shape. AFlow [8] , published around the same time, makes a different trade: it searches a graph over a fixed library of operators with Monte Carlo tree search. ADAS and AFlow leave open whether to search over open-ended code or a fixed operator graph.
The archive both enables the search and makes it expensive: Meta Agent Search is a novelty-seeking search with an LLM as the mutation operator, and the archive of past designs lets each round build on earlier ones. That same archive makes each step expensive: 25 iterations on ARC and 30 on the reasoning benchmarks, each generating one candidate, running two self-reflection passes, and allowing up to five error-driven refinements, with every accepted candidate scored on the full validation set. Scaling to harder benchmarks runs into the sample-efficiency limit that prompt-optimization methods like OPRO [3] also hit, and surrogate scoring to avoid running every candidate on the full eval set is the obvious follow-up.
On the intrinsic-to-extrinsic spectrum of self-improving agents: that spectrum [9], from Liu and van der Schaar, runs from agents that set their own learning loop (intrinsic) to loops fully fixed by humans (extrinsic). ADAS is more intrinsic than the earlier prompt-search optimizers: the meta agent reasons over the archive in an open-ended code space to decide what to build next, which is autonomous metacognitive planning rather than algorithmic mutation, and code can in principle express agents that improve themselves. But the parts that decide what counts as better stay human-fixed: the objective (validation accuracy on a chosen benchmark), the evaluation function, the archive mechanism, the stopping point. So it is a mixed case, not the fully extrinsic end: autonomous proposal inside a human-designed objective and loop. The paper’s own thesis, that hand-designed solutions are eventually replaced by learned ones, applies to the agents but not yet to the loop that finds them. Making that loop learned, a self-referential meta agent that improves itself, is the direction the authors flag as future work. The same team took that step in the Darwin Gödel Machine [10] , where agents rewrite their own code against a growing archive of variants.
The “provided we develop it safely” caveat points at a real property of the method: the abstract’s closing line is not boilerplate. A loop that proposes and executes arbitrary code is a capability-elicitation concern once it is pointed at an open-ended objective rather than a sandboxed benchmark, closer in shape to AutoGPT-style self-improvement than to prompt search. Clune’s earlier argument for AI-generating algorithms [11] is the right context for reading the paper’s scope.

title: Early-Token Confidence Predicts Reasoning Quality in Multi-Agent LLM Debate
text:
Token-level log-probability trajectories for the Advocate and Skeptic on Essay Sets 7 (left) and 8 (right). Solid lines are mean trajectories, shaded bands the 25–75 and 10–90 percentiles. The opening tokens are the most spread out, and so the most informative. Figure 2 from the paper [1].
In Early-Token Confidence Predicts Reasoning Quality in Multi-Agent LLM Debate [1], Keramati et al. (UC Irvine) show that the confidence of an LLM’s first few generated tokens predicts how a judge rates the quality of its reasoning in a debate-based essay-scoring system, often better than statistics taken over the whole response.

title: Early-Token Confidence Predicts Reasoning Quality in Multi-Agent LLM Debate
text:
Methods
The framework scores essays through a structured debate, then mines the debaters’ own decoding signals rather than any reference answer:

Two debating agents: an Advocate argues an essay’s strengths against a rubric trait and a Skeptic rebuts with limitations, both producing open-ended argument without assigning a score. Both are generated by GPT-4o-mini.
Confidence signals: during decoding, each agent’s per-token log-probabilities \(\ell_t = \log p(t_t \mid t_{<t}, x)\) are recorded as an intrinsic confidence trace over the response.
Windows and statistics: from each trace they extract a handful of candidate windows anchored at the start or end of the response — the first or last \(k\) tokens (a fixed count; the paper’s features span \(k\) of 3, 5, 10, and 30) and the first or last \(\alpha T\) tokens (a fraction \(\alpha\) of the response length \(T\), e.g. the final half) — plus the full response, and summarize each window by its mean, median, min, max, variance, standard deviation, range, and trajectory slope.
LLM-as-judge targets: a separate GPT-5-mini judge reads the debate transcript and scores each argument on five targets, which the confidence statistics are then tested against:

Instruction following — three-point ordinal (1 = Low, 2 = Medium, 3 = High)
Justification quality — three-point ordinal
Evidence grounding — three-point ordinal
Aggregate score — the composite, in \([0,9]\)
Critical failure — a binary flag for a severe error; when it fires, the aggregate score above is overridden to 0 Prediction quality is measured per target by its natural metric: Spearman’s \(\rho\) (and Kendall’s \(\tau\)) for the four ordinal targets, AUROC for the binary critical-failure flag. So “critical-failure detection” is just the binary-classification slice of the analysis — predicting that flag — as opposed to rank-correlating the ordinal scores.





The multi-agent debate and LLM-as-judge evaluation framework: an Advocate argues an essay’s strengths and a Skeptic rebuts, both exposing token-level log-probabilities, which are compared against a judge’s rubric scores. Figure 1 from the paper [1].

title: Early-Token Confidence Predicts Reasoning Quality in Multi-Agent LLM Debate
text:
Results
The data is the ASAP automated-essay-scoring benchmark (the Hewlett Foundation’s Automated Student Assessment Prize), restricted to Essay Sets 7 and 8 (the only sets with trait-level human annotations). Advocate and Skeptic arguments come from GPT-4o-mini, and the judge is a deterministic GPT-5-mini. Table 1 reports, for each role–target pair, the top three confidence features ranked by their fit to the judge score and the best score achieved.
Early-token confidence is the standout predictor, most clearly for catching severe failures and on the harder essay set:

Critical-failure detection is strong. The max of the first 3 tokens reaches AUROC 0.849 for the Advocate on Set 7, and the median of the first 5 tokens reaches 0.759 on Set 8, so severe errors tend to show up as localized confidence spikes or drops right at the opening.
Fine-grained quality ranking is weak. The best Spearman correlations with ordinal scores top out near 0.39 (Advocate, Set 7), and the Skeptic’s barely reach 0.11 to 0.27.
Roles are asymmetric. Confidence aligns with judged quality far better for the supportive Advocate than the adversarial Skeptic, across both sets.
Not uniformly early-token. On Set 7 the Advocate’s best ordinal predictor was the full-response median, not an opening-window feature. The early-token advantage shows up mainly on Set 8 and for critical-failure detection.




Top-3 confidence features for each role–target pair across Essay Sets 7 and 8. For the ordinal targets the final column reports Spearman’s \(\rho\); for critical-failure detection it reports AUROC. Early-\(k\) refers to statistics over the first \(k\) generated tokens, final-half to the last 50%. Table 1 from the paper [1].


The judge leans hard on its top score — it assigns a 3 to 77% of essays on instruction following, 79% on justification quality, and 93% on evidence grounding. Evidence grounding is so saturated it behaves almost like a constant, which leaves little rank variation for any confidence feature to align with and mechanically holds its correlation down — a ceiling in the labels, not a failure of the signal.



Distribution of LLM-as-judge scores by dimension: evidence grounding saturates at the top score, while instruction following and justification quality vary more. Figure 3 from the paper [1].

title: Early-Token Confidence Predicts Reasoning Quality in Multi-Agent LLM Debate
text:
My Notes

Intrinsic confidence works for open-ended reasoning too. Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know established that a model’s token probabilities track correctness on closed-form tasks. This paper extends the idea to open-ended, reference-free reasoning and localizes it: the first three to five tokens hold more predictive signal than the full sequence, which makes the proxy a cheap decoding-time read rather than a separate calibration model [1].
Confidence is diagnostic for advocacy, not for critique. The Skeptic’s log-probability confidence barely correlates with judged quality (Spearman 0.11 to 0.27) while the Advocate’s does (up to 0.39, AUROC 0.85). That matches a known soft spot: MAST found verification failures — a system not checking its own work — to be a recurring multi-agent breakdown. Here the critique role is also where intrinsic confidence is least informative, so monitoring helps least on the function that most needs a second look.
It is a failure flag, not a fine scorer. Rank agreement with graded quality is weak (Spearman around 0.39 at best), but critical-failure detection is strong (AUROC up to 0.85). And the abstract’s “consistently the strongest” is set-dependent: on Essay Set 7 the Advocate’s best ordinal predictor was the full-response median, not an early-token feature.
What can we do with token logits reliably? Only one thing transfers across the paper’s two essay sets: the predictive signal lives in the opening three to five tokens, so early-token statistics make a cheap decode-time screen for severe failures (AUROC up to 0.85 within a set). The specific feature and its direction do not transfer — the top detector is the max of the first three tokens on Set 7 but the median of the first five on Set 8, and the signs even disagree (a confident early spike flags failure, a wide early spread suppresses it). So the reliable recipe is narrow: read the first few tokens, but fit which statistic and which sign on your own data rather than lifting a fixed rule from this paper.

title: Pramaana Labs Raises $27M to Bring Formal Verification to AI
text:
A Doric temple overlaid with formal measurements and proportions. Image from TechCrunch.
TechCrunch reports that Pramaana Labs has raised a $27M seed round led by Khosla Ventures to apply formal verification, specifically the Lean proof language used to check mathematical proofs, as a deterministic layer on top of an LLM. The LLM still answers the natural-language question. A Lean-style system then checks that the answer obeys a formalized rulebook. Pramaana is targeting rule-dense, high-stakes verticals like law, tax preparation, and drug discovery, building a separate verification system per domain with oversight from experts such as former IRS commissioner Danny Werfel. The company was founded by three IIT Madras alumni whose backgrounds run through Google Maps moderation, Glean, and Google DeepMind’s Gemini team. Co-founder Ranjan Rajagopalan frames the bet this way: “The world’s hardest problems are not unsolvable. They are unformalized.”
What Pramaana is building:

title: Pramaana Labs Raises $27M to Bring Formal Verification to AI
text:
My Notes

The bottleneck moves from the model to the spec. The deterministic layer checks that the LLM’s output obeys a formalized rulebook, but it cannot check that the rulebook itself is correct or complete. A proof of conformance is only as good as the formalization, and turning law or tax into Lean means making thousands of interpretive choices that can each be wrong. Verified Doesn’t Mean Nothing Can Go Wrong is the sharp version of this: a Claude agent found a buffer overflow in the Lean runtime under code that was itself formally verified.
The verticals are rule-dense, but not equally formalizable. Law and tax are good fits because they are written rules, and France’s CATALA project already turns much of the French tax and benefit code into executable form. Drug discovery is a harder case: much of it is empirical and statistical rather than a codified rulebook, so the pitch that codifying the rules makes the reasoning deterministic fits tax far better than it fits biology. The ongoing cost is also real, since a formalization of the tax code has to be re-checked every time the code changes.
This is a per-domain build, not a horizontal product. Each vertical gets its own Lean-style system overseen by domain experts: a former IRS commissioner for tax, named professors for cybersecurity and drug discovery. That makes the moat the formalization work and the expert relationships, which reads closer to a high-end services model than to software that scales by adding users. The Project 1729 fellowship, which embeds a Pramaana engineer with each outside team, fits that shape: each new domain is its own formalization project. The same LLM-plus-Lean toolchain is being pushed on open math problems in Advancing Mathematics Research with AI-Driven Formal Proof Search, where the binding constraint is likewise how much gets formalized, not the model.
The competitive landscape, especially in law and tax. The field splits on what makes a high-stakes answer trustworthy, and Pramaana’s wager is on machine-checkable proof:

The proof camp (Pramaana’s own): Axiom, founder Carina Hong’s Lean-based startup, runs the same deterministic-formal-layer thesis aimed at mathematics. Imandra sells “reasoning as a service,” applying automated reasoning and formal verification to mission-critical and financial-regulatory decisions, which puts it closest to Pramaana’s professional territory.
The retrieval camp (what Pramaana positions against): X’s Moonshot for Specialized Professional Intelligence and Harvey chase the legal market with LLM analysis over private documents, while Thomson Reuters and LexisNexis tools still hallucinate more than 17% of the time. In tax, Black Ore’s “Tax Autopilot” automates tax preparation for CPA (certified public accountant) firms with a claimed 99% accuracy, and France’s CATALA remains the closest formal precedent.

title: Pramaana Labs Raises $27M to Bring Formal Verification to AI
text:
Related Posts

title: Spiking Neural Networks: A Primer
text:
A surrogate-gradient spiking network reading a dynamic-vision-sensor (event-camera) gesture stream, with local readout costs at each step. Figure from Neftci, Mostafa & Zenke [1].
Spiking neural networks (SNNs) are often called the “third generation” of neural network models, a term due to Maass [2], after the McCulloch–Pitts threshold unit [3] and the continuous-valued, rate-based units of modern deep learning. The idea is older than the name: the integrate-and-fire neuron goes back to Lapicque in 1907, Hodgkin and Huxley’s 1952 model of the action potential [4] earned a Nobel Prize, and computing with spikes drew sustained interest through the 1990s before energy-efficient neuromorphic hardware revived it in the 2010s. The defining difference: SNN neurons communicate with discrete, asynchronous, binary events called spikes placed in continuous time, rather than with real-valued activations exchanged synchronously layer by layer. Computation becomes a function not just of which neurons fire and how much, but of when they fire.

title: Spiking Neural Networks: A Primer
text:
Research questions and goals
The field is pulled by three partly-overlapping agendas, and it’s worth being explicit about which one a given paper is serving, because the three imply different success criteria.

Energy-efficient computation. Spikes are sparse and event-driven: a neuron does work only when it receives or emits a spike, and a multiply-accumulate collapses to an accumulate (no weight is multiplied by a graded activation, just an accumulate when a spike arrives). On the right hardware this promises orders-of-magnitude lower energy than dense matrix multiplication. The central question is whether that advantage holds on real tasks at competitive accuracy.
Computational neuroscience. SNNs are the natural modeling substrate for how biological brains actually compute, since real neurons spike. Here the goal is explanatory: understanding coding, plasticity, and dynamics. Biological plausibility is a feature rather than a constraint to relax.
Temporal computation. Because state and timing are intrinsic, SNNs are a candidate substrate for streaming, event-based, low-latency signals (event cameras, audio, sensor streams) where the input is naturally a sparse stream of events rather than a sequence of dense frames.

The hard open problem cutting across all three agendas is training. The spike-generating function is a threshold (a step), so its derivative is zero almost everywhere and undefined at threshold, leaving standard backpropagation no gradient to descend. Most methodological research of the last decade is, directly or indirectly, an answer to a handful of open questions:

The non-differentiability problem. How do you train a network whose core nonlinearity is a non-differentiable step? The two leading answers are surrogate gradients [1] and conversion from a trained artificial neural network (ANN) [5].
What should spikes encode? Rate, precise timing, or something in between? Does that choice change what the network can compute, and how cheaply?
Can learning be local and online? Global backpropagation-through-time [6] works but is biologically implausible and awkward for hardware. The leading local alternative is spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP), which adjusts each synapse using only the relative timing of its own pre- and post-synaptic spikes [7], [8]. Today it does not close the gap: unsupervised STDP reaches about 95% on MNIST [9] against the 99%+ of backprop-trained networks, and the gap widens sharply on harder benchmarks, with pure STDP yet to produce competitive results on ImageNet. Whether a local rule can ever match backprop on accuracy is the open question.
Can the accuracy gap close without re-importing the cost? SNNs still trail conventional networks on large-scale tasks: on ImageNet the best directly-trained SNNs reach roughly 80% top-1 accuracy against the ~90% of leading conventional models (details below). Closing that gap while keeping the sparsity and energy advantage, rather than reintroducing the dense computation that made conventional networks expensive, is the open engineering question.

title: Spiking Neural Networks: A Primer
text:
Techniques and the mathematics

The neuron model
The most widely used model is the leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) neuron, whose membrane potential \(V(t)\) integrates incoming current and leaks back toward rest. It is defined by its rate of change:
\[\frac{dV(t)}{dt} = \frac{-\big(V(t) - V_\text{rest}\big) + R\,I(t)}{\tau_m}\]
You integrate this over time to get \(V(t)\), the “integrate” in integrate-and-fire. (The literature usually writes the equivalent form \(\tau_m\,\frac{dV}{dt} = -(V - V_\text{rest}) + R\,I(t)\), with the time constant multiplying the derivative.)
In plain terms: the voltage leaks steadily back toward its resting level while incoming current pushes it up. When the push wins and the integrated voltage reaches threshold, the neuron fires and resets.
Here \(I(t)\) is the input current (the summed synaptic drive) and \(R\) the membrane resistance, so \(R\,I(t)\) is the voltage the input would drive the membrane to at rest. When \(V\) crosses a threshold \(V_\text{th}\), the neuron emits a spike and \(V\) is reset (to \(V_\text{rest}\) or by subtracting \(V_\text{th}\)). The constant \(\tau_m = RC\) is the membrane time constant, the timescale over which the voltage relaxes back toward rest once input stops, much like an \(RC\) circuit discharging. A large \(\tau_m\) means a slow leak and a long memory of past input. A small one means the neuron forgets almost immediately and responds only to near-coincident spikes.
For simulation and training this is discretized. A common form, written as a recurrent unit over time steps \(t\):
\[U[t] = \beta\,U[t-1] + W X[t] - S[t-1]\,U_\text{th}, \qquad S[t] = \Theta\big(U[t] - U_\text{th}\big)\]
In plain terms: this is the same leaky neuron rewritten so a computer can step through it in time. At each tick it keeps the previous voltage but shrinks it by the decay \(\beta\), adds the new weighted input \(W X[t]\), and subtracts the threshold to reset if it fired on the last tick.
where \(U[t]\) is the membrane potential at time step \(t\) (the discrete-time counterpart of \(V\)), \(W\) the synaptic weights, \(X[t]\) the input spikes arriving at that step, \(\beta = e^{-\Delta t/\tau_m} \in (0,1)\) the decay factor, \(S[t]\in\{0,1\}\) the output spike, and \(\Theta\) the Heaviside step function (\(\Theta(x) = 1\) when \(x \geq 0\), else \(0\)), so the neuron emits a spike (\(S[t]=1\)) exactly when the potential \(U[t]\) reaches the threshold \(U_\text{th}\) and stays silent (\(S[t]=0\)) below it. The last term subtracts the threshold after a spike, implementing reset-by-subtraction. In this form an SNN is essentially a recurrent network with a binary activation and a built-in leak, which is exactly why deep-learning training methods can be brought to bear.
Other neuron models trade biological fidelity against cost:

Hodgkin–Huxley [4] (1952): a system of coupled nonlinear ordinary differential equations (ODEs) modeling ion-channel conductances. Biophysically faithful, expensive.
Izhikevich [10] (2003): two coupled equations, \(\dot v = 0.04v^2 + 5v + 140 - u + I\) and \(\dot u = a(bv - u)\) with after-spike reset. A celebrated sweet spot: it reproduces a large repertoire of cortical firing patterns (bursting, chattering, fast-spiking) at roughly the cost of LIF.
Spike Response Model [11] (Gerstner): an integral, kernel-based reformulation convenient for analysis.



What spikes encode
A spiking network has to commit to what a spike means: how information is read out of a spike train. Rate and temporal/latency coding are the two ends of a spectrum, differing in how much they rely on the precise timing of spikes rather than their average count, and a real code can sit anywhere between them. Population coding is a separate question (which neurons in a group fire) and combines with either. What matters in practice is how a use case maps the code onto the output format it needs:

Rate coding → a class label. Each input (say, a pixel) drives a spike train whose rate is proportional to its value, and a downstream neuron’s firing rate then stands in for a real-valued activation (80 spikes in 100 steps ≈ an activation of 0.8). The output layer has one neuron per class, and the prediction is the output neuron with the highest spike count over the window, the spiking analogue of taking an ANN’s largest logit. This is the default for ANN-to-SNN conversion and deep-SNN image classifiers, where accuracy matters more than latency. The cost is the many time steps needed to estimate each rate, and that when spikes occur is discarded.
Temporal / latency coding → a fast decision. Information lives in when a neuron first fires: a stronger or more salient input fires earlier (time-to-first-spike). The readout watches for the earliest output spikes and settles on a class as soon as one fires, often before the full window elapses. That is what suits it to ultra-low-latency, low-power inference (always-on keyword spotting or fast detection on neuromorphic chips) and to models of the brain’s rapid visual categorization. It is sparse (potentially one spike per neuron) but harder to train and more fragile.
Population coding → a continuous value. Each neuron has a preferred value (a tuning curve), and a quantity is represented by the pattern of activity across the group. The output is decoded as a weighted combination of the population’s firing (a population vector, or a learned linear decoder), yielding a continuous vector rather than a discrete class. This underlies continuous-variable tasks like motor control and robotics: it is the basis of the Neural Engineering Framework [12] behind Nengo, and of the classic decoding of movement direction from motor-cortex activity [13].



Training methods
Three broad families of methods are used to train an SNN.
ANN-to-SNN conversion. Train a conventional rectified-linear-unit (ReLU) network normally, then map activations to firing rates and copy the weights into a rate-coded SNN, calibrating thresholds [5], [14]. Achieves near-ANN accuracy and sidesteps the gradient problem entirely, but typically needs many time steps (high latency, eroding the energy win) and only yields rate codes.
Surrogate gradients. The dominant direct-training approach. Use the hard step \(\Theta\) on the forward pass, but substitute a smooth surrogate derivative on the backward pass, pretending (only for gradient purposes) that the spike function had a soft slope. A common choice is the derivative of a fast sigmoid [15] or a triangular/boxcar function centered at threshold:
\[\frac{\partial S}{\partial U} \;\approx\; \frac{1}{\big(1 + |U - U_\text{th}|\big)^2} \quad\text{(one popular surrogate)}\]
In plain terms: a real spike is all-or-nothing, so its true slope is zero almost everywhere and undefined at threshold, useless for gradient descent. On the backward pass we pretend the neuron responded smoothly, with sensitivity highest right at threshold and tapering off as the voltage moves away from it.
Unrolling the LIF recurrence over time and applying backpropagation-through-time then trains the network end-to-end. This is the core idea behind STBP (spatio-temporal backpropagation) [16] and is surveyed definitively by Neftci, Mostafa & Zenke [1]. The broader set of supervised and unsupervised methods is reviewed by Tavanaei et al. [17].
Local / biologically-inspired plasticity. STDP is an unsupervised, local rule: a synapse strengthens if the presynaptic spike precedes the postsynaptic one (causal, “pre-before-post”) and weakens otherwise. The dependence was characterized experimentally by Markram et al. [8] and Bi & Poo [7]. A standard form:
\[\Delta w = \begin{cases} A_+\, e^{-\Delta t/\tau_+} & \Delta t > 0 \ (\text{pre before post}) \\[4pt] -A_-\, e^{\Delta t/\tau_-} & \Delta t < 0 \ (\text{post before pre}) \end{cases}\]
In plain terms: if the input spike lands just before the neuron fires, the synapse is strengthened (it helped cause the spike). If it lands just after, it is weakened, and either effect fades the further apart in time the two spikes are.
with \(\Delta t = t_\text{post} - t_\text{pre}\). STDP needs no labels or global error signal and maps cleanly onto on-chip learning, but on its own it lags supervised methods on accuracy. Diehl & Cook [9] is the canonical demonstration, reaching competitive MNIST accuracy with STDP alone. It remains central to the neuroscience agenda and to online-learning hardware.

title: Spiking Neural Networks: A Primer
section: How biologically realistic is it, really?
text:
How biologically realistic is it, really?
SNNs are routinely described as “more biologically realistic” than conventional networks. That’s true, but in a narrower sense than the phrase suggests, and it’s worth separating what holds from what gets oversold.
The claim holds at the level of signal representation. Real neurons communicate with discrete action potentials whose timing encodes information, and SNNs do the same. Conventional rate-based networks do neither: each unit emits a single continuous value with no temporal structure. SNNs also maintain intrinsic state (membrane potential, leak) and event-driven dynamics that mirror real neural behavior. STDP in particular was discovered experimentally in biology and then imported into SNNs, so that learning rule is genuinely biologically grounded rather than reverse-engineered. By this measure an SNN is unambiguously closer to a brain than a ReLU multilayer perceptron (MLP).
But “more realistic than an ANN” is a low bar, and most working SNNs clear it and then stop:

The standard LIF neuron is a gross simplification: a single compartment, no dendritic computation, no ion-channel dynamics, a fixed threshold. Real neurons are closer to small nonlinear networks in themselves. Hodgkin–Huxley is far more biophysically detailed, but its cost and stiff dynamics keep it almost entirely out of trained networks. It lives in computational-neuroscience simulation instead.
The most successful SNNs are trained with surrogate-gradient backpropagation-through-time, and backprop is exactly the part that is biologically implausible, since it needs a global error signal, symmetric weight transport, and a backward pass the brain has no obvious mechanism for [18]. The systems that perform best are realistic in their neurons and implausible in their learning.
Rate coding, the easiest regime to train, discards the spike-timing information that motivated the realism argument in the first place, leaving a spiking implementation of essentially rate-based computation.
Connectivity structure, neuromodulation, glia, conduction delays, the diversity of neuron types: none of it is in a typical SNN.

Biological realism is really an argument for using SNNs in neuroscience rather than in engineering. For the energy and edge-AI agenda the operative property is sparse, event-driven computation on neuromorphic hardware, an efficiency argument rather than a fidelity one. The two get conflated because “brain-like” sells, but a system can be brain-like in the way that matters for power (sparse spikes) while being quite unbrain-like in how it learns.

title: Spiking Neural Networks: A Primer
text:
Potential impact

Edge and always-on AI. Ultra-low-power inference for wearables, hearing aids, keyword spotting, and battery-constrained sensors: the most credible near-term commercial case.
Event-based vision and robotics. Pairing with event cameras (dynamic vision sensors), which output sparse per-pixel brightness-change events [19], SNNs offer microsecond-latency, low-power perception for drones, autonomous systems, and high-speed tracking.
Neuroscience. Large-scale spiking simulations test theories of coding, plasticity, and circuit dynamics, feeding back into our understanding of biological computation.
Sustainability. If the energy advantage holds at scale, neuromorphic computing is one of the few proposals that attacks the rising energy cost of AI at the architectural level rather than the process-node level.

The honest caveat: most efficiency claims are realized only on matched neuromorphic hardware. On a graphics processing unit (GPU), simulating an SNN over many time steps is often slower and more energy-hungry than the equivalent conventional network. The advantage is a hardware–algorithm co-design story, not an algorithm-alone story.

title: Spiking Neural Networks: A Primer
text:
Current status
Hardware is the most mature dimension. Intel Loihi 2 (with the open Lava software framework), IBM NorthPole [20], Manchester SpiNNaker 2 [21], Heidelberg BrainScaleS-2 [22], and commercial parts like BrainChip Akida and SynSense processors are all available to researchers or in products. These demonstrate real energy and latency wins on sparse, event-driven workloads.
Software has matured rapidly: snnTorch, Norse, SpikingJelly, BindsNET, and Nengo make surrogate-gradient training routine on top of PyTorch, and standardized event-based datasets (N-MNIST [23], DVS-Gesture [24], CIFAR10-DVS [25]) support benchmarking.
Accuracy. The gap with conventional networks is narrowing but not yet closed:

Small-to-medium and event-based tasks: surrogate-gradient SNNs are now competitive with conventional networks, and the gap is nearly closed.
Large-scale (ImageNet): directly-trained SNNs reached about 75% top-1 accuracy in 2023 (Spikformer [26]) and roughly 80–81% by 2024 (Spikformer V2 [27]), against the 85–90%+ of leading vision transformers and convolutional networks, narrowing from wide to a few points but not yet closing.
Overall: the synthesis from Roy, Jaiswal & Panda [28] and the Eshraghian et al. tutorial [29]: the building blocks exist and the energy case is real on the right substrate, but no general-purpose, clearly-superior spiking system at scale has arrived yet.
The frontier: closing the accuracy gap while preserving sparsity, and developing learning rules that are both effective and hardware-local.

title: Spiking Neural Networks: A Primer
text:
People and institutions
Foundations and theory. Wolfgang Maass (TU Graz) framed spiking networks as the third generation and established much of their computational theory. Eugene Izhikevich (then UCSD/NSI) gave the field its most-used efficient neuron model. Wulfram Gerstner (EPFL) co-authored the standard textbook Spiking Neuron Models. Terrence Sejnowski (Salk Institute) and Sander Bohte (CWI) contributed early coding and learning work.
Training methodology. Emre Neftci (now Forschungszentrum Jülich / RWTH Aachen) and Friedemann Zenke (Friedrich Miescher Institute, Basel) are central figures in surrogate-gradient learning. Timothée Masquelier (CNRS, Toulouse) works on STDP and temporal coding. Kaushik Roy (Purdue) leads spike-based deep learning and its hardware co-design. Jason Eshraghian (UC Santa Cruz) authored the widely-used snnTorch tutorial-paper and library.
Neuromorphic hardware. Carver Mead (Caltech) coined “neuromorphic” in the 1980s [30]. Giacomo Indiveri (Institute of Neuroinformatics, ETH Zurich / University of Zurich) is a leading mixed-signal neuromorphic engineer. Steve Furber (University of Manchester) built SpiNNaker [31]. The late Karlheinz Meier (Heidelberg) drove BrainScaleS. Dharmendra Modha led IBM TrueNorth [32] (and later NorthPole [20]). Mike Davies leads Intel’s Loihi [33] program. These efforts were heavily catalyzed by the EU Human Brain Project (2013–2023, now continued as the EBRAINS research infrastructure) and the US DARPA SyNAPSE program (2008–2014).
Today. The field’s center of gravity is shifting from big-science programs to a commercial wave: BrainChip (Akida), SynSense, and Innatera now ship neuromorphic silicon aimed at low-power edge sensing, while the academic side stays active through Intel’s Neuromorphic Research Community and continued SpiNNaker 2 work at Manchester and TU Dresden.

Related Posts

Physical Neural Networks: the closest sibling — training non-digital substrates (optics, electronics, mechanics) by backpropagation, the same “compute outside the von Neumann box” instinct that motivates neuromorphic SNN hardware.

title: Estonia Intends to Recognize AI Agents With Digital IDs
text:
A page from a 1979 internal IBM training manual. Image via Simon Willison.
The Register reports that Estonia plans to give AI agents their own digital identities, so an agent acting for a person can be verified and audited. The primary source is a statement from the Estonian Government Office: at the second meeting of the Eesti.ai advisory board on 17 June 2026, the board agreed to move forward with digital identities for AI agents, which it calls an “AI ID.” Prime Minister Kristen Michal put the goal in terms of one question:
What the proposal says:
The Register places the move in a wider scramble over who answers for an agent’s actions. Argentina’s president Javier Milei has endorsed “non-human corporations” run by software with limited liability. In commerce, Target’s terms now treat actions by an agent you authorized as transactions you made, while American Express goes the other way and promises to cover customers when an authorized agent makes a purchase in error. The piece also revives the line from IBM’s 1979 training manual, that a computer can never be held accountable and so must never make a management decision, and notes that courts are filling the gap anyway, holding Air Canada liable for bad chatbot advice.

title: Estonia Intends to Recognize AI Agents With Digital IDs
text:
My Notes

A digital ID is really about who to blame. A software agent can’t be punished the way a person can, as Mark Riedl and Deven Desai point out: you can fine or jail a human, not a piece of software. So an AI ID doesn’t make the agent answerable. It records who authorized the agent and how much it was allowed to do, so there is finally a clear human to hold responsible when something goes wrong. The commerce terms above are early, ad hoc stabs at the same problem. A national identity layer would settle it the same way every time.
Estonia can be first because the hard part is already built. The AI ID is an increment on e-Estonia’s digital identity, X-Road data exchange, and digital signatures, not a greenfield project. The same fact makes the “first country” claim credible and the approach hard to copy elsewhere: a state without an e-government foundation would have to stand up the identity layer before it could scope an agent’s powers at all.

title: The ACUTE Protocol: Operationalizing Language Model Activations for Better Calibration, Utility, and Trust
text:
The ACUTE protocol: input features drawn from a model’s internal activations train a confidence estimator that decides whether to trust or abstain from each output. Figure 2 from the paper [1].
In The ACUTE Protocol: Operationalizing Language Model Activations for Better Calibration, Utility, and Trust [1] (ICML 2026), Nishant Subramani, Palash Goyal, Yiwen Song, Mani Malek, Yuan Xue, Tomas Pfister, and Hamid Palangi (CMU, Google, Scale AI) train lightweight classifiers on a model’s own hidden states to decide when to trust its output, and propose a utility metric, EURO, that scores confidence estimates on whether they help a downstream decision rather than on calibration alone.

title: The ACUTE Protocol: Operationalizing Language Model Activations for Better Calibration, Utility, and Trust
text:
Methods
The paper has two parts: a metric EURO and a confidence estimator ACUTE.
EURO (expected utility renormalized by the oracle) answers a complaint about calibration scores. The expected calibration error (ECE) and its smoothed variant (smECE) measure whether stated confidences match observed accuracy, but a model that reports the base rate on every example is perfectly calibrated and useless. EURO instead frames confidence as a trust-or-abstain decision and scores the utility of acting on it, in four steps:

Assign rewards to the four outcomes: the trust-or-abstain decision has four cases, each with a task-set reward. Trusting a correct answer earns \(R_{tp}\), abstaining on a wrong one earns \(R_{tn}\), trusting a wrong one earns \(R_{fp}\), and abstaining on a correct one earns \(R_{fn}\), with correct calls rewarded (\(R_{tp}, R_{tn} \ge 0\)) and mistakes penalized (\(R_{fp}, R_{fn} \le 0\)).
Reduce them to one knob.

Net utilities: \(U_{ct} = R_{tp} - R_{fn}\) is the gain from correctly trusting a correct answer instead of abstaining, and \(U_{ca} = R_{tn} - R_{fp}\) the gain from correctly abstaining on a wrong answer instead of trusting. The subtracted terms are penalties (\(R_{fn}, R_{fp} \le 0\)), so each difference is the full swing between the two outcomes.
Normalize: rescale the pair to sum to one, \(u_{ct} = U_{ct}/(U_{ct}+U_{ca})\) and \(u_{ca} = U_{ca}/(U_{ct}+U_{ca})\).
The threshold falls out: the minimum-Bayes-risk threshold works out to exactly \(\tau = u_{ca}\), so the estimator trusts when its confidence \(\hat{p}\) exceeds \(u_{ca}\). A plain classifier (reward 1 for a correct call, 0 for a mistake) gives \(\tau = 0.5\).
Penalties steer it: making a wrong trust expensive (\(R_{fp} \ll 0\)) raises \(u_{ca}\) toward 1, so the estimator demands more confidence before trusting, while making a wrong abstention expensive (\(R_{fn} \ll 0\)) grows \(U_{ct}\) and lowers \(u_{ca}\) toward 0, so it trusts more readily.

Renormalize to a fixed scale: score the estimator’s utility at a given \(u_{ca}\) against a perfect oracle (1) and a worst-case anti-oracle (0), so the number is comparable across tasks.
Sweep risk levels: the four rewards are application-specific, so rather than fix them per task the experiments leave them unset and sweep \(u_{ca}\) across its whole range \((0, 1)\), which is enough because \(\tau = u_{ca}\) collapses the reward structure into that one number. The area under the resulting curve, auc-euro, is the headline number, reported both over the full range and over three bins: low \(u_{ca} \in (0, 1/3)\), medium \([1/3, 2/3)\), and high \([2/3, 1)\), identically across MMLU, APIGen, and SCITLDR.

Figure 1 shows why this matters: ECE and smECE rank the two worst estimators (a base-rate predictor and a noisy base-rate predictor) above a probabilistic oracle, while auc-euro orders all four correctly.



Four confidence estimators ranked from best to worst, scored by ECE, smooth ECE, and the paper’s auc-euro (higher auc-euro is better, lower ECE/smECE is better). ECE and smECE rate the two base-rate estimators above the probabilistic oracle, while only auc-euro orders all four correctly. Figure 1 from the paper [1].


ACUTE (activation-based confidence, utility, and trust estimation) is the estimator. For each output it reads the model’s internal activations and trains a random forest to predict whether the output is correct. The features aren’t concatenated into one model: each of three feature families trains its own estimator, and the paper reports six configurations in total:

Mean-pooled activations: the hidden states at a layer, averaged over tokens. Trained per layer, this yields three configurations, the best estimator from the early, middle, and late third of layers (acute early/mid/late act).
Layer-wise cosine similarities with the final layer: a low-dimensional summary of how each layer’s activation aligns with the last, one configuration (acute cosine).
PCA-transformed activations: a layer’s activations reduced to their top 10 or 20 principal components, two configurations (acute pca10, acute pca20).

Random forests are the classifier throughout because they slightly outperformed logistic regression and support vector machines in early experiments, and because a well-trained forest needs no post-hoc recalibration. A single decision tree reads its probability off leaf purity and pushes toward 0 or 1, the reason tree estimators have traditionally needed post-hoc scaling such as Platt scaling [2] [3]. A forest instead reports the vote fraction across many decorrelated trees, a smoother estimate that is already close to calibrated when the forest is well-trained [4].

title: The ACUTE Protocol: Operationalizing Language Model Activations for Better Calibration, Utility, and Trust
text:
Results
The protocol is evaluated on six models from four families (gemma-3-4b-it, gemma-3-12b-it, Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507, Qwen3-14B, phi-4, and SmolLM3-3B) across three deliberately distinct tasks: MMLU multiple-choice question answering [5] (5-shot, scored over its 57 subtasks), APIGen tool-calling [6] (zero-shot, approximate exact match), and SCITLDR scientific-abstract summarization [7] (zero-shot, ROUGE-L). The two generation tasks force the estimator to work from multi-token output, not a single classification logit. ACUTE’s six configurations are compared against raw confidences and two strong, cheap baselines, a histogram regression estimator (HRE) and Nadaraya-Watson kernel regression (NWKR), with calibration measured by smECE (lower is better) and utility by auc-euro (higher is better) at low, medium, and high risk.
The headline numbers (Table 1, averaged across models) decompose by task:

Tool-calling shows the largest gain. On APIGen, acute pca20 reaches 0.88 auc-euro versus 0.78 for both HRE and NWKR, roughly 0.10 ahead of the strong baselines and 0.35 ahead of raw confidences (0.53).
Multiple-choice shows a modest gain. On MMLU, acute late act reaches 0.83 versus 0.79 for NWKR, with the edge concentrated at high risk (0.80 versus 0.74).
Summarization shows essentially none. On SCITLDR, every method including the histogram baseline scores 0.77–0.78, and ACUTE matches the baselines without beating them.
Calibration holds throughout. smECE stays low (around 0.07–0.09), comparable to the calibration baselines, so the utility gains do not come at the cost of miscalibration.




smECE (lower is better) and auc-euro at low/medium/high risk on MMLU, APIGen, and SCITLDR, averaged across the six models. The ACUTE rows lead on APIGen and MMLU, especially at high risk, and sit level with the baselines on SCITLDR. Table 1 from the paper [1].


Figure 4 shows where that high-risk edge on MMLU comes from. The y-axis is EURO, the oracle-renormalized expected utility where 1.0 matches a perfect oracle and higher is better. The x-axis is the risk level \(u_{ca}\), the normalized abstention utility defined above (equivalently the trust threshold \(\tau\)), running from low-risk settings on the left to high-risk on the right, where wrongly trusting a bad answer is costliest. Each line is one estimator, one of the three baselines or ACUTE’s six configurations, averaged over the 57 MMLU subtasks. At low risk, where abstaining is cheap, every estimator including the baselines performs about the same and the curves overlap. As the risk level rises the ACUTE estimators pull away from raw confidences, HRE, and NWKR, which is why ACUTE’s MMLU advantage is modest in the pooled score but pronounced at high risk.



EURO versus risk level on MMLU for four of the six models, averaged over the 57 subtasks, with three baselines and ACUTE’s six configurations. All policies are close at low risk, but ACUTE pulls ahead at high risk. Figure 4 from the paper [1].


The analysis sections add three supporting results:

Sample-efficient. ACUTE reaches its accuracy with small training sets.
Middle and late layers win. Those depths give the strongest mean-pooled signal.
Generalizes to a mixture-of-experts model. On Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 (Table 2), an MoE with 30B total but only ~3B active parameters, acute pca20 and acute late act reach roughly 0.87 auc-euro on APIGen against about 0.82 for the calibration baselines, with the SCITLDR result flat again. The active footprint is on par with the smallest dense models tested, so this checks the MoE architecture rather than a larger compute budget.




Results on the APIGen and SCITLDR tasks for the mixture-of-experts model Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507. The ACUTE configurations again lead on APIGen while staying level with the baselines on SCITLDR. Table 2 from the paper [1].

title: The ACUTE Protocol: Operationalizing Language Model Activations for Better Calibration, Utility, and Trust
text:
My Notes

What EURO adds beyond proper scores. EURO is motivated by the fact that ECE rewards a base-rate predictor, the failure I worked through in a primer on calibration metrics, where a constant-0.5 model scores a perfect zero while saying nothing. But the Brier score and log loss already can’t be gamed that way, so EURO’s real addition is not gaming-resistance but the risk-level framing: it scores confidence by the utility of trusting or abstaining and sweeps that utility across risk levels. The paper’s Appendix B agrees: minimizing the Brier score gives a Bayes-optimal predictor, but Brier still ignores the task’s risk level, the same blind spot as ECE.
It needs access to the model’s internals. ACUTE reads activations, so only whoever holds the weights can run it, which the paper accepts as fine for model developers. That makes it a first-party tool, unlike verbalized confidence (Just Ask for Calibration) or logit-based self-knowledge (Kadavath et al.), which a caller can use through an API. It is closest to reading confidence off the residual stream (metacognitive monitoring and control through activations), but trains an external probe instead of asking the model to report on itself.
The gain depends on the scoring metric. ACUTE helps a lot on tool-calling, a little on multiple choice, and not at all on summarization. Tool-calling is judged by near-exact match, close to a yes/no, while a ROUGE-L summary score is fuzzy, and there even the histogram baseline is near the ceiling. The activation signal for whether an answer is right seems strongest when “right” is close to binary, which suggests ACUTE will help most on verifiable tasks and least on open-ended generation.

title: Conformal Certification of Reasoning Trace Prefixes
text:
CROP returns a green certified prefix and routes the red uncertified suffix to a blue repair pass, shown on an Arithmetic and a GSM8K trace. Figure 1 from the paper [1].
In Conformal Certification of Reasoning Trace Prefixes [1] (arXiv preprint, May 2026), Matt Y. Cheung, Ashok Veeraraghavan, Hanjie Chen, and Guha Balakrishnan (Rice University) introduce CROP, a calibration layer that returns the longest leading slice of a reasoning trace whose steps provably contain no annotated error, given any step-level risk signal.

title: Conformal Certification of Reasoning Trace Prefixes
text:
Methods
CROP operates downstream of a completed reasoning trace and asks a narrower question than most uncertainty quantification (UQ) work. Not “is the final answer right?” but “how much of this trace can I keep before the first error?” A reasoning instance is a question plus its trace of \(T\) steps, each step labeled with a binary error flag in the data. CROP turns step-level risk scores into a single calibrated cut-off, then keeps everything up to that cut-off. The pieces:

Step-level risk proxy: a fixed function \(s_t(\cdot)\) that scores each step, with larger values meaning higher estimated error risk. The proxy can be a process reward model (PRM), a model trained to judge whether each reasoning step is correct (the kind of step scorer the literature calls a verifier), or a plainer signal such as a likelihood statistic, a hidden-state feature, or a hand-built heuristic. CROP is verifier-agnostic: it consumes whatever the proxy outputs, which need not be calibrated or even accurate, only fixed before calibration.
Retained prefix: at a threshold \(\lambda\), CROP keeps the longest leading run of steps whose risk all stays at or below \(\lambda\), a prefix of length \(M_\lambda = \max\{m : s_t \le \lambda \text{ for all } t \le m\}\). The uncertified suffix after the first threshold crossing is split off for downstream review or repair.
Monotone contamination loss: for an instance \(Z\), the loss \(L_\lambda(Z) \in \{0, 1\}\) flags the failure event “the kept prefix contains an annotated error.” Because raising \(\lambda\) can only lengthen the prefix, and once a bad step enters it never leaves, this binary loss is monotone in \(\lambda\). Monotonicity is the condition conformal risk control (CRC) [2] requires, so CROP applies it directly.
Calibration rule: on \(n\) held-out labeled instances \(Z_1, \dots, Z_n\) and a target risk \(\alpha\), CROP picks the largest threshold \(\lambda\) whose corrected empirical contamination rate \((1 + \sum_i L_\lambda(Z_i))/(n+1)\) (the mean loss over those instances, with the \(+1\) a finite-sample correction) stays at or below \(\alpha\). A larger \(\lambda\) means longer prefixes, so this is the longest prefix subject to the risk budget. If no threshold qualifies, it falls back to the empty prefix.

The guarantee that follows, the paper’s Proposition 1, Clean-Prefix Risk Control, is finite-sample and marginal: under exchangeability of the calibration and test instances, the returned prefix contains an annotated error with probability at most \(\alpha\). Writing \(\hat{\lambda}\) for the calibrated threshold and \(Z_{n+1}\) for a fresh instance, that is \(\mathbb{P}(L_{\hat{\lambda}}(Z_{n+1}) = 1) \le \alpha\). The reason is the standard split-conformal count: the calibration rule sets \(\hat{\lambda}\) so that at most \(\lfloor \alpha(n+1) \rfloor - 1\) of the \(n\) calibration instances come out contaminated, and a fresh instance, being exchangeable with those \(n\), is equally likely to fall at any rank among the \(n+1\), so its chance of landing in the contaminated group is at most \(\lfloor \alpha(n+1) \rfloor / (n+1) \le \alpha\). The exchangeable unit is the whole instance, not the step, so steps inside a trace may depend on each other arbitrarily.
The cover figure shows what CROP produces on two worked traces: a green certified prefix, a red uncertified suffix, and a blue repair pass on the suffix. The Arithmetic example clears its prefix at a strict threshold (\(\lambda = 0.995\)). The GSM8K example, where the proxy is noisier, certifies far less (\(\lambda = 0.156\)) and cuts after the second step. Each \(\lambda\) here is its dataset’s single calibrated threshold, fixed once on that dataset’s calibration split and applied to every instance, so the two values differ because they come from two separate calibrations, not because \(\lambda\) is tuned per problem. What changes from trace to trace is only where that fixed threshold falls.

title: Conformal Certification of Reasoning Trace Prefixes
text:
Results
The authors evaluate CROP across six process-supervision datasets: Arithmetic and GSM8K (Llama-generated chain-of-thought traces with dense first-error labels, from the circuit-based reasoning verification (CRV) dataset [7]), plus ProcessBench [8], Math-Shepherd [9], PRMBench [10], and PRM800K [3]. The main benchmark is 2,819 traces over Arithmetic and GSM8K (19,311 steps, 1,006 annotated errors).
They compare five step-level risk proxies on a 60/20/20 train/calibration/test split:

Random: random step scores, the floor baseline.
Token/format: a logistic regression over cheap text features (step length, position, punctuation).
Trace features: a logistic regression over those text features plus Llama-3.1-8B likelihood and hidden-state summaries.
Direct PRM: a frozen Qwen2.5-Math-PRM-7B, scored directly as one minus its step-correctness probability.
Trace features + PRM: a joint logistic regression over the trace features and the PRM score.

The target risk is fixed at \(\alpha = 0.05\), and downstream repair is measured by feeding the certified prefix to four separate repair models (Gemma 4, Qwen2.5-7B, DeepSeek-R1-0528-Qwen3-8B, Llama3.1-8B) and parsing the final answer.
CROP’s repair is compared against three baseline interfaces:

Question-only: the repair model sees only the original question, with the trace discarded entirely.
Full-trace: the repair model sees the complete trace, warned that it may contain mistakes.
Conformal whole-trace abstention: an all-or-nothing conformal decision that either accepts the entire trace or backs off to the bare question, with no partial prefix.

At a fixed risk target, the more of each trace CROP can certify, the better, since the certified prefix is valid reasoning kept for downstream use rather than discarded. Figure 2 plots this retained-prefix fraction as the risk target \(\alpha\) is relaxed.



Across six process-labeled datasets, the certified prefix kept rises as the target risk \(\alpha\) is relaxed. PRM-backed proxies (Direct PRM in blue, Trace features + PRM in green) retain long prefixes even at strict \(\alpha\), while random and cheap token/format signals stay flat. Figure 2 from the paper [1].


The findings:

AUROC does not predict prefix utility. Step-level AUROC (the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve) measures how well a proxy ranks erroneous steps above correct ones, the usual yardstick for choosing among proxies. Here it is the wrong one: Figure 3’s red segments mark inversions where the higher-AUROC of two proxies certifies the shorter prefix, and the appendix proves two proxies can share identical AUROC yet certify different prefix lengths under the same calibration. The paper recommends selecting proxies by certified prefix length instead.
PRM signals dominate, and not as an artifact. PRM-backed proxies retained the longest prefixes at fixed risk across datasets (for example 97.5% retained on Arithmetic and 81.7% on GSM8K at \(\alpha = 0.05\), versus 77.5% and 39.8% for token/format). After balancing trace length, formatting, and answer-format cues, PRM still kept ~27 percentage points more prefix than the token/format baseline, so the gain is not explained by exploitable formatting regularities.
CROP’s cut is closer to the oracle clean boundary. Against the annotated first-error position, CROP’s boundary deviation was 1.1% on Arithmetic and 9.9% on GSM8K, beating whole-trace abstention (4.6% and 14.1%) by avoiding both over-withholding of clean steps and unsafe overshoot past the first error.
Repair gains are real but model-dependent. CROP beat the best deployable non-CROP input in five of eight repair settings, with the largest lift on Arithmetic for DeepSeek (+5.5 points) and Gemma (+5.3). Llama posted negative deltas in both domains, which the authors trace to same-family answer repetition: the Arithmetic and GSM8K traces were originally generated by Llama, so the Llama repair model is unusually prone to copying the trace’s own wrong answer.




Step AUROC versus retained-prefix fraction across six datasets at \(\alpha = 0.05\). Gray segments mark agreement between ranking and prefix utility; red segments mark inversions where higher AUROC yields a shorter prefix. Figure 3 from the paper [1].


Figure 3 ties the first two findings together: PRM proxies retain the most prefix, but the red segments show that moving to a higher-AUROC proxy sometimes costs retained prefix.
Beyond accuracy, CROP changes what the downstream workflow sees. Whole-trace abstention is all-or-nothing: it accepts a full trace or falls back to the bare question. CROP instead returns a partial prefix, salvaging the clean opening of traces that abstention would reject outright.



Table 3 from the paper [1].


Table 3 shows the tradeoff: with the PRM proxies, CROP keeps more total step mass (92.0% and 95.1%) than whole-trace abstention at a matched empirical risk, even while accepting fewer whole traces.

title: Conformal Certification of Reasoning Trace Prefixes
text:
My Notes

CROP extends the conformal-for-LLMs line to a new object. Conformal Language Modeling [4] certifies a set of candidate generations, and Conformal Thinking [5] calibrates stop/continue thresholds for a compute budget. CROP applies the same conformal risk control [2] machinery to a third object, a contiguous reasoning prefix.
The coverage guarantee holds in aggregate, not per question. Like all conformal prediction [6], CROP controls the contamination probability averaged over the calibration distribution, so a particular question from a topic rare in that set can still contaminate well above \(\alpha\).
Rewarding global ranking does not necessarily yield the longest prefixes at a fixed risk. The process-reward-model literature CROP builds on, from PRM800K and Let’s Verify Step by Step [3] onward, ranks proxies by pooled step accuracy and best-of-\(N\) selection, both global-ranking objectives. Prefix certification instead rewards keeping the opening clean, so a PRM that tops those leaderboards need not certify the longest prefix at the same risk. A deployment that cares about prefix length should re-rank its proxies by certified prefix length directly.
