title: Just Ask for Calibration: Strategies for Eliciting Calibrated Confidence Scores from Language Models Fine-Tuned with Human Feedback
text:
Reliability diagrams for gpt-3.5-turbo on SciQ. Raw token-level probabilities (top-left, orange) are consistently overconfident. Verbalized numerical probabilities (bottom, blue) track empirical accuracy much more closely, and asking the model to “consider more answer choices” (bottom-right) improves calibration further. Figure 1 from the paper [1].
In Just Ask for Calibration [1] (EMNLP 2023), Katherine Tian, Eric Mitchell, Allan Zhou, Archit Sharma, Rafael Rafailov, Huaxiu Yao, Chelsea Finn, and Christopher D. Manning (Harvard + Stanford) show that for RLHF-tuned large language models (LLMs), a verbalized confidence score prompted from the model is typically better-calibrated than the model’s own token-level probabilities.

title: Just Ask for Calibration: Strategies for Eliciting Calibrated Confidence Scores from Language Models Fine-Tuned with Human Feedback
text:
Methods
The starting point is a known regression: RLHF degrades the calibration of a model’s token-level probabilities. The authors first reproduce it on Llama-2-70B, comparing the base model against its RLHF-tuned chat version.



Figure 2 from the paper [1].


Figure 2 plots two calibration metrics, expected calibration error (ECE, lower is better) and area under the selective-accuracy curve (AUC, higher is better), for the base and chat models on each dataset. RLHF raises ECE and lowers AUC across the board, and the gap is widest on TruthfulQA. The rest of the paper shows that for several strong RLHF models, reading the confidence out of the model’s text output recovers much of this lost calibration, again most strongly on TruthfulQA.
The evaluation spans five RLHF-tuned models (gpt-3.5-turbo, GPT-4, Claude-1, Claude-2, and Llama-2-70B-Chat) on three factual question-answering benchmarks: TriviaQA (1,000 sampled questions), SciQ (1,000), and TruthfulQA (all 817), the last of which is adversarial, with questions written to draw out common human misconceptions. Exact-match scoring would count a correct answer phrased differently as wrong, so correctness is judged by GPT-4 or GPT-3.5 checking whether the response is semantically equivalent to the gold answer.
The methods for extracting a confidence score fall into two families:

Sampling the model’s conditional probability. Because the closed models don’t expose token log-probabilities, both methods in this family estimate the probability from \(n = 10\) samples. Label prob. draws ten answers, returns the most common one, and uses its sampled frequency as the confidence. ‘Is True’ prob. (a variant of Kadavath et al. [2]) samples a single answer, then asks the model whether that answer is true and reads the probability it assigns to “True.”
Verbalizing the confidence in token space. The model writes its confidence as part of its response, with no fine-tuning to teach it the skill.

Verbalized numerical (Verb. 1S / 2S top-\(k\)) asks for a probability between 0 and 1. The one-stage (1S) version emits the answer and the probability together; the two-stage (2S) version answers first, then assigns a probability in a second turn. The top-\(k\) variants ask for \(k\) guesses (\(k = 1, 2, 4\)) and take the highest-probability one.
Verbalized with chain of thought (Verb. 2S CoT) adds a reasoning step before the answer, then asks for the probability.
Verbalized linguistic (Ling. 1S-human / 1S-opt) has the model pick a phrase such as “highly likely” or “almost no chance” instead of a number. The human variant maps each phrase to a probability using a 123-respondent survey; the optimized variant fits the mapping on a held-out calibration set.


The paper’s “consider the opposite” prompt asks for more than one guess before the confidence, borrowing a psychology finding that enumerating alternatives reduces overconfidence.
Calibration is reported on four metrics, each explained in more depth in a companion primer on confidence-calibration metrics:

ECE bins predictions by stated confidence and averages the gap between confidence and empirical accuracy across bins, weighted by bin size.
ECE-t is the same metric after temperature scaling, a one-parameter recalibration that replaces each confidence \(c\) with \(\sigma\!\left(\sigma^{-1}(c)/T\right)\), the logit of \(c\) divided by a single temperature \(T\) and mapped back through the logistic \(\sigma\). The temperature is fit to minimize negative log-likelihood, and one value applies to every prediction: above 1 it softens the confidences toward 0.5, below 1 it sharpens them.
BS-t is the Brier score [3] on temperature-scaled confidences, the mean squared error between confidence and correctness. Because a model that answers “50%” on every binary question scores a perfect ECE while telling you nothing, BS-t adds a metric that rewards discrimination.
AUC is the area under the selective-accuracy-versus-coverage curve from the selective-classification literature.

title: Just Ask for Calibration: Strategies for Eliciting Calibrated Confidence Scores from Language Models Fine-Tuned with Human Feedback
text:
Results
Across the five models and three datasets, the verbalized methods are better-calibrated than the sampled conditional probabilities for the strong closed models, with the effect largest on the adversarial TruthfulQA. Table 1 shows the full picture for gpt-3.5-turbo.



Table 1 from the paper [1].


The findings:

Verbalized confidence beats sampled probability. For gpt-3.5-turbo (Table 1), one-stage verbalized confidence cuts ECE on TriviaQA from 0.140 (Label prob.) to 0.068; for GPT-4, the strongest verbalized method drops SciQ ECE from 0.219 to 0.056. The relative reduction is around 50% on TriviaQA and SciQ and larger on TruthfulQA.
Generating multiple guesses improves calibration. Asking for the top 2 or top 4 answers before the confidence lowers gpt-3.5-turbo’s SciQ ECE from 0.234 (one guess) to 0.065 (four guesses), and its TruthfulQA ECE from 0.389 to 0.203.
Numbers work as well as words. Verbalized numerical probabilities match or beat the linguistic-expression methods on most settings, despite the known difficulty language models have with numbers. The exception is TruthfulQA, where the optimized linguistic mapping reaches the lowest error for several models (0.082 ECE for GPT-4).
Chain of thought does not help. Adding a reasoning step before the confidence leaves verbalized calibration essentially unchanged across all three datasets.
Temperature scaling narrows but does not close the gap. Fitting a temperature to the sampled probabilities improves them, but they stay worse-calibrated than the raw verbalized confidences (the ECE-t columns in Table 1).
The effect is model-dependent. Claude-1 verbalizes poorly: on SciQ its verbalized ECE (0.265) is worse than its own sampled probability (0.216). Claude-2 is comparable to gpt-3.5-turbo and beats the GPT models on TruthfulQA (0.099 ECE with the optimized linguistic mapping, down from 0.409). Llama-2-70B-Chat improves over its own probabilities on some metrics but inconsistently, most clearly on TruthfulQA.

title: Just Ask for Calibration: Strategies for Eliciting Calibrated Confidence Scores from Language Models Fine-Tuned with Human Feedback
text:
My Notes

RLHF does not wreck a model’s calibration so much as relocate it. Since Guo et al. (2017) [4], calibration has been treated as a property of the softmax, repaired by post-processing (temperature scaling, Platt, isotonic). The result here is that for RLHF models the calibrated signal has not disappeared, it has moved to a channel no post-processing can reach: the model’s own words. Calibration for instruction-tuned models is then less a recalibration problem (rescale the logits) than an elicitation one (ask for the number). But eliciting a calibrated confidence and acting on it are different things: AbstentionBench finds reasoning fine-tuning cuts abstention recall by 24%, so the same post-training that keeps confidence elicitable weakens the link between that confidence and the answer-or-abstain decision it should drive. Later work tempers the optimism: Xiong et al. [5]  find that across GPT-4 and LLaMA-2-Chat, elicited verbalized confidences beat the logprobs but are still systematically overconfident, so eliciting the number improves calibration without solving it.
The verbalized-beats-logprob result holds for RLHF models, not language models in general. Pre-RLHF base models typically have well-calibrated token probabilities, so the gap this paper documents comes from RLHF. For practitioners: with a fine-tuned instruction model whose logprobs you can read, verbalized confidences are probably the better move, but with a base model the logprobs are still the honest signal. The paper is careful about this, but the headline is easy to over-generalize.
A verbalized confidence is produced after the answer and conditioned on it, so it can encode reliability information the answer’s own token probabilities cannot. This is related to but distinct from self-consistency [6] sampling: both recruit the model’s own generation to estimate answer reliability, but self-consistency uses disagreement across samples while Just Ask uses within-sample reflection.
The “consider the opposite” prompt (asking for several guesses before the confidence) improves calibration with nothing more than a prompt change. Forcing the model to enumerate alternatives before stating a confidence is inference-time debiasing against anchoring on its first answer. It connects to self-reflection and verification prompts like CRITIC [7] , and suggests a shared mechanism: breaking the model’s commitment to a single chain of thought improves calibration, correctness, and hallucination rates together.

title: A Primer on Confidence-Calibration Metrics: ECE, Brier, AUROC, and What Each One Misses
text:
Figure 1. Reliability diagrams for the three models in the worked example below. Each solid bar is the accuracy of the answers whose stated confidence falls in that bin, and the dashed line is perfect calibration. The gap to that line is hatched with forward slashes where the model is overconfident (accuracy below confidence) and with crosses where it is underconfident (accuracy above confidence). Model B, which says “0.5” to everything, falls exactly on the diagonal and scores zero calibration error while being useless. Model C is severely overconfident.
A confidence score is a number a model attaches to an answer to say how likely that answer is to be correct: 0.9 means “almost certainly right,” 0.5 means “a coin flip.” For a language model the number can come from several places, the probability the model assigns to its own answer tokens, a value it states in words (“about 80% sure”), or the rate at which sampled answers agree. Wherever it comes from, the reason to want one is to act on it: defer the low-confidence cases to a person, abstain instead of guessing, or weight the answer in a downstream decision. That only works if the number can be trusted.
Whether a confidence score can be trusted is itself something we measure, and “good” turns out to have more than one meaning. The calibration literature reports a confusing spread of numbers for it: expected calibration error (ECE), Brier score (BS), negative log-likelihood (NLL), area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC), and several selective-prediction variants. A single paper often reports four of them at once. Just Ask for Calibration [1], for instance, scores every method on ECE, temperature-scaled ECE, temperature-scaled Brier, and an AUROC-style selective-accuracy curve.
Are these metrics redundant, or do they measure different things? This post works one small example through each of them. The example is rigged so that three models give the same answers and get the same number right, and differ only in how they report confidence. That isolates the confidence signal from accuracy, and it turns out to be enough to make every metric disagree about which model is best.

title: A Primer on Confidence-Calibration Metrics: ECE, Brier, AUROC, and What Each One Misses
section: What we want from a confidence score
text:
What we want from a confidence score
The setup is the one used for question answering. A model answers a question and attaches a confidence \(c \in [0,1]\), its own estimate that the answer is correct. We observe the outcome \(y \in \{0,1\}\), whether the answer was actually right. Over \(N\) questions we have pairs \((c_i, y_i)\). There are two distinct properties we might want from those confidences, and a model can have either one without the other.

Calibration (reliability): among the answers given confidence \(\approx 0.8\), about 80% should be correct. The stated number means what it says.
Discrimination (resolution): the model assigns higher confidence to answers that turn out correct than to ones that turn out wrong. The number ranks answers by reliability, whatever its absolute scale.

These come apart. A model can be perfectly calibrated and useless (predict the base rate every time), or perfectly discriminating and badly calibrated (rank correctly but report inflated numbers). A third thing we might want is a single number that rewards both at once and cannot be gamed by a trivial strategy. That is what a proper scoring rule provides, and it is where the metrics below end up.

title: A Primer on Confidence-Calibration Metrics: ECE, Brier, AUROC, and What Each One Misses
text:
Measuring calibration: expected calibration error (ECE)
ECE (lower is better, zero is perfect) measures calibration. Introduced by Naeini et al. [2] and brought to deep networks by Guo et al. [3], it bins predictions by stated confidence and averages the gap between confidence and accuracy across bins, weighted by bin size:
\[\mathrm{ECE} = \sum_{b=1}^{B} \frac{n_b}{N}\,\bigl|\, \mathrm{acc}(b) - \mathrm{conf}(b) \,\bigr|\]
where \(B\) is the number of bins, \(n_b\) the count in bin \(b\), \(\mathrm{acc}(b)\) the fraction correct in the bin, and \(\mathrm{conf}(b)\) the mean confidence in the bin. With five equal-width bins:

Model A: 0.225. Spread along the diagonal, with moderate gaps in both directions.
Model B: 0.000. Every prediction lands in the bin around 0.5, where accuracy is also 0.5. The gap is zero.
Model C: 0.445. All ten predictions sit in the top bin, where the mean confidence is 0.945 but accuracy is 0.5.

Figure 1 plots these as reliability diagrams, where the hatched gap to the diagonal is the quantity ECE averages. ECE asks one question, whether a stated 0.8 corresponds to 80% correct, and the model that knows nothing scores a perfect zero. That is its blind spot: ECE rewards calibration and is indifferent to whether the confidences separate right answers from wrong ones. It earns its place anyway: ECE isolates calibration in interpretable units, a 0.05 ECE meaning stated confidence is off from accuracy by about five points on average. The proper scores introduced later fold calibration together with discrimination, so they cannot report that gap on its own.
A second problem is that ECE is not even a single number, because it depends on the binning scheme. The same Model A predictions give:



Bins

A single bin lets over- and under-confidence cancel within it and reports near-perfect calibration. Many bins, with one or two points each, overstate the error. The number is not even monotone in the bin count. A bare ECE in one paper is not comparable to one in another unless the binning matches, which is the motivation for adaptive (equal-mass) binning [4] and debiased estimators [5].

title: A Primer on Confidence-Calibration Metrics: ECE, Brier, AUROC, and What Each One Misses
text:
Measuring discrimination: AUROC
A discrimination metric ignores the absolute scale of the confidences and asks only whether they rank correct answers above wrong ones. AUROC (higher is better, 1.0 is a perfect ranking and 0.5 is chance) is the probability that a randomly chosen correct answer gets a higher confidence than a randomly chosen wrong one, with ties counting as half. Writing \(\mathcal{P} = \{i : y_i = 1\}\) for the correct answers and \(\mathcal{N} = \{i : y_i = 0\}\) for the wrong ones, it is the fraction of all correct–wrong pairs that the confidence ranks the right way:
\[\mathrm{AUROC} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{P}|\,|\mathcal{N}|} \sum_{i \in \mathcal{P}} \sum_{j \in \mathcal{N}} \Bigl[\, \mathbf{1}(c_i > c_j) + \tfrac{1}{2}\,\mathbf{1}(c_i = c_j) \,\Bigr]\]
With the example’s five correct and five wrong answers, that is 25 pairs:

Model A: 0.96. One misranked pair out of 25.
Model B: 0.50. All confidences tie, so it ranks no better than chance.
Model C: 1.00. Every correct answer outranks every wrong one.

Now the overconfident model is perfect, because ranking is all AUROC sees. AUROC’s blind spot is the mirror of ECE’s: it ignores calibration completely. The deeper fact is that AUROC is invariant to any order-preserving rescaling of the confidences. Pass Model C’s confidences through a temperature scaling that pulls them toward 0.5 and its calibration error collapses, while its AUROC stays at 1.00 because the ranking is untouched. So AUROC measures the calibration the model could reach after recalibration, not the calibration it has now. The practical corollary: a poor ECE is often a recalibration away from good, but a poor AUROC is not, because the model has thrown away the information that recalibration would need. This reframes a result like Just Ask for Calibration. The question worth asking is not only whether verbalized confidences are better calibrated than token probabilities, but whether they rank answers better, since only a ranking gain survives recalibration.

title: A Primer on Confidence-Calibration Metrics: ECE, Brier, AUROC, and What Each One Misses
section: The selective-prediction view: risk–coverage and AURC
text:
The selective-prediction view: risk–coverage and AURC
AUROC collapses the ranking into a single scalar. But deciding what to answer and what to defer is a trade-off between coverage and risk, which the selective-prediction literature [6] draws as a risk–coverage curve (Figure 2): answer only the most confident questions and abstain on the rest, then track how the error rate (the risk) changes with the fraction of questions answered (the coverage). Writing \(y_{(j)}\) for correctness in descending-confidence order, the risk at a coverage of \(k/N\), keeping the \(k\) most confident answers, is \(r_k = \tfrac{1}{k}\sum_{j \le k}(1 - y_{(j)})\), and the area under the curve is
\[\mathrm{AURC} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{k=1}^{N} r_k \qquad (\text{lower is better, ties averaged}).\]



Figure 2. Risk–coverage curves for the same three models: the error rate among the answers kept (risk) as the most-confident fraction (coverage) grows. Model B (dashed) stays flat at 0.5 because it cannot tell its right answers from its wrong ones. Model A (solid, circles) and Model C (dotted, squares) hold risk near zero over the confident half, then climb. A and C trace the same curve except at coverage 0.5, where A’s one ranking inversion admits a wrong answer before a right one, spiking its risk before the next, correct answer pulls the rate back down. This is the exact reversal of the calibration view in Figure 1, where B looked perfect and C looked broken.


Plotting accuracy (\(1 - r_k\)) instead of risk gives the selective-accuracy curve, whose area is the “AUC” that Just Ask and much of the LLM work report. It is just \(1 - \mathrm{AURC}\) (higher is better). These areas are summaries for comparing models, and on this example AURC, that “AUC,” and AUROC all order the three the same way (C best, A close behind, B at chance), so the scorecard later reports only AUROC. What you actually deploy against, though, is the curve, not its area: you read an operating point off it, the confidence threshold that answers as many questions as possible while holding risk under a budget. The single number averages over every threshold and hides the one you would pick.

title: A Primer on Confidence-Calibration Metrics: ECE, Brier, AUROC, and What Each One Misses
section: Measuring both: Brier score (BS) and log loss (NLL)
text:
Measuring both: Brier score (BS) and log loss (NLL)
A proper scoring rule rewards calibration and discrimination at once, in a single number (lower is better) that is minimized, in expectation, only when the stated confidence equals the true probability of correctness. The Brier score [7] is the mean squared error between confidence and outcome:
\[\mathrm{BS} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} (c_i - y_i)^2\]

Model A: 0.120.
Model B: 0.250.
Model C: 0.424.

Now A wins and B is in the middle. The constant predictor that aced ECE is penalized for providing no information, and the overconfident C for its inflated numbers. Neither can game a proper score.
Log loss, also called negative log-likelihood (also lower is better), is the other proper scoring rule in common use:
\[\mathrm{NLL} = -\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} \bigl[\, y_i \ln c_i + (1 - y_i)\ln(1 - c_i) \,\bigr]\]

Model A: 0.404.
Model B: 0.693 (which is \(\ln 2\), the score of a coin flip).
Model C: 1.286.

The ranking matches Brier, but the spread is wider, and the reason matters. Log loss is unbounded: a confident wrong answer drives one term toward infinity. Raise a single wrong answer’s confidence from 0.70 to 0.99, and its Brier contribution goes from \(0.49\) to \(0.98\), a doubling against a ceiling of 1, while its log-loss contribution goes from \(-\ln(0.30) = 1.20\) to \(-\ln(0.01) = 4.61\), almost a quadrupling with no ceiling. Log loss punishes catastrophic overconfidence far harder than Brier, which is why C looks worst of all under it. The choice between the two proper scores is mostly how harshly to treat the confidently-wrong tail.

The metrics are not redundant and not interchangeable: each rewards a different property, and optimizing the wrong one selects a degenerate model.

title: A Primer on Confidence-Calibration Metrics: ECE, Brier, AUROC, and What Each One Misses
section: Why the proper scoring rules see both
text:
Why the proper scoring rules see both
That Brier and NLL pick the right model is not luck. Murphy’s decomposition [8] splits the Brier score into three terms:
\[\mathrm{BS} = \underbrace{\mathrm{reliability}}_{\text{calibration gap}} - \underbrace{\mathrm{resolution}}_{\text{discrimination}} + \underbrace{\mathrm{uncertainty}}_{\text{base rate}}\]
The reliability term is the squared calibration gap. ECE measures the same gap in absolute value. The resolution term rewards predictions that separate from the base rate, the quantity AUROC proxies, and it enters with a minus sign so more of it lowers the score. The uncertainty term depends only on the data. A proper scoring rule already contains a calibration component and a discrimination component, which is exactly why B (zero resolution) and C (large reliability term) both score badly. The two one-sided metrics from the sections above are the two halves of this split: ECE is roughly the reliability piece in isolation, and AUROC is a rank-based proxy for the resolution piece. Reporting ECE and AUROC side by side is, in effect, reconstructing a proper score’s decomposition by hand. The calibration-versus-refinement split goes back to DeGroot and Fienberg [9]. The general theory of proper scoring rules is laid out by Gneiting and Raftery [10].

title: A Primer on Confidence-Calibration Metrics: ECE, Brier, AUROC, and What Each One Misses
text:
Other metrics worth knowing

Maximum calibration error (MCE): the worst single bin’s gap rather than the average (lower is better). Model A’s MCE at five bins is 0.30, against an ECE of 0.225. Useful when a single badly-calibrated region is a safety problem.
Adaptive / equal-mass ECE: bins by equal count instead of equal width [4], so a region with few predictions does not get its own noisy bin. Reduces, but does not remove, the binning dependence.
Debiased and binning-free estimators: the plug-in ECE is a biased estimator of the true calibration error. Debiased versions [5] and kernel or Kolmogorov–Smirnov variants estimate it without committing to a bin grid.
Reliability diagram: the visual in Figure 1, and the thing every scalar calibration metric is summarizing.

title: A Primer on Confidence-Calibration Metrics: ECE, Brier, AUROC, and What Each One Misses
text:
Which metric to use
The right metric follows the downstream use, because optimizing the wrong one selects a degenerate model: train against ECE alone, and the constant predictor B is a global optimum. Common cases:

Routing unconfident cases to a human (triage or abstention): only the ranking matters, so use AUROC, and read the operating point off the risk–coverage curve to set how much to defer.
Showing the number to a user as a probability: it has to mean what it says, an “80% sure” that is right about 80% of the time, so use ECE and the reliability diagram.
Feeding the confidence into a decision or expected-value calculation: the number enters arithmetic (act when probability times payoff clears a threshold), so calibration is the requirement. Use ECE, with a proper score as a backstop.
Selecting the best model, or training against the confidence as a loss: use a proper score (Brier or NLL), which a one-sided strategy cannot game.
Penalizing confident mistakes hardest (safety-critical answers): use NLL, which is unbounded, and report MCE for the single worst region.
Comparing calibration numbers across papers: distrust a bare ECE unless the binning matches, and prefer a proper score or a debiased estimator.

When one headline number is needed, a proper score is the safe default, since it already includes both a calibration and a discrimination term. ECE and AUROC are then most useful as a diagnosis of which way a model fails: a good Brier with a bad ECE means the ranking is sound and recalibration will help, while a bad AUROC means the information to rank was never there.

title: A Primer on Confidence-Calibration Metrics: ECE, Brier, AUROC, and What Each One Misses
section: Caveat: sometimes the correctness label is not fixed
text:
Caveat: sometimes the correctness label is not fixed
One assumption runs under all four metrics: that \(y\), whether an answer was correct, is known. For multiple-choice or short-answer tasks it is. For open-ended question answering, \(y\) is itself a model’s judgment of whether the response is semantically equivalent to the reference answer, and switching from exact match to a GPT-4 grader changes which answers count as correct. That moves accuracy, every bin’s contents, and the ranking all at once. The comparison above holds \(y\) fixed. For language models graded by another model, the label is one more moving part, and a calibration number is only as trustworthy as the grader that defined correctness.

title: AI Researchers’ Perspectives on Automating AI R&D and Intelligence Explosions
text:
Participant predictions on whether AI companies will publicly deploy models capable of meaningfully accelerating AI research, grouped by affiliation. Each dot is a participant who gave a clear opinion, sorted into “Expects Internal,” “Nuanced,” and “Expects Public” (participants with an unclear opinion are omitted). Six gave nuanced answers, contingent on government intervention or inter-lab differences. Overall, 17 of 25 participants expected ASARA-class systems (AI Systems for AI R&D Automation) to be increasingly reserved for internal use. Figure 1 from the paper [1].
In AI Researchers’ Perspectives on Automating AI R&D and Intelligence Explosions [1] (arXiv preprint, March 2026), Field, S., Douglas, R., and Krueger, D. (the ML Alignment and Theory Scholars Program, Berkeley) interview 25 frontier-lab and academic AI researchers and find converging predictions on a path to autonomous AI developers, paired with a sharp epistemic split on timelines, deployment, and governance.

title: AI Researchers’ Perspectives on Automating AI R&D and Intelligence Explosions
text:
Methods
The study draws on semi-structured interviews with 25 AI researchers conducted in August and September 2025. Participants were recruited from frontier AI labs (Google DeepMind, OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta) and academia (UC Berkeley, Princeton, Stanford), with selection prioritizing diversity of perspectives among researchers with published work on recursive improvement or comparable capability forecasting. The interview protocol covers three sections:

Conceptualizing ASARA (“AI Systems for AI R&D Automation,” the paper’s operational term for systems that can meaningfully contribute to frontier-AI development): what such a system would look like.
Organizational dynamics: how labs would deploy such systems.
Risk and governance: risk assessment plus governance preferences.

Transcripts are qualitatively coded for themes. Participant affiliations span five types (frontier-lab, ex-frontier-lab, academic, industry, and nonprofit), used to show where opinions cluster and where they diverge.

title: AI Researchers’ Perspectives on Automating AI R&D and Intelligence Explosions
text:
Results
The paper organizes findings around five themes:

what participants imagine ASARA looking like
public versus internal deployment
trajectory clarity
risk perception
views on red lines

The findings, with the figures that ground them:

Severe-and-urgent risk: 20/25. Twenty of the 25 participants identified automating AI research as one of the most severe and urgent AI risks. The two most-frequently raised concerns were power concentration and AI-augmented progress accelerating behind closed doors. The most common specific worry, in 18 of 25 transcripts, was that recursive self-improvement amplifies every other AI risk at once. Figure 3 sorts participants by how they rank ASARA risk, from minimal concern through serious risk to the primary driver of AI risk, and groups them by affiliation. Most fall in the serious-to-primary range, with academics the affiliation most represented at the minimal-concern end.




Participant risk priority for ASARA, grouped by affiliation. Figure 3 from the paper [1].



Internal-only deployment: 17/25. Seventeen participants expected ASARA-class systems to be increasingly reserved for internal use at AI companies or governments rather than publicly deployed (Figure 1, the cover image). Reasons offered include too-valuable-to-share, higher returns from internal R&D than from API revenue, and competitive dynamics.
Trajectory clarity by affiliation. Figure 2 places each participant on a spectrum from “Clear Path” through “Major Obstacles” to “Unknown/Unknowns.” Frontier-lab researchers cluster toward “Clear Path,” while academic researchers spread across the spectrum, with several identifying “Major Obstacles” and no participant in the “Unknown/Unknowns” category. Section 4.1 names this “Schism Between Silicon Valley and Academia.”




Participant views on the clarity of the trajectory toward ASARA, grouped by affiliation. Figure 2 from the paper [1].



Red lines: split. Transparency: near-universal. Participants divided on whether regulatory “red lines” (limits whose breach should trigger major response by labs or governments) were a good idea. Figure 4 shows the split between favoring, being unsure about, and opposing red lines, roughly balanced across affiliations. Concrete objections include definitional ambiguity, enforcement difficulty, and a fear that lines drawn at the wrong threshold could backfire by promoting workarounds. Almost all participants favored transparency-based mitigations as either complement or alternative.




Participant views on red lines for autonomous research, grouped by affiliation. Transcripts with no clear perspective are omitted. Figure 4 from the paper [1].

title: AI Researchers’ Perspectives on Automating AI R&D and Intelligence Explosions

title: What Remains Scarce After AGI: Alex Imas and Phil Trammell on Labor, Capital, and Redistribution
text:
Alex Imas and Phil Trammell on the Dwarkesh Podcast. Watch on YouTube or read the transcript on Dwarkesh’s site.
In the June 4 episode of his podcast, Dwarkesh Patel talks with Alex Imas, Director of AGI Economics at Google DeepMind and an economist at Chicago Booth, and Phil Trammell, Head of Economics at Epoch and a research scholar at Stanford, about what economics predicts for a world of advanced AI: what stays scarce, whether the labor share collapses, and how you would tax and redistribute the wealth.
The through-line is methodological. Imas argues economists should stop making point forecasts, which have a bad track record, and instead lay out the possible scenarios and ask what data would tell them apart. His refrain is that the data does not exist yet. We do not measure consumer demand elasticities, and we barely track which jobs are being created or destroyed.
With the help of AI, I’ve built an enriched transcript at the bottom of this post. It is Dwarkesh’s published transcript, sliced into chapter and topic subsections, with inline hyperlinks, acronym expansions, and editor’s-note callouts. See the preamble of that section for details.
Some of the points I found most useful:
YouTube chapters (jump to the enriched transcript below, or watch on YouTube):

title: What Remains Scarce After AGI: Alex Imas and Phil Trammell on Labor, Capital, and Redistribution
text:
Transcript
What’s here is Dwarkesh’s published transcript, reorganized into a reader-friendly form. The dialog itself is verbatim, with no words added, cut, or reworded, but four layers of editorial structure sit on top:

Chapter + topic outline. The 7 YouTube chapters, each linking to its timestamp, sliced into finer topic subsections. The subsection titles are editorial summaries of what’s being discussed, not verbatim speaker quotes. The full outline is in the right-hand sidebar.
Inline hyperlinks. Dwarkesh’s team already hand-linked most salient terms, and those links are preserved as published. A handful of missing first mentions (people, companies) were added, and two tracking-laden source URLs were cleaned to canonical links.
Bracketed acronym expansions. Where an acronym appears for the first time without being expanded in speech, the expansion is inserted in [square brackets] (e.g. HBM [high-bandwidth memory]) to mark the addition as editorial.
Editor’s notes in blue callout boxes flag claims that are verifiable and look slightly off, or attributions worth double-checking against the primary source.

Every paper cited in the body has a [[N]](#ref-N) cite linking to the References block at the bottom.

0:00:00 — Will capital share increase?

What will be scarce: the relational sector
Dwarkesh Patel: Today I’m chatting with Alex Imas, who is Director of AGI Economics at Google DeepMind and Professor of Economics at the University of Chicago, and Phil Trammell, who is Head of Economics at Epoch and research scholar at Stanford.
In general what I want to understand in this interview is what economics tells us about what we can expect in a world with more and more automation and more advanced AI. I want to understand what that tells us about what will happen to wages and the labor share, what the best way to tax and redistribute the wealth generated by AGI will be, and what kinds of things will be scarce. What is scarce tells you where the value will accrue.
I want to start there. What are some plausible candidates of what will be scarce?
Alex Imas: Something like the relational sector, which is defined as services and goods where the fact that a human was in the loop is part of the value of that product. Because humans are naturally scarce, if we have automation where a lot of other things stop being scarce, we will still have scarcity in the things that humans are involved in and in the loop for.


Is the human-only economy doomed to shrink? Imas’s case for forecasting humility
Dwarkesh Patel: I’m curious to understand whether humans doing services for other humans can ever be a big part of the economy. Here’s maybe one intuition pump. In a world where AI can physically do anything humans can do, there’s this whole machine economy where they’re building factories and doing research and coming up with new ideas.
Humans may or may not be involved in the physical production of those things, but probably not in the ultimate limit, if robotics is solved. If you don’t care about humans being involved in that process, why would they be?
But then there are these other things you point out where we actually do want the ballerina or the barista to be a human. That’s part of the value of going to a cafe or a performance. But only humans have that preference. So there’s this human economy where humans are doing services for each other, and part of their wealth is flowing to other humans.
But part of their wealth is also flowing out, because they will want some of the automated goods this machine-only economy is creating. This is not a closed loop. A lot of things in the machine-only economy are a closed loop because the machines don’t care about getting the human barista to make them a coffee.
Within that model, isn’t it intrinsic that the human-only economy will become a smaller and smaller share?
Alex Imas: I would like to pitch a rephrasing of that question. My view is that the individual forecasts economists like us would make, as individual forecasts, are not necessarily very useful.
There was a blog post by Andrey Fradkin, Brian Jabarian, and Andrew Koh that came out yesterday looking at economists’ forecasts about the labor market. What they found is that there’s a ton of disagreement in every single direction.
What they advocate for, and I’m in agreement here, is that rather than thinking about individual forecasts, we should be generating prediction markets where you get aggregate forecasts and wisdom-of-the-crowd effects. The reason I think this is because we have been famously terrible at forecasting.
Let’s go all the way back to 1820. This debate we’ve been having is actually 200 years old. David Ricardo is one of the classical economists, not neoclassical.
When the Industrial Revolution started happening, he wrote a bunch of stuff saying, “This is going to be great for everybody. Prices are going to come down.” But then he turned around and said, “Wait, I can see all these jobs that are creating value are going to be automated by these machines. This is going to be really bad. Everybody’s going to become unemployed, and there’s going to be political unrest.”
And if you look at Ricardo’s predictions, they’re actually right. All those jobs that made money in Ricardo’s time got automated.
If David Ricardo woke up and somebody told him all those jobs did get automated, and then asked him, “What do you think the prime-age employment rate is in 2026?”, I think he’d be surprised to be told it was the highest it’s ever been other than 2000.
We have the highest number of employed people that could potentially be employed since 2000. That was the peak and now it’s the second peak basically.
What David Ricardo ended up missing is that you have these economics of structural change, where everything that got automated became cheap. People had more money to spend, and then they started spending it on services. This is the lump-of-labor fallacy. David Ricardo didn’t consider that new jobs would be created.
But it’s not obvious that money would go to services. Why wouldn’t it go to more automated goods and something like that? I’m not using this anecdote to say this is what’s going to happen now and that we’re going to have full employment. I’m using it to say it’s really hard to make predictions.
What may be a really useful tool that economists have is to instead start with a premise. Maybe we start today: labor share is zero. Labor share has gone down. What could possibly explain this? Let’s write down an economic model of what happened. Phil will talk about this later today. Or you can write down a model that asks, “What if labor share just stays the same? What can make that happen?”
If you don’t take anything else out of this conversation from me: We don’t have any data. I’ve been saying we need a Manhattan Project for data. We don’t have data on consumer demand elasticities. We don’t know what they are. We’re not really tracking what jobs are getting created or destroyed. The O*NET database [Occupational Information Network], with all of the tasks and different jobs, has been rarely updated and is super low quality.
What is really useful is to think about the potential scenarios, map them out, and say what dimension of scarcity will generate each scenario. If there’s full employment, we can talk about the relational sector. If the labor share collapses, we can talk about other sorts of scenarios. That will tell us what data we should be collecting.


Defining labor share and capital share; the Kaldor fact
Dwarkesh Patel: It’s probably worth defining labor share and capital share real quick. The whole economy, the total sum of goods and services sold, is either paid out to people in wages or it’s paid out to capital, which is to say, there’s rent on buildings and shareholders of companies that get paid out.
For many hundreds of years, ~60% of the economy basically gets paid out to humans in wages, and the other 30-40% gets paid out to people who own machines and land and claims on companies. The question is, if 60% is going to wages right now, does that shrink as AIs get smarter and better?
Alex Imas: This is a Kaldor fact. We should stress this. It’s incredibly surprising that it’s over 60% after the Industrial Revolution and all of the automation we’ve ever seen. Some people are worried it’s an accounting error that it’s been so constant.
There’s even a controversy right now. Some might say labor share has been falling in the last 20 to 30 years. But there have been a lot of accounting changes in the last 30 to 40 years. For example, Atkinson has a paper showing [1] that if you keep the accounting constant over the years, labor share hasn’t even fallen ever.






Note



Editor’s note. The paper linked here is Elsby, Hobijn, and Şahin, “The Decline of the U.S. Labor Share” (Brookings Papers on Economic Activity, 2013), not a paper by Tony Atkinson (a different economist, known for inequality measurement). As its title suggests, that paper documents a decline in the US labor share over recent decades and attributes much of it to import competition. The “labor share hasn’t fallen once you hold the accounting constant” claim is a separate, contested measurement argument about how items like proprietors’ income get classified.


Dwarkesh Patel: But it’s not that surprising, right? Phil, you made this point that if labor and capital are complements, you need both to do anything. It would make sense that you’d need to pay both of them to get something done.
Alex Imas: You have had stuff be completely automated.


Network-adjusted factor shares: nothing is fully automated yet
Phil Trammell: There’s a sense in which nothing has yet been completely automated. Look at the network-adjusted factor shares of a good. Look down the supply chain and not just the final step and how much of that is done by capital and labor, but what went into the machines that can automate that final step. You’ll find that labor is adding a lot of value down the supply chain.
Computer and electronic products in the US have a very stable network-adjusted capital share of around 50%. It’s not 100%. I do think there’s this qualitative shift that I think we agree is coming, which is that there will be at least some goods whose network-adjusted capital share goes to one. The whole supply chain can be automated, and there’s no part in it that we care intrinsically about having a human do. That will be a qualitative shift.
Interestingly, the implications of that shift for the overall capital share are ambiguous. Let’s say we’ve got two sectors: the human-intrinsic sector with the ballerinas, and everything else.
Right now, everything else has been scarce because of the lack of labor in it. But if we fully automate the supply chains for everything else, and we satiate in everything else really fast, then the quantity of everything that’s not a ballerina goes to infinity, but the marginal utility in that stuff goes to zero faster than the quantity is rising.


The task-based model: why “ballerina” is the wrong reference class
Alex Imas: I also want to move away from the ballerina example. The point I was trying to make in my post—working backwards from a particular scenario—was that the ballerina and the performer are the wrong reference class. Right now we have a lot of jobs where you have different tasks. This is the task-based model of jobs. Take a doctor, what is their job? They’re filling out insurance documents. They’re going and calling different pharmaceutical companies. One of their tasks is to see the patient and talk to them, but that’s not the main part of the job.
You could have a job and a service or a good be a product of different types of tasks, and you can automate a ton of those tasks. If the consumer is willing to pay more for a product or service where every single task is automated except for that one part where the doctor is delivering the diagnosis and providing support, we would call that job part of the relational sector. People are willing to pay more for the human to stay in the loop in the job.
We don’t have data to say, “Here are relational jobs, here are not.” You literally need to collect data of the following sort. Do a conjoint analysis of your willingness to pay for this service or good. Here’s the counterfactual where everything is produced by machine. Here’s the counterfactual where this one task is not produced by a machine. What is your willingness to pay? What is your elasticity for the human to not be in the loop?
If I don’t have that data, what prediction am I going to make in this story?
Dwarkesh Patel: Isn’t there another point, which is that there are a lot of fully automated goods that don’t even exist yet? And you can’t collect any data right now about, say, how much people will want to keep buying more and more of some drug that makes you healthier that is fully produced by the AIs.
Alex Imas: Absolutely. That’s kind of Phil’s point. You could have an increase in variety in capital where you don’t get the satiation. You’re increasing variety, so you’re not hitting that diminishing marginal utility point where most of your income is going to the human sector.
If that increasing variety is fast enough, and there is no such increasing variety in the human sector, then you can get all of the relational goods you want, but it doesn’t matter for labor share. It goes to zero.


The Mongolian-economist analogy
Dwarkesh Patel: Phil, I liked your analogy to some Mongolian economist sitting around in 1400 thinking about what will be scarce and the limits of that kind of analysis. I think you should talk about that.
Phil Trammell: Just look at the goods available to a Mongolian of the distant past. I’m no expert on this society, but I know that they didn’t have nearly the variety that we have now. Look at the jobs that were intrinsically human, like being a singer. And then you look at the things that were not intrinsically human, like the transportation services provided by their horses or the different kinds of food they had.
If they just held the varieties fixed in both categories and asked, “What will happen once we have a lot more automation?”, they might have said, “We’ll just satiate in horse-like transportation and in yogurt and in yurts. Those shares will all go to zero, and we’ll be left spending all of our money on singers.”
But of course, that’s not what happened. As we’ve accumulated more wealth and more advanced machines, we’ve expanded the range of things other than singers to spend our money on, and the share spent on singers has stayed negligible. Likewise, that’s my central prediction about how the future unfolds, though it could go either way.


Moore’s law and the falling value of compute
Dwarkesh Patel: I was going to make a point and I realize it’s a fallacy, but the reason it’s a fallacy is interesting. It’s just hard to imagine a world where there are trillions upon trillions of robots, but there’s only some billion-odd humans, and the cumulative amount we’re spending on robots is less than what we’re spending to pay Magnus Carlsen or—
Alex Imas: Financial advisors or doctors or tutors.
Dwarkesh Patel: Right, or podcasters or whatever. But then I realized why it’s a fallacy. The number of transistors in the world has literally trillion-X’d, maybe quadrillion-X’d.
Your colleague Chad Jones has a very interesting result [2] about how the share of the economy that is going towards paying for computing, paying for the transistors, has been decreasing.
The point you made is that one way to think about Moore’s law is… What sets price? Supply and demand. So not only are we producing more transistors more cheaply, but also the value of the marginal transistor is decreasing. As you were saying, another way of saying Moore’s law is…
Phil Trammell: I like the pessimistic framing of Moore’s law: every 18 months, the value of computation halves. We’re running out of uses for computation so fast that it’s sustaining Moore’s law.
Dwarkesh Patel: This is relevant to a conversation about AI where maybe for the first time, this is no longer true. The famous fact here is that an H100 costs more to rent now than it did three years ago, even though we have much superior technology and much more compute in the world. Because as models get smarter, the opportunity cost of compute gets higher.






Note



Editor’s note. Public GPU rental price indices show the opposite trend for the H100 specifically. On-demand H100 rates fell from roughly $8/hour around its 2023 launch to about $2/hour or less by 2025 as supply caught up with demand. The broader point, that the opportunity cost of compute rises as models get smarter, can still hold, but the specific claim that an H100 rents for more now than three years ago runs against the published pricing.


Alex Imas: This is Phil’s point about increasing variety. What we have done is increased the types of things that people demand from capital. Now all of a sudden you have a new variety that you could be using capital for, and you jump back up.
Dwarkesh Patel: You could imagine we just never satiate demand for compute. As long as that stays the case, the share of the economy that is going towards compute would keep increasing.


Do we ever satiate demand? The art-print experiment
Alex Imas: That’s the big question. That is the ultimate question that we need to be looking at. What number of new uses are we finding for that compute where you have the demand for these uses? What I want to emphasize is that a lot of models in economics, especially in the space that we’re talking about, take demand as almost exogenous. They don’t unpack the psychology of what people actually want.
What got me thinking about the idea of the relational sector is work that I was doing on the fact that there does seem to be this intrinsic value. It’s not just because it’s scarce; it’s because there’s some intrinsic preference that people have for empathy, connection, and interacting with another person.
One of the experiments that we ran involved an art print. We have an incentive-compatible way of asking, “How much are you willing to pay for this art print?” People are actually paying real money for it. Then we say, “Look, there’s only one of those art prints, and it’s either made by AI or by a person.” These are between-subject conditions. With one, you get the effect that the person-produced art print is valued much higher than the AI version.
Then, in a set of other conditions, we say there’s 500 of these being produced. For the human-made one, the price goes down a lot because it’s no longer seen as making a connection with this one artist. With AI there’s no difference. AI is already viewed as a commodity.
We need to do a lot more research on this, but it seems that’s the key difference between this and something like a horse. A horse was an input into an output, where you can replace the horse with something else. You only care about the output.
The only way this relational story works—and this is what we need more data on—is if a human is not a horse in the sense that they are providing value from the output, where if you replace the human, the value of the output decreases. If that’s not strong enough, and if it doesn’t hold for enough sectors or enough jobs, then this story doesn’t work anymore.



0:19:36 — Messy Middle scenario

The “Messy Middle”: automation without enough wealth to redistribute
Dwarkesh Patel: There’s one possibility which Molly Kinder has written about, this “Messy Middle” scenario. That possibility made me think about whether it might be better to have—at least as far as wealth distribution and redistribution go—a much faster AI takeoff.
I want to ask you whether the following possibility is at all likely, or if there’s any set of assumptions that can make it so. AI makes it possible to automate jobs such that many people are losing their jobs, but it doesn’t create enough wealth, while the process of automation is happening, to basically pay off the people who are getting laid off and create a Pareto improvement, where everybody’s getting better as a result of AI automation.
Of course, there’s a trivial sense in which that must be true. Whatever money the company is saving by not paying the humans instead of just paying the AIs, those resources still exist in the economy and can just be paid out to people.
But there’s going to be some allocative inefficiency. The government doesn’t know exactly who got laid off because of AI.
There’s a political problem. If the Meta worker gets laid off first and they were making $200,000 a year, is there a politically sustainable situation where you give them a $200,000 check a year when there are many working people making much less?
Do you find this scenario plausible, where AI is automating a bunch of things, but there isn’t as much wealth creation as there is automation?
Phil Trammell: I think it’s possible. To me, it does seem like a pretty narrow window. My guess is that if we have the technology to automate so many jobs that it becomes a new kind of political problem, then the pie will also be growing really fast.
Well, unless in all of those professions it’s automating, it’s just a hair more productive. So the cost of all the capital to replace all the software engineers is just a hair less than the cost of what we’ve been paying the software engineers.


Political economy and the drip: phone operators, COVID, Andy Hall
Dwarkesh Patel: Why is it implausible that a company can save money by laying off a bunch of software engineers? And in the long run, there’s a Jevons paradox, and we can’t anticipate in advance what we’d do with more software, and surely there will be more uses. But in the short run, the effect is just that a lot of people are laid off, and they still need to figure out how they can use a million times more JavaScript tokens.
Alex Imas: Phil and I have been writing about these things, and we have mathematical models in the back of these things. We don’t have any political economy in any of our models.
Andy Hall wrote a really nice blog post about the politics of AGI, and he made a really interesting observation. If there’s a 2% increase in unemployment, the political winds completely change. Unemployment has a huge effect on what happens politically.
Referring to Molly’s excellent essay, I think in some ways one of the worst scenarios is a drip scenario because of the political economy piece. What you might see is people not really being unemployed en masse, but moving into sectors that pay them less money.
This is what happened with phone operators between 1920 and 1940. Phone operators were completely automated, but it took 20 years, even though the technology existed. There was this drip. It wasn’t like this giant sector just disappeared.
There’s a really nice QJE [Quarterly Journal of Economics] paper [3] on this showing that they got reabsorbed into the economy, but at lower salaries, and they were mostly underemployed. That’s the scenario Molly was writing about, this messy middle where things aren’t a disaster.
We saw with COVID that the fiscal response can move quickly if there’s an emergency. An emergency is a quick uptick in unemployment, which could even look like 2-3%. That becomes a national emergency if it happens fast.


Did the pie actually grow?
Dwarkesh Patel: The concern is that whatever you’re saving on those white-collar workers, if that’s not growing the economy but just creating saved resources that can be allocated elsewhere, is that enough to do a broad-based redistribution scheme?
You have the money you’ve saved off a couple of people. Unless you can figure out exactly how to get it to them specifically, you have the problem of, “Can I do a UBI [universal basic income] off the money I saved by laying off…?”
Alex Imas: You’re basically saying the pie did not grow that much. You’re just displacing a bunch of people, but that didn’t grow the technological frontier of what the economy can produce.
Dwarkesh Patel: Then there’s a question of whether every time this has happened in history, the technological frontier has expanded a bunch.
Alex Imas: I think that’s the case. Simply in history, the technological frontier has expanded. I think Phil made the same point. It’s hard to imagine that sort of scenario where you are getting intelligence that’s just enough to replace the software engineer but still costs a lot of money. It’s just a hair less expensive than the software engineer, so you’re not getting this abundance effect. Where is the redistribution going to happen because the pie didn’t grow?
Dwarkesh Patel: This is very helpful. Many different things have to be true for this scenario to come to pass, each of which seem unlikely.
One, it has to be the case that it is possible to automate entire white-collar jobs, but only in a piecemeal way. That is to say that you can only automate software engineers, but that same program can’t also automate an accountant and an analyst and whatever.
My model of intelligence is such that—both the breadth of tasks it requires to do something like software engineering and what intelligence is—if you can really just lay off all the software engineers, you’ve got enough in the bucket there that you could automate all kinds of white-collar work. There are huge amounts of potential savings that have happened as a result of these layoffs, and also AI is going to be cheaper than human labor.
If both of those things are true, this messy middle scenario where we literally don’t have the wealth to go around seems unlikely. Then the question is, what is the best way to tax it and redistribute it?



0:25:57 — How to tax and redistribute AI wealth

Layering the instruments: negative income tax, UBI, universal basic capital
Alex Imas: I have some thoughts. I think it’s really important to outline the costs and benefits. First, there’s differential complexity in implementing these things. Two, they differ in the timeline of being actually helpful. Something like universal basic capital is not going to generate returns for something that happens in six months. You probably are going to end up with a layer of things.
Take a negative income tax, for example. You implement it, and the day it turns into law, you already have this insurance that there’s a floor where everybody gets a certain amount of money, and if you earn more money, you get taxed more. But there are positives and negatives to a negative income tax.
With UBI, for example, I worry a lot about the political economy implications. If people are just dependent on a check, it really matters who’s in power. Right now, we’re endowed with labor that can turn into income. When that is no longer the case and we are at the mercy of the elected official for basic needs, that feels like a power-sharing arrangement that’s really dangerous.
Dwarkesh Patel: But wouldn’t that be true of any sort of government redistribution program?
Alex Imas: With something like universal basic capital, where you have an ownership share and property rights for capital, you just have a share.
Dwarkesh Patel: You’re a normal shareholder.
Alex Imas: You’re just a normal person.


Universal basic capital and the indexing problem
Dwarkesh Patel: But this goes back to the question of indexing, because if indexing is hard, then universal basic capital is hard.
Alex Imas: That’s the problem of universal basic capital: targeting. What do you target to put into people’s portfolios?
Dwarkesh Patel: Like, what if Anthropic goes to zero, but some random robotics company takes all this over?
Alex Imas: Exactly. That’s the risk of universal basic capital. With a negative income tax, you have the same sort of issues as with UBI, where somebody comes into power and says, “We’re not going to do that anymore,” and people can’t work, and then you have the issue of the floor being gone.


Wealth tax, capital tax, and investment distortion
Dwarkesh Patel: One concern with the wealth tax is that there’s no politically sustainable equilibrium at a 0.5% wealth tax. This happened with the income tax, of course. Maybe they would’ve just decided to have their heirs index the economy and have their wealth grow at the rate of economic growth, and their heirs would be trillionaires by now.
Before index funds existed, it was just very hard. A very small fraction of the economy, going back 100 years, accounts for a majority of the value created now. If you missed those particular things, your wealth would’ve just stagnated.
Maybe there was a brief golden window from the creation of index funds up until five years ago where you could actually index the economy and have your wealth grow at the rate the economy grows. But now we’re in this world with very concentrated returns, especially to private companies. As we were making the point in our blog post, this is capital that the average person has disproportionately less access to. Most of their capital is having a random house, at least in the US.
Phil Trammell: Or a part of a house.
Dwarkesh Patel: Which, as we were saying, is capital that is uniquely ill-suited to be complementary to the production of AI or the serving of AI or to robots.
Phil Trammell: Or the kinds of goods that the rich will bid up the prices of.
Dwarkesh Patel: Exactly. What is the value of a house currently? It’s that the land is close to other humans and modulo relational stuff that is just not going to be the main factor of production in the future.
Alex Imas: This would be why a Georgist tax would not raise enough money for the sort of programs that we will be discussing.
Dwarkesh Patel: Right. But stepping back, the point I was trying to make is, if it gets harder to index the economy now, and that is the main way in which normal people are supposed to—modulo some sort of universal basic income—
Phil Trammell: In the developed world.
Dwarkesh Patel: —are supposed to have some purchase on the wealth from AI. And it’s also the way that developing countries are supposed to have some purchase on the wealth gains from AI.
But it’s very hard. Does Nigeria own a lot of SK Hynix and Anthropic? I’m guessing not. It’s not enough for them to just own the S&P 500.


Is AI like electricity or social media?
Alex Imas: This brings up a really important point. Is AI going to be like electricity or social media?
Think about ConEd, or whatever the electricity provider here is. It’s a monopoly. It provides a resource that everybody uses. But do we think about electricity as creating a concentration of power? Does ConEd have this huge amount of political power, social power, or something like that? No, because with electricity, a lot of the downstream benefits actually came to the users of the electricity rather than the actual entity producing it.
On the other hand, with social media, it was the opposite case. Social media was everywhere. Everybody uses social media, but the rents went to the platform.
Dwarkesh Patel: That’s a really interesting point. I don’t endorse this take yet, I’m going to talk out loud. The more you think our economy is going to be run on AGI the way our economy currently runs on electricity—that is, there’s a broad fundamental transformation of the entire economy—the more it looks like electricity… Every company in the S&P of the future, if it’s going to make it to the S&P 500, it is because it has leveraged AI.
Alex Imas: Exactly. And then you’re indexed again.
Dwarkesh Patel: But then again, I guess if you just look at how concentrated the S&P is over time, just these big tech companies much more so… I guess this goes to a fundamental point that it’s hard to reason about how much of the gains from AI these individual private companies will be able to control.


Open models and the commoditization question
Alex Imas: I think the open model thing is going to be a big point here. If we’re indeed in a world where the open models are six months behind the frontier—or nine months—then we’ll hit AGI, we’ll hit whatever, and in six months, everybody has access to this resource.
Dwarkesh Patel: This goes to show you that every question is connected to every other. That question about whether there’s runaway gains connects to questions about recursive self-improvement. Even if not recursive self-improvement, then continual learning, or online learning, which lets a model learn on the job. So if it’s deployed, it gets to learn more.
These are just forecasting technical questions which then impact whether Uganda will have any purchase on the returns of AGI.
The reason I’m emphasizing the question is I think both for the messy middle and for developing countries, a recommendation that is often made naively is that you’ve got to do some kind of retraining. You’ve got to do some kind of jobs program, or you’ve got to have them build data centers in your country. I think you guys are suggesting something closer to just buying the index of AGI. That’s probably a much cleaner strategy and much more likely to succeed.
Alex Imas: These are the two scenarios. I think there is a world where it is concentrated, in which case it’s going to be really hard to index AGI. There is another world where it is electricity. Basically every company has access to AGI. So you just buy the index. Nigeria just needs to buy the index, and Nigeria has access to AGI because of the open models.


Retrain or index?
Phil Trammell: Just to get back to the question about whether to go with retraining or trying to index. I would prioritize trying to index, just given how fast AI could hit the world. But I definitely wouldn’t just rely on that.
In the messy middle cases or the long-timeline cases where we don’t get anything like AGI all that soon, it would be leaving a lot of value on the table if you could have retrained to be a bit better educated on how to use the latest wave of computing. I don’t think there’s that much of an either/or there.
Dwarkesh Patel: Maybe the reason to be pessimistic about this is because one of the reasons a country is poor is that it has a bad education system, so becoming the best in the world at retraining people at using AI doesn’t seem like a particularly promising strategy for that poor country.


Leapfrogging: mobile banking in Nigeria
Alex Imas: Although there are cases where, in developing countries, you had this leapfrogging effect with, for example, mobile banking. It’s much more prevalent in Nigeria than it is in Germany.
Everybody is doing mobile banking. They have it on their phones, and they’re constantly doing this sort of thing.
Again, I’m not putting probabilities on this, but with a transformative technology like AI, you could get leapfrogging where you skip the step in the middle and get really astronomical growth.


Commoditization vs the safety race: the Defense Production Act threat
Phil Trammell: Just about the ease of indexing, I think it’s definitely something to worry about a bit and keep an eye on. But as discussed in our own essay, and as other people have pointed out, it’s already not that hard to index. There’s been a bit of an increase in the privatization of returns, but still, well under 20% of the total market cap of non-tiny companies in the US is private.
Everyone thinks about OpenAI and Anthropic. If that’s where all the wealth will accrue, then all these questions about whether open models will stay only a little bit behind, those are important. But even they look like they’re going public before too long, probably. The frictions that have been keeping companies from going public might themselves be alleviated by AI a lot, just all of the disclosure requirements and whatnot. They want to get access to more potential investors, too.
If I had to guess, I would guess that the long general trend of lowering those frictions and making it easier for more and more people to index will continue, despite the recent bump in the other direction.
Dwarkesh Patel: This actually makes me hope even more so than before that the labs do get commoditized, or at the very least they go public as soon as possible. But hopefully they just get totally commoditized. I think AI will be much more popular and, more importantly, will be much more likely to lead to broad increases in prosperity if it is as hard to capture the gains of AI as it is to capture the gains of electrification.
Alex Imas: Exactly. There’s no anti-electricity people out there.
Dwarkesh Patel: I mean electricity doesn’t take your job, but—
Phil Trammell: Well, it takes some people’s jobs.
Dwarkesh Patel: It took some people’s jobs, yeah.
Alex Imas: This is maybe tangential to the conversation but I think narratives matter. There’s this really negative narrative around AI right now, but that’s because people are not putting out the positive narrative.
There’s a reason. It’s more difficult to imagine a good thing that doesn’t exist than losing something that exists.
It’s much easier for somebody to go on a podcast and say, “These jobs that you like, they’re going away,” than for somebody to spin up a utopia which doesn’t exist yet.
Phil Trammell: I hope this isn’t too out of left field, but I would be remiss if I didn’t point out one big cost of having commoditized frontier AI models, which is the tech race dynamic. For safety purposes, you might want fewer frontier companies so that each one has a buffer in case they want to slow things down to make things safer.
The way this relates to our point before about the widespread access of the returns, is that I think there’s a lot less of a trade-off there than some people imagine.
Some people think either frontier AI gets commoditized and we all enjoy the benefits—but there might be some risk, because the market’s really competitive and cutthroat—or things are safer because there’s a big gap between the leader and the laggard.
But that means the leaders get fantastically wealthy? No. You could just have a relatively big gap, but it’s a public company, and ownership in it is widely distributed.
Dwarkesh Patel: More recently, I have been thinking that the risk of commodification—which is that it diffuses the ability to use AI to harmful ends—is worth the benefit. I worry that having these concentrated labs not only makes it so that the surplus isn’t as widely distributed through society, but also creates a very tangible, clear political target for the government.
We saw this with the Defense Production Act threat against Anthropic. If there wasn’t one lab, or a couple of labs, that are clearly ahead of others, this kind of threat would be much harder to make.
Thank you guys for doing this. I feel like there’s a lot of unresolved questions, but it is helpful to know what the first branch is along all these important dimensions.
Phil Trammell: Great.
Alex Imas: Thank you.
