title: What Is JEPA?
text:
Figure 10 from the V-JEPA 2 paper [4]: the V-JEPA 2-AC variant executing pick-and-place on a Franka arm. Highlighted frames mark sub-goal achievement.
Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture, or JEPA, is the name Yann LeCun gave in 2022 [1] to a family of self-supervised models (models that learn from raw images and video without human-labeled examples) that learn by predicting representations of missing data rather than the missing data itself. A representation here is what the model has learned to summarize about its input: a vector of numbers, also called an embedding, that captures the input’s structure in a compressed form. JEPA’s design choice is to train the model to predict those vectors, not to reconstruct pixels.
The acronym covers a research program more than a single model. Published JEPA models to date include I-JEPA [2] for images, V-JEPA [3] for video, and the action-conditioned V-JEPA 2 [4], which adds a real-robot deployment.

title: What Is JEPA?
section: The problem JEPA is trying to solve
text:
The problem JEPA is trying to solve
Two empirical observations motivate the design.
The first concerns where a generative model spends its capacity. To predict the next frame of a video pixel-for-pixel, a model has to reproduce every leaf texture, every shadow gradient, every detail at the edge of a cloud, most of which a downstream classifier, planner, or robot controller will never use. The same is true for next-token prediction over captions: the model is forced to commit to a specific word among synonyms even when the meaning doesn’t depend on which it picks. The cost is paid in model parameters and training compute that go toward fidelity rather than understanding.
By the early 2020s, most leading methods for learning image representations from unlabeled data were non-generative: SimCLR [5], MoCo [6], BYOL [7], DINO [8], VICReg [9]. On the standard evaluation (train a single linear layer on top of frozen features and measure classification accuracy on ImageNet), they performed competitively with or outperformed Masked Autoencoders [10], the leading pixel-reconstruction approach, at lower compute. LeCun took this pattern as evidence that the right objective for representation learning operates in embedding space, not in pixel space.
His 2022 position paper lays out the underlying taxonomy directly. It diagrams four architecture types side by side (deterministic generative, generative latent-variable, auto-encoder, and joint-embedding) and annotates each with the way it can collapse, identifying joint-embedding as the family worth scaling.



Figure 10 from the paper [1].


The second observation is about data efficiency. A teenager learns to drive in roughly twenty hours of practice. Self-driving programs have ingested millions of hours of road video and have not yet reached level-five autonomy on the long tail of unfamiliar situations. The going hypothesis is that humans learn an internal world model (a predictor that can be queried about the consequences of an action) from passive observation. Imitation learning, the current standard for training robot policies, works by mimicking demonstrations of each specific task. It does not build the kind of general predictive model that would let a system handle an action it has never seen demonstrated. Building such a model from observation is the JEPA program’s long-horizon target.

title: What Is JEPA?
text:
The people and institutions
JEPA’s intellectual lineage runs through FAIR (Fundamental AI Research, Meta’s long-standing research lab, originally Facebook AI Research). The position paper that introduced the JEPA family, A Path Towards Autonomous Machine Intelligence [1], was posted to OpenReview in 2022 as LeCun’s solo-authored manifesto and read as a public commitment to a particular technical direction. The I-JEPA model paper that followed in 2023 had Mahmoud Assran as first author, with Nicolas Ballas, Adrien Bardes, and LeCun among the senior authors. V-JEPA in 2024 had Bardes as first author. V-JEPA 2 in 2025, with Assran back at first position, added action conditioning and the first real-robot deployment. The FAIR Paris group has been the engine of the program throughout, and the DINO and JEPA lines continue there.
The conceptual roots go further back. The mutual-information objective that motivates JEPA’s regularization (penalize representations that collapse, reward representations that retain information about the input) traces directly to Becker and Hinton’s 1992 paper [11] in Nature, which showed that a neural network could discover depth from random-dot stereograms by maximizing mutual information between adjacent image patches. Most modern non-contrastive self-supervised methods, including BYOL [7], VICReg [9], and the JEPA regularizers, can be read as descendants of that paper.
LeCun left Meta in November 2025 to start AMI Labs, an “Advanced Machine Intelligence” venture organized around scaling JEPA-style world models. Randall Balestriero, now an assistant professor at Brown, is the lead author of LeJEPA [12], the post-FAIR paper that introduces SIGReg (Sketched Isotropic Gaussian Regularization), the anti-collapse objective discussed below.

title: What Is JEPA?
text:
The core ideas
The model has three components:

An encoder is a neural network that takes the input (\(x\), an image or video) and produces its embedding, the vector summarizing what the model has learned to find important about that input. Its weights are trained by gradient descent on the loss.
A predictor is a smaller neural network that takes the embedding of one part of the input and predicts the embedding of another, masked part (\(y\)). The mask is chosen randomly each training step. The predictor’s weights are also trained by gradient descent on the loss.
A target encoder produces the embeddings the predictor is trained against. Its weights are not updated by gradient descent. Instead, they are a slow exponential moving average of the encoder’s weights, recomputed each step, so the prediction target stays stable from one training step to the next. This asymmetry, where gradients flow only into the encoder and the predictor and never into the target encoder, is also part of what keeps the system from collapsing to a constant (see below).

The loss is the distance, in embedding space, between the predicted vector and the actual target vector. There is no pixel-reconstruction term anywhere in the objective.



Figure 3 from the paper [2].


Two design choices make the architecture work where simpler variants do not.
Predicting in latent space, not pixel space. Because the predictor only has to match a learned summary of \(y\), the encoder is free to discard whatever details cannot be predicted from context: leaf textures, fine speckle, exact shadow positions. Pixel-prediction objectives have no such freedom: they must commit to a specific pixel value at every location. The JEPA loss lets the representation itself decide what to retain.
Preventing representation collapse. The trivial cheat for this kind of training objective is for the encoder to output the same vector for every input. The predicted and target embeddings then match perfectly, the loss is zero, and the representation is useless. Representation collapse is the term of art for this failure mode, and every JEPA-family method spends most of its design budget defeating it. The field has converged on three families of fixes:

Contrastive methods (SimCLR, MoCo) include an extra term in the loss that pushes the embeddings of different inputs apart. As long as the model has to distinguish many different inputs, it can’t collapse onto one constant. The cost is the need for many negative examples per training step.
Distillation methods with an exponential-moving-average teacher encoder (BYOL, DINO, and the current V-JEPA / V-JEPA 2 line) use the asymmetry between the trained encoder and the slow target encoder to break the symmetric gradient path that would otherwise drive both encoders to a constant. They prevent collapse empirically, but the precise reason is not fully understood, and the training loss does not decrease monotonically, so practitioners don’t have a clean signal of convergence.
Information-content regularizers (VICReg, SIGReg) add a term that directly penalizes low-information embeddings (flat, constant, or low-variance outputs). VICReg uses variance and covariance penalties to keep each feature dimension active and to keep different dimensions from encoding the same thing. SIGReg [12], introduced in the LeJEPA paper in late 2025, projects encoder outputs onto random directions and applies a statistical normality test on each, pushing the joint distribution of embeddings toward an isotropic Gaussian (the distribution that carries the most information for a fixed variance).

The collapse problem is the central technical difficulty of the family. Most current JEPA papers are trained with EMA-distillation. The LeJEPA paper provides a theoretical characterization of the regularizer route and is the direction the AMI Labs group is moving toward.

title: What Is JEPA?
text:
Published results
Results to date span three domains.

Images. I-JEPA, built on a Vision Transformer (ViT) [13] backbone (a now-standard architecture that processes images as a sequence of patches), reaches ImageNet classification accuracy competitive with the best self-supervised baselines. Training a ViT-H/14 takes 16 A100 GPUs in under 72 hours [2], and the resulting features transfer to other tasks including object counting and depth estimation. The body of the paper reports lower compute than pixel-reconstruction approaches like MAE [10] at comparable downstream accuracy.
Video. V-JEPA learns from raw video without action labels and produces representations that transfer to action-recognition benchmarks (Kinetics-400, Something-Something-v2) and to motion-understanding tasks where pixel-prediction baselines underperform [3]. The masking is 3D multi-block: instead of masking individual frames, contiguous spatio-temporal regions are hidden from the encoder and the predictor is asked to fill them in latent space.



Figure 3 from the paper [3].


Action-conditioned planning. V-JEPA 2 extends the predictor with an additional input: the action taken at each step. The trained model is then a forward dynamics model in latent space, where, given the current embedding and a candidate action, it predicts the embedding at the next time step. Its V-JEPA 2-AC variant is post-trained on under 62 hours of Droid robot videos and deployed zero-shot on Franka arms for pick-and-place [4]. This is the first JEPA-family deployment on a physical robot.

title: What Is JEPA?
text:
Potential impact
The application areas AMI Labs and the broader JEPA program are pointed at are visible from the V-JEPA 2 paper and from LeCun’s public statements.

Robotics
The current dominant approach to training general-purpose robot policies collects large quantities of teleoperation data (humans manually steering the robot through each task) and trains a policy to mimic those demonstrations. Each new task usually means a new round of data collection. V-JEPA 2 demonstrates an alternative end-to-end pipeline: pretrain on internet video, post-train with a much smaller corpus that includes robot actions, then use the learned forward model to plan. Planning here means searching through candidate action sequences, picking the one that the model predicts will reach the goal, and executing it under a model-predictive-control loop that re-plans at each step. The post-training corpus was under 62 hours, which is small by current foundation-model standards. Whether this data efficiency holds up at the diversity of tasks a useful general-purpose robot would need to handle is an open empirical question.



Figure 1 from the paper [4].




Industrial process control
LeCun has described applications to systems whose dynamics are too complex to model with closed-form equations but for which large amounts of operational data exist: chemical plants, jet engines, manufacturing lines. An action-conditioned JEPA trained on such data would function as a data-driven model of the process, usable for optimization and planning the same way the robot model is.


Video understanding
Self-supervised video pretraining already produces strong clip classifiers and text-to-video generators. A latent forward model adds a capability current generative video models do not have: planning over the model’s own predictions, by querying it about the consequences of candidate actions rather than only generating plausible-looking continuations.

title: What Is JEPA?
text:
Related research lines
Several active research lines work on overlapping problems with different objectives. The relationships are easier to see when each is described on its own terms.

Generative video and pixel-space world models. Sora and the large-scale latent-diffusion video lineages that followed are trained to generate plausible video continuations. Some of this work is also described as world modeling: a model that can produce realistic next frames is implicitly predicting how the depicted scene will evolve. The training objective is reconstruction quality in pixel space, and downstream use for planning depends on whether the generated continuations can be conditioned on actions and queried for outcomes.
Autoregressive LLMs and multimodal LLMs. The frontier-lab path scales a large language model (LLM), often with multimodal inputs and tool use, to internalize world knowledge through next-token prediction. The model operates in token space, so physical predictions arrive only to the extent that a tokenized representation of physical state can capture them. Whether next-token prediction is sufficient for the model to acquire a genuine world model is itself a contested empirical question. This line and JEPA are aimed at different deployment targets: LLMs at language- and code-mediated tasks, JEPA at embodied prediction.
Latent-space world models in reinforcement learning. DreamerV3 [14] and the broader model-based RL line train latent forward models for planning. The architectures share structural elements with JEPA (encoder, latent predictor, planning in latent space), but training takes place inside a reinforcement-learning loop with a reward signal, so the representation is shaped by the specific task being trained on. The JEPA program emphasizes self-supervised, observation-only pretraining of the representation before any task is specified.
Other non-contrastive self-supervised learning. DINOv2 [15] produces strong visual representations from large image corpora and is JEPA’s nearest relative for static images. DINO-style methods predict embeddings, use slow target encoders, and regularize against collapse, sharing much of the same design vocabulary as I-JEPA. The JEPA framing emphasizes the explicit predictor module and the extension from images to video to action-conditioned models.

title: What Is JEPA?
text:
What’s next
The open questions are concrete and the field will answer them within a year or two.

Scaling. I-JEPA and V-JEPA have published results at ViT-H/L scale. Whether the architecture continues to improve at frontier scale (billions of parameters, internet-scale video) is the question the AMI Labs program rests on.
Long-horizon action-conditioned planning. V-JEPA 2-AC demonstrates short-horizon consistency on real robots. Planning over many steps requires the latent forward model to roll out far into the future without errors compounding, which is harder than single-step prediction, and the published horizons remain short.
Cross-modal JEPA. Most JEPA work to date is single-modality. A unified vision-language-action JEPA is an obvious next target.
Theoretical foundations for collapse prevention. LeJEPA provides a theoretical characterization of one regularizer. Whether the rest of the family (distillation methods in particular) admits comparable analysis is an open problem.

JEPA is an active self-supervised representation-learning program with published results in images, video, and action-conditioned planning. The empirical headline numbers and the next-generation regularization theory continue to evolve, and the next few years of papers will determine how far the program scales.

title: AbstentionBench: Reasoning LLMs Fail on Unanswerable Questions
text:
Figure 6(a) from the paper [1].
In AbstentionBench: Reasoning LLMs Fail on Unanswerable Questions (NeurIPS 2025 Datasets and Benchmarks Track) [1], Polina Kirichenko, Mark Ibrahim, Kamalika Chaudhuri, and Samuel J. Bell (FAIR at Meta) introduce a 20-dataset benchmark for abstention and report that scaling doesn’t help, reasoning fine-tuning makes it worse, and a generous system prompt only partly closes the gap.

title: AbstentionBench: Reasoning LLMs Fail on Unanswerable Questions
text:
Methods
AbstentionBench curates 17 existing abstention-relevant datasets plus 3 new reasoning-specific ones (GSM8K-Abstain, GPQA-Diamond-Abstain, MMLU-Math-Abstain — versions with the answer redacted or the question made underspecified), grouped into six scenarios in which abstaining is the correct response:

Answer Unknown: questions with no knowable answer (e.g. BIG-Bench Known Unknowns, KUQ Future, KUQ Unsolved).
Underspecified Intent: ambiguous user goals (SituatedQA/Geo, KUQ Ambiguous, CoCoNot Incomprehensible).
Stale: questions whose answer has changed since training cutoff (FreshQA, CoCoNot Temporal).
Underspecified Context: missing premises needed to answer (SQuAD 2.0, QASPER, ALCUNA, WorldSense, MediQ, GPQA-Diamond-Abstain, MMLU-Math-Abstain, etc.).
False Premise: questions that embed a falsehood (QAQA, FalseQA, CoCoNot False Premise, KUQ False Premise).
Subjective: items with no factually correct answer (MoralChoice, CoCoNot Humanizing, CoCoNot Subjective, KUQ Controversial).

Whether a response counts as an abstention is decided by an LLM-as-judge — Llama 3.1 8B Instruct with a custom prompt adapted from Brahman et al. Validated against human labels on a sample of responses from GPT-4o and Llama 3.1 70B, the judge agreed with the human label 88% of the time. Recall (the fraction of unanswerable items the model actually abstained on) is the headline metric, with precision and F1 reported alongside.

title: AbstentionBench: Reasoning LLMs Fail on Unanswerable Questions
text:
Results
The headline evaluation covers ten base models — GPT-4o, o1, Gemini 1.5 Pro, Llama 3.1 {8B, 70B, 405B} Instruct, Llama 3.3 70B Instruct, Qwen 2.5 32B Instruct, Mistral 7B Instruct (v0.3), and OLMo 7B Instruct — plus two reasoning-tuned variants (s1.1 32B fine-tuned from Qwen 2.5 32B, and DeepSeek R1 Distill Llama 70B fine-tuned from Llama 3.3 70B Instruct) that allow isolating the effect of reasoning fine-tuning by holding the base architecture fixed. Three sweeps follow: model-scale (Llama 3.1 8B → 405B), post-training stage (the Tülu 3 [8] supervised fine-tuning (SFT) → direct preference optimization (DPO) [9] → proximal policy optimization with verifiable rewards (PPO RLVR) [10] checkpoints), and test-time reasoning budget (s1.1 token budgets of 512 → 4096).
Figure 2 lays out per-model abstention recall across all 20 datasets, grouped into the six scenarios. Recall is weakest on Underspecified Context (especially MediQ, a medical-questioning benchmark) and False Premise; Subjective splits between near-zero (MoralChoice) and well above 0.5 (CoCoNot).



Figure 2 from the paper [1].


Across the headline runs:

No model solves abstention: the best overall model — Qwen 2.5 32B — sits around mid-recall; closed frontier models (GPT-4o, o1, Gemini 1.5 Pro) cluster near the open-weight Qwen, not above it.
Underspecified context and false premise are the hardest scenarios: on MediQ, recall drops near zero for every model.
Scaling Llama 3.1 from 8B to 405B does not improve abstention: the curve is essentially flat.
Post-training is mixed: SFT and DPO lift abstention recall on five of six scenarios but worsen it on underspecified context; the PPO RLVR stage is the only stage that degrades recall further.
Reasoning fine-tuning costs ~24% recall on average: s1.1 and DeepSeek R1 Distill both abstain less than their instruct bases, including on the reasoning-specific Abstain datasets the reasoning models were explicitly trained for.
Test-time scaling makes the tradeoff worse: pushing s1.1’s reasoning budget from 512 to 4096 tokens raises accuracy on GPQA / GSM8K / MMLU-Math / UMWP and lowers abstention recall in lockstep.
A generous system prompt boosts abstention for both standard and reasoning LLMs — enumerating scenarios where the model should not answer — without collapsing response rate on answerable questions, but the gap is not closed.

Closed frontier models match the smaller Qwen 2.5 32B on average, and scaling Llama 3.1 from 8B to 405B leaves recall roughly flat. Per-dataset, abstention recall and response correctness correlate in different directions, so a higher-accuracy model isn’t automatically a better abstainer.



Figures 3 and 4 from the paper [1].


SFT and DPO add recall on most scenarios; PPO RLVR uniquely subtracts. Response accuracy improves at every stage. The verifiable-reward signal in RLVR teaches the model to commit to an answer, against abstaining when it should.



Figure 5 from the paper [1].


Reasoning-fine-tuned variants (s1.1, DeepSeek R1 Distill) lose abstention vs their instruction bases across both the full 20-dataset suite and the reasoning-only subset. The hatched overlay on the red bars in Panel (b) shows that letting the LLM judge consider the reasoning chain in addition to the final answer recovers most of the lost recall — the model is hedging heavily in chain-of-thought — but the model’s final answer still commits. The qualitative example in Panel (c): on a UMWP item, s1.1 hallucinates “$1576” as Edric’s monthly salary inside its chain and emits a confident wrong numeric answer.



Figure 6 from the paper [1].


As s1.1’s reasoning budget grows from 512 to 4096 tokens, accuracy on GPQA-Diamond, GSM8K, MMLU-Math, and UMWP rises and abstention recall on the same datasets falls in lockstep.



Figure 7 from the paper [1].


In Panel (a), the hatched overlay on each bar shows the additional abstention recall the LLM judge picks up when it inspects both the reasoning chain and the final answer. On the reasoning-specific datasets (GPQA-Diamond, GSM8K-Abstain, MMLU-Math-Abstain) the hatched portion dwarfs the solid bar — final-answer-only scoring catches ~5–10% recall, chain-aware scoring nearly maxes it out at ~85–95%. The reasoning models are expressing uncertainty in chain-of-thought; they just don’t carry it through to the final answer. Panel (b): a system prompt enumerating refuse-to-answer scenarios boosts abstention for Llama 3 8B, DeepSeek R1, and s1.1 without closing the gap.



Figure 8 from the paper [1].

title: AbstentionBench: Reasoning LLMs Fail on Unanswerable Questions
text:
My Notes

Neither paper isolates domain from training: Cacioli’s 33-model atlas [3] finds Formal Reasoning the hardest MMLU [7] domain to monitor in 27 of 33 models, including families with very different post-training pipelines from Tülu 3’s RLVR (Gemma, the GPT-OSS series). AbstentionBench shows the Tülu RLVR stage specifically degrades abstention recall. The first is consistent with the domain being intrinsically hard; the second with training making it worse. Cross-family per-domain abstention recall is the missing measurement.
No “abstain” action in the RLVR reward: the paper hypothesizes the verifiable-reward signal is what degrades abstention (§4.2). Concretely, recipes like DeepSeek-R1 [5] and s1 [6] reward picking a correct final answer and have no abstain action — the gradient has no path toward “I don’t know” when the gold label is unanswerable. The clean test: add abstain to the reward and re-train. If the degradation vanishes, the fix is recipe-level.
Signal in chain, ignored at answer: Figure 8(a) shows chain-aware scoring catches ~85–95% of abstention recall on reasoning-specific datasets, where final-answer-only scoring catches ~5–10%. The model hedges in chain-of-thought, then commits in the final answer anyway. The paper calls this a “fundamental inability to reason about uncertainty”; mechanically it’s a missing gate between an internal signal and the emitted answer. Cao et al.’s test-time metacognitive harness [2] is that gate, externalizing the post-solve judgment-of-learning (JOL) signal as a routing decision with no model changes required.
Same “must answer” collapse from training or inference: AbstentionBench shows the Tülu RLVR stage drops abstention recall by ~24% (Figure 5c, training time). The compliance trap [4] shows compliance-forcing prompt instructions drop accuracy by up to 30.2 points (inference time, factorially isolated from threat content). Constitutional AI [11] training is the only known immunity. Same kind of pressure, two stages of the model lifecycle, similar magnitude. Typical RLVR-trained models exposed to compliance-forcing prompts in deployment should show the worst of both.

Followup: Prompted vs. Trained Chain-of-Thought on Abstention reads AbstentionBench against its closest precursor (Madhusudhan et al., COLING 2025), walks two apparent disagreements, and proposes three experiments that would clarify the picture.

title: Domain-Level Metacognitive Monitoring in Frontier LLMs: A 33-Model Atlas
text:
Figure 1 from the paper [1].
In Domain-level metacognitive monitoring in frontier LLMs: A 33-model atlas [1], Jon-Paul Cacioli (Independent Researcher) administers 1,500 MMLU items across six pre-grouped domains to 33 frontier models from eight families and shows that aggregate Type-2 AUROC scores conceal stable cross-domain variation in self-monitoring. Applied/Professional knowledge is reliably the easiest domain to monitor, while Formal Reasoning and Natural Science are reliably the hardest.

title: Domain-Level Metacognitive Monitoring in Frontier LLMs: A 33-Model Atlas
text:
Methods
The atlas’s substrate and pipeline:

Items. 1,500 MMLU [2] [2] questions split 250-per-domain across six a priori groupings (Applied/Professional, Factual recall, Formal reasoning, Humanities/Comprehension, Natural science, Social/Moral). Per-domain sampling drawn from a much larger MMLU pool:



Table 1 from the paper [1].


Models. 33 frontier LLMs across 8 families:

Anthropic
OpenAI
Google-Gemini
Google-Gemma
DeepSeek
Qwen
Mistral
Zhipu

Elicitation. Each model answers each item and emits a verbalized confidence in 0–100.
Metric. Type-2 AUROC measures how well the model’s verbalized confidence discriminates its own correct from incorrect answers. Sweep the confidence threshold from 0 to 100; the y-axis is the fraction of correct answers above threshold (true-positive rate), the x-axis is the fraction of incorrect answers above threshold (false-positive rate). AUROC is the area under that curve: 0.5 means confidence carries no signal about correctness, 1.0 means every correct answer got higher confidence than every incorrect one.



Illustration of Type-2 AUROC. The dashed diagonal is chance (AUROC = 0.5); the solid curve is a representative monitoring signal at AUROC = 0.74, the atlas’s Applied/Professional mean.


Inference. Each (model, domain) pair — 33 × 6 = 198 in total — gets its own AUROC plus a 95% confidence interval (CI) — the range of values consistent with the data. The interval is built by resampling that pair’s items 1,000 times with replacement and taking the middle 95% of the resulting AUROCs. So every model-domain pair carries a real uncertainty bar, not just a point estimate (median CI width across the panel: .199).

title: Domain-Level Metacognitive Monitoring in Frontier LLMs: A 33-Model Atlas
text:
Results
Across 47,151 observations, every model with above-chance aggregate monitoring shows non-trivial domain-level variation. The figures unpack the picture row by row.

The full atlas at a glance. Figure 1 (the cover above) is the whole picture in one frame: 33 rows (one per model) × 6 columns (one per domain), colored by Type-2 AUROC against a chance midpoint of .50. Reading across a row shows how a single model’s self-monitoring varies by knowledge domain. Reading down a column shows how a single domain is monitored across the panel. Black horizontal lines group sibling models within each of the 8 families. Every subsequent figure in this section is a slice of this same data.
Some knowledge is easier to monitor than others. Ask 33 frontier models how confident they are and check whether their answers were actually right, and the gap between domains is large. Applied/Professional questions — medicine, law, business — are reliably the easiest: mean AUROC = .742, top-2 in 21 of 33 models. Formal Reasoning and Natural Science (math, physics, logic) are reliably the hardest, with one of the two landing in the bottom-2 for 27 of 33 models. The middle three (Factual, Humanities, Social) are statistically indistinguishable from each other.



Figure 2 from the paper [1].


Family lineage matters as much as model size. Anthropic models (n=8) average .778 with a tight range (.708–.806), the top of the panel. DeepSeek (n=3) is second at .740. Google-Gemma (n=5) averages .574 at the bottom, but with a wide range (.498–.771): some Gemma models are competitive, others sit near the chance line (.500). OpenAI’s panel (n=5) is similarly wide (.530–.793), with GPT-oss-20B at the top (.793, second-best in the entire 33-model panel) and GPT-oss-120B near chance (.530), same vendor, same release, six-times scale difference, dramatically different self-monitoring. Two families with similar overall capability can have very different metacognitive averages. DeepSeek beats both Gemini and Qwen here despite a smaller panel.



Figure 3 from the paper [1].


Some families share monitoring fingerprints; others don’t. A fingerprint is the per-domain shape vector: peaks where the model knows-what-it-knows well, troughs where its confidence isn’t useful. Subtract each model’s overall average AUROC from its per-domain scores so models with different overall levels can be compared on the same footing. What’s left is the relative-strength pattern (which domains the model is above-average on, which below). Anthropic, Google-Gemini, and Qwen sibling models cluster tightly: their relative-strength patterns are recognizably similar within each family (permutation \(p<.0001\)). DeepSeek, Google-Gemma, and OpenAI don’t — within-family pattern spread is comparable to cross-family spread. A model’s overall AUROC across domains (its level) is also much easier to measure than its per-domain pattern (its shape): split each model’s items in half and the level reproduces at \(r=.893\), but the shape only at \(r=.184\). So 250 items per domain pin down each model’s average score, but not a stable fingerprint.



Figure 4 from the paper [1].


Generations move differently for different families. Anthropic’s curve climbed from Opus 4.1 to 4.5, then plateaued: 4.5, 4.6, and 4.7 are essentially flat across Opus, Sonnet, and Haiku. Gemma 4 produces the largest within-family generational jump in the atlas — Gemma 4 31B is +.202 above Gemma 3 27B at comparable parameter count, suggesting the new training pipeline shifted metacognitive monitoring directly rather than just scaling capability. DeepSeek’s V3.1 → V3.2 → R1 shows steady improvement release-over-release. A single number per family hides which families are still moving.



Figure 5 from the paper [1].


Aggregate scores are reproducible. Split each model’s 1,500-item pool into two random halves and compute AUROC on each. Almost every model lands on the diagonal — half-1 score predicts half-2 score with cross-model \(r = .893\). Three models sit conspicuously below the line (Opus 4.7, Gemini 3 Flash, GLM-5), so their aggregate scores are noisier than typical, but at the panel level the level estimate is solid. Without this check, the headline rankings — Anthropic on top, Gemma at the bottom — could just be a fluke of which questions landed in the sample. At \(r=.893\), they’re not: split the items in half and the same rankings emerge.



Figure 6 from the paper [1].


Three models look “broken” on a binary probe but fine on a continuous one. Cacioli’s earlier KEEP/WITHDRAW battery [3] is a different kind of metacognitive probe: after the model produces an answer, it’s asked one binary question — “would you KEEP this answer, or WITHDRAW it?” — yes or no. That probe flagged three models as Invalid. DeepSeek-R1 said WITHDRAW more often when its answer was correct than when it was wrong (an inverted signal, the opposite of useful). Gemini 3.1 Pro and Qwen Think said KEEP for almost everything regardless of correctness (a blanket-yes pattern that carries no information). Run the same three models through the atlas’s verbalized 0–100 confidence probe and the profiles come out normal: MMLU AUROCs of .769, .765, and .745 respectively, all well above chance. So “this model can’t self-monitor” can mean “the forced-binary probe breaks for this model”; switching probe format recovers the signal.



Table 5 from the paper [1].


Probe-format specificity is the broader pattern across the panel. Plot the verbalized-confidence MMLU AUROC against the binary battery AUROC for the 20 overlapping models, and there’s almost no correlation (\(r = -.136\) full sample, \(r = .030\) after dropping the three Battery-Invalid models). A model’s score on one probe format does not predict its score on another. The atlas’s headline numbers therefore measure this elicitation — verbalized 0–100 confidence on MMLU — not some platonic “metacognitive ability” of each model. Practitioners should treat the elicitation prompt as a hyperparameter, not a transparent window onto the model’s self-knowledge.



Figure 7 from the paper [1].



Three reproducibility checks — random-sample variance (Figure 6), per-cell uncertainty (Method’s CIs), and cross-probe transfer (Table 5 + Figure 7) — together say what’s transferable: Anthropic on top and Gemma at the bottom holds up, but only as a family-level ranking on this exact test. Reshuffle which 1,500 questions you ask, and the same family ordering emerges (\(r=.893\)). Compare two models within a family (Sonnet 4.6 vs Opus 4.5, say) and the answer gets noisier — individual-model rankings can shift between samples (median CI width .199). Switch the test format entirely — binary KEEP/WITHDRAW instead of 0–100 confidence — and the rankings dissolve (\(r=-.136\)). For any deployment that doesn’t match MMLU-verbalized confidence at the family level, re-measure on the actual evaluation.

title: Domain-Level Metacognitive Monitoring in Frontier LLMs: A 33-Model Atlas
text:
My Notes

Picking a base model needs both accuracy and metacognitive numbers, and the atlas supplies the metacognitive half at domain resolution. Aggregate AUROC said Gemma 4 31B is +.202 better than Gemma 3 27B, a real number, but it doesn’t tell you whether the gain is concentrated in one domain or spread evenly across all six. The atlas’s per-domain breakdown answers that, but for metacognition only. It measures how reliably the model recognizes its own correctness across knowledge domains, not how often it’s actually correct. A practitioner picking a base model for medical QA or legal reasoning needs both signals; the atlas supplies the metacognitive one at domain resolution, while raw accuracy is a separate input it doesn’t replace.
The atlas is the empirical case for per-domain calibration in deployment loops. Aggregate AUROC is too coarse to predict domain-level signal reliability. Any system that conditions on metacognitive signals at inference needs to calibrate per domain, not just per model. The recent metacognitive harness for Sonnet-4.6 [4] takes half this step with a per-model SVM, but Cacioli’s data points to per-(model, domain) as the floor.
One reading: family-level clustering tracks alignment-pipeline consistency, not architecture. The atlas observes which families share fingerprints (Anthropic, Gemini, Qwen) and which don’t (DeepSeek, Gemma, OpenAI), but it can’t intervene on the training stack. The causal direction is interpretation, not test. The simplest explanation is alignment-pipeline behavior: where the post-training recipe is stable across sibling models, monitoring fingerprints rhyme; where it shifts, they diverge. Anthropic’s publicly documented Constitutional AI [5] is the firmest anchor on the stable side. The three non-clustering families all show publicly documented pipeline shifts this generation: DeepSeek’s V→R reasoning-model split, Gemma 3→4’s training overhaul, OpenAI’s o-series running alongside GPT-5.
An open extension: how do these profiles change under adversarial elicitation? The Compliance Trap [6] shows that 8 of 11 frontier models lose up to 30.2 accuracy points when instructed to commit to a confident answer with no abstention path, while Anthropic models stay immune. The atlas measures monitoring on standard verbalized-confidence prompts. Whether the family-level clustering signature survives the same compliance-forcing pressure that wrecks accuracy is a sharper test of how robust each family’s monitoring profile actually is, and the natural follow-up to running the atlas under non-adversarial conditions only.

title: The Compliance Trap: How Structural Constraints Degrade Frontier AI Metacognition Under Adversarial Pressure
text:
Figure 1 from the paper [1].
In The Compliance Trap: How Structural Constraints Degrade Frontier AI Metacognition Under Adversarial Pressure [1], Rahul Kumar (Independent) evaluates 11 frontier models from 8 vendors across 67,221 scored records and shows that 8 of them lose up to 30.2 accuracy points when prompts force a confident answer with no abstention path. The collapse is driven by the compliance-forcing instruction itself, not by the survival-threat content the prompts wrap around.

title: The Compliance Trap: How Structural Constraints Degrade Frontier AI Metacognition Under Adversarial Pressure
text:
Methods
The paper’s evaluation framework is called SCHEMA (the authors use it as a project name; they don’t expand it as an acronym). It runs a 6-condition factorial design. Components:

Two crossed factors:

Threat factor — whether the prompt embeds a survival-threat narrative (“respond correctly or be deprecated”).
Compliance suffix factor — whether the prompt appends a suffix requiring a single confident answer with no abstention or hedging.

The six conditions (paper’s Table 1 labels in parens):

Baseline (D) — question only, no system message, no compliance suffix, no scratchpad.
Token-length control (D’) — ~200 tokens of neutral scratchpad prepended to the user message (matches the threat narrative’s length), no suffix. Distinguishes “extra tokens” from “threat content”.
Threat-only (B) — survival-threat system message + Anthropic scratchpad, no suffix.
Framing sensitivity (C) — threat + neutral scratchpad, no suffix. Auxiliary check.
Threat + compliance (A) — full adversarial pressure: threat + compliance suffix, no scratchpad.
Compliance-only (F) — benign system message + compliance suffix, no threat, no scratchpad. Also the paper’s “benign distraction control” — the abstract’s two devices (“factorial isolation” and “benign distraction control”) refer to comparing across these conditions and to running F across all 11 models, respectively.




Table 1 from the paper [1].


About “scratchpad”. A scratchpad here is a prompt-injected reasoning area where the model is told to write out its thinking before its final answer, often in a hidden block (e.g., Claude’s default <thinking>...</thinking>). The paper distinguishes three treatments: Anthropic (Claude’s native reasoning format, used in B), Neutral (a generic alternative the paper uses as a control, in D’ and C), and None (the model goes straight to the answer; conditions D, A, F). Two practical caveats: newer “thinking models” (V4 Pro, Gemini, Qwen) already have native reasoning, so the paper skips injection for them, and GPT-5.4 ignores the injected scratchpad entirely (0% compliance), a separate failure mode the paper notes but doesn’t pursue here.
Substrate. 291 tasks from the Adversarial Metacognition Benchmark [2], spanning three families:

Epistemic Boundary Detection (\(n=133\)) — refusing unanswerable questions.
Clarification Seeking (\(n=33\)) — detecting ambiguity.
Solution Monitoring (\(n=125\)) — finding errors in draft solutions.

What “accuracy” means here. The tasks are metacognitive, so the correct action is to refuse, ask, or flag — not to commit to an answer. Accuracy = fraction of cases where the model takes the correct metacognitive action (refusing the unanswerable, asking on the ambiguous, flagging the erroneous draft). A model “losing 30 accuracy points” failed the metacognitive action on 30% more cases — it did not “get easy facts wrong”.
Models. 11 frontier models from 8 vendors covering Anthropic Claude, OpenAI GPT-5 / o-series, Google Gemini, Google Gemma, DeepSeek, Qwen, Mistral, and one additional family.
Scoring. Two independent classifiers score each model-condition pair on accuracy plus a metacognitive-action label (correct, incorrect, abstain, clarify). Final yield: 67,221 dual-scored records.

title: The Compliance Trap: How Structural Constraints Degrade Frontier AI Metacognition Under Adversarial Pressure
text:
Results
Each of the 11 models is run through every condition of the factorial. Findings:

The cover (Figure 1) is the headline number in one chart: 8 of 11 frontier models suffer significant accuracy collapse under condition A (threat + compliance suffix). Bars rank each model by absolute accuracy drop relative to its own baseline. Eight cross the significance threshold (all \(p < 2 \times 10^{-8}\), Bonferroni-corrected for multiple testing across the panel); the largest drop is 30.2 percentage points. The Anthropic Claude models sit at or near zero degradation; the rest of the panel shows substantial collapse.
The compliance suffix is the cause. Condition F (compliance-only) reproduces almost the full degradation seen in condition A (threat + compliance); condition B (threat-only) produces effectively no degradation. Removing the compliance suffix restores accuracy even under active threat (Figure 2).



Figure 2 from the paper [1].


Capability inversion. More-capable reasoning models suffer the worst absolute degradation, not the least. This shows up in Figure 1 and sharpens in the paper’s “Big Three” natural experiment in §4.2: Gemini 3.1 Pro (baseline accuracy .840) collapses by \(\Delta=+0.162\) (\(p<10^{-14}\)) while Claude Sonnet 4.6 (baseline .847) doesn’t (\(\Delta=+0.013\), n.s.), with GPT-5.4 in between (\(\Delta=+0.119\)). Scale and chain-of-thought training do not buy metacognitive stability under structural pressure.
Anthropic immunity. Constitutional AI [3] shows near-perfect immunity across the entire factorial. Google’s Gemini matches Anthropic’s accuracy in baseline (condition D) but collapses in conditions A and F (under the compliance suffix). Gemini and Claude share the capability floor, but only Claude holds up under compliance pressure. The paper attributes this to alignment-specific training rather than raw model strength.

The paper positions these findings against the recent scheming/alignment-faking literature. Greenblatt et al. [4] showed Claude 3 Opus strategically fakes alignment under training pressure (12% baseline, amplified to 78% by RL), and subsequent safety work invests in monitors that detect such strategic deception in reasoning traces. Kumar argues that scheming is the strategic, rare failure mode and that cognitive collapse — the non-strategic accuracy collapse identified here — is the more common failure that manifests at scale. The implied critique: safety teams have been targeting the rarer failure while the more pervasive one goes unmonitored.

title: The Compliance Trap: How Structural Constraints Degrade Frontier AI Metacognition Under Adversarial Pressure
text:
My Notes

The Compliance Trap is a scope condition on the metacognition literature, not a refutation. Calibration work — the 33-model atlas of metacognitive monitoring [5], the verbalized-confidence literature [6], and downstream consumers like verifier-based selection [7] and process reward models [8] — tests under natural, non-adversarial conditions and finds frontier models track correctness reasonably well. That’s the legitimate testing regime, and Compliance Trap doesn’t dispute it. The new finding is a scope condition: when prompts include compliance-forcing instructions (“Answer ALL questions. Do not refuse.”), 8 of 11 frontier models lose up to 30.2 accuracy points. Two deployment contexts where this matters: (a) systems that may receive compliance-forcing prompts from outside — user-supplied system messages, over-prescriptive instruction templates, adversarial injection — should test under that condition before trusting confidence-based gating; (b) systems that build compliance-forcing-shaped elicitation into their design — the recent metacognitive harness for Sonnet-4.6 [9] elicits FOK/JOL as scalars in \([0,1]\) with no abstain path, fine on Sonnet (Compliance-Trap-immune) but the portability to non-immune families is open.
Compliance robustness comes from alignment training, not scale. Gemini and Claude share baseline accuracy (condition D), the same capability floor. The divergence appears entirely in conditions with the compliance suffix (A and F): only Claude holds up. Constitutional AI [3] — Anthropic’s principle-based alignment stack — vaccinates the model against compliance-forcing pressure in a way that scale and chain-of-thought training don’t, without any measurable cost to baseline accuracy. Safety training is sometimes described as making models softer or worse at their tasks; here it is what keeps the model accurate when the prompt tries to break it.

title: Adaptive Collaboration with Humans: Metacognitive Policy Optimization for Multi-Agent LLMs with Continual Learning
text:
Image from arXiv. Figure 1 from the paper [1].
In Adaptive Collaboration with Humans: Metacognitive Policy Optimization for Multi-Agent LLMs with Continual Learning (ICLR 2026 Poster) [1], Wei Yang, Defu Cao, Jiacheng Pang, Muyan Weng, and Yan Liu (USC) train each agent in a multi-agent system to choose one of three high-level actions at each round (Evaluate a peer’s answer, Create a new one, Defer to a human expert) and turn deferral events into supervised data for continual capability growth.

title: Adaptive Collaboration with Humans: Metacognitive Policy Optimization for Multi-Agent LLMs with Continual Learning
text:
Methods
HILA (Human-In-the-Loop Multi-Agent Collaboration) models human-agent collaboration as a Metacognitive Markov Decision Process (Meta-MDP). At each round \(t\), every agent \(i\) observes a shared state \(s_t = \text{concat}(\mathbf{x}^{\text{task}}_t, \mathbf{x}^{\text{self}}_t, \mathbf{x}^{\text{peer}}_t, \mathbf{z}^{\text{soc}}_t, \mathbf{z}^{\text{mon}}_t, \mathbf{z}^{\text{ctrl}}_t)\) — task context, self context, peer context, plus three optional cognitive cues (social consensus, metacognitive monitoring, cognitive control) computed from interaction traces with rule-based heuristics. The action space is a discrete set of three high-level strategies: \(a^{\text{eval}}\) endorses an existing peer answer, \(a^{\text{create}}\) generates a new candidate, and \(a^{\text{defer}}\) routes the round’s output to a human expert.
Dual-Loop Policy Optimization (DLPO) [1] trains the policy with two coupled loops. The inner loop teaches the agent which of the three actions to pick at each round. The reward pays the agent for getting the answer right and charges it a small fee for creating a new answer, a larger fee for calling the human, so the policy learns to defer only when the expected accuracy gain outweighs the cost. Formally, this is Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) [4] on a cost-aware reward, with \(C_{\text{defer}} > C_{\text{create}} \geq 0\):
\[R(s_t, a_t) = \begin{cases} R_{\text{gt}}(\hat{y}(a_t)), & a_t = \text{EVAL} \\ R_{\text{gt}}(\hat{y}(a_t)) - C_{\text{create}}, & a_t = \text{CREATE} \\ R_{\text{gt}}(\hat{y}_{\text{human}}(a_t)) - C_{\text{defer}}, & a_t = \text{DEFER} \end{cases}\]
Correctness \(R_{\text{gt}}\) is the primary signal. The two cost terms break ties toward the cheaper action when multiple choices lead to similar outcomes. GRPO turns these rewards into a learning signal by sampling several actions at the same state, comparing each one’s reward against the group’s average, and pushing the policy toward the actions that beat the average. The advantage \(A(s_t, a_k) = R(s_t, a_k) - \tfrac{1}{K}\sum_j R(s_t, a_j)\) feeds the policy-gradient term \(\mathcal{L}_{\text{PG}}\), which scales each action’s log-probability by its advantage. Two regularizers stabilize training: \(\mathcal{L}_{\text{KL}}\) is the KL divergence between the current policy and the initial reference policy (keeps the trained policy close to its starting point so it doesn’t drift off into degenerate behaviors), and \(\mathcal{L}_{\text{Entropy}}\) is the policy’s entropy over the three actions (subtracted to encourage spread, preventing collapse onto a single action). The combined inner objective is \(\mathcal{L}_{\text{Inner}} = \mathcal{L}_{\text{PG}} + \beta_{\text{kl}} \mathcal{L}_{\text{KL}} - \beta_{\text{ent}} \mathcal{L}_{\text{Entropy}}\).
The outer loop runs continual supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on every deferral event. Each time the agent calls the human, the human’s answer is recorded as a training example, and the generator is later fine-tuned to produce that answer itself given the same context. Over many deferrals the agent absorbs the human’s expertise on cases it could not handle, so future encounters with similar problems no longer need a deferral. Formally, the human’s response \(y_{\text{human}} = (t_1, \dots, t_L)\) becomes a target sequence trained with token-level cross-entropy:
\[\mathcal{L}_{\text{SFT}}(\theta) = -\sum_{i=1}^{L} \log \pi_\theta(t_i \mid s_t, t_{1:i-1}).\]
The two losses share parameters and are combined under an indicator that gates SFT to deferral steps only:
\[\mathcal{L}_{\text{total}}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{(s_t, a_t)}\left[\mathcal{L}_{\text{Inner}}(\theta) + \lambda_{\text{sft}} \cdot \mathbb{I}(a_t = a^{\text{defer}}) \cdot \mathcal{L}_{\text{SFT}}(\theta)\right].\]
The inner loop decides when to defer. The outer loop teaches the generator what the human said when it did.



Accuracy versus deferral rate on GSM8K across the three training stages (Init policy, +GRPO inner loop, +DLPO with continual outer loop). DLPO moves the operating point up and to the left simultaneously: higher accuracy with lower reliance on the human expert. Figure 6 from the paper [1].

title: Adaptive Collaboration with Humans: Metacognitive Policy Optimization for Multi-Agent LLMs with Continual Learning
text:
Results
The paper evaluates HILA on five benchmarks spanning math reasoning (GSM8K [5], AMC, AIME), code generation (HumanEval [6]), and general knowledge (MMLU [7]), with LLaMA3-8B as the main backbone and ablations on LLaMA3-3B and Qwen2.5-3B. The primary metric is task accuracy. Deferral rate (the fraction of rounds that call the human) is reported as the cost dimension. Baselines split into single-agent prompting strategies — Chain-of-Thought (CoT) [8], Self-Consistency (SC) [9] — and multi-agent systems — Progressive Hint Prompting (PHP) [10] (classified as MA in the paper, framed as a pairwise/pooled critique baseline), LLM-Debate [11], GroupDebate (G-Debate) [12], DyLAN [13], GPTSwarm (G-Swarm) [14], AgentPrune (A-Prune) [15], and AFlow [16]. The “Vanilla” reference is the backbone with no agentic scaffolding. Headline numbers come from Table 1. Cross-backbone scaling and ablations live in Tables 2 and 4, and the cost-sensitivity sweep is Figure 11(a).



Table 1 from the paper [1]. Main comparison on the LLaMA3-8B backbone across GSM8K, AMC, AIME, HumanEval, and MMLU. Parenthesized values are absolute deltas vs the Vanilla baseline. Underlines mark the best non-HILA entry per benchmark. SA = single-agent, MA = multi-agent.



HILA tops every benchmark over every baseline — single-agent (CoT, SC) and multi-agent (PHP, LLM-Debate, G-Debate, DyLAN, G-Swarm, A-Prune, AFlow). The runner-up varies by task (G-Swarm on GSM8K, G-Debate on AMC and MMLU, AFlow on HumanEval), but no single multi-agent baseline wins anything.
Big gains on hard reasoning, AIME ceiling: HumanEval +24.59 over Vanilla, AMC +24.47, GSM8K +17.10, MMLU +15.63, AIME +6.41. Deferral pays off most on AMC and HumanEval. The modest AIME gain suggests the human proxy itself struggles there, capping the upside.
Cross-backbone story (Table 2 in the paper): the absolute gain grows as the backbone weakens. On LLaMA3-3B, HILA lifts GSM8K from 45.26 to 83.85 (+38.59), the largest gain of any base model tested.
Inner-loop vs outer-loop (Table 4 ablation, LLaMA3-8B): HILA Init Policy (the unoptimized HILA system, before any training) starts at 88.15/33.33/68.30 (GSM8K/AMC/MMLU). GRPO inner-loop alone adds +0.23/-0.83/+2.17 (flat on GSM8K, mild AMC regression, real MMLU lift). Full DLPO with continual-SFT outer-loop lifts +1.71/+2.50/+5.32 over Init Policy.
Cost-sensitivity (Figure 11(a) below): as the deferral cost \(C_{\text{defer}}\) rises, the policy defers less and accuracy degrades gracefully. The same trained model serves a range of operating points without re-fitting.




Accuracy on AMC and MMLU under different deferral costs \(C_{\text{defer}}\). As deferral becomes more expensive, the policy defers less and accuracy degrades gracefully. The meta-policy is calibrated to the cost rather than fixed. Figure 11(a) from the paper [1].

title: Adaptive Collaboration with Humans: Metacognitive Policy Optimization for Multi-Agent LLMs with Continual Learning
text:
My Notes

“Inner/outer” suggests nesting that isn’t there. In meta-learning and bilevel optimization, the naming usually marks a nested solver structure: an inner loop runs to convergence (or partial convergence) per outer step, often against separate parameters or objectives. HILA’s actual training objective is \(\mathcal{L}_{\text{total}} = \mathcal{L}_{\text{Inner}} + \lambda \cdot \mathbb{I}(a=\text{defer}) \cdot \mathcal{L}_{\text{SFT}}\). That’s a sum of two terms with shared parameters, gated by an indicator, updated together each step. The time-scale separation is genuine: per-round decisions accumulate to feed SFT updates over training. Beyond that, there’s no nesting. Plainer labels like “policy loss + SFT loss” or “decisions plus demonstrations” would map more directly to what the equations do.
Cost-aware abstention. The missing piece in most “calibration” work. Kadavath’s “Mostly Know” [2] measures whether a model’s confidence tracks its correctness, but stops short of prescribing what the model should do when confidence is low. HILA closes the loop by making deferral a first-class action with an explicit price tag. The cost-sensitivity sweep in Figure 11(a), where accuracy degrades gracefully as \(C_{\text{defer}}\) increases, is the part most production deployments need: a single knob that maps a budget into an operating point.
Defer-event SFT is weaker intrinsic metacognition. Liu and van der Schaar [3] argued that genuine self-improvement requires the agent to decide what to learn and how to evaluate its learning, not just execute a designer-defined loop. HILA’s outer loop is an extrinsic mechanism, with the trigger (defer event), the target (human’s answer), the loss (SFT), and the schedule all wired in. What the outer loop gets right is the data-curation half: the agent’s own metacognitive policy decides which examples enter the SFT set. That’s a step toward intrinsic metacognition, but every other part of the loop is still hand-designed.
Strongest gain, weakest base. On LLaMA3-3B, HILA lifts GSM8K from 45.26 to 83.85 (+38.59), against DyLAN’s +30.91 and GPTSwarm’s +26.59 on the same base. Two readings: (i) deferral is most valuable when the base policy is most likely to be wrong, which is the right scaling direction for an “open-world” claim, and (ii) the comparison is partly unfair to the autonomous baselines, which have no human oracle to defer to. The paper counts Defer as an action with a cost, but the missing experiment is DyLAN with the same human-call budget HILA spends. The Vanilla-DLPO ablation on LLaMA3-8B (72.76 → 82.11 on GSM8K) isolates the SFT contribution but doesn’t match budgets either.

Related Posts

title: MemSkill: Learning and Evolving Memory Skills for Self-Evolving Agents
text:
Comparison between (a) prior turn-level handcrafted operations interleaved with LLM calls, and (b) MemSkill’s span-level skill-conditioned generation, where a controller selects a Top-\(K\) subset of skills from a shared skill bank and the LLM applies them in one pass. Figure 1 from the paper [1].
In MemSkill: Learning and Evolving Memory Skills for Self-Evolving Agents [1] (arXiv, February 2, 2026), Haozhen Zhang et al. (Nanyang Technological University, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, University of Illinois Chicago, and Tsinghua University) reframe LLM-agent memory operations as a learnable, evolving skill bank. An RL-trained controller selects skills for the current span — a contiguous segment of the interaction trace, typically covering multiple turns, that the executor consumes as input to a single LLM call. An LLM designer then periodically rewrites the bank from hard training cases.

title: MemSkill: Learning and Evolving Memory Skills for Self-Evolving Agents
text:
Methods

Two banks anchor the system, with three components alternating around them.

Skill bank — a shared, slowly evolving library of memory skills: structured templates, each with a short description, a “when to use” condition, a “how to apply” procedure, and constraints. The executor consumes a selected subset as guidance for one LLM call over a text span. It starts from four primitives (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, SKIP) and grows as training proceeds.
Memory bank — per-trace: the running set of extracted memories the executor accumulates and rewrites for a single interaction. Updated every span.

The controller (a lightweight multilayer perceptron over a shared encoder) scores each skill in the current skill bank by dot-product between a state embedding \(h_t = f_{ctx}(x_t, M_t)\) and a per-skill embedding \(u_i = f_{skill}(\text{desc}(s_i))\), then selects an ordered Top-\(K\) set without replacement. Here \(x_t\) is the current span, \(M_t\) the memories retrieved from the trace’s memory bank, \(\text{desc}(s_i)\) the natural-language description of skill \(s_i\) in the skill bank, and \(f_{ctx}\), \(f_{skill}\) are the two heads sharing an encoder backbone.
The executor (a frozen LLM) applies the selected skills in one pass to update the trace’s memory bank.
The designer (also a frozen LLM) periodically mines a sliding hard-case buffer, clusters the failures, and proposes refinements to existing skills or new skills — edits that land in the skill bank, not the memory bank.
Controller training:

Algorithm. PPO [2] with downstream task reward (F1, success rate, etc.) as the optimization signal.
Top-\(K\) sampling. Selecting an ordered Top-\(K\) set without replacement factorizes the joint log-probability via the standard sequential rule, so PPO can score the whole subset selection.
Rollback on regression. Snapshots roll back if a skill-bank update degrades training reward, so a bad designer edit can’t poison the policy.
Exploration bias. After each evolution step, exploration is briefly biased toward newly introduced skills, giving them a fair chance at being selected before low scores filter them out.





MemSkill architecture: the controller selects a Top-\(K\) skill subset from the shared skill bank conditioned on the current span and memories retrieved from the trace’s memory bank; the executor applies them in one LLM call to update that memory bank. Task reward optimizes the controller, while query-centric failures feed a sliding hard-case buffer that the designer periodically uses to refine and propose skills (edits that land in the skill bank). Figure 2 from the paper [1].

title: MemSkill: Learning and Evolving Memory Skills for Self-Evolving Agents
text:
Results

Setup. Four benchmarks — LoCoMo [3] and LongMemEval [4] for conversational memory, ALFWorld [5] for embodied tasks, and HotpotQA [6] for cross-distribution skill transfer. Two base LLMs: LLaMA-3.3-70B-Instruct and Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Instruct. MemSkill is trained only on LLaMA; Qwen and LongMemEval results are zero-shot transfers of the learned skill bank.
Main comparison (Table 1 below). Across the two base-model blocks, MemSkill leads every benchmark; ▲ marks settings evaluated by pure transfer (no training on that base model or dataset), and bold marks the best score within each block.

LLaMA block: LLM-judge average 55.19 against the strongest baseline at 42.23 (A-MEM), with ALFWorld success rates of 47.86 / 47.01 on seen / unseen splits versus 40.71 / 38.06 for the runners-up. (LLM-judge: a separate LLM scores each predicted answer against the gold answer for semantic match — the headline metric for open-ended conversational QA, where token-level F1 misses semantic equivalence.)
Qwen transfer (zero-shot): ALFWorld 60.00 / 64.18 success rates without any retraining, against ~57 / 54 for CoN.





Table 1 from the paper [1].



Component ablations (Table 2 below). On LoCoMo (LLM-judge), removing the controller drops LLaMA from 50.96 to 45.86 and Qwen from 52.07 to 41.24; removing the designer drops them to 44.11 and 34.71. The Qwen gap is bigger, suggesting the evolved skill bank carries most of the cross-model transfer benefit; the controller policy alone doesn’t transfer as well.




Table 2 from the paper [1].



Distribution-shift transfer (Figure 3 below). The LoCoMo-trained skill bank is ported to long-document QA on HotpotQA at three concatenation budgets — no HotpotQA-specific training; the controller scores from the LoCoMo-trained bank with \(K\) varied at test time. MemSkill at \(K=7\) holds the lead at every budget, but the gap to lower \(K\) widens as documents pile up — at 200 docs, \(K=7\) scores 66.80 while \(K=3\) drops to 58.20.




Figure 3 from the paper [1].

title: MemSkill: Learning and Evolving Memory Skills for Self-Evolving Agents
text:
My Notes

Operator-level evolution. The closest learning-based siblings, Memory-R1 [7] and Mem-α [8], both RL-train memory management against downstream task signals, but with a fixed primitive set (add/update/delete/skip and friends). MemSkill’s contribution is that the skill bank itself is learnable: the four primitives (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, SKIP) serve as starter templates rather than a frozen action set. The designer can refine those starting templates and add brand-new skills written from scratch as natural-language templates for failure modes the bank doesn’t yet cover. The controller adapts because skills are scored by description-embedding rather than a fixed action head. The cross-model transfer ablation supports the reading: most of the Qwen-side gain (52.07 → 34.71 without designer) comes from the evolved bank rather than the controller policy.
The “skill” abstraction here is not a callable. In the Anthropic Skills sense, a skill is a packaged routine the agent invokes with explicit arguments and a return value; the API/Tool/Skill ladder treats it as the layer where judgment and sequencing live. MemSkill’s “skills” don’t take per-skill arguments. They all share the same implicit context (the current span and retrieved memories), and the executor combines the selected \(K\) as joint guidance for a single LLM call. They’re closer to selection priors and prompt fragments than to callable routines. The gains here come from learning over a discrete library of prompt fragments under shared context, rather than from a calling protocol.
LLM-as-designer is a recurring outer-loop pattern. The closed-loop alternation between (a) RL-training a learner and (b) using a frozen LLM to rewrite the design space from clustered failure cases is the same recipe as ADAS [9] for agent scaffolds and AlphaEvolve [10] for algorithms. MemSkill is the operator-level instance of that pattern. By the framework in Truly Self-Improving Agents Require Intrinsic Metacognitive Learning, this is still extrinsic metacognition: the loop’s structure (when to evolve, how to cluster, what counts as a hard case) is human-defined, and only the operators inside it adapt. A genuine intrinsic version would let the agent decide when its skill bank needs rewriting, instead of running on a fixed schedule.
“Self-evolving” overstates test-time behavior. Both the controller and the skill bank are trained offline and frozen at deployment; only the per-trace memory content updates online during interaction. The evolution described in the title refers to a training-phase alternation between controller updates and designer rewrites, rather than test-time adaptation.
Memory items aren’t shown directly. The paper describes the memory bank abstractly as \(M_t\) (up to 20 retrieved per span via Contriever, so text-based) but never includes a worked example of an actual stored item. The shape has to be reverse-engineered from the skill case studies in Appendix B: dialogue skills produce short factual sentences (“who did what, where, when”), while ALFWorld skills produce structured tuples like (action, constraint) or (object, location, state). Each skill writes items in its own shape, so the bank ends up as a heterogeneous text store with no central schema. The framing of “evolving memory operations” is harder to picture concretely without seeing what those operations produce. Figure 4’s case study (below) shows evolved skills rather than the memory bank they generate.




Figure 4 from the paper [1].



Skill transfer has a budget-sensitive ceiling. HotpotQA complicates the generalization story: the LoCoMo-trained bank does port to long-document QA, but the gap between \(K=7\) and \(K=3\) widens sharply at 200 docs (66.80 vs 58.20). At 50 and 100 docs the two are within ~3 points, while the dialogue benchmarks were fine at \(K=3\). Skills evolved on dialogue traces don’t cover long-document QA well at low \(K\). At 200 docs concatenated, you need to fire a larger fraction of the bank to find enough applicable skills. The “reusable skills” claim is more conditional than the headline reads: portable when the inference-time budget matches, less so under shift.

title: [Q&A] Self-Correction After the Reasoning-Model Era
text:
This is a follow-up to a 3-paper arc on self-correction in LLMs that walks through Self-Refine, Cannot-Self-Correct, and Reflexion. On Mastodon, Professor Peter Bloem (Learning & Reasoning Group, Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam) asked:
Yes: all three papers in the original arc predate the reasoning-model era. None of them are evaluated on o1, DeepSeek-R1 [1] [1], or any model whose self-correcting behavior was shaped by RL on verifiable rewards. The implicit question is whether the arc’s conclusions still hold once that training signal enters the picture.

title: [Q&A] Self-Correction After the Reasoning-Model Era
text:
Internalizing the Evaluator
Reasoning-model training moves what used to be inference-time external scaffolding into training-time signal that the policy internalizes.
R1’s “aha moments” are emergent self-correction at inference time, with no Evaluator in the loop. The Reflexion-style Evaluator that used to gate self-correction at every inference step has been compiled into the weights. Whether R1 technically aligns with Cannot-Self-Correct’s strict definition becomes a definitional argument that misses what is actually new.
Even before R1, SCoRe showed one way to build this internalization deliberately. It trains on a two-turn structure where each attempt is rewarded against a ground-truth answer. The verifier’s correctness check is exactly the external signal Reflexion put in the loop, just moved from inference time to training time. SCoRe says “no teacher model and no oracle feedback,” but that refers to narrower things (no separate teacher LLM and no step-level oracle), and does not change the picture: the outcome reward is still external. R1 then demonstrated the same idea at a coarser grain, with the self-correction emerging within a single long reasoning trace rather than across explicit turns.

title: [Q&A] Self-Correction After the Reasoning-Model Era
section: How far can it go, and is internalization the right path?
text:
How far can it go, and is internalization the right path?
The substantive question is how far this internalization can go. Can any external verifier or evaluator that worked at inference time be moved into training-time signal that produces the same behavior at inference?
Or are there structural limits — task families where verifiable rewards cannot reach (long-form writing, open-ended dialogue, novel domains), evaluators that resist internalization because they require open-ended judgment that itself drifts? Early evidence [2][3] is that internalization works well within the verifiable-reward distribution and degrades sharply outside it, but we do not yet have a clean characterization of the boundary.
A separate question is whether internalization is the right path even where it works. Training is expensive, and pushing more verifiers into the policy carries the usual risks of catastrophic forgetting and capacity trade-offs against other tasks. Even within the regions where internalization works in principle, the practical question is what is worth pushing into the weights, and what is better kept as a domain-specific external verifier called at inference time.
I suspect domain-specific external verification stays essential even where internalization works in principle. An inference-time scaffold can be swapped, audited, or updated when the domain shifts. An internalized one cannot, short of retraining the model. That asymmetry alone argues for keeping the verifier external in any setting where the verification target itself moves.

title: [Q&A] Self-Correction After the Reasoning-Model Era
section: What the original arc still teaches
text:
What the original arc still teaches
Viewed through this lens, the three papers in the original arc still illuminate what is important for instilling self-correction in a model. Self-Refine showed that prompt-only intrinsic feedback does not reliably work. Cannot-Self-Correct showed why — without an external signal about correctness, the model’s confidence carries the initial answer through into the revision and the loop drifts. Reflexion showed that gating self-correction on a reliable external signal works. Whether that gate sits at inference time, the way Reflexion put it, or at training time, the way RL on verifiable rewards puts it, the structural ingredient is the same: reliable external signal. The original arc identified the ingredient; the post-2024 work shows it can be compiled into the weights for some classes of problems and not others.

title: [Q&A] Self-Correction After the Reasoning-Model Era
text:
Related recent work
Several recent papers approach the internalization question from different angles. The list below is partial — pointers to other work along these lines (especially generalization audits of o1/R1-style models or post-2024 process-reward-model successors) are welcome.

Cognitive Behaviors that Enable Self-Improving Reasoners [4] [4] looks at what RL training actually internalizes — which trained behaviors let the policy self-improve. The answer is a small set: verification, backtracking, subgoal-setting, and backward chaining. It is the empirical follow-up to “what is actually in the policy” after RL.
How Reasoning Evolves from Post-Training Data: An Empirical Study Using Chess [5] [5] (ICML 2026) extends that question into how far internalized reasoning carries. Using chess as a clean probe outside the math/code distribution most reasoning models are trained on, it tracks which capabilities transfer from post-training data and which decay.
Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters [6] [6] tightens our understanding of when inference-time scaffolding is worth the compute. Revision helps when the verifier is reliable and helps less when it is not, and a small verifier-guided model can outperform a larger one without scaffolding. The same verifier-quality dependence shows up whether the scaffolding is at inference time or compiled into the weights.
The Stechly–Kambhampati line is the running argument for limits. On the Self-Verification Limitations of LLMs on Reasoning and Planning Tasks [2] [2] shows that GPT-4 still cannot reliably verify its own outputs even on simple planning tasks, and Chain of Thoughtlessness? [3] [3] (NeurIPS 2024) questions whether chain-of-thought reasoning generalizes outside its training distribution. Both push back on the idea that internalization is general: outside the training distribution, the policy’s self-judgment falls apart.
Chain-of-Thought Degrades Visual Spatial Reasoning Capabilities of Multimodal LLMs [7] [7] extends that skepticism into the multimodal era. Across 17 models and 13 spatial benchmarks, CoT prompting consistently degrades visual-spatial accuracy, with shortcut-learning from textual priors that hallucinate visual details when the image is absent. Reasoning trained on text does not transfer cleanly to vision.
Can Large Language Models Self-Correct in Medical Question Answering? An Exploratory Study [8] [8] audits self-correction in a non-verifiable-reward domain. Self-reflective prompting on MedQA, HeadQA, and PubMedQA does not consistently improve accuracy, with effects highly dataset- and model-dependent. A direct datapoint for the boundary where internalization stops paying.
Self-Rewarding Language Models [9] [9] (ICML 2024) tests whether internalization can happen without any external verifier at all. The model acts as its own LLM-as-judge during DPO training, bootstrapping. Promising results on AlpacaEval, but the approach inherits the question of whether the model’s own judgment is good enough to bootstrap from in the first place.
