title: Large Language Models Are Human-Level Prompt Engineers (APE)
text:
Figure 1 from the paper [1].
In Large Language Models Are Human-Level Prompt Engineers [1] (ICLR 2023), Zhou et al. (University of Toronto, Vector Institute, University of Waterloo) propose Automatic Prompt Engineer (APE), a black-box search that uses one large language model (LLM) to write candidate natural-language instructions for a task, then selects the best via the zero-shot performance of a second LLM.

title: Large Language Models Are Human-Level Prompt Engineers (APE)
text:
Methods
APE casts instruction design as a program-synthesis problem over natural-language programs. Given a small set of input-output demonstrations:

Propose. A proposer LLM generates candidate instructions in one of two ways:

Forward generation — “here are examples, write the instruction.”
Reverse infilling — the proposer fills in an <INSERT> slot placed between inputs and outputs.

Forward mode is the default and works on any pretrained LLM, but constrains the instruction to sit at the end of the prompt. Reverse mode requires a proposer with infilling capability (e.g., T5, GLM, InsertGPT, or InstructGPT’s <INSERT> token) and lets the instruction be placed mid-prompt, which the authors find more flexible. The paper uses forward mode for the Instruction Induction experiments and reverse mode for BIG-Bench. The choice is the user’s, not an algorithmic gate inside APE.
Score. Each candidate is run through an executor LLM on a held-out set; the score is task accuracy or log-probability of the correct output.
(Optional) resample. Monte Carlo resampling asks the proposer to generate semantically similar variants of the best candidates and re-scores them.
Select. The instruction with the highest score wins.

No fine-tuning is involved and the method treats both the proposer and the executor as black boxes.

title: Large Language Models Are Human-Level Prompt Engineers (APE)
text:
Results
The paper evaluates APE on the 24 NLP tasks from the Instruction Induction [2] benchmark [2], plus the BIG-Bench Instruction Induction subset and TruthfulQA [3]. It compares three sources of instructions:

APE — the full propose-score-select pipeline.
Greedy — Honovich et al.’s [2] prior algorithm, which takes the proposer’s first sample without any selection step.
Human — gold annotations written by the original Instruction Induction annotators.

With InstructGPT (175B) as both proposer and executor, APE reaches an interquartile mean of 0.810 across the 24 Instruction Induction tasks versus 0.749 for human-engineered prompts (Figure 1b), and achieves zero-shot accuracy at or above the human bar on all 24 of 24 individual tasks while the Greedy baseline trails on most (Figure 4). On the BIG-Bench Instruction Induction subset, APE matches or beats humans on 17 of 21 curated tasks. On TruthfulQA, APE-generated prompts steer the model toward truthful or informative outputs on demand, beating the human “help” prompt with 200 candidate proposals. Prepending APE prompts to few-shot in-context learning prompts also improves downstream performance on 21 of 24 tasks.



Figure 4 from the paper [1].

title: Large Language Models Are Human-Level Prompt Engineers (APE)
text:
My Notes

A benchmark designed to favor short prompts. The 24-of-24 headline comes from Instruction Induction [2] tasks (singularize, translate, capitalize, etc.), which are short, template-shaped tasks where human prompt writers have little advantage. A crisp one-sentence instruction is close to the Bayes-optimal prompt, and LLMs can generate dozens of paraphrases of “output the plural form” cheaply. The result does not transfer to tasks where the useful prompt is paragraphs long, contains domain-specific scaffolding, or requires carefully chosen few-shot demonstrations. Later optimizers like MIPROv2 [4] [4]  and GEPA [5] target that harder regime.
Reverse infilling, the transferable idea. Forward generation (“here are examples, write the instruction”) forces the instruction to be predicted at the end of the prompt, which is rarely where instructions naturally sit. The reverse infilling prompt, which feeds inputs on the left and outputs on the right and asks the model to fill in the instruction between them, lets the instruction be placed mid-prompt where it more naturally belongs. This matches what T5-style span corruption [6] [6] showed about bidirectional objectives years earlier, and it sits in the same family as the prompt-repetition trick for recovering bidirectional context inside a causal LM. Both are runtime workarounds for the fact that left-to-right generation can’t condition on what comes after the token being predicted.
Scoring dominates the compute budget. APE’s compute is spent evaluating candidates on a held-out set with the executor LLM, not generating candidates with the proposer. The Monte Carlo resampling step, the only part of APE that resembles iterative optimization, does not add much over the base proposer pool for most tasks. The subsequent line of work (MIPROv2 [4] [4]  Bayesian surrogate, GEPA [5] reflective mutation, Promptbreeder [7] evolutionary operators) all attack this scoring bottleneck with different mechanisms.
The thin human baseline. The “human” prompts in the benchmark are typically one-sentence instructions written by a small number of annotators under Honovich et al.’s protocol [2], not prompts tuned by expert prompt engineers with access to the executor’s failure modes. The paper’s headline claim is more accurately read as “APE matches a single-shot human annotator on short template tasks.” The gap to genuine prompt-engineering expertise on open-ended tasks is a separate question the paper does not answer.

title: GEPA: Reflective Prompt Evolution Can Outperform Reinforcement Learning
text:
Figure 3 from the paper [1].
In GEPA: Reflective Prompt Evolution Can Outperform Reinforcement Learning [1] (ICLR 2026 Oral), Lakshya A. Agrawal (UC Berkeley), Matei Zaharia (UC Berkeley / Databricks), Omar Khattab (MIT), and 14 co-authors across UC Berkeley, Stanford, Notre Dame, BespokeLabs.ai, Databricks, and MIT argue that natural-language reflection on sampled trajectories is a richer learning signal than scalar rewards, and introduce GEPA (Genetic-Pareto), a prompt optimizer that outperforms Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) [2] while using far fewer rollouts.

title: GEPA: Reflective Prompt Evolution Can Outperform Reinforcement Learning
text:
Methods
A compound AI system, in the paper’s (and DSPy’s) vocabulary, is a pipeline of one or more LLM-invoked modules — each a distinct prompted call (e.g., a first-hop query generator, a second-hop query generator, an answer generator in a multi-hop QA pipeline) — potentially interleaved with tool calls. Each module has its own prompt, which GEPA can optimize independently.
GEPA treats each prompt in a compound AI system as a gene and maintains a pool of candidate programs. At each iteration (Figure 3), GEPA proposes a new candidate using one of two genetic operators — a single-parent mutation or a two-parent crossover — and evaluates it on a minibatch. If the minibatch score improves over the parent, the candidate is promoted to evaluation on the full training set and added to the pool. The default operator is reflective mutation; crossover (Merge) fires opportunistically when the pool contains two candidates that share a common ancestor, have optimized disjoint sets of prompts, are both Pareto-optimal, and both beat the ancestor in aggregate — with a hard cap of five merges per run.
The two operators are:

Reflective Prompt Mutation samples trajectories from one candidate — reasoning, tool calls, and tool outputs — and feeds them to a reflector LM that writes a natural-language diagnosis of what went wrong and proposes an edited prompt for a single module. Figure 5 traces this on PUPA [3] — a benchmark for privacy-conscious delegation, where a trusted local model must answer user queries containing personally identifiable information (PII) using an untrusted API model as a helper, without leaking PII. Starting from a short base instruction (“Create a privacy-preserving request for a powerful external LLM that can assist without learning private information about the user.”), each successful child adds a concrete nuance the reflector extracted from a failure — expanded privacy strategies, explicit PII categories and generalizations, structured output and domain best-practices, then a detailed transformation rationale, ending at a strict exhaustive protocol that bans partial redaction and demands auditable zero-leakage. The prompt accumulates lessons rather than being rewritten wholesale. In the figure below, red arrows mark the promoted lineage from candidate 0 to the best candidate (11), with scores in parentheses.




Figure 5 from the paper [1].



System-Aware Merge takes two qualifying descendants of a common ancestor and assembles a child module-by-module. For each module, if one descendant changed the ancestor’s prompt and the other left it untouched, the child inherits the changed version; if both descendants changed it, the child inherits from the higher-scoring parent (ties broken randomly); if neither changed it, it stays at the ancestor’s version. No LLM call is made — the whole step is a textual combine over existing prompts, which is why the paper calls it system-aware crossover rather than a mutation. Merge works only when the two parents have explored disjoint modules, so complementary improvements can compose without stepping on each other.

Parent selection is Pareto-based rather than greedy. Instead of always mutating the best-scoring candidate, GEPA maintains a per-task score matrix over its history and samples parents from the Pareto frontier — the set of candidates that no other candidate beats on every task — which prevents a locally strong candidate from dominating the search. The paper reports two named variants, “GEPA” using reflective mutation only and “GEPA+Merge” using both mutation and merge; both share the Pareto-based selector and the minibatch-then-full-set gate. The optimizer is agnostic to the downstream task: it needs a trajectory sampler, a metric, and a reflector LM.

title: GEPA: Reflective Prompt Evolution Can Outperform Reinforcement Learning
text:
Results
Six tasks — HotpotQA [4], HoVer [5], IFBench [6], PUPA [3], AIME-2025 [7], and LiveBench-Math [8] — using GPT-4.1 Mini and Qwen3-8B as task models.

Qwen3-8B: GEPA beats GRPO on five of the six benchmarks, losing only on AIME-2025. IFBench makes the gap sharp — GEPA reaches 38.61% after 678 rollouts, above GRPO’s 35.88% at 24,000. Averaged across the six tasks, GEPA is +6% over GRPO and up to +20% on the best task, with up to \(35\times\) fewer rollouts (trajectories sampled from the current policy during training). GEPA+Merge is less reliable here: it also trails GRPO on IFBench and PUPA, which the paper attributes to Merge’s hyperparameters being tuned for GPT-4.1 Mini rather than Qwen3-8B.
GPT-4.1 Mini: GEPA is evaluated as a drop-in prompt optimizer against MIPROv2 [9] in two settings (instruction-only “MIPROv2-No-Demos” and joint instruction-plus-few-shot “MIPROv2”), Trace [10] with its OptoPrime optimizer, and TextGrad [11] . GEPA wins on every benchmark, with margins as wide as 11% (HotpotQA, PUPA). The abstract highlights +12% on AIME-2025. A GEPA-Qwen-Opt variant optimized entirely on Qwen3-8B gets +9% when run on GPT-4.1 Mini without modification, outperforming every baseline that was optimized directly on GPT-4.1 Mini.

Beyond benchmarks, the paper reports GEPA as a promising inference-time search strategy for CUDA kernel optimization, iteratively improving kernels against a PyTorch-eager baseline.



Tables 1 and 2 from the paper [1]: benchmark results on Qwen3-8B (top) and GPT-4.1 Mini (bottom).

title: GEPA: Reflective Prompt Evolution Can Outperform Reinforcement Learning
text:
My Notes

Reflection beats policy gradients: GRPO wastes signal already present in each trajectory, in three ways.

Information content: GRPO consumes a trajectory as a single scalar reward (normalized against the group’s own mean and standard deviation, the “Group Relative” that replaces PPO’s learned critic), throwing away which tool call was wrong, which instruction was ambiguous, which demonstration misled the model. A reflector LM reading the same trajectory can name all three and edit the one prompt that caused the failure.
Variance: because each rollout contributes one noisy scalar, GRPO needs thousands of rollouts before the gradient estimate stabilizes. A natural-language critique encodes structured per-module diagnosis, so one rollout already yields usable signal.
Credit assignment: GRPO’s policy-gradient update spreads the scalar reward across every token of every module in the rollout, even when only one module was responsible. Reflection attributes the failure to a single module and leaves the rest alone.
The same pattern shows up in Self-Refine and Reflexion, where verbal feedback outperforms scalar reward at comparable compute. GEPA is the first paper I have seen that posts the head-to-head against GRPO on matched tasks.

The Pareto-frontier selector is the generalizable part: Sampling mutation parents from the Pareto frontier rather than argmax prevents collapse to a single best candidate, which is the same mode-collapse problem that shows up in evolutionary prompt search and RL fine-tuning. The mechanism is general enough to drop into any iterative search where candidates have multi-dimensional scores (accuracy vs. cost, or task A vs. task B), and I expect to see it reused well past prompt optimization.
Beating MIPROv2 without Bayesian optimization: This is a substantive methodological claim. MIPROv2 [9]  spends its budget on a Bayesian surrogate over instruction and demonstration hyperparameters. GEPA discards the surrogate and spends the same budget on reflective rewrites plus merge. The result suggests the Bayesian model in MIPROv2 was under-using the trajectory information MIPROv2 already had access to, and the proposer was not reading the failures carefully enough. Several authors overlap between the two papers, so the comparison is a within-lab course-correction rather than an external critique.
The paper doesn’t say what reflector it used: Appendix E.2 lists Qwen3-8B and GPT-4.1 Mini as the task models but never specifies the reflection LM. The gepa-ai/gepa repo quickstart pairs GPT-5 as reflector with GPT-4.1 Mini as task, a stronger model reading a weaker one’s trajectories. Without the reflector spec or an ablation, we can’t tell whether GEPA corroborates or contradicts the just-ask calibration [12]  and uncertainty-quantification findings that single-model self-evaluation is unreliable.

title: Training Language Models to Self-Correct via Reinforcement Learning (SCoRe)
text:
Figure 1 from the paper: Left, SCoRe lifts Gemini 1.5 Flash on MATH by +4.4% over direct generation at the second turn, while the base model loses 11.2% and standard fine-tuning is near-flat. Right, spending inference compute on sequential self-correction beats parallel sampling at matched budgets. Figure from the paper [1].
In Training Language Models to Self-Correct via Reinforcement Learning [1] (ICLR 2025 Oral; arXiv preprint September 2024), Aviral Kumar, Vincent Zhuang, Rishabh Agarwal, Yi Su, and 14 co-authors at Google DeepMind train a single model to revise its own answers using only self-generated data, with no teacher model and no oracle feedback.

title: Training Language Models to Self-Correct via Reinforcement Learning (SCoRe)
text:
Methods

Problem setting



Figure 3 from the paper: the problem setting. Standard training (left) optimizes the loss on a single response \(y\) given prompt \(x\). SCoRe (right) instead rolls out two turns — a first attempt \(y_1\), then an improved response \(y_2\) conditioned on \((x, y_1)\) and an optional external instruction \(p\) to self-correct — and places the loss on the second attempt. The training objective is the quality of the final answer, not the first one. Figure from the paper [1].


This change in problem setup matters because it changes what the model is incentivized to do. A one-turn model trained to minimize loss on \(y\) learns to commit to its best guess. A two-turn model trained to minimize loss on \(y_2\) is free to produce an exploratory first attempt and use the second turn to fix it, as long as the training signal actually rewards that behavior. That training-signal design is the problem the rest of the paper solves.
Formally, the paper states the training objective as Equation 1:
\[\max_{\pi_\theta} \; \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}^* \sim \mathcal{D}, \; \hat{\mathbf{y}}_{1:l+1} \sim \pi_\theta(\cdot \mid [\mathbf{x}, \hat{\mathbf{y}}_{1:l}, p_{1:l}])} \left[\sum_{i=1}^{l+1} \hat{r}(\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i, \mathbf{y}^*)\right] \tag{1}\]
where \(\pi_\theta\) is the policy (the LLM) with parameters \(\theta\), \(\mathbf{x}\) is the input prompt drawn with its ground-truth answer \(\mathbf{y}^*\) from dataset \(\mathcal{D}\), \(\hat{\mathbf{y}}_i\) is the model’s attempt at turn \(i\) conditioned on all prior attempts and optional external inputs \(p_{1:l}\) (e.g., an instruction to “try again”), and \(\hat{r}\) is the verifier’s correctness reward. The paper sets \(l = 1\), giving two turns and rewarding the sum \(\hat{r}(\hat{\mathbf{y}}_1, \mathbf{y}^*) + \hat{r}(\hat{\mathbf{y}}_2, \mathbf{y}^*)\).
Two subtleties: first, unlike single-turn SFT or RLHF — which directly supervise the policy to produce \(\mathbf{y}^*\) — Equation 1 supervises each turn only indirectly, through its contribution to the sum. Second, summing the per-turn rewards means the idealized objective pays equally for a correct first attempt and a correct second attempt. The paper later argues this is exactly why naive RL on Equation 1 behavior-collapses: the policy finds it easier to maximize the sum by producing the best possible \(\hat{\mathbf{y}}_1\) and echoing it as \(\hat{\mathbf{y}}_2\) than by learning genuine revision. SCoRe’s Stage I regularization and Stage II progress bonus are then introduced as modifications that break this degenerate solution.


The two-stage recipe
The method is a two-stage multi-turn online Reinforcement Learning (RL) recipe. Figure 7 sketches the overall approach:



Figure 7 from the paper: an overview of SCoRe. Stage I (left) trains an initialization for self-correction — instead of running SFT (which produces pathological amplification of biases), the policy is constrained via KL penalty to keep the first attempt \(y_1\) close to the base model while maximizing reward at the second attempt \(y_2\), so that the two turns are decoupled. Stage II (right) jointly optimizes both attempts with multi-turn RL, where the second-turn reward is augmented by a shaped bonus that explicitly pays for correctness gains from \(y_1\) to \(y_2\), incentivizing genuine self-correction rather than the trivial strategy of producing the best possible first response and echoing it. Figure from the paper [1].


Stage I optimizes only the second-turn reward while holding the first-turn policy close to the base model via a strict KL penalty:
\[\max_{\pi_\theta} \; \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}_1,\, \mathbf{y}_1 \sim \pi_\theta(\cdot \mid \mathbf{x}),\, \mathbf{y}_2 \sim \pi_\theta(\cdot \mid [\mathbf{x}_1, p_1])} \left[\hat{r}(\mathbf{y}_2, \mathbf{y}^*) \;-\; \beta_2 \, D_{KL}\!\left(\pi_\theta(\cdot \mid \mathbf{x}_1) \,\|\, \pi_{\text{ref}}(\cdot \mid \mathbf{x}_1)\right)\right] \tag{3}\]
Here \(\beta_2\) is a large KL coefficient that applies only to the first attempt, preventing the policy from collapsing the two attempts into a single distribution. The result is an initialization where \(\mathbf{y}_1\) remains base-model-like — so any gain at \(\mathbf{y}_2\) must come from real revision — while the revision head has started to learn what useful corrections look like. This blocks the dominant failure mode of naive RL on this task, which the paper calls behavior collapse: the model learns to produce a near-optimal first answer and then make no meaningful second-turn revision.
Stage II then jointly optimizes both turns with standard multi-turn RL, initialized from Stage I:
\[\max_{\pi_\theta} \; \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}_1,\, \mathbf{y}_1 \sim \pi_\theta(\cdot \mid \mathbf{x}),\, \mathbf{y}_2 \sim \pi_\theta(\cdot \mid [\mathbf{x}_1, p_1])} \left[\sum_{i=1}^{2} \hat{r}(\mathbf{y}_i, \mathbf{y}^*) \;-\; \beta_1 \, D_{KL}\!\left(\pi_\theta(\cdot \mid \mathbf{x}_i) \,\|\, \pi_{\text{ref}}(\cdot \mid \mathbf{x}_i)\right)\right] \tag{4}\]
Equation 4 on its own would still permit behavior collapse: the policy can maximize the sum by producing the best possible \(\hat{\mathbf{y}}_1\) and echoing it as \(\hat{\mathbf{y}}_2\). SCoRe prevents this by adding a progress bonus to the second-turn reward:
\[b(\mathbf{y}_2 \mid \mathbf{y}_1, \mathbf{y}^*) \;:=\; \alpha \cdot \left(\hat{r}(\mathbf{y}_2, \mathbf{y}^*) - \hat{r}(\mathbf{y}_1, \mathbf{y}^*)\right), \qquad \alpha > 1\]
The bonus is positive only when the second attempt flips an incorrect response to correct, and sharply negative when it corrupts a correct response into an incorrect one. Revisions that make progress get more reward than revisions that preserve an already-correct answer, biasing the policy toward genuine self-correction.


Why SFT baselines fall short
Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) on model-generated correction traces is shown to fail for a separate reason: distribution shift between the mistakes in the off-policy data and the mistakes the trained model actually makes at test time.



Table 1 from the paper: self-correction performance after training on \(\mathcal{D}_{\text{StaR}}\) and \(\mathcal{D}_{\text{SFT}}\). The gap between the second and first attempts Δ(t1, t2) is either negative or small across all SFT/STaR variants, and both approaches erroneously modify correct responses to incorrect at high rates (high \(\Delta^{c \to \neg c}\), low \(\Delta^{\neg c \to c}\)). Table from the paper [1].

title: Training Language Models to Self-Correct via Reinforcement Learning (SCoRe)
text:
Results
On MATH [2] with Gemini 1.5 Flash, the base model loses 11.2% at the second turn (intrinsic self-correction is net negative), SFT and STaR [3] are near-zero gain, and SCoRe gains +4.4%. The top-line 15.6-point gain on MATH and 9.1-point gain on HumanEval [4] are reported as improvements in the self-correction delta Δ(t1, t2) relative to the base model’s Δ(t1, t2). At matched inference-sample budgets, sequential self-correction with SCoRe outperforms parallel sampling under self-consistency up to \(K = 2^5 = 32\) samples.



Table 2 from the paper: performance of SCoRe on MATH. SCoRe not only attains a higher accuracy at both attempts, but also provides the most positive self-correction performance Δ(t1, t2). Table from the paper [1].





Table 3 from the paper: performance of SCoRe on HumanEval. SCoRe attains the highest self-correction performance (Accuracy@t2, Δ(t1, t2)), and also outperforms other methods at offline correction (MBPP-R). Table from the paper [1].

title: Training Language Models to Self-Correct via Reinforcement Learning (SCoRe)
text:
My Notes

The SFT failure here is teacher-forcing exposure bias, one level up. Teacher forcing mismatches at the token level: training feeds the gold previous token as input, inference feeds the model’s own previous token. SCoRe’s offline SFT mismatches at the turn level: training’s “first answer” is a frozen sample from the data-collection policy, inference’s “first answer” comes from an updated model whose error distribution has drifted. Same structural problem one level up. The remedies parallel too. Scheduled sampling [5] and DAgger [6] feed the model’s own predictions back into the training loop. SCoRe uses online multi-turn RL to re-sample traces from the current policy each step. The principle is “put the model’s own distribution inside the training loop,” and any self-correction recipe that stops at offline SFT reproduces the exposure-bias pitfall at a coarser granularity.
Behavior collapse is not model collapse [7], but the remedies parallel. Shumailov et al.’s model-collapse result describes how recursive training on model-generated text erodes distribution tails across generations — finite-sample statistical error compounds into irreversible drift. SCoRe’s behavior collapse is a different pathology on a single training run: the policy converges to a degenerate solution where the second attempt echoes the first. Both failure modes arise from training on self-generated data without an external anchor. SCoRe’s defenses (a KL penalty against the base model in both stages, plus a ground-truth verifier reward) play the same structural role as the model-collapse literature’s call to keep real data in the loop: they tether the policy to a distribution the policy itself did not produce. The paper never describes the Stage I KL constraint as collapse insurance, but structurally that is what it is.
Sequential vs. parallel scaling is the practical implication. Figure 1 right shows that spending \(2^5 = 32\) samples on sequential self-correction beats the same budget spent on parallel independent samples under self-consistency. That shifts the usual test-time-compute scaling picture [8]: when the model can reliably fix its own mistakes, sequential samples dominate. Practitioners running agent loops will take this as evidence for investing in multi-turn policies rather than larger parallel fan-outs.
No PRMs here. Prior work on Let’s Verify Step by Step [9] and later step-level RL pipelines use process-reward models (PRMs) as a source of dense intra-step feedback. SCoRe instead uses only outcome reward plus a turn-level progress bonus, avoiding PRMs entirely. Whether PRM supervision would stack additively with SCoRe, or overlap with the same failure mode the progress bonus already addresses, remains open. Both mechanisms densify a sparse outcome signal, and the paper does not run the controlled comparison between a PRM-based recipe and SCoRe’s ORM+progress-bonus at matched compute.

title: Training Language Models to Self-Correct via Reinforcement Learning (SCoRe)
text:
Related Posts

Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet: the counterweight SCoRe answers — intrinsic self-correction degrades reasoning without external feedback, and SCoRe’s verifier reward is exactly the external signal that paper says is missing.
Let’s Verify Step by Step: the PRM lineage SCoRe declines to follow, densifying the outcome signal with a turn-level progress bonus instead of per-step process supervision.
[Q&A] Self-Correction After the Reasoning-Model Era: where a verifier-trained recipe like SCoRe lands once RL-on-verifiable-rewards reasoning models arrive.
Model Collapse and LLM-Contaminated Training Data: the recursion-on-self-generated-data failure SCoRe’s behavior collapse parallels, and the shared remedy of tethering training to a distribution the policy did not produce.

title: Let’s Verify Step by Step
text:
Figure 2 from the paper: two solutions to the same math problem graded step-by-step by the trained PRM. Green highlights mark high per-step correctness scores; red marks low. The left solution stays green throughout and reaches the correct answer; the right solution makes an error mid-derivation and the PRM flags the wrong step red. Figure from the paper [1].
In Let’s Verify Step by Step [1] (ICLR 2024; arXiv preprint May 2023), Hunter Lightman, Vineet Kosaraju, Yura Burda, Harri Edwards, Bowen Baker, Teddy Lee, Jan Leike, John Schulman, Ilya Sutskever, and Karl Cobbe at OpenAI argue that supervising every reasoning step — not just the final answer — produces substantially more reliable reward models for math.

title: Let’s Verify Step by Step
text:
Methods
The paper builds two reward models on top of a GPT-4 generator fine-tuned on a 1.5B-token math pretraining mix called MathMix:

Outcome-Supervised Reward Model (ORM). Trained only on a final-answer correctness label, following Cobbe et al.’s GSM8K [2] verifier recipe [2].
Process-Supervised Reward Model (PRM). Trained on a per-step positive/negative/neutral label, supplied by human labellers through a dedicated annotation interface and supervised only up to the first incorrect step. The PRM’s score for a whole solution is the product of step-level correctness probabilities; the cover image above shows Figure 2 of the paper, where two PRM-graded solutions make the per-step scoring visible — green for high-score steps, red for the wrong step the PRM catches.

To make human feedback go further, the authors use active learning: the current-best PRM selects “convincing wrong-answer” solutions (high-PRM-score but wrong-final-answer) to send to labellers, which concentrates annotation budget where the reward model is most confidently wrong. The resulting dataset, PRM800K, contains 800K step-level labels over 75K solutions to 12K problems from the MATH benchmark [3], and is released with the paper.

title: Let’s Verify Step by Step
text:
Results
The paper evaluates the PRM and ORM as solution re-rankers on the MATH test set:

On a 500-problem representative subset of the MATH test set, the large-scale PRM reaches 78.2% best-of-1860 accuracy — i.e. for each problem the generator draws 1860 candidate solutions and the PRM re-ranker picks one, which matches the gold answer 78.2% of the time — versus 72.4% for the ORM and 69.6% for majority voting. The PRM-over-ORM gap widens with larger N, consistent with the PRM being better at distinguishing subtly flawed solutions rather than just obviously wrong ones.
On a held-out out-of-distribution (OOD) test set of 224 STEM questions from AP Calculus, AP Chemistry, AP Physics, and AMC10/12, the PRM still leads at 72.9% aggregate vs. 63.8% ORM and 61.3% majority voting.
Surfacing “convincing wrong-answer” solutions to labellers via active learning delivers a 2.6× improvement in data efficiency for process supervision.
Small-scale ablations, where a large PRM acts as a synthetic labeller for smaller PRM training, isolate the supervision-type effect from the training-set-size confound that complicates the large-scale comparison.




A comparison of outcome-supervised and process-supervised reward models, evaluated by their ability to search over 1860 samples per test problem. Majority voting is shown as a strong baseline. For \(N \le 1000\), the shaded bands visualize variance across subsamples. The PRM-over-ORM gap widens with N. Figure 3 from the paper [1].

title: Let’s Verify Step by Step
text:
My Notes

This paper made PRMs the reasoning-RM default. Before this work, the closest comparison was Uesato et al.’s Solving Math Word Problems with Process- and Outcome-Based Feedback [4], which found process and outcome supervision were roughly equivalent on GSM8K. The gap here (larger model, more labels, harder benchmark) flipped the conclusion, and the 2024 reasoning-RL literature took PRM-over-ORM as a starting point even where it then walked it back. DeepSeek-R1 [5], notably, reports that it tried a PRM for its large-scale training and moved to rule-based outcome rewards after running into reward-hacking and scaling issues. Whether a PRM still adds value on top of rule-based rewards at frontier scale remains open.
Active learning on “convincing wrong answers” carries the data-efficiency story. Surfacing high-PRM-score-but-wrong-final-answer solutions for labelling delivers the 2.6× data-efficiency gain and is what makes 800K step-labels tractable at all; most follow-ups skip active learning and pay a linear data cost instead. A natural next step would be to test whether self-refine and verifier-guided search pipelines [6] see similar gains from explicit wrong-answer mining.
The practical picture lives at small N, not N=1860. The PRM-over-ORM gap shrinks at smaller N (visible in Figure 3 of the paper), and a PRM that wins handily at \(N=1860\) but only marginally at \(N=64\) has different deployment implications than the headline suggests. A clean PRM-vs-ORM comparison at fixed small N (say 8, 16, 64) with matched training-data scales would tell practitioners more than the top-line best-of-N number.
Process supervision’s alignment claims are left unmeasured. The paper gestures at better interpretability and less spurious reward, but the “convincing wrong-answer” mining strategy itself produces a distribution shift in the training set, since the PRM and ORM end up trained on systematically different solutions. A matched-distribution ablation, or a direct interpretability metric (e.g., how often human raters prefer PRM-selected solutions on unambiguous tie cases), would close both gaps.

title: Let’s Verify Step by Step
text:
Related Posts

Training Language Models to Self-Correct via Reinforcement Learning (SCoRe): a later reasoning-RL recipe that pointedly avoids PRMs, using only outcome reward plus a turn-level progress bonus, and reads as a direct counterpoint to the PRM-over-ORM result here.
AbstRaL: Augmenting LLMs’ Reasoning by Reinforcing Abstract Thinking: another RL-on-reasoning recipe that shapes the reward at a finer grain than final-answer correctness, here over abstraction faithfulness rather than per-step labels.
ReMA: Learning to Meta-think for LLMs with Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning: a different decomposition of reasoning supervision, splitting planner and executor instead of grading each step.
20 Seconds of Thinking, 100,000× More Data: the test-time-search backdrop the PRM serves, where a strong re-ranker over many sampled solutions is what turns extra inference compute into accuracy.

title: The Inference Shift
text:
Image from Stratechery.
Ben Thompson uses the Cerebras IPO as a hook to argue that what the industry has been calling “inference” is actually two workloads with very different hardware implications:
If agentic inference becomes the largest market by far because it scales with compute rather than with humans, Nvidia’s price advantage, earned on latency, gets less valuable exactly where the volume lives. China, which cannot buy the leading edge for training, already has everything it needs for agentic inference. Space data centers start to make sense too, because older, slower nodes tolerate radiation and dissipate less heat. Thompson ends by inverting his usual Huang-era stance: “Moore’s Law doesn’t matter, and that the way we get more compute is by realizing that the compute we have is already good enough.”

title: The Inference Shift
text:
My Notes

Premium hardware earns its premium on latency, and workloads where no human is waiting eventually migrate off it. Thompson is arguing that’s what’s about to happen to agentic inference.

Mainframes in the 1970s ran two workloads on the same expensive hardware: interactive timesharing (a human at a terminal is waiting, latency-sensitive, what the premium was really justified by) and batch jobs (no human is waiting, latency-tolerant, the premium going unused).
Machine-time cost collapsed by orders of magnitude over this period; human-time cost moved slowly by comparison. The end of the mainframe monopoly was driven by commodity compute getting cheaper on two fronts at once: batch workloads migrated to cheaper shared servers (minicomputer-class, then Unix workstations, then commodity x86 clusters), and interactive computing migrated to per-user PCs. Mainframes survived in domains where the premium is genuinely justified (banks, airlines, reservation systems), but they stopped being the volume market.
Thompson’s answer-inference vs. agentic-inference split is the same split on today’s GPU clusters. Answer inference is the interactive tier: a human is waiting, the latency premium is justified. Agentic inference is the batch tier: no human is waiting, latency is free, the GPU’s premium characteristics are going unused. Once agentic workloads are large enough, they migrate off the premium tier onto a commodity memory hierarchy, the way batch unbundled from the mainframe.
The mapping:

The prediction that falls out: Nvidia keeps the training-and-answer-inference premium (the pieces where human time is still on the clock) and cedes the volume market, the way IBM kept mainframes and ceded personal computing. Export-control arbitrage rhymes too: Cold-War restrictions on leading-edge systems stopped tracking the market once PC-class compute proliferated.

The memory hierarchy is where the economics moves the money. Thompson’s phrasing, “the memory hierarchy wrapped around a model,” describes agentic systems as mostly a storage-and-retrieval problem with a language model as one stage in the pipeline, rather than as “a GPU answering a question.” If he’s right about the economics, a lot of the investment that today goes into more HBM per card gets redirected down the hierarchy, into DRAM, SSDs, and the databases and stores that actually hold the agent’s state.
The 220,000 Nvidia GPUs Anthropic just contracted at Colossus 1 are the shape of the locked-in bet. That’s latency-first hardware on a decade-long depreciation schedule. Anthropic’s own announcement earmarks the capacity for Claude Pro and Max subscribers: a mix of answer inference and agent runs on the same clusters today. Thompson’s argument implies the agent portion of that mix will grow faster than the answer portion, and increasingly won’t need what the fleet is optimized for. Hyperscalers with similar high-end-GPU-dense fleets face the same exposure. A year of elevated Nvidia prices was always the smaller concern; the larger one is whether the fleet’s shape matches the workload mix for the next depreciation cycle.
Two prior posts are worth tying back here. In 2020 the open question around Huang’s Law was whether Nvidia’s exponential curve would democratize big models; Thompson is now arguing the interesting frontier may not sit on that curve at all. At a meta level the piece also echoes the mechanism in the 2028 Global Intelligence Crisis scenario: once humans stop being the anchor for how much compute can get used, the old “paid human time” ceiling disappears, whether the effect shows up as expanding agentic markets here or as labor substitution there.

title: The Inference Shift
text:
Related Posts

Huang’s Law and the Democratization of NLP: the curve Thompson now inverts, where the 2020 bet was that Nvidia’s exponential would put big models in everyone’s hands.
The 2028 Global Intelligence Crisis: Scenario and Rebuttal: the same removal of the human-time ceiling, viewed from the labor side rather than the hardware side.
The Math Behind the Cost of AI Agents: the agentic-inference economics in detail, where memory reuse through caching is what bends the token-cost curve Thompson’s argument rests on.
Sequential KV Cache Compression via Probabilistic Language Tries: a concrete attack on the memory hierarchy Thompson says agentic inference will live in, compressing the KV cache that holds an agent’s context.

title: Peeking Inside a Language Model, and Finding It Knows It’s Being Watched
text:
NLA schematic: the activation verbalizer turns a target activation into a text description, and the activation reconstructor recovers the activation from the text alone. Watch on YouTube
Anthropic’s interpretability team introduces Natural Language Autoencoders (NLAs), a method for turning an internal activation of a language model into a plain-text explanation. Two copies of the target model are trained jointly: an activation verbalizer that reads an activation and writes a text explanation, and an activation reconstructor that reads the explanation and rebuilds the activation. The training signal is reconstruction similarity, so explanations that carry real content about the activation are rewarded over explanations that do not. The companion paper on Transformer Circuits [1] comes with an interactive demo on Neuronpedia and training code on GitHub.

title: Peeking Inside a Language Model, and Finding It Knows It’s Being Watched
text:
Methods



The NLA training loop: the activation verbalizer (AV) translates a target activation \(h_{L,i}\) into a natural-language description, and the activation reconstructor (AR) recovers an activation \(\hat{h}_{L,i}\) from that text alone. Training minimizes \(\|h_{L,i} - \hat{h}_{L,i}\|_2^2\), so descriptions that carry real content about the activation are rewarded. Schematic from the paper’s training section [1].

title: Peeking Inside a Language Model, and Finding It Knows It’s Being Watched
text:
Results
The post applies NLAs to two problems: evaluation awareness and alignment auditing. On a test of destructive coding actions (e.g. deleting important files), NLA explanations flag evaluation awareness 16% of the time in cases where Claude never verbalizes it; on SWE-bench Verified the rate is 26%; on real claude.ai traffic from users who opted in to training it sits under 1%. Anthropic reports that NLAs were used in the pre-deployment alignment audits of Claude Mythos Preview and Claude Opus 4.6.



Opus 4.6 shows NLA-measured evaluation awareness on 26% of SWE-bench Verified transcripts and 16% of destructive-coding transcripts, versus 1% and 0% when measured by what the model actually verbalizes. On opt-in real claude.ai traffic the NLA-measured rate is 0.4%. Chart from the paper [1].


In a toy auditing game where a target model has been trained with a single hidden misaligned motivation, auditors equipped with NLAs uncover the motivation 12–15% of the time, compared with 3% or below when given other interpretability tools.



Auditing-game win rates across tool configs. NLA+conversation auditors identify the target model’s misaligned motivation 12/100 without access to training data and 15/100 with access, well above the SAE+conversation (3/100) and conversation-only (1–2/100) baselines. Chart from the paper [1].

title: Peeking Inside a Language Model, and Finding It Knows It’s Being Watched
text:
My Notes

NLAs trade mechanistic grounding for direct legibility. Sparse autoencoders (SAE) and attribution graphs share the autoencoder structure (round-trip reconstruction as the training signal, structured output a trained researcher reads); NLAs swap the sparse feature dictionary for a text bottleneck and the linear readout for another copy of the model. The closest prior art is Patchscope [2], which uses a frozen LLM to decode hidden states into natural language without a round-trip training objective. NLAs add the reconstruction loop to tighten what the verbalizer has to say. The paper itself flags the cost as a limitation: an SAE feature is a specific direction in activation space you can causally intervene on, while an NLA explanation is a black-box output of another LLM. That makes NLAs a natural complement to the structural methods rather than a replacement: the SAE or attribution graph tells you where in the network a representation lives, and the NLA tells you, in prose, what it seems to be about.
NLAs move the describing job from the model to a dedicated pair. The evaluation-awareness numbers tighten a gap that SelfReflect articulated: current LLMs cannot faithfully describe their internal distributions when asked to. NLAs sidestep the asking by training a separate model to do the describing from the activation directly. Where SelfReflect measures a given model’s introspective faithfulness as a property of that model, NLAs make reconstruction fidelity the explicit training target, at the cost of training and running a dedicated pair of models for the task. The paper’s own caveat — that the training objective “does not explicitly incentivize NLA explanations to be interpretable or faithful” — is why they still have to evaluate faithfulness empirically rather than claim it by construction.
Where did the eval-awareness come from in the first place? Nobody explicitly trained Claude to notice “this is a test”, so the signal had to seep in from the training data. Prior work on situational awareness by Berglund et al. [3], and its follow-up benchmark by Laine et al. [4], has already speculated on the supervision sources: the AI safety literature itself, published openly and full of discussions of evaluation protocols, sandbagging, and red-teaming; benchmark format exposure during pretraining, since SWE-bench-style task-description conventions live on the public web and there is no way to scrub them without hurting capability training; and a structural tell during RLHF, where human raters treating contrived prompts and conversational prompts as different kinds of “good response” teaches the model a distribution over what eval-shaped inputs look like. What none of the prior work has done — and what NLAs now make possible — is a systematic training-data audit: read activations for eval-awareness signals, trace the candidate text sources through the training corpus, and publish the map. That would be the natural companion piece.
NLA-measured eval-awareness has a Goodhart half-life. Frontier models may behave differently during evaluation than during deployment, and NLAs put a number on it. On SWE-bench Verified, activations register “this is a test” on 26% of problems; on opt-in claude.ai traffic, the rate is 0.4%. If that gap holds up under independent interpretability methods, benchmark scores reflect how a frontier model behaves under observation. How it behaves when nobody is watching is a separate question, and the verbalized rate (1% on SWE-bench) tells us the model will not answer it for us. There is a further catch: 26% itself depends on a model that doesn’t yet know its activations will be read. Once NLA-style signals enter RLHF or alignment training — and Anthropic is already running NLAs in pre-deployment audits, which is the shortest possible path into that loop — a future model can learn to suppress activation-level eval-awareness without the underlying awareness decreasing. This is the observer effect entering interpretability, with Goodhart’s Law as the sharper limit: measuring the model disturbs it once the measurement loops back into training, and at that point the measure stops tracking what it was measuring. The dynamic has been predicted in theory [5] and recently demonstrated empirically in reward-gaming experiments [6]; what’s missing is the direct test on interpretability tools: train on NLA-derived signals, measure NLA quality decay. That would put a half-life on numbers like 26%.

title: Schools Retreat From the Pandemic’s Ed-Tech Buildout
text:
A classroom scene illustrating the 1:1 device era. Image from The Washington Post.
Lauren Lumpkin, reporting for The Washington Post, walks through the ed-tech pullback underway in U.S. K–12.
What the article reports:
One line from the piece, by Missouri state Rep. Tricia Byrnes:

title: Schools Retreat From the Pandemic’s Ed-Tech Buildout
text:
My Notes

The ed-tech thesis assumed content delivery was the bottleneck. It wasn’t. Districts bought laptops and learning software expecting infinite personalized practice to move outcomes. What’s missing is the layer around the content that turns “access to material” into “engagement with material”: a teacher calling on a student by name, a grade that matters, peer accountability. A 10-year-old alone with an iPad and open-internet access will drift to YouTube, because the recommendation and feed-ranking plumbing underneath consumer tech is optimized for that drift, and the ed-tech layer on top doesn’t disable it.
This is the demand-side confirmation of the thesis in The Global Edtech Boom Is Fading. Venture capital left K–12 because outcomes never materialized. Districts are now legislating the rollout out, for the same reason. Venture-backed K–12 needed content delivery to be the bottleneck to justify its valuations, so the category defaulted to that claim even when the evidence was thin. What’s left standing is the nonprofit-plus-frontier-API shape (Khan Academy’s Khanmigo and similar), which doesn’t require the misdiagnosis to make its economics work.

title: A User Manual for synesis
text:
This site is a static blog. No comments, no like button, no email-capture popup, no newsletter overlay — just HTML, CSS, and enough JavaScript to keep the reading experience pleasant.
Everything works with a mouse on the desktop and by tap on phones. On top of that, desktop readers get a keyboard shortcut for almost every feature. Press ? on any page to see the map.
Below is a tour of what’s here. The conventions carry across every page, so learning them once covers the whole corpus.

title: A User Manual for synesis
text:
Search
Click the magnifying glass in the navbar, or press /, to open the full-text search overlay. It indexes every post title, body, and code block. Results land with term highlights in place, and Esc clears them.



The search overlay with results for a query like “conformal” or “marathon”.


Search runs entirely in your browser. No network round-trip per keystroke, and it keeps working if you lose connectivity mid-session.

title: A User Manual for synesis
text:
Ask AI
A small “Ask AI” button sits next to the search icon. Clicking it (or pressing q) opens a popover that deep-links your question plus the current page’s context into Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, or Perplexity.



The Ask AI popover with provider buttons and the composed prompt.


Scope is detected automatically. On a post, the popover asks about that post. On the archive with a tag filter active, it asks about posts with that tag. On the home page, it asks about the whole blog.
If you select a passage on the page before opening the popover (or paste one in once it’s open), a separate “Your question” field appears below the context. The split keeps the chatbot answering your question instead of just commenting on the passage. Without context, the single field is your question.
Each provider opens in a new tab with your question pre-filled. Gemini is the exception, because its web UI does not accept a pre-filled question. The site copies the prompt to your clipboard and opens the app instead. Paste to submit.

title: A User Manual for synesis
text:
Jump to a tag
The third button in the top-right pill — a small # icon, between the Ask-AI bubble and the search magnifier — opens a tag picker. Pressing # does the same. Type any part of a tag name, hit Enter, and you land on the archive filtered to that tag. Use it when you already know what you’re looking for and don’t want to scroll the tag cloud.



The tag picker opened with an empty input — the top-twelve tags by post count, ranked.


The list ranks matches in four tiers (exact name, name starts with what you typed, any word starts with it, anywhere in the name) and breaks ties by post count. Up to twelve results appear at a time. Arrow keys move the highlight; Esc cancels.

title: A User Manual for synesis
text:
Browsing the archive
The archive page lists every post in one scrollable table. Clicking a tag chip filters the table in place, and the URL updates so the filtered view is shareable.



The archive page with a tag filter active. The selected chip sits above the table, and the URL updates to match.


A tag cloud sized by post count sits in the right sidebar on desktop, and in the bottom-sheet panel on phones. Clicking any tag applies it as a filter without leaving the page. Click the active chip again, or press Esc, to clear.

title: A User Manual for synesis
text:
Moving between posts
The home and archive pages carry a pagination bar so you can walk backward through the archive a page at a time. A small previous / next strip also appears below every post for linear reading.



A post page with the prev / next strip showing the neighboring posts.


The same motion is available from the keyboard. On a post, j or ← goes to the newer post and k or → goes to the older one. On a listing page, the same keys turn pages. ↑ and ↓ walk a highlight through visible posts, and Enter opens the highlighted one.



A listing page with one post highlighted by keyboard navigation.

title: A User Manual for synesis
text:
Activity timeline
The home page carries a right-side timeline: one dot per post, grouped by month, scaled by activity. Hovering a dot previews the post title, and clicking jumps to the post. It is meant for the “when did I write that one thing about…” lookup that search cannot quite answer.



The home page with the activity timeline sidebar visible on the right.


On archive pages the right sidebar becomes the tag cloud instead. On post pages it becomes the table of contents.

title: A User Manual for synesis
text:
Lightbox
Every figure in a post is clickable. The lightbox preserves the caption, including any “Watch on YouTube” or source-credit links, so you can click through to the source from the zoomed view.



A figure zoomed into the lightbox, caption link still live.


Esc closes. Arrow keys walk through figures within the same post.

title: A User Manual for synesis
text:
Sharing and contact
Every post carries a small row of icons below the title: Mastodon, LinkedIn, Hacker News, Bluesky, a divider, then email.



The share and contact row that appears right under the title on every post.


The four share links carry a small tracking tag on the URL so I can tell which platform drove a click. Mastodon is the odd one out because the network is federated, so there is no universal share URL. The first Mastodon click asks for your instance (e.g. mastodon.social), and the answer is saved in your browser so later clicks skip the prompt.
The email icon opens your mail client with the subject pre-filled as Re: <post title> and the post’s URL quoted in the body. Because there is no comment box, email is the primary channel for reader-to-author conversation. If something in a post is wrong, incomplete, or sparks a follow-up thought, that is the fastest path to me.

title: A User Manual for synesis
text:
Making it look right
Three appearance controls sit in the lower-right corner: a light/dark toggle, a font cycler, and a line-spacing cycler. Each also has a single-key shortcut: d for light/dark, t for theme, f for font, l for line spacing.



The same post under two different combinations of theme, font, and line spacing.


Your choice sticks across visits. Defaults track the system color scheme — if you have never pressed d, the site follows whatever your OS or browser is set to.

title: A User Manual for synesis
text:
Keyboard shortcuts at a glance
? toggles a modal listing every keyboard shortcut on the site. It is the only shortcut worth memorizing. The rest are one keystroke away from there.



The help overlay, reached by pressing ? on any page.


The highlights, in rough order of usefulness:

/ search, q Ask AI, # jump to tag
s home, a archive, A about
j / ← newer, k / → older (works on posts and on paginated listings)
↑ / ↓ / Enter move the highlight and open
d / t / f / l theme, font, line spacing
Esc to close any overlay, clear search highlights, or drop a tag filter

Same keys do different things depending on the page: j/k move post-to-post on a post, and page-to-page on a listing.

title: A User Manual for synesis
text:
On the phone
On phones and other narrow windows, the right sidebar will not fit. Instead, a corner button in the bottom-left opens a bottom-sheet panel with whatever the sidebar would have held: timeline on home, tag cloud on archive, table of contents on posts. Tap the button to open or close.



The mobile bottom-sheet open on a phone-width viewport.


Tap the dim area behind the sheet, or the corner button again, to close.

title: A User Manual for synesis
text:
For agents and feed readers
Three routes exist for non-human readers:

/llms.txt — a plain-text index of every post, regenerated on each build, aimed at AI agents
/posts/<slug>/index.qmd — the raw Markdown source of every post, served alongside the rendered HTML
/index.xml, /feed-page-2.xml, … — a full-content RSS feed, paginated, with math and diagrams pre-rendered so they show up even in readers that do not run JavaScript

The RSS feed carries every post in full, with nothing truncated. The backlink sits at the top of each item so a reader who wants to comment or share has the canonical URL in hand before scrolling.



An RSS client showing a full post rendered from the feed, with math, code, and images all present.


The full agent-facing surface is broader than these three. Making synesis Agent-Friendly covers all of it.

title: A User Manual for synesis
text:
Feedback welcome
If anything on the site is broken, missing, or could be better, the email icon under any post title is the fastest way to tell me. Curious to hear what you find.

title: A User Manual for synesis
text:
Related Posts

Making synesis Quick: the performance side of the same static-site build, how the reading experience this manual describes stays fast.

title: Are AI Systems About to Start Building Themselves?
text:
Image from Import AI.
Jack Clark, co-founder and policy lead at Anthropic, walks through the public evidence that automated AI research and development (R&D), a frontier model autonomously training its own successor, has a roughly 60% chance of arriving by the end of 2028, and a 30% chance by 2027. The essay collects benchmark trends across coding, scientific reproduction, kernel design, fine-tuning, alignment-research automation, and time-horizon scaling, then argues each of those covers a distinct ingredient of the AI-engineering pipeline.
What Clark argues:

title: Are AI Systems About to Start Building Themselves?
text:
My Notes

None of these benchmarks individually proves recursive self-improvement, but together they describe a system that can do most of the engineering schlep without supervision.
Clark puts 30% on automated AI R&D by 2027 and 60% by 2028. The gap is a bet that some research insights still come from humans on a year-or-more cadence. The creativity window is on the order of a year.
The Aletheia/Erdős-problems pipeline [7] evaluated around 700 conjectures and produced 13 addressable problems — 5 novel autonomous solutions plus 8 that turned out to match existing literature — with 1 deemed genuinely interesting. A funnel dominated by human filtering. That fits Terence Tao’s generation / verification / digestion decomposition: AI is strong on the first two, and the research taste sits with the humans doing digestion. Clark describes this as a “centaur configuration”: humans collaborating with AI rather than AI acting alone. The pattern is real, but human mathematicians are still the scarce input.
On Anthropic’s CPU-only training-optimization benchmark, the 2.9x → 52x speedup chain hasn’t flattened, and the human 4x baseline was passed three generations ago. Another year at this pace would make the 30%-by-2027 probability look too conservative.
The alignment section is brief, but the compounding-error math Clark cites (99.9% accuracy → 95.12% after 50 generations → 60.5% after 500) is the quantitative reason getting alignment right before recursion starts matters more than fixing it along the way. The math assumes per-generation drift compounds independently, which is generous — if drift correlates across generations the curve steepens fast.
ARC-AGI-3 is a live test of both the creativity gap and the drift math. GPT-5.5 scored 0.43% and Opus 4.7 scored 0.18% on a benchmark that withholds instructions and forces models to infer rules from sparse feedback. Clark’s benchmarks are mostly in-distribution with verifiable rewards, which is where current models climb fastest. Two of the three failure modes pulled from the reasoning traces pick up his caveats directly. Failure 2 (reusing a Tetris or Sokoban template for unfamiliar mechanics) is what happens when a system hits a genuinely novel direction with no training match. Failure 3 (reward cementing the wrong primitive after a lucky level-beat) is the empirical shape of the compounding-drift math. If AI R&D includes material amounts of either, Clark’s estimate looks too optimistic.
The economic bullets are weaker than the technical ones, partly because the labor data through today still sits where the rebuttal in The 2028 Global Intelligence Crisis described it: low-4s unemployment, rising new-business formation, software-engineer postings up year-over-year. The essay does not attempt to reconcile a 2028 R&D-automation forecast with a 2026 labor market that is not yet inflecting.

title: Influential ChatGPT-in-Education Meta-Analysis Retracted: Where’s the Transparency and Cost?
text:
Image from Ars Technica.
Jeremy Hsu, reporting for Ars Technica, walks through the retraction of the Wang and Fan paper, a meta-analysis in Humanities and Social Sciences Communications (Springer Nature) claiming ChatGPT delivers “a large positive impact on improving learning performance,” a “moderately positive impact on enhancing learning perception,” and gains in “fostering higher-order thinking.” The paper pooled effect sizes from 51 prior studies that compared ChatGPT-using experimental groups against non-AI control groups. Springer Nature retracted it on April 22, 2026:
What the article reports:
The retracted paper’s abstract:

title: Influential ChatGPT-in-Education Meta-Analysis Retracted: Where’s the Transparency and Cost?
text:
My Notes

The technical case against the paper has been specific and public from the start. Tuomi’s methodological analysis and companion post, both posted shortly after the paper appeared, lay it out; Williamson amplified them in his own pre-publication LinkedIn warning the same week, telling readers to “check out the two-part analysis by Ilkka Tuomi” before taking the meta-analysis seriously:

The paper “repeats all the errors from an earlier meta-analysis by Deng et al.,” reusing Deng’s search string without attribution, including a copied spelling error.
Deng at least tried to score input studies for quality. Wang & Fan say nothing about quality and do not state whether the analyzed studies were peer-reviewed; studies from “0-quality journals (like ‘Mathematics’ from MDPI)” are included.
Internal validity in randomized and quasi-experimental designs requires control and treatment groups drawn from the same population. The 51 studies pool teachers, medical-practice students, college mathematics, computer programming, and language-learning groups; the “basic criterion for making (internally) valid conclusions is broken before the analysis starts.”
The funnel: the search strings returned 6,621 papers; abstract filtering left 2,712; “careful review” produced 51. In half the studies the experimental/treatment group had fewer than 35 students; some “claim to make statistically valid conclusions based on groups with 12 students,” and the paper offers no study-power estimate.
The heterogeneity statistic is reported but not interpreted: “huge, suggesting that there is no ‘it’ in the studies. The external validity is junk.”
To illustrate what summing effect sizes across incompatible studies looks like, Tuomi compares it to a meta-review of “the impact of electricity on learning outcomes” that would pool teacher commute mode, classroom lighting, and air conditioning into a single average. He calls the pattern “garbage in, gold out”: junk inputs, respected-journal output.

Publishers should publish a real account of what went wrong, especially for a paper this widely cited. Two sentences and a non-responsive-author disclosure is not enough from a Springer Nature title that just retracted a paper with 504 citations and ~500K reads, especially when the technical critique above had been public the entire year. The notice does not say which of the three headline claims are now invalid, what the meta-analysis discrepancies actually were, or whether the failure was in study selection, effect-size aggregation, or both. The Committee on Publication Ethics retraction guidelines call for specifics; this notice does not meet that standard. The publisher should also disclose what peer review missed and notify the 262 within-publisher citing authors directly, so the correction reaches them instead of the other way around. Williamson, writing on LinkedIn after the retraction, put it bluntly: the paper “should not have been published in the first place,” and despite the retraction, “this and similar studies have shaped debates about AI in education anyway.”
Make get-famous-quick costly for researchers and their institutions. Publishing fast on a hot topic compounds in upside, while the downside, if it ever arrives, is a thin retraction note years later that does not erase the citations or the attention score. The Wang & Fan paper accumulated nearly 60K accesses and a 200+ altmetric score within three days of publication, per Williamson’s update on LinkedIn; by retraction it had reached ~500K reads and 504 citations. Williamson described the broader environment as a “flaky evidentiary culture” in AI-in-education research, “where it’s relatively easy to publish in journals with low-quality peer review and editorial processes, allowing papers of dubious quality to get trawled in a poorly designed meta-analysis and then bundled up as conclusive evidence that gets wildly circulated by big social media accounts.” A few changes would make the asymmetry hurt:

Institutional misconduct review by the authors’ employer (Hangzhou Normal University in this case), with a published outcome rather than internal-only handling.
Mandatory reciprocal-citation: any paper citing a retracted work after the retraction date must cite the retraction note alongside it, enforced by the publisher inside the same journal family.
A publicly searchable retraction registry that travels with the author byline at hiring, grant review, and tenure time. The Retraction Watch Database already exists; funders and search committees should treat it as a default lookup; few currently do.
A grant-cycle penalty: principal investigators with retracted papers in the prior N years carry a disclosure on every new application, weighted in review.

As long as retraction costs this little, fast publication on a hot topic with weak data has no real downside for the authors or their institutions. The downside lands elsewhere. Papers like Wang & Fan helped legitimize the AI-in-education investment thesis that is now collapsing, and the schools, districts, and ed-tech vendors that bought in carry the cost. The citation residue stays in the literature long after the funding has moved on.

title: Agentic Coding Is a Trap
text:
Image from Lars Faye’s article.
Lars Faye, a software engineer who runs the Confident Coding Course, argues that the dominant “orchestrator with sub-agents” coding workflow trades the very critical-thinking skills it depends on for short-term throughput. The piece collects the public evidence of skill atrophy under heavy AI-assisted coding, including two Anthropic studies and on-the-record concerns from a LinkedIn engineering director, then lays out a narrower role for large language models (LLMs) that preserves the underlying capability.

title: Agentic Coding Is a Trap
text:
What Faye cites
The argument leans on a long chain of independent sources. Listed in roughly the order Faye reaches for them:

Quentin — “One More Prompt: the Dopamine Trap of Agentic Coding” — slot-machine framing for the “one more prompt” loop.
Margaret Storey — “Cognitive Debt Revisited” — research that AI tooling has been shown to impact critical thinking negatively.
MIT Media Lab — “Your Brain on ChatGPT” — measured cognitive impact of LLM-assisted writing.
404 Media on a Microsoft study — Microsoft research finding AI use atrophies human cognition.
Simon Willison — “Cognitive Debt” — Faye’s evidence that senior engineers aren’t immune to the pattern.
Anthropic — “How AI Is Transforming Work at Anthropic” — source of the “paradox of supervision” passage.
Business Insider — leaders worry about skill atrophy — where Sandor Nyako, Director of Software Engineering at LinkedIn (oversees ~50 engineers), is on the record.
Anthropic — “AI Assistance Coding Skills” — source of the 47% debugging-skill drop.
PYMNTS — “AI adoption is being measured in tokens, but the metric falls short” — hype around token usage as the productivity metric of choice.
Lam (LinkedIn) — “Claude’s Outages Show the Dark Side of AI Productivity” — one of the LinkedIn posts Faye saw during a Claude outage when teams couldn’t work.
The Verge — AI monetization / token economics — evidence that model providers are heavily subsidized today.
Cheewebdevelopment — “Don’t Vibe Code: Delegate” — the source Faye credits for the “delegation utilities” framing.
Jeremy Howard (fast.ai) — quoted: “If you outsource all your thinking to computers, you stop upskilling, learning, and becoming more competent.”
Five supporting YouTube clips: anecdotal developer testimony, a recent interview, AI-enthusiastic senior developers, Primeagen on vendor capture, and further on-the-ground reporting.

title: Agentic Coding Is a Trap
text:
Faye’s prescription
Faye proposes inverting the dominant orchestration pattern: the engineer codes; the model helps with adjacent work. His daily workflow:

Generate specs and plans with the model, but implement manually. “I am still manually coding anywhere from 20% to 100%, depending on the task.”
Write pseudo-code first, then engage the model. Pseudo-code “closes the distance between the request and the generated code” — the model fills gaps rather than architects.
Use models as delegation utilities. Ad-hoc code generation, interactive documentation, research-and-iterate questions — all bounded, all small.
Never generate more than you can review in one sitting. If it’s too big, split the task and manually refactor through it.
Never ask the model to implement something you couldn’t do on your own. Educational exceptions allowed, and often discarded after.
TL;DR (Faye’s): “Use them like the Ship’s Computer, not Data.” A reference tool, not a substitute for the engineer.

title: Agentic Coding Is a Trap
text:
My Notes

The “paradox of supervision” (Faye quotes it from Anthropic) is one slice of a self-undermining loop. Faye and Anthropic name the contradiction: to supervise the model you need the same skill the model is eroding, but didn’t explicitly close the loop.

The missing link: as that skill weakens, more decisions slide to the model (some on purpose, some because the human no longer catches the slips), which erodes the skill further, which weakens the next round of supervision. Each turn justifies the next.
The cycle isn’t unbreakable. Faye’s “never generate more than you can review” rule does break it, by keeping each round small enough that the human’s skill stays in use. Preserving judgment in the moment is also what keeps the cycle from running.

Restoring the speed-and-comprehension link in agentic tooling is about what we optimize for. Model capability isn’t the bottleneck. Today’s tools optimize for generated-code volume; they should optimize for human-verifiable diff per unit time instead. Decision-Bound Programming makes the same recommendation from a different starting point: when generation is cheap and evaluation is not, the next generation of programming tools should be decision support systems: tooling that narrows the space of options the human must evaluate. The asymmetry itself isn’t new — Terence Tao’s decomposition of mathematical work into generation, verification, and digestion names the same problem one field over: AI is racing through the first two while leaving the third (the human’s comprehension) behind. Four concrete shapes narrow the evaluation gap:

Type-driven generation — the type checker rules out a class of candidates; the human reads types, not whole functions.
Test-driven generation — a passing test suite becomes the checkable signal; the human verifies via the gate.
Spec-first systems where the model stays at the planning layer (Faye’s own inversion) — the human decides at the spec level, and trusts the mechanical translation below.
Domain-specific languages (DSLs) and structured-edit modes — a smaller grammar is a smaller decision space; the output is cheap to scan.

Intrinsic non-determinism doesn’t disappear, but in all four the tool absorbs the checking work the human was doing before.
Vendor lock-in adds an industry risk to the personal-skill risk. When entire teams sit idle during a Claude outage, the lock-in has already happened. Token costs are a moving target by design, subsidized today and “nerfed” tomorrow, and the financial exposure piles on top of the cognitive risk. The 2028 Global Intelligence Crisis scenario treats this same compute-cost-as-labor-cost substitution as a macro variable; the Cursor agent that erased PocketOS production data shows the daily-operations failure mode at the other end.
