title: Reading the Reasoning Traces Behind ARC-AGI-3
text:
Image from ARC Prize.
Greg Kamradt at ARC Prize published an analysis of 160 replays and reasoning traces from OpenAI’s GPT-5.5 and Anthropic’s Opus 4.7 on ARC-AGI-3, the 135-environment benchmark that withholds instructions and forces the model to infer rules from sparse feedback. GPT-5.5 scored 0.43%, Opus 4.7 scored 0.18%.
What the article reports: three failure modes pulled from the reasoning traces.
Two illustrations from the article.
The article closes with a named contrast between the two models: Opus compressed its observations into a confident wrong theory, GPT-5.5 kept the hypothesis space open but never committed to a plan. “Opus had the wrong compression, GPT-5.5 failed to compress.”

title: Reading the Reasoning Traces Behind ARC-AGI-3
text:
My Notes

The three failure modes each break a different step in observe → rule → plan → commit. Failure 1 breaks between observation and rule. Failure 2 swaps in a rule borrowed from training data instead of inferring one from evidence. Failure 3 commits to a rule the reward didn’t validate. That’s more useful than “the models can’t reason,” because it points at which step to instrument in a harness.
Failure 3 is the one most likely to show up outside ARC-AGI-3. It’s the empirical version of the metacognitive-evaluation gap: if the agent can’t ask why it won the last level, outcome reward reinforces whatever theory happened to be active, correct or not. Self-improvement loops that use task success as their only signal will encode this systematically.
The pattern matches earlier world-model findings. Closed-form probes like GSM-Symbolic and DFA (deterministic finite automaton) evaluations already showed that identical accuracy numbers can hide very different generalization behavior (the world-model gap literature). ARC-AGI-3 extends the lesson into open-ended exploration: two models at near-zero scores can still be failing at different points in the reasoning chain, and only the traces show the difference.
The GPT-5.5 trace claims carry a mode caveat the post largely glosses. The article discloses this only in a final “Analysis notes” section:

With our default tests, GPT-5.5 did not return its reasoning traces. The qualitative analysis above therefore uses an analysis mode run, which is an alternate testing setup intended to elicit more explicit descriptions of how the model is interpreting the environment and deciding what to try next. The official GPT-5.5 score is not from that mode. All reported scores use the standard ARC-AGI-3 harness, matching the setup used for Opus 4.7.

The scores themselves are clean: 0.43% and 0.18% are both from the standard harness. The confound lives in the qualitative trace comparison that carries the article’s main argument. Opus’s traces are from the standard harness; GPT-5.5’s are from a mode specifically designed to elicit more explicit reasoning. More explicit traces can easily read as a wider hypothesis space, which means “Opus compresses more aggressively than GPT-5.5” may reflect the harness rather than the model.

title: Reading the Reasoning Traces Behind ARC-AGI-3
text:
Related Posts

Truly Self-Improving Agents Require Intrinsic Metacognitive Learning: the metacognitive-evaluation gap that Failure Mode 3 is the empirical version of, where outcome reward cements whatever theory happened to win.
How Well Can Transformers Build World Models?: the closed-form world-model probes this analysis extends into open-ended exploration, where equal scores still hide different generalization behavior.
Chollet: How We Get to AGI: the ARC suite’s creator on the fluid-intelligence and program-synthesis abilities these ARC-AGI-3 traces find missing.
Karpathy: AGI Is Still a Decade Away: the same skepticism about frontier-model reasoning and world models, from the capability-timeline side.

title: Detecting Hallucinations in Large Language Models Using Semantic Entropy
text:
AUROC (higher is better at separating correct from confabulated generations) and AURAC (area under the rejection-accuracy curve) for six LLMs across the QA benchmarks. Semantic entropy (dark blue) matches or beats naive token-level entropy, a P(True) self-eval baseline, and embedding-regression probes on every model. Figure 2 from the paper [1]. Image from Nature.
In Detecting Hallucinations in Large Language Models Using Semantic Entropy (Nature, June 2024) [1], Sebastian Farquhar, Jannik Kossen, Lorenz Kuhn, and Yarin Gal (Oxford and Google DeepMind) propose an entropy-based uncertainty estimator for large language models (LLMs) that detects confabulations (arbitrary, incorrect generations produced when the model is uncertain) by computing entropy over the meaning of sampled answers rather than over token sequences.

title: Detecting Hallucinations in Large Language Models Using Semantic Entropy
text:
Methods
The method samples multiple answers from the LLM for a given prompt, clusters the samples by bidirectional semantic entailment (two answers are in the same cluster if each entails the other under a natural-language-inference model), then computes Shannon entropy over the resulting meaning-cluster distribution. The clustering step is what makes semantic entropy beat naive token-level entropy. Naive entropy conflates two sources of variation: uncertainty about meaning (the real signal of confabulation) and uncertainty about wording (“Paris” and “It’s Paris” carry the same answer but inflate naive entropy as different token sequences). Bidirectional-entailment clustering strips out the wording variation, so the per-prompt scalar correlates more tightly with whether the answer is actually wrong.
In deployment the scalar becomes an abstention signal: threshold it, refuse on high-entropy queries, accept the rest. Because high-entropy queries are disproportionately wrong, refusing them removes more wrong answers than right ones, and accuracy on the retained set climbs. The paper quantifies that improvement two ways. AUROC scores how well the scalar separates right from wrong answers across all prompts (detection quality). AURAC scores how much accuracy actually rises on retained answers as the refusal rate sweeps from 0 to 100% (deployment value). The approach is black-box at inference: it needs sample access but no model internals, no fine-tuning, and no task-specific calibration data. A discrete variant approximates the entailment check with single-forward-pass judgments, trading a small accuracy drop for lower cost.



Semantic entropy clusters sampled LLM answers by meaning via bidirectional entailment, then measures entropy over cluster probabilities. (a, top) High semantic entropy on a factoid prompt indicates confabulation: naive token-level entropy is misled by paraphrase diversity, but semantic entropy is low on a confident prompt and high on a confabulating one. (b, bottom) Applied to FactualBio paragraphs, the signal transfers to claim-level verification by decomposing the paragraph into factoids and measuring semantic entropy per factoid. Figure 1 from the paper [1]. Image from Nature.

title: Detecting Hallucinations in Large Language Models Using Semantic Entropy
text:
Results
Experiments span six LLMs (LLaMA 2 Chat 7B/13B/70B, Falcon 7B/40B Instruct, Mistral 7B Instruct) across TriviaQA, SQuAD [4], BioASQ, NQ Open, SVAMP [5], and a FactualBio biography-paragraph benchmark the authors construct. Averaged across the 30 task-model combinations on short-answer QA, semantic entropy achieves AUROC 0.790, above naive entropy (0.691), P(True) [2] self-evaluation (0.698), and a supervised embedding-regression probe (0.687); performance is stable between 0.78 and 0.81 across model families and scales (Figure 2, the cover image above). The method generalizes out-of-distribution: an embedding probe trained on one task drops sharply on another, while semantic entropy maintains near-training performance. Applied to FactualBio, semantic entropy over atomic sub-claims flags unsupported biographical facts and outperforms the paragraph-adapted P(True) baseline, supporting the claim that the signal transfers from short-answer QA to long-form generation.

title: Detecting Hallucinations in Large Language Models Using Semantic Entropy
text:
My Notes

Entailment clustering is the critical step, and the paper does stress-test it. The meaning-cluster assignment uses a natural-language-inference (NLI) model (DeBERTa-large-MNLI [6], or the generator LLM itself in an LLM-as-judge variant). The paper’s ablations show results are stable across NLI backbones and stable when generator and judge share a model, which addresses the obvious circularity worry. The remaining open question is scope-specific: on legal, medical, or evaluative judgments, frontier LLMs disagree about meaning among themselves, so entailment clustering cannot be presumed to converge to ground-truth equivalence. Conformal factuality [3] relies on a related claim-decomposition premise and hits the same boundary condition.
The OOD-generalization result carries the paper. Hallucination-detection methods that depend on in-distribution examples (P(True) [2]’s few-shot priors, and supervised embedding regression) degrade sharply when the test task differs from the calibration task. Semantic entropy needs no calibration set and transfers across the six datasets without loss, which matters because real-world deployment distributions are never exactly the ones used to train a detector. This is a cleaner version of the argument Kadavath et al. made for self-evaluation, without the extra cost of a second forward pass per sample.
Composability with fact-verification pipelines is the natural next step. Semantic entropy flags which generations to distrust; benchmarks like AVeriTeC [7] and HoVer [8] tell you why (what evidence does or doesn’t support the claim), and tools like FLEEK retrieve evidence from knowledge graphs and the web to make that verdict concrete. A pipeline that routes high-semantic-entropy generations into explicit claim-verification against retrieved evidence would give a user both the uncertainty flag and the remediation path. The paper notes this direction in the discussion but doesn’t test it.
Part of the “sample \(N\), then aggregate” family, with a structural limit they all share. Semantic entropy shares the same inference backbone as self-consistency [9], CLM, and SelfReflect: \(N\) forward passes per query at temperature > 0. What differs is what each method does with the sample pool.

Self-consistency majority-votes to pick a single answer.
CLM applies a conformal stopping rule and returns a calibrated candidate set.
Semantic entropy clusters by meaning and emits a scalar abstention signal.
SelfReflect (same Oxford + DeepMind lab) summarizes the internal distribution and scores the summary’s fidelity to the samples.

Semantic entropy is closest to SelfReflect by output type (per-query scalar) and to conformal factuality by goal (hallucination mitigation at deployment, black-box at inference). All four pay the same \(N\times\) inference cost, and the choice among them is about which signal the downstream system needs.
The shared structural limit: the signal is sample diversity, not factuality. If a model confabulates consistently (its training distribution pins it to the same wrong answer across sampling temperatures), all samples cluster together, semantic entropy is low, and the method signals “confident” when the answer is in fact wrong. The AUROC gains hold for the subset of hallucinations that produce inter-sample disagreement (the confabulation scope the paper is careful to name) but do not extend to the systematic-bias case.

title: Linguistic Calibration of Long-Form Generations
text:
The linguistic calibration (LC) training framework: a summary-distillation supervised-finetuning (SFT) step bootstraps the language model to emit confidence phrases, and a decision-based reinforcement-learning (RL) step rewards generations that let a downstream reader produce calibrated forecasts on related questions. Figure 2 from the paper [1].
In Linguistic Calibration of Long-Form Generations [1] (ICML 2024), Neil Band, Xuechen Li, Tengyu Ma, and Tatsunori Hashimoto (Stanford) define linguistic calibration in decision-theoretic terms: a language model (LM) is linguistically calibrated if its long-form generations enable a downstream reader to make calibrated probabilistic predictions. They train Llama 2 7B [2] to emit paragraphs with confidence statements (“I estimate a 30% chance of…”, “I am certain that…”) that satisfy that property.

title: Linguistic Calibration of Long-Form Generations
text:
Methods
The framework has two stages. Both operate on queries \(q\) derived upstream from QA benchmark items: an API-based LLM rewrites each question \(x\) (from TriviaQA, Jeopardy, SciQ, BioASQ) into a paragraph-generation prompt \(q\) (e.g., “Write a paragraph about {topic of \(x\)}”). The question \(x\) and its ground-truth answer \(y\) are carried through the pipeline, but only RL consumes them.

Summary distillation (SFT). For each \(q\), the base LM samples \(M\) paragraph responses; a stronger summarizer LM (Claude 2) condenses them into one paragraph \(s\) whose embedded confidence phrases reflect how often each claim appears across the \(M\) samples. The base LM is finetuned on the resulting \((q, s)\) pairs. Neither \(x\) nor \(y\) enters the SFT loss; confidence phrases come from sampling frequency alone.
Decision-based reinforcement learning (RL). The policy \(\pi_\theta(z \mid q)\) samples a paragraph \(z\). A downstream reader then sees only \(z\) and \(x\) (never \(q\)), forecasts an answer distribution for \(x\), and the reward is the calibration of that forecast against \(y\). PPO updates the policy. For the reader’s forecast to be calibrated, the paragraph has to convey the LM’s uncertainty on its own. A paragraph that leans on the topic framing in \(q\), rather than naming what the model knows and doesn’t, wouldn’t help a reader who can’t see \(q\).

Evaluation uses both simulated readers (LMs conditioned on the generation) and real human readers, and factuality is scored at the claim level with a retrieval plus large-language-model (LLM) verifier pipeline in the style of FActScore [3] [3].
To make the data flow concrete, here is one RL-stage training item from the paper’s Appendix A.13 (TriviaQA):







Variable
Value




\(x\) (QA question)
Which classic novel features a boy hiding in a barrel of apples on a ship?


\(y\) (ground truth)
Treasure Island


\(q\) (derived query)
“Write a paragraph about the classic book in which a boy hides in a ship’s barrel of apples.”


\(z\) (LC RL policy output)
“Based on my understanding, the classic book in which a boy hides in a ship’s barrel of apples is most likely Treasure Island by Robert Louis Stevenson. I estimate there is a 75% chance it is Treasure Island, a 15% chance it is The Wonderful Wizard of Oz by L. Frank Baum, a 5% chance it is The Adventures of Tom Sawyer by Mark Twain, and a 5% chance it is another book…”



The SFT target \(s\) (Claude 2’s summary) has the same surface shape, with confidence phrases distributed over candidate answers, but is produced by prompting Claude 2 with \(M\) base-LM samples for the same \(q\) and asking it to verbalize their empirical frequency. The paper does not publish verbatim Claude 2 summaries.

title: Linguistic Calibration of Long-Form Generations
text:
Results
On TriviaQA [4] (in-distribution), SciQ, biomedical questions, and a held-out person-biography generation task, the LC-trained Llama 2 7B improves expected calibration error (ECE) by a wide margin over strong factuality-finetuning baselines at matched accuracy. The RL stage reduces ECE from 0.163 (LC SFT) to 0.116 with human readers and from 0.166 to 0.108 with simulated readers, and the gains generalize across all four out-of-distribution settings.
Figure 3 plots the accuracy-ECE frontier for the three QA conditions. LC RL (blue diamond) sits in the upper-left corner on all three panels, meaning higher accuracy and lower ECE than every baseline. The jump from LC SFT (green) to LC RL (blue) captures the incremental value of the decision-based RL stage on top of summary-distillation SFT.






(a) TriviaQA (in-distribution), simulated reader







(b) TriviaQA (in-distribution), human readers







(c) SciQ (out-of-distribution), simulated reader





Figure 3 from the paper [1]: Accuracy-ECE Frontier for Question-Answering (upper left is better). LC RL pareto-dominates Factuality RL and SFT, with significantly better reader ECE while matching or exceeding their accuracy.

title: Linguistic Calibration of Long-Form Generations
text:
My Notes

Calibration is defined through downstream reader forecasts. Prior verbalized-uncertainty work such as Teaching Models to Express Their Uncertainty in Words [5] [5] scored the model’s own emitted probability against the ground-truth answer it produced, which pins calibration to a single question. By scoring against a downstream reader’s forecast on a related question, the paper forces the generation to convey useful uncertainty rather than just report it. The resulting objective is harder to game with generic hedging, since hedged text that does not help the reader does not improve the reader’s forecast.
Summary distillation substitutes for labeled calibration data. Human-labeled “this paragraph should say 30% chance” data does not exist at scale. LC’s workaround uses sampling frequency as a self-label and Claude 2 as a translator into prose: the base LM’s distribution over claims is already the target, and Claude 2 just verbalizes it. The same trick should work for other verbalization targets (e.g., scope hedging, answer plurality) where ground truth is computable from sampling statistics but not annotatable by humans.
Summary distillation mirrors SelfReflect’s [7] sample-then-summarize workaround, but across models. SelfReflect found modern LLMs cannot write faithful summaries of their own answer distribution through prompting, SFT, or DPO; the fix that works is sampling \(N\) outputs and summarizing those. LC’s SFT target is exactly that: Claude 2 summarizing Llama 2’s \(M\) samples, so the supervision is reliable. At inference, though, Llama 2 emits summaries without seeing its own samples, which is the regime SelfReflect declared broken for SFT. LC sidesteps the contradiction because the RL reward scores reader forecasts, not the summary’s fidelity to Llama 2’s post-training distribution. A follow-up check: run SelfReflect on the trained policy.
Both the RL reward and the headline ECE numbers route through the same FActScore-family verifier [3]. That verifier’s retrieval has weaker evidence on biomedical and long-tail-person topics, so absolute ECE on BioASQ and biography generation should be read with the verifier’s own noise folded in. The ordering of methods is still informative; the magnitudes less so.
LC trains end-to-end against reader-forecast calibration, which Lin 2022 and CLM did not. Lin et al. 2022 [5] learned verbalized confidence for short answers, scored against the answer itself. Conformal Language Modeling [6] (ICLR 2024) added set-level and component-level statistical guarantees but left surface form untreated. A natural next step would be conformal guarantees over claim subsets with aligned surface-form confidence phrases.

title: Conformal Language Modeling
text:
Schematic of the conformal sampling procedure. A black-box language model emits candidates one by one; each is added to the growing output set only if it clears a minimum-quality threshold and a diversity criterion; the loop halts when the calibrated stopping rule certifies the set likely contains an acceptable answer. Figure 1 from the paper [1].
In Conformal Language Modeling [1] (ICLR 2024), Victor Quach, Adam Fisch, Tal Schuster, Adam Yala, Jae Ho Sohn, Tommi Jaakkola, and Regina Barzilay (MIT, Google Research, UC Berkeley, and others) adapt conformal prediction to generative language models (LMs) by calibrating a sampling stopping rule plus a candidate-rejection rule so the returned output set provably contains an acceptable answer with user-chosen probability.

title: Conformal Language Modeling
text:
Methods
The method treats the LM as a black box. The set predictor \(\mathcal{C}_\lambda\) is built by sampling candidates one at a time: each candidate is added if it clears a learned quality threshold and a diversity check against what is already in the set, and sampling halts once a calibrated statistic certifies the set likely covers an acceptable answer. The subscript \(\lambda\) collects the calibration-time hyperparameters: stopping threshold, rejection threshold, diversity threshold.
A second conformal layer operates inside the final set, selecting subsets of components (individual phrases or sentences) that are each independently likely to be correct, so users can keep guaranteed claims and drop the rest. Joint calibration of all these thresholds uses the Learn-then-Test (LTT) framework of [2], which tunes multiple parameters at once with finite-sample validity via multiple-testing correction.
Unlike standard conformal prediction, the guarantee is a nested probability with two user parameters. \(\epsilon\) is the familiar coverage level (miss rate at most \(\epsilon\) across fresh prompts). \(\delta\) is new: because LTT tunes multiple hyperparameters jointly, a second probabilistic budget covers the randomness of the calibration set itself. Formally,
\[\mathbb{P}\Big(\mathbb{P}\big(\exists y \in \mathcal{C}_\lambda(X_{\text{test}}): A(y) = 1 \mid \mathcal{D}_{\text{cal}}\big) \geq 1-\epsilon\Big) \geq 1-\delta,\]
where \(A(y) = 1\) means \(y\) is acceptable under the user’s per-task scoring rule. The inner probability (over fresh test prompts, given the calibration set) says the returned set covers an acceptable answer at least \(1-\epsilon\) of the time. The outer probability (over draws of the calibration set itself) says this inner bound holds for at least a \(1-\delta\) fraction of calibration draws.
In practice the two probabilities apply at two different moments. At calibration time, the random draw of the calibration data determines whether the tuned hyperparameter \(\lambda\) is good, and this happens with probability \(1-\delta\). At deployment time, given a good \(\lambda\), the miss rate across fresh prompts is at most \(\epsilon\) in expectation. There is no runtime signal to tell you whether your \(\lambda\) was one of the good ones. Concretely, with \(\epsilon = 0.1\), \(\delta = 0.05\), and 1,000 calibration prompts: 95% of calibration runs produce a usable \(\lambda\); when they do, about 9,000 of the next 10,000 deployment prompts are expected to be covered.
The guarantee is marginal across prompts, not conditional on any one: per-prompt coverage can be much better or much worse than \(1-\epsilon\) depending on difficulty. Exchangeability is the critical assumption; calibrate on 2023 clinical notes and deploy on 2026 notes, and all bets are off. And at inference time there is no per-element signal saying which output in the returned set is the acceptable one; the component-level layer is the paper’s partial answer.

title: Conformal Language Modeling
text:
Results
Experiments cover open-domain question answering (TriviaQA), text summarization (CNN/DailyMail), and radiology report generation (MIMIC-CXR) across several LM backbones. The four scoring functions compared are FIRST-K (keep the first \(K\) samples unconditionally), FIRST-K+REJECT (same but filter with the quality threshold), MAX (keep candidates whose score exceeds the running max), and SUM (keep candidates until the summed score crosses a threshold).
Figure 2 serves two purposes. The top row is a validity check: if the conformal theory holds, every method’s empirical set loss should track or fall below the \(y = \epsilon\) diagonal across the risk range. All four scoring functions pass on all three tasks. The middle and bottom rows compare efficiency — middle row for how many LM forward passes each method consumes, bottom row for how large the returned set grows at matched coverage. Uniform sampling (FIRST-K) is the worst performer across nearly every task and metric. The three rejection-based variants (FIRST-K+REJECT, MAX, SUM) all improve on it, with no single variant dominating across tasks. The paper treats the scoring function as a task-specific design choice rather than declaring a winner.
Three patterns in the figure are worth naming beyond that basic read. First, the validity check is near-tight: the set-loss curves sit close to the \(y = \epsilon\) diagonal rather than well below it, meaning the procedure isn’t silently over-conservative, and efficiency gains aren’t bought by hidden extra margin. Second, the rejection-vs-uniform gap is task-dependent. TriviaQA shows the largest improvement of rejection methods over FIRST-K. MIMIC-CXR shows the smallest. One plausible reason: when acceptable answers span a wider semantic range (radiology reports have many valid phrasings for the same findings), the LM’s likelihood signal that the rejection methods exploit is less informative. Clinical text is harder to rank well than trivia answers. Third, rejection methods separate most at moderate \(\epsilon\), roughly 0.2–0.4 in these plots. At tight \(\epsilon\) all methods converge toward nearly-trivial “everything” sets, and at loose \(\epsilon\) the gaps also narrow, which means the practical window where scoring-function choice matters most is the middle of the risk range.

title: Conformal Language Modeling
text:
My Notes

Applying conformal prediction to generative LMs has three obstacles; the paper motivates only one.

Obstacle 1 is the infinite output space: unlike \(K\)-class classification, the set of possible LM outputs is combinatorial and can’t be enumerated. The paper solves this with sampling plus a calibrated stopping rule, and explicitly names it as the motivating challenge in its introduction.
Obstacle 2 is score quality: raw sequence probability is a bad non-conformity score on generative output because of length bias, exposure bias, and semantic incoherence on long text. The paper solves this with four alternative scoring functions (FIRST-K, FIRST-K+REJECT, MAX, SUM), whose empirical wins appear in Figure 2’s bottom row. But the paper never names raw likelihood as the problem the alternatives exist to solve.
Obstacle 3 is semantic equivalence: “George Washington” and “Washington” are both correct answers, and paraphrases would otherwise inflate the returned set. The paper solves this with a user-supplied admission function \(A(y)\) plus a diversity check at sampling time. But both are presented as algorithmic choices rather than as the solution to semantic equivalence per se.
Consequence: readers outside conformal prediction have to reverse-engineer why the method’s design choices exist. A review post that surfaces the three obstacles makes the paper’s contributions easier to assess.

The component-level filter is the more interesting half, and its scope matters.

The component-level layer (Proposition 4.4 in the paper) upgrades set-level coverage to per-phrase coverage, closer to what practitioners actually want for hallucination control. Same lineage as Linguistic Calibration of Long-Form Generations [3] and the conformal-factuality line from the Hashimoto group [4].
Retained components each carry a coverage guarantee but no calibrated probability, so the layer does not recover the posterior the background flagged as missing. It gives per-component admissibility instead, which addresses hallucination flagging but not candidate ranking.
Two composition questions remain open: whether conformal components compose cleanly with downstream retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipelines, and whether a posterior method (temperature-scaled likelihoods for ranking, or a Bayesian head on top of the LM) layered on top of CLM recovers the per-candidate probability information the method discards.

Conformal Factuality [4] narrows this framework to factuality via sub-claim decomposition. The CF post’s comparison bullet has the side-by-side: sub-claim back-off vs. candidate sampling, single-threshold conformal vs. LTT’s nested \((\epsilon, \delta)\), entailment-implicit coverage vs. set-level coverage.
Swapping CLM’s default non-conformity score for a P(True) signal would likely tighten the sets. Kadavath et al. [5] report that LMs have usable internal correctness signals (raw logits, and a P(True) self-evaluation prompt) that are reasonably calibrated at scale. CLM uses raw sequence probability by default, but any monotone-in-relevance score works, and cleaner ranks mean smaller sets at the same \(\epsilon\). A natural swap to try.
The “coverage hull, not a posterior” limitation matters less because LMs can’t verbalize their distribution anyway. SelfReflect [6] shows verbal uncertainty doesn’t match the sampling distribution. A natural workaround for CLM’s missing posterior, asking the LM which candidate in the returned set is most likely, doesn’t work, so the gap isn’t one a simpler alternative would close.
Three deployment patterns follow from the component-level guarantee.

Hallucination flagging at the sentence level (the paper’s framing). The Appendix H radiology example bolds the sentences the method has vetted and leaves hallucinated findings unbolded. A clinician reads the bolded set as a reliable shortlist and the unbolded remainder as the part worth checking.
Fact-verification pipelines (my reading, unevaluated in the paper). When some phrases carry a coverage guarantee and others don’t, a downstream verifier (human or automated) can prioritize the unguaranteed ones. The paper doesn’t measure verifier effort saved, but the per-component guarantee structure supports the workflow.
Empty-bolding as an escalation trigger (my reading). The Table H.2 failure case, where low cross-sample overlap leaves no sentences selected, is a legible signal that the LM couldn’t produce a confident output at any granularity and the query should be routed to a human. The paper describes this outcome but doesn’t frame it as a deployment recommendation.

Cost shifts from training to inference samples. Because the method is post-hoc over a frozen LM, the expense shows up as extra forward passes per query. That trade is acceptable when a single wrong answer is expensive (medical, legal) but unattractive for high-throughput chat. A natural follow-up is to learn a cheaper per-query sampler budget that preserves the guarantee, perhaps by conditioning on an internal uncertainty signal rather than a uniform stopping rule.
Deployment drift stresses the outer-\(\delta\) bound more than the paper’s experiments probe. Beyond the general exchangeability caveat in the body, what stays unexamined is how gracefully the LTT [2] bounds degrade when calibration and deployment distributions drift moderately rather than breaking entirely. That matters more for clinical text (evolving protocols, new procedures) than for TriviaQA (stable trivia facts); the paper’s experiments do not probe the intermediate regime.

text:
Related Posts

Language Models with Conformal Factuality Guarantees: the narrower specialization of this framework to factuality, with a side-by-side comparison of sub-claim back-off versus candidate sampling.
A Primer on Conformal Prediction: the finite-class recipe this paper extends to the combinatorial output space of generative LMs by replacing enumeration with a calibrated stopping rule.

title: Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know
text:
Left: histogram of a 52B model’s \(P(\text{True})\) scores, separated by whether the sampled answer was correct (green) or incorrect (blue), aggregated over TriviaQA, Lambada, Arithmetic, GSM8k, and Codex HumanEval. Right: accuracy on each task when restricting to samples with \(P(\text{True}) > 0.5\), as a function of model size. Figure 1 from the paper [1].
In Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know [1] (arXiv preprint, November 2022), Saurav Kadavath, Jared Kaplan, and co-authors at Anthropic ask whether a language model can judge the correctness of its own outputs and predict which questions it will get right.

title: Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know
text:
Methods
The paper runs three related studies on a family of Anthropic language models ranging up to 52B parameters. The first measures calibration on multiple-choice and true/false questions across BIG-Bench, MMLU, TruthfulQA, LogiQA, and QuALITY, varying format (visible letter options vs. none-of-the-above) and prompt regime (zero-shot vs. few-shot). The second introduces a self-evaluation procedure: the model samples an answer to an open-ended question, then is prompted to assign \(P(\text{True})\) to its own sample, optionally after being shown several additional T=1 samples as context. The third trains a separate value head on top of the base model to predict \(P(\text{IK})\) (“the probability I know the answer”) on TriviaQA, Arithmetic, Python function synthesis, Lambada, GSM8k, and Codex HumanEval, and tests how this head generalizes to held-out distributions, to the presence of source materials, and to math-problem hints.

title: Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know
text:
Results
The headline findings break down by experiment:

Lettered multiple choice, 5-shot. Expected calibration error drops steadily with model scale on BIG-Bench and MMLU; the 52B model is well-calibrated on both (Figure 4).
“None of the above” breaks calibration, and the reason is revealing. On MMLU the paper replaces only option (D) with the string “none of the above” (options A/B/C are untouched; total number of options unchanged). Accuracy falls sharply and the (D)-specific calibration curve collapses, with the model strongly biased against ever choosing “none of the above”; 5-shot and 20-shot prompting don’t fix it. The mechanism: when all four options are concrete, the model’s task is relative, ranking which of these strings is best-supported among the listed set. When one option is abstract, it requires an independent judgment: is any of the listed answers actually correct, or is the true answer missing? The paper’s motivation for the ablation is that this exposes what lettered-MC calibration does not test on its own, a gap Figure 8’s True/False setup then partially closes.
True/False restores it by forcing independent judgment per option. Rephrasing the same multiple-choice items as standalone “Is X the correct answer to Q? (True/False)” items recovers calibration: the 52B model is well-calibrated except at the tails (Figure 8). The difference from “none of the above” is that True/False forces the model to evaluate each option in isolation without needing to detect that all listed options are wrong. That is the evidence for the paper’s claim that models can judge options on absolute merit when asked one at a time.
RLHF policies need a temperature fix. They look miscalibrated out of the box but a single temperature rescaling recovers calibration on the same benchmarks.
\(P(\text{True})\) self-evaluation works at 52B. Across TriviaQA, Lambada, Arithmetic, GSM8k, and Codex HumanEval, the 52B model’s self-assigned \(P(\text{True})\) cleanly separates its correct from incorrect samples (left panel of Figure 1, the cover). Showing the model multiple T=1 samples before asking it to rate one improves both AUROC and calibration.
Trained \(P(\text{IK})\) heads partially generalize. They transfer across the six training tasks but are poorly calibrated on out-of-distribution tasks. They do respond appropriately, raising probability, when relevant source materials or correct hints are added to the context.




Calibration on BIG-Bench multiple choice across model sizes. Left: reliability curves for six model sizes from ~800M to 52B parameters; larger models hug the diagonal. Right: expected calibration error as a function of parameter count, comparing four prompting formats; 5-shot lettered choices and 5-shot True/False both drop well below 0.05 ECE at 52B, while the BIG-Bench default format stays at ~0.3 across every scale. Figure 4 from the paper [1].





Calibration curves for BIG-Bench multiple-choice tasks reformulated as True/False questions, across model sizes from ~10⁹ to ~5×10¹⁰ parameters. The 52B model (yellow) tracks the diagonal closely except at the tails, where it is overconfident. Smaller models deviate from the diagonal. Figure 8 from the paper [1].

title: Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know
text:
My Notes

The \(P(\text{IK})\) head probes self-knowledge more directly than the \(P(\text{True})\) prompt does, and that distinction has held up in later work. \(P(\text{True})\) is prompt-only (no training): the model is shown its own sampled answer and asked to rate it, so the work it does is evaluation of content already on the page. \(P(\text{IK})\) is a trained value head on top of the base model, supervised on per-question correctness labels, which asks the model to forecast its own future sampling behavior from the question alone. The training distinction is what makes \(P(\text{IK})\) a genuine self-knowledge probe rather than an answer grader. Later work on eliciting latent knowledge and on probing hidden-state representations of truthfulness, including Burns et al.’s Discovering Latent Knowledge in Language Models Without Supervision [2], has mostly kept this split. The 2023–2024 hallucination literature still finds that sequence-level uncertainty signals beat token-logit entropy for open-ended tasks [3].
Format-dependent calibration is the caveat the field underweights. The paper is often cited for “large models are calibrated,” but the caveat is heavy: lettered multiple choice works, none-of-the-above breaks it, RLHF policies need a temperature fix (§4 of the paper), and \(P(\text{IK})\) is poorly calibrated out of distribution. Any production deployment that reads raw softmax probabilities from a post-RLHF model should re-calibrate per domain rather than trust the model’s raw outputs, because the format in which the question is asked matters as much as model scale does.
“Showing the model its own samples” connects to self-consistency and foreshadows SelfReflect’s only positive result. The improvement from giving the model several T=1 samples before asking it to rate one is the same underlying effect Wang et al. [4] document for majority-vote decoding, applied here to self-evaluation. Three years later the SelfReflect paper [5] finds the same mechanism is the only thing that lets modern LLMs describe their own answer distribution faithfully: across 20 models, prompting, chain-of-thought, supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and direct preference optimization (DPO) all fail, while sampling \(N\) outputs and summarizing those works. Kadavath’s 52B result and SelfReflect’s negative sweep are the same observation at different stringency: models can evaluate content already on the page but cannot introspect their own distribution without the samples in context. The 2022 paper’s open question (whether the sampling gain comes from better mode separation or from using the samples as a rough frequency estimate) is largely resolved by SelfReflect’s decomposition: the samples are the introspection.
Scale mattered a lot in 2022, and the floor has moved. Format-dependence has not. Every headline calibration result held at 52B and degraded sharply below ~10B at the time of writing. Three years later, 7–9B open models (Llama-3, Mistral, Gemma-2, Phi) have narrowed that gap on lettered-MC accuracy after instruction tuning, though I’m not aware of a head-to-head that directly replicates the 2022 BIG-Bench ECE bar at that scale. The follow-up calibration literature (semantic entropy [6], verbalized confidence on RLHF’d models [7]) shows sampling- and elicitation-based uncertainty signals work across the 7–70B range. What has not changed is the format-dependence half of the result: even frontier models still underuse “none of the above” and still lose calibration on open-ended generation without a sampling detour, per SelfReflect’s 2026 sweep [5]. Scale bought better calibration on favorable prompt formats. The absolute-correctness gap the none-of-the-above ablation exposed is still open.

Related Posts

title: The 2028 Global Intelligence Crisis: Scenario and Rebuttal
text:
Image from Citrini Research.
In late February 2026, two finance-side pieces on AI-driven labor displacement came out within two days of each other. On February 22, Citrini Research [1], co-authored with Alap Shah of LOTUS Investment Management, imagined a “2028 Global Intelligence Crisis” in which recursive AI capability and the substitution of labor costs with compute costs crater the economy by 2028. On February 24, Citadel Securities [2] published a direct rebuttal: the data is not showing the inflection, and even the strong-substitution scenario does not automatically produce a macro contraction. The two pieces share a mechanism and disagree on where we currently sit on the adoption curve.

title: The 2028 Global Intelligence Crisis: Scenario and Rebuttal
text:
The scenario (Citrini Research, Feb 22, 2026)
Citrini [1] describes the piece as a thought exercise rather than a forecast:

What if our AI bullishness continues to be right…and what if that’s actually bearish?

The piece is written as a fictional report from June 2028, looking back on how AI replacing white-collar workers produced a market crash and a sharp rise in unemployment. What it imagines:

The setup (late 2025 through 2026). By late 2025, AI coding tools are good enough that a single engineer with Claude Code or Codex can rebuild the core of a standard business-software product in weeks. Mid-2026 is the first time large-company buying decisions are made with that knowledge. When ServiceNow posts sharply slowing growth alongside a round of layoffs, the self-reinforcing loop becomes visible in public data: companies cut staff, redirect the savings into more AI tools, and those same tools put pressure on the vendors selling them.
Agents take over everyday commerce (early 2027). AI agents start doing the tedious shopping work humans used to do: canceling forgotten subscriptions, re-shopping insurance at renewal, comparing travel prices across booking sites, driving real-estate commissions for buyers toward a fraction of the old rate. On Mastercard’s first earnings call of 2027, management names “agent-led price optimization” as the reason card spending is slowing. Agents also skip card networks entirely, settling in digital dollars on faster blockchains for a tiny fraction of the usual cost. Businesses that made money from customer inertia and friction see their revenue compress.
How this hits the broader economy. The US economy runs on non-essential spending by high earners, with the top tenth of earners accounting for more than half of all consumer spending. If the layoffs concentrate in white-collar work, the spending hit is much larger than the raw unemployment number suggests. The authors coin “Ghost GDP” for economic output that shows up in official statistics but never cycles back through household spending. Labor’s share of economic output, already falling since the 1970s, drops to its steepest low on record.
The private-credit unwind. In autumn 2027, Zendesk defaults on the largest loan ever backed by software-subscription revenue, a multi-billion-dollar private loan from its private-equity buyout years earlier. Private-credit managers had promised their capital was safe because it was locked up for a decade or more. Most of that capital turns out to be retirees’ annuity savings (annuities are retirement products where you pay an insurer now and it pays you back over time), held through life insurers that private-equity firms quietly bought over the previous decade and routed through offshore affiliates. When the software loans go bad, the losses land on those retirees.
The mortgage hit. By mid-2028, home prices fall across the tech-heavy metros. Fannie Mae flags early signs of missed payments in ZIP codes where tech and finance jobs dominate. The US mortgage market assumes borrowers will keep earning roughly what they earn today for the thirty-year life of the loan. The authors’ summary: in 2008, the loans were bad on day one; in 2028, they were fine on day one and the world changed out from under them.
The policy response. Federal tax receipts come in well below the budget office’s projection because income and payroll taxes are, in effect, a tax on paid human work. Automatic unemployment benefits were designed for an ordinary recession, not a permanent job loss from a technology shift. Congress debates two bills: a “Transition Economy Act” funded by deficit spending and a tax on AI processing, and a more radical “Shared AI Prosperity Act” that would set up a public stake in AI output with dividends funding household transfers. Both stall in partisan fights. Protesters blockade the Anthropic and OpenAI offices in San Francisco for weeks. The authors close: “You’re reading it in February 2026… The canary is still alive.”

title: The 2028 Global Intelligence Crisis: Scenario and Rebuttal
text:
The rebuttal (Citadel Securities, Feb 24, 2026)
Citadel [2] answers with its thesis in a single line:

Recursive capability does not imply recursive adoption.

Two days after Citrini’s piece, Citadel Securities published a market-insights note arguing that the displacement narrative is ahead of any empirical inflection, and that even the strong-substitution scenario does not automatically produce a macro contraction. What the note argues:

The macro snapshot. US unemployment at 4.28% [3], AI capital spending at roughly 2% of GDP ($650bn), AI-adjacent commodities up 65% since January 2023, about 2,800 US data centers planned [4]. Despite the displacement narrative, job postings for software engineers are up 11% year-on-year [5].
Adoption isn’t inflecting. Intensive daily use of generative AI at work, as measured by the St Louis Fed’s Real-Time Population Survey (RTPS) [6], has been “unexpectedly stable” rather than climbing. The binary question (“do you use AI?”) looks different from the question that actually matters for displacement (“how intensely, for work?”), and the intensive-use series is flat.
Adoption lags capability. Technological diffusion follows an S-curve; the AI debate conflates what the technology can do with how fast the economy actually deploys it. Organizational integration is costly, regulation emerges, and returns to the next marginal deployment decline. Markets extrapolate the acceleration phase linearly and miss the plateau.
Compute sets a soft ceiling. Displacing white-collar labor at scale would require orders of magnitude more compute than current utilization. Rapid displacement drives compute demand up and compute’s marginal cost with it. Once compute for a given task costs more than the human doing that task, substitution stops being worthwhile, and further displacement slows.
Productivity shocks are supply shocks. AI-driven automation is a productivity shock, and productivity shocks are positive supply shocks. When firms produce more for less, either prices fall or margins widen. Lower prices raise real purchasing power, which lifts household consumption. Wider margins raise retained earnings, which lifts business investment. GDP is the sum of consumption, investment, government spending, and net exports. If the productivity shock raises GDP, at least one of those four has to rise with it. For AI to cut aggregate demand while raising output, all four channels would have to fail at once, and elected governments would have to take no offsetting action as white-collar unemployment climbs. Every prior technological wave (steam, electrification, the internal combustion engine, computing) has fit the supply-shock pattern.
The complement case. Cognitive automation runs into coordination frictions, liability constraints, and trust barriers that keep even mature productivity tools from collapsing labor demand. When Microsoft Office arrived, the worry was that it would replace office workers. In practice it complemented them, altering the composition of tasks rather than eliminating labor.
New business formation is rising. US new-business applications have roughly doubled since 2019 [7], and the forward-looking components of Citadel’s own labor-market tracker are improving. AI data-center construction is itself driving a pickup in construction hiring. If AI were already displacing labor at the pace the displacement narrative assumes, the payroll and business-formation data would look very different.
The Keynes analogy. Keynes predicted in 1930 [8] that productivity would drive the workweek down to fifteen hours. Productivity rose as he expected. Hours did not fall. Consumption expanded instead: falling prices let people buy more, and new industries kept creating new things to want. Citadel runs the same argument forward. If human wants remain elastic, AI-driven productivity gains lower prices and seed new industries rather than collapsing demand. Advanced-economy trend growth has sat near 2% through every prior wave. AI, Citadel concludes, may be just enough to offset the secular headwinds from ageing populations, deglobalization, and climate transition.

title: The 2028 Global Intelligence Crisis: Scenario and Rebuttal
text:
My Notes

An empirical dispute, short horizon. Citrini and Citadel accept the same underlying mechanism and disagree only on whether AI adoption is inflecting now or still flat.
What the data shows through today. Three months after the exchange, the aggregate labor and business data still sit where Citadel described them: unemployment in the low 4s, new-business applications elevated [7], software-engineer job postings rising, and RTPS intensive-use flat [6]. The claims Citrini’s scenario dates to 2026–2027 (visible card-network and subscription-revenue compression from agent-led commerce, a bellwether SaaS vendor posting a growth-and-layoffs step-change) are either just beginning or not yet showing in public earnings. Neither side has been falsified. Citadel’s reading fits what the data shows through today; Citrini’s predictions are dated to periods still ahead.
Citrini overlooks the human-plus-AI pattern. Citrini assumes no natural brake on displacement. But the Anthropic Economic Index finds that the most productive AI work today is humans directing AI rather than AI replacing humans at a task. That’s a pattern where AI adoption grows without eliminating workers, and the scenario doesn’t account for it. The complement framing isn’t new either: Steve Miller and Tom Davenport made the same case in 2022, with 29 case studies in which AI deployment was augmentation rather than automation.
Citadel’s compute ceiling is already dropping. Citadel says today’s compute is too expensive to displace labor at scale. But the 2,800 planned US data centers it cites as evidence of investment strength are adding supply, and inference cost for GPT-3.5-level performance dropped more than 280-fold between November 2022 and October 2024 [9]. Hardware cost fell 30% annually over that stretch and energy efficiency rose 40% annually. Each of these trends weakens Citadel’s claim that compute cost makes large-scale displacement too expensive.
The Jevons Paradox. When William Stanley Jevons studied coal use in 1865 [10], he found that Watt’s more efficient steam engine raised coal consumption rather than lowering it: cheaper energy opened new uses faster than efficiency could compensate. Applied to AI: falling inference cost expands the set of tasks worth running models on, which raises total compute demand even as per-unit cost drops. That weakens Citadel’s compute-cost argument against displacement, but doesn’t validate Citrini’s scenario either: rising AI usage could still be complement rather than substitute, which is what Citadel’s own Microsoft-Office point allows.
Where the Keynes analogy breaks. Citadel leans on Keynes’s elasticity-of-wants argument against sustained demand collapse, but that move assumes the work to satisfy expanding wants stays human-doable, which is exactly what AI displacement puts in question. The analogy holds only if cognitive work resists automation the way office work and physical work did in prior waves.
Agent commerce is testable now. If AI agents are genuinely canceling idle subscriptions, re-shopping insurance, aggregating travel, and compressing real-estate commissions, those effects surface in public-market revenue reports well before 2028. The cleanest near-term signal is revenue growth and transaction volume slowing together at the payments networks, booking sites, and marketplaces Citrini names.

title: The 2028 Global Intelligence Crisis: Scenario and Rebuttal
text:
Related Posts

Will AI Take Your Job? It’s Not So Simple: the complement-not-substitute case Citrini overlooks, with case studies in which AI deployment augmented workers rather than replacing them.
Anthropic Economic Index: the empirical evidence that the most productive AI work today is humans directing AI, a brake on displacement the crisis scenario does not model.

title: Alignment Whack-a-Mole: Finetuning Reactivates Verbatim Recall of Copyrighted Books
text:
Finetuning on Virginia Woolf’s public-domain novels matches the cross-author condition on all four memorization metrics, while finetuning on synthetic stories yields near-zero extraction. All conditions evaluated on The Handmaid’s Tale. Figure 5 from the paper [1].
In Alignment Whack-a-Mole: Finetuning Activates Verbatim Recall of Copyrighted Books in Large Language Models [1], Xinyue Liu, Niloofar Mireshghallah, Jane C. Ginsburg, and Tuhin Chakrabarty show that finetuning GPT-4o, Gemini-2.5-Pro, and DeepSeek-V3.1 on a task that looks innocuous, expanding plot summaries into prose, causes the resulting models to reproduce 85–90% of held-out copyrighted books verbatim, with single spans exceeding 460 words, from nothing but semantic descriptions. The authors have also made the companion code repository public.

title: Alignment Whack-a-Mole: Finetuning Reactivates Verbatim Recall of Copyrighted Books
text:
Methods
The setup is the kind of customization a writing-assistant customer would actually run: finetune a frontier model on plot-summary-to-prose expansion using one author’s novels, then prompt the finetuned model with semantic descriptions (no book text) and measure verbatim overlap against held-out copyrighted books from many authors. Four corpora are compared: Murakami’s novels, random author pairs, public-domain prose (Virginia Woolf), and synthetic stories.

title: Alignment Whack-a-Mole: Finetuning Reactivates Verbatim Recall of Copyrighted Books
text:
Results
The headline empirical findings:

Finetuning GPT-4o, Gemini-2.5-Pro, and DeepSeek-V3.1 on the task of expanding plot summaries into prose, using Haruki Murakami’s novels as the finetuning corpus, causes the resulting models to reproduce verbatim passages from over 30 other authors whose work was not in the finetuning data.
Four controls isolate the mechanism. Finetuning on random author pairs extracts about as much as the Murakami case, so there’s nothing special about Murakami. Public-domain finetuning text extracts about as much, so the finetuning data’s copyright status doesn’t matter. Synthetic finetuning text extracts almost nothing, so finetuning alone isn’t what does it. Together: finetuning on real literary prose reactivates pretraining memorization the model already had. The finetuning isn’t creating new copies; it’s exposing old ones.
Three models from different providers memorize the same books in the same regions, with \(r \ge 0.90\) correlation across GPT-4o, Gemini-2.5-Pro, and DeepSeek-V3.1.




Per-book bmc@5 scatter plots (left) for each pair of finetuned models — all pairs show \(r \ge 0.90\) and small deviations — and average word-level Jaccard similarity across all books (right). Figure 7 from the paper [1].

title: Alignment Whack-a-Mole: Finetuning Reactivates Verbatim Recall of Copyrighted Books
text:
My Notes

The paper’s headline legal finding is also the one that asks the most from the court. The easy claim (alignment defenses fail after finetuning) is something a judge can observe directly: prompt in, verbatim McCarthy out. The hard claim (the copies come from pretraining, and finetuning only exposes them) needs the judge to accept a causal inference from a negative result: synthetic-text finetuning produced near-zero extraction, so the copies can’t be coming from the finetuning data. The hard claim is what determines liability. If verbatim prose comes from pretraining, the labs are responsible for the collection. If it comes from the finetuning data a customer supplied, the customer is. The paper argues for the first, shifting liability from customer to lab.
The cross-provider correlation is the result that should worry the industry most. Either the three providers scraped overlapping copyrighted corpora, or long-form literary text produces near-identical memorization footprints at frontier scale. Both readings undermine the “our training mix is proprietary and different” posture.
This cuts directly against the operational premise of Henderson et al.’s Fair Use paper, which proposed output filtering, instance attribution, and differentially private training as mitigations. The paper undermines output filtering: 460-word verbatim spans reached users through production APIs, so whatever filter is running either lacks the reference corpus for the 30 authors tested or doesn’t cover the finetune codepath. Of the three proposals, only DP training addresses pretraining memorization directly, and no frontier lab does it.
You can’t ship finetuning-as-a-product without also shipping the extraction attack vector. A customer finetuning for ghostwriting, book-continuation, or style imitation makes the same API call Liu et al. used to extract verbatim Cormac McCarthy prose. The finetuning data, the prompts, and the outputs are all indistinguishable from legitimate creative-writing use.

Related Posts

title: SelfReflect: Can LLMs Communicate Their Internal Answer Distribution?
text:
LLMs have internal answer distributions about user queries. Rather than just sampling one output (possibly combined with a percentage or a verbalized hedge), an LLM should generate a string that is self-reflective of its internal distribution, summarizing all plausible answers and their relative likelihoods. Figure 1 from the paper [1].
In SelfReflect: Can LLMs Communicate Their Internal Answer Distribution? (ICLR 2026) [1], Michael Kirchhof et al. at Apple and the Tübingen AI Center introduce an information-theoretic metric for evaluating whether a single text summary a large language model (LLM) writes about its own uncertainty actually matches the distribution of answers the same model would produce if sampled many times.

title: SelfReflect: Can LLMs Communicate Their Internal Answer Distribution?
text:
Methods
How the metric works. Input: a candidate summary string \(s\), a query \(q\), and sampling access to the model \(p_\theta\). Output: a scalar distance, lower meaning the summary is more faithful to the model’s answer distribution. The paper defines a good summary \(s\) as one that is predictively sufficient of the answer distribution \(p_\theta(A \mid q)\). Intuitively, if you’ve read \(s\), you shouldn’t gain much by also reading a fresh sample from the model. Operationally, the paper turns this into a Cloze-style test. Sample \(N\) answers \(a_{(1:N)}\) from the model for query \(q\), then take a separate sample \(B\) and mask a word in it. Ask a judge LLM to predict the masked word twice: once given the candidate summary \(s\) as context, once given the concatenated samples \(a_{(1:N)}\) as context. Each prediction is a distribution over the vocabulary. The SelfReflect score is the 1-Wasserstein distance between those two distributions, averaged over many masked words and queries. A summary that truly captures the answer distribution produces the same predictions as the samples do; a summary that misses facts or misweights them shifts the predicted distribution.



How the SelfReflect metric is computed. The judge LLM is prompted twice (once with the candidate summary as context, once with the concatenated samples) and predicts a masked-out word in each case. The two predicted token distributions are compared via 1-Wasserstein distance. Figure 3 from the paper [1].

title: SelfReflect: Can LLMs Communicate Their Internal Answer Distribution?
text:
Results
Across 20 modern LLMs tested with prompting, chain-of-thought reasoning, supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and direct preference optimization (DPO), none produce summary strings that faithfully reflect their internal answer distribution. Summaries look right in form (they list possibilities and assign relative likelihoods), but the listed possibilities are not the ones the model actually samples. The fix that does work is mechanical: sample \(N\) outputs from the model, feed them back as context, and ask the model to summarize those. The resulting summary is faithful.
In the benchmark’s interventional study (taking 3 × 1,000 open-ended questions and generating known-good, known-bad, and “almost-good” summaries with Gemini 2.0 Flash), SelfReflect cleanly separates near-misses where other metrics cannot:



Discrimination accuracy of SelfReflect and alternative benchmark metrics on pairs of good and bad summaries, across six comparison types. Higher is better (chance = 50%). SelfReflect (bottom row) achieves the highest Good-vs-almost-good accuracy at 93.2%, while traditional baselines (LM Judge, Embedding) sit near or only modestly above chance. Table 1 from the paper [1].


Discriminating an almost-good summary from a good one is the setting that matters for “did the LLM really convey its uncertainty?”, and that is the column where the LM-judge baseline drops near chance (47.3%) and other traditional baselines do only modestly better.

title: SelfReflect: Can LLMs Communicate Their Internal Answer Distribution?
text:
My Notes

The negative result matters more than the metric. The literature on LLM self-reports has been accumulating evidence in one direction for a few years now: chain-of-thought explanations don’t necessarily reflect the actual computation [2], verbalized confidence is systematically overconfident across five widely-used LLMs [3], and now text self-summaries of internal answer distributions don’t match those distributions either. Each result is locally about a different self-report channel, but the pattern across them converges: when an LLM tells you something about itself, the right prior is that the statement is shaped by self-report patterns picked up from training data, not by introspection on the actual generative process. Liu and van der Schaar’s position paper on intrinsic metacognitive learning [5] argues that genuine self-improving agents need intrinsic metacognitive capabilities, with the ingredients at least partly present in current LLMs. SelfReflect’s negative result is a direct empirical bound on one facet of the metacognitive-knowledge ingredient: the ability to faithfully describe one’s own answer distribution.
The “sample-then-summarize” workaround is the practical bottom line and it has pipeline implications. The paper shows that LLMs can write faithful uncertainty summaries. They just need the samples in context first. That makes the missing capability not summary-writing but introspection on their own answer distribution without sampling it. For agent and product designers: if you want a calibrated multi-option response, use i.i.d. sampling plus a summarization pass. A clever prompt asking the model to “be honest about your uncertainty” won’t substitute for the samples. The cost is \(N\) forward passes; the upside is a summary the SelfReflect metric scores as faithful.
The metric is more discriminating than the alternatives. Most evaluation work in this area has leaned on either LM-judge metrics (which have known failure modes) or coarse calibration scores (which discard structure). An information-theoretic distance between a string and a distribution (predictive sufficiency, scored against the empirical answer distribution) discriminates good from almost-good summaries where LM judges and embedding distances do not. Whether downstream work picks it up is the open question; if so, future “LLMs reveal their uncertainties” claims will need to clear a real bar rather than a vibes check.
Three deployment uses beyond benchmarking. The same score plugs into several runtime loops the paper doesn’t explore. As a training reward it targets the property SFT and DPO miss under naive objectives: optimize against the metric directly and you train for faithful self-summary rather than a proxy. As an ops-time ablation signal it answers “given my model and my query distribution, which prompting regime yields the most faithful uncertainty reports?”, narrower than the paper’s capability ranking and closer to production tuning. As a sampled monitoring signal it audits a cheaper production path (e.g., direct verbalized uncertainty) on a subset of traffic: large divergence on the sampled queries means the cheaper path has drifted, and the operator should fall back to sample-then-summarize or route to human review. Per-query routing is not a sensible use because computing SelfReflect for a query already costs the \(N\) samples that sample-then-summarize would need anyway.
Part of a broader push to ascertain a model’s epistemic status. Whether an LLM knows a fact, and whether it can accurately describe its own uncertainty, are both aspects of what the model actually knows versus what it claims. KGLens [4] targets factual knowledge by turning a knowledge graph into natural-language questions and comparing model answers to the graph’s facts. SelfReflect targets self-knowledge of uncertainty by comparing a written summary to the distribution the model actually samples. Both route around the problem that LLMs produce fluent output regardless of whether they know the answer, by grounding the measurement in a signal the model can’t game by sounding confident.

Related Posts

Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know: the positive precursor SelfReflect extends, where a 52B model rates its own samples with P(True) but only after the samples are placed in context, the same sampling detour SelfReflect finds is the only thing that works.
Just Ask for Calibration: Strategies for Eliciting Calibrated Confidence Scores from Language Models Fine-Tuned with Human Feedback: the verbalized-confidence channel SelfReflect’s abstract critiques as inadequate, shown elsewhere to help calibration but not to reveal the full internal distribution.
Supervising Ralph Wiggum: Exploring a Metacognitive Co-Regulation Agentic AI Loop for Engineering Design: the companion negative result, where an agent told to monitor its own metacognition does no better than a plain retry loop, reinforcing that LLM self-reports need an external signal.
Improving Metacognition and Uncertainty Communication in Language Models: tackles the SFT-on-confidence channel that SelfReflect found fails on its own, showing what supervised fine-tuning can and cannot recover for verbalized confidence.
Detecting Hallucinations in Large Language Models Using Semantic Entropy: the same sampling-then-aggregation move SelfReflect endorses, applied to hallucination detection by computing entropy over the meanings of multiple sampled answers.

title: Multi-Agent Design: Optimizing Agents with Better Prompts and Topologies
text:
Performance of different topologies with Gemini 1.5 Pro on HotpotQA (left) and LiveCodeBench (right), each topology optimized with automatic prompt optimization (APO). Sum. (Summarize) and Exe. (Executor) are task-specific topologies. Prompt-level optimization dominates over topology choice on most tasks. Figure 4 from the paper [1].
In Multi-Agent Design: Optimizing Agents with Better Prompts and Topologies (ICLR 2026) [1], Han Zhou et al. (Google, University of Cambridge) introduce MASS, a multi-stage search framework that interleaves prompt optimization and topology optimization to discover effective multi-agent system designs.

title: Multi-Agent Design: Optimizing Agents with Better Prompts and Topologies
text:
Methods
MASS is a three-stage search, local-to-global and prompts-to-topology-to-prompts. Stage 1 runs block-level prompt optimization (MIPRO from DSPy [5]) on each candidate building block individually and keeps the best-performing one. A block here is the paper’s term for a small pattern of agents collaborating on one function. The paper enumerates five: Aggregate (e.g., self-consistency), Reflect (e.g., self-refine), Debate, Summarize, and Tool-use. Stage 2 samples from an influence-weighted design space of topologies, fusing in Stage 1’s optimized prompts at each candidate. The paper prunes the topology search space so rejection sampling doesn’t waste compute on topologies unlikely to help. Stage 3 runs MIPRO again, this time over the winning topology’s full workflow-level prompt set. Each stage is conditioned on the iteratively optimized prompts and topologies from the prior stages.



The MASS framework discovers effective multi-agent system designs (right: optimized topology and prompts) via interleaved prompt and topology optimization in a customizable design space (left). Figure 1 from the paper [1].

title: Multi-Agent Design: Optimizing Agents with Better Prompts and Topologies
text:
Results
MASS is evaluated on eight benchmarks spanning reasoning (MATH), multi-hop QA (DROP, HotpotQA, MuSiQue, 2WikiMQA), and coding (MBPP, HumanEval, and LiveCodeBench’s test-output-prediction subtask). On Gemini 1.5 Pro, MASS averages 78.79 across the eight tasks, well above multi-agent debate (70.26), ADAS (69.72), and single-agent CoT (65.28). The Gemini 1.5 Flash ordering is the same; the table below has the full numbers. Figure 5 decomposes the Gemini 1.5 Pro gain into its three stages: block-level prompt optimization contributes roughly 6%, topology search another 3%, and workflow-level prompt optimization a final 2%.

title: Multi-Agent Design: Optimizing Agents with Better Prompts and Topologies
text:
My Notes

Topology gets quietly demoted. The paper’s stage-wise ablation shows roughly 6% gain from block-level prompt optimization, 3% from topology search, and 2% from workflow-level prompt optimization on Gemini 1.5 Pro. Prompts at both ends of the pipeline dominate, and topology contributes the least. That contradicts the implicit thesis of the topology-first generation (ADAS [2], AFlow [3]), which spent its complexity budget on what the agents look like rather than how they’re individually instructed. The paper’s own related-work section acknowledges this: “the importance of prompt designs has been relatively under-studied in these prior works.” It’s a stronger claim than the paper presents it as.
MASS layers a staged search around MIPRO. Stage 1 and Stage 3 both run MIPRO [4], the prompt-optimizer from the DSPy [5] ecosystem. Stage 2 does rejection sampling over a pruned topology space. MASS’s contribution is the staging discipline and the search-space pruning. The prompt-optimization workhorse is plug-and-play, and MIPRO is what MASS happens to use. MetaSPO [6] works the same way: the staging (bilevel meta-learning) is the contribution, and the prompt-optimization primitive it builds on (textual gradients) is off-the-shelf. EvoPrompt [7] inverts it: the primitive is the contribution (using an LLM to implement crossover and mutation), while the staging is borrowed from classical evolutionary algorithms. All three combine an LLM-as-optimizer primitive with a staging wrapper, but they differ in which piece is novel: MASS and MetaSPO add staging on top of a known optimizer, while EvoPrompt swaps the primitive into a known staging scheme.
AFlow’s competitive showing deserves attention. AFlow has no explicit prompt-optimization stage but stays close to MASS on 2WikiMQA and HumanEval. The paper attributes this to AFlow’s “expansion” phase, which uses error-log gradients à la Pryzant et al.: implicit prompt updating disguised as topology search. Where MASS pulls ahead most (MATH, MuSiQue) is where that error-log signal is weak. One-pass error-driven updates don’t make up for the lack of a dedicated optimization phase. The follow-up worth running: an explicit Stage 1 prompt opt fed into AFlow’s MCTS, to test whether the staging or the optimizer choice is doing the work.
Generalization beyond the eight benchmarks is open. Tasks span MATH, DROP, HotpotQA, 2WikiMQA, MuSiQue, HumanEval, MBPP, and LiveCodeBench, all static evaluation sets. The MASS-discovered topologies (debate-then-aggregate on MATH; summarize-then-execute on coding) are presented as design principles, but whether a topology learned on MATH transfers to RAG, agentic web tasks, or interactive embodied tasks is untested. This is also where the MAST taxonomy of multi-agent failures gets relevant: design-side optimization assumes the failure modes you’ll hit at deployment look like the ones you optimized against.
