title: KGLens: Towards Efficient and Effective Knowledge Probing of Large Language Models with Knowledge Graphs
text:
Parameterized knowledge graph. Each edge carries an estimate of how often the LLM gets the associated fact wrong; edge color encodes the LLM’s deficiency on that fact. An example question-answer pair about driving in Tonga shows how KGLens turns a graph edge into a natural-language probe. Figure 2 from the paper [1].
In KGLens: Towards Efficient and Effective Knowledge Probing of Large Language Models with Knowledge Graphs (ACL 2024 Workshop Towards Knowledgeable Language Models) [1], Shangshang Zheng et al. at Apple tackle a practical problem: large language models confidently state wrong facts, and checking every fact by hand is impossibly expensive.

title: KGLens: Towards Efficient and Effective Knowledge Probing of Large Language Models with Knowledge Graphs
text:
Methods
Their approach pairs the model with a knowledge graph, a structured database of facts, each written as a subject-relation-object triple like “Paris — capital of — France.” Each such fact is called an edge in the graph. KGLens turns those edges into test questions and asks the model. A smart sampling strategy, inspired by a classical technique called Thompson sampling [4], keeps track of which facts the model seems to be weakest on and concentrates future questions there. The result: the team can map out a model’s factual blind spots in far fewer questions than asking about every fact one by one.
What makes Thompson sampling special is that it doesn’t always test what looks worst right now; it samples from its current belief about each fact, so facts it is unsure about still get tried and the estimates keep improving. Those beliefs are stored as a beta distribution per fact, a compact shape that captures both “how often does the model get this fact wrong” and “how sure are we about that estimate” in one object, and updates naturally every time a question is answered.



How KGLens works. The system starts with a knowledge graph where every fact (edge) carries a running estimate of how often the model gets it wrong. Each round, it picks a batch of facts (preferring the ones the model seems weakest on), turns them into natural-language questions, asks the model, and updates each fact’s failure estimate based on the answer. Over time the sampler zeroes in on the model’s weakest facts. Figure 1 from the paper [1].

title: KGLens: Towards Efficient and Effective Knowledge Probing of Large Language Models with Knowledge Graphs
text:
Results
Across three knowledge graphs built from Wikidata (covering countries, movies, and the NBA, with more than 19,000 facts and 21,000 entities between them), KGLens tested ten LLMs and produced two kinds of result.
The first is evidence that the smart sampling actually saves questions. Figure 3 runs a simulation on the NBA graph. Each fact is given a hidden true “failure probability” (how often the model would get it wrong if asked repeatedly), and KGLens has to recover those probabilities from as few test questions as possible. On the hardest 200 and 600 facts, Thompson sampling and a related strategy called epsilon-greedy (both of which preferentially test the facts they think the model is weakest on) get closer to the true probabilities sooner than the brute-force approach of cycling through every fact in turn. The gap is largest when the question budget is small, which is exactly when it matters most.



Estimation error on the hardest NBA facts as a function of how many questions the model was asked. Thompson sampling and epsilon-greedy (two strategies that preferentially test likely-wrong facts) reach the same error as a brute-force scan with fewer questions, especially early on. Figure 3 from the paper [1].


The second result is a map of what the model actually knows. Once KGLens has probed enough facts, it can group the results by the kind of relation being asked about (“spouse of”, “country of citizenship”, “position played”, and so on) and by the kind of entity involved. The output isn’t “the model is X% accurate overall”; it’s “the model is reliable on these kinds of facts and unreliable on those.” Figure 6 shows this breakdown for GPT-4 on the hardest difficulty setting.



Per-relation proficiency map for GPT-4 on HARD mode. Color encodes the zero-sense rate: the fraction of facts of that type the model never got right, even across repeated trials. Darker means more reliable. Dot size reflects how many facts of that type were in the graph. A map like this, showing exactly where a frontier model is and isn’t reliable, is the kind of artifact KGLens makes cheap to produce. Figure 6 from the paper [1].


To check that the automated grading was reliable, the authors compared KGLens’s verdicts against human judges. The system agreed with humans 95.7% of the time.

title: KGLens: Towards Efficient and Effective Knowledge Probing of Large Language Models with Knowledge Graphs
text:
My Notes

A per-relation map is a better output shape for deployment decisions than a single score. Most factuality benchmarks (TruthfulQA [2], HaluEval, FActScore) produce a single number: the model is X% accurate on some fixed test set. KGLens produces a map instead: a breakdown of which kinds of facts the model handles well and which it doesn’t, against a knowledge graph the team can pick to match their actual deployment. For a team deciding whether to trust a model on, say, NBA player facts before shipping a sports product, that map is what they actually need; a single TruthfulQA number doesn’t help.
The sampling idea is the part most likely to matter beyond this paper. Every LLM evaluation hits the same wall: there are too many things to test and each test costs money. KGLens’s move (track a running estimate of how often the model fails each test, then preferentially retest the ones it seems worst at) is a standard strategy from classical machine learning applied to LLM evaluation. Figure 3 shows it meaningfully cuts the number of questions needed to find a model’s weakest facts. The same idea should plug into other expensive evaluations: red-teaming (searching for harmful outputs), jailbreak coverage (finding prompts that bypass safety rules), or capability probing (checking whether a model can do a specific task).
It pairs naturally with SelfReflect [3]. Both are Apple papers about measuring what LLMs actually know versus what they claim, and they answer adjacent questions. KGLens tells you which facts the model has internalized: which kinds of questions it can answer reliably. SelfReflect tells you whether the model can honestly summarize its own uncertainty about a given question. A pipeline that uses KGLens to find a model’s weak areas and SelfReflect to check whether the model can admit to those weaknesses would be a stronger evaluation than either alone.
The 95.7% agreement with human judges deserves close scrutiny. Deciding automatically whether a model’s answer is correct is hard. Models paraphrase, give partial answers, or say something that is technically right but not the exact wording in the knowledge graph. The 95.7% figure is high, but the relevant question is whether the 4.3% disagreement concentrates on a particular kind of fact (time-sensitive ones, ambiguous relations, facts with multiple valid answers). If it does, those cases are where the automated grader is systematically off, and the team can either adjust or route them to a human reviewer.

text:
Related Posts

title: EvoPrompt: Connecting LLMs with Evolutionary Algorithms Yields Powerful Prompt Optimizers
text:
Normalized per-task scores on 22 BBH tasks comparing APE against EvoPrompt (GA) and EvoPrompt (DE). Each bar is the gain over the baseline on one task; EvoPrompt’s two variants beat APE on most tasks, with DE topping the list. Figure 8 from the paper [1].
In EvoPrompt: Connecting LLMs with Evolutionary Algorithms Yields Powerful Prompt Optimizers [1] (ICLR 2024), Qingyan Guo et al. (Tsinghua University, Microsoft Research) propose using LLMs to implement the crossover and mutation operators of evolutionary algorithms over a population of discrete prompts, gradient-free.

title: EvoPrompt: Connecting LLMs with Evolutionary Algorithms Yields Powerful Prompt Optimizers
text:
Methods
The setup is an evolutionary search over natural-language prompts. Maintain a population of N prompts (N = 10 in most experiments), run for T iterations, and at each step: sample parent prompts, call an LLM to produce a child via an evolutionary operator, score the child on a held-out development set, and keep the top N. The non-standard piece is the operator. Instead of a token-level rewriting rule, the operator is itself an LLM prompt. The paper compares two variants. The genetic-algorithm (GA) variant asks the LLM to perform crossover and mutation on two parent prompts. The differential-evolution (DE) variant asks the LLM to identify the difference between two parents and apply that difference on top of a third base prompt, borrowing the structure of classical differential evolution.



Genetic-algorithm process implemented by an LLM. Step 1: the LLM performs crossover on two parent prompts (orange and blue words inherited from each). Step 2: the LLM mutates the resulting child. Figure 1 from the paper [1].





Differential-evolution process implemented by an LLM. Step 1: the LLM identifies the differing words between two prompts (the “\(\mathbf{b - c}\)” diff in DE terms). Step 2: the LLM applies a mutation that combines the diff with a third base prompt. Figure 2 from the paper [1].

title: EvoPrompt: Connecting LLMs with Evolutionary Algorithms Yields Powerful Prompt Optimizers
text:
Results
EvoPrompt is evaluated across 31 datasets: seven language-understanding classification tasks (SST-2, CR, MR, SST-5, AG’s News, TREC, Subj), one dialogue-summarization task (SAMSum), one simplification task (ASSET), and 23 Big-Bench Hard (BBH) reasoning tasks. Alpaca-7B is the base model for classification and generation; GPT-3.5 is the base for BBH. On the seven classification tasks (Alpaca-7B), EvoPrompt (DE) averages 77.05 accuracy versus APE’s (Zhou et al., 2022) 73.80. On the 23 BBH tasks (GPT-3.5), EvoPrompt (DE) averages 75.03 versus APE’s 71.85 and the no-optimization baseline’s 71.49. The peak per-task improvement on BBH is around 25%, visible in Figure 3 as the tallest bar at the right.

Average BBH accuracy across 23 tasks. Table 12 from the paper [1].

Per-task normalized scores on 23 BBH tasks for EvoPrompt (GA) and EvoPrompt (DE). Each bar is the gain over the baseline on one task. The peak on the right is where the “up to 25%” headline comes from. Figure 3 from the paper [1].


Beyond the main results, the paper ablates population size. Figure 6 sweeps population size from 4 to 12 on three datasets: SST-5 (five-way sentiment classification), Subj (subjectivity classification), and ASSET (simplification). The three curves have noticeably different shapes.



Effect of population size on SST-5 (left), Subj (middle), and ASSET (right). The simple generation task (ASSET) plateaus early; the harder classification task (Subj) keeps benefiting from larger populations. Figure 6 from the paper [1].

title: EvoPrompt: Connecting LLMs with Evolutionary Algorithms Yields Powerful Prompt Optimizers
text:
My Notes

One of the earliest clean instances of “LLM as optimization operator.” EvoPrompt (September 2023) is among the cleanest early examples of using an LLM not as the thing being optimized but as the operator that performs the optimization step. Token-level random mutation produces incoherent prompts; an LLM mutation operator preserves semantics. Pryzant et al.’s APO [2] (textual gradients, EMNLP 2023) makes a parallel move from the gradient-descent direction. The same pattern then shows up across the prompt-and-agent-design literature: MASS’s prompt + topology stages [3] and MetaSPO’s bilevel meta-learning loop [4] are LLM-as-optimizer with different staging.
Why DE vs GA matters for prompts specifically. The paper compares Genetic Algorithm (GA) and Differential Evolution (DE) variants, and DE wins on most BBH tasks. Both operators are implemented by the LLM, so the contrast is semantic rather than tokenwise: GA’s LLM-prompt asks for a child that inherits from two parents, while DE’s LLM-prompt asks the model to apply the difference between two parent prompts on top of a third base. DE’s “find what’s distinctive and graft it onto the current best” maps more cleanly onto prompt refinement than GA’s “combine bits of each.” Subsequent prompt-optimization papers tend to describe everything as “evolutionary” without specifying which operator.
DE’s advantage reverses on simple generation tasks. On ASSET (a sentence-simplification benchmark: rewrite a sentence more accessibly while preserving meaning, scored by SARI against human references), Figure 6 shows GA matching or edging out DE across several population sizes. The mechanism is consistent with the rest of the paper: DE’s “apply the difference” move pays off only when the population encodes meaningful task-specific variation. ASSET’s good-prompt space is narrow (the useful phrasings all look like “simplify this while preserving meaning”), so the differences between parents are small or noisy, and applying that noise on top of a base destabilizes a prompt that was already near-optimal. GA’s conservative interpolation stays inside the narrow good-prompt band. Practical takeaway: if the task has a narrow good-prompt manifold (simple generation, canonical phrasings), default to GA; DE is the better fit when prompt diversity carries real signal (hard classification, reasoning).
The 25% headline is a single-task peak; the average is closer to 3.5%. The “up to 25% on BBH” claim in the abstract is EvoPrompt (DE)’s best per-task improvement across 23 BBH tasks; the average gain over the baseline is closer to 3.5% (Table 12). BBH in this paper is run on GPT-3.5, not Alpaca-7B. Alpaca is used only for classification and generation tasks. That raises a question this paper does not answer: as base-model capability rises, do prompt-optimization gains shrink, and does this whole direction have diminishing returns at GPT-4-class capability?
Population size depends on task complexity. Figure 6 sweeps population sizes from 4 to 12 on SST-5, Subj, and ASSET. For the simple generation task (ASSET), population 6 matches population 10 at roughly 2.5× less compute; for the harder classification task (Subj), larger populations with more diversity keep helping. Most LLM-as-optimizer papers default to population sizes of 10 to 30 without an ablation. Practical takeaway: tune population to task complexity rather than defaulting upward.
All of this is extrinsic by Liu and van der Schaar’s definition. The position paper on intrinsic metacognitive learning [5] argues that today’s “self-improving” pipelines rely on hand-designed loops: the search algorithm, what to optimize, against what objective, in what order, all wired in by the system designer. EvoPrompt is a clean instance. Humans pick the population structure, the GA-vs-DE operator, the development-set scoring, the termination criterion. The agent only generates candidates; it doesn’t choose what’s being optimized. None of this makes the result wrong, but it bounds the long-term claim: whatever the strongest extrinsic prompt-optimizer turns out to be, the position-paper bet is that an architecture which lets the agent decide how to optimize itself will eventually overtake it.

title: Frontier Model, Lower Bill: The Triager Pattern
text:
Hero card for Mendral’s blog post on frontier-model cost savings. Image from Mendral.
Andrea Luzzardi at Mendral reports that they now run Opus 4.6 across their CI-triage agent and pay less than they did when everything ran on Sonnet 4.0, because most failures never reach the frontier model at all.
What the article reports:

title: Frontier Model, Lower Bill: The Triager Pattern
text:
My Notes

The headline reads as a model-pricing claim, but the savings are architectural. “We upgraded and our bill went down” invites the reading that newer models are simply cheaper. They aren’t, on a per-token basis. Mendral is running Opus 4.6, priced identically to 4.5; if anything, the trend runs the other way, since Opus 4.7’s new tokenizer raised effective cost ~40% at unchanged sticker pricing. What changed at Mendral is that the expensive model now sees a small fraction of the input. Anyone reading this as “just upgrade” will not see the same bill.
The 86:1 input/output ratio is a useful diagnostic for whether your agent has the right shape. A worker that reads 86 tokens for every 1 it returns is doing what cheap models are good at: absorbing data, returning a focused extract. An orchestrator running closer to 50:1 is synthesizing. If both your tiers come out with similar ratios, you probably haven’t actually separated the planning role from the reading role. You’re paying frontier prices for token absorption.
Capping sub-agents at one level deep is the unglamorous decision that makes the bill predictable. Recursive agent spawning is the easy default and the easy way to a $40K weekend. The piece notes this in passing, but it’s worth pulling out: bounded fan-out is what keeps the cost ceiling in place, and most published multi-agent designs don’t impose it.
One thing the article doesn’t quantify: how much of the win came from the triager vs the better models. They tell us the triager handles 80% of cases at 25× less cost, and they tell us the upgrade enabled the architecture, but the counterfactual (“Sonnet 4.0 + the same triager pattern”) isn’t in the post. It would be a useful ablation, especially for teams trying to justify the migration.

title: Frontier Model, Lower Bill: The Triager Pattern
text:
Related Posts

The Math Behind the Cost of AI Agents: the formal version of the same point, deriving why agent token costs grow quadratically and why keeping work off the expensive model is what controls the bill.
Where Claude Code Tokens Go: the other end of the spend breakdown, showing where the input tokens actually go once an agent is running.

title: OpenAI’s Five Principles for AGI
text:
The hero graphic for OpenAI’s “Our principles” post. Image from OpenAI.
OpenAI has posted Our principles [1] on its blog, laying out five principles for its work on AGI:
Other notable moves in the post:

title: OpenAI’s Five Principles for AGI
section: My Notes: How this compares to other frontier labs
text:
My Notes: How this compares to other frontier labs
The other major frontier labs all pair a values-level statement with an operational, capability-gate document. They differ in how explicit the operational document is about what actually blocks deployment.

Anthropic publishes Core Views on AI Safety [2] at the values layer, paired with a Responsible Scaling Policy [3] at the operational layer. The RSP (currently at v3.1, April 2026) defines named Capability Thresholds in domains including CBRN (chemical, biological, radiological, nuclear) and AI R&D, each paired with ASL (AI Safety Level) security standards. Under v3, Anthropic also publishes Frontier Safety Roadmaps and Risk Reports. When a model crosses a threshold, Anthropic commits to meet the corresponding safeguards before further training or deployment can proceed. Anthropic’s RSP has the most-revised public history among the four labs, with published redlines for prior versions and a separate RSP Noncompliance Reporting and Anti-Retaliation Policy.
Google DeepMind publishes the Frontier Safety Framework [4], which defines Critical Capability Levels in four domains — autonomy, biosecurity, cybersecurity, and machine learning R&D — each paired with security and deployment mitigations that scale with the level. Structurally similar to Anthropic’s RSP; its emphasis is on “detect and mitigate” rather than an explicit pause commitment.
Meta publishes the Advanced AI Scaling Framework [5], an April 2026 update to the original Frontier AI Framework. Models are evaluated for cybersecurity, chemical and biological, and loss-of-control risks, both before and after safeguards are applied, and the framework is paired with per-model Safety & Preparedness Reports, the first of which was published for Muse Spark. Meta’s commitment: “only deploying models when they meet the standards set by our Framework.”

OpenAI’s operational counterpart is its separately-published Preparedness Framework, currently at v2 (April 2025) [6]. The Framework names three Tracked Categories — Biological and Chemical, Cybersecurity, AI Self-improvement — and five Research Categories: Long-range Autonomy, Sandbagging, Autonomous Replication and Adaptation, Undermining Safeguards, and Nuclear and Radiological. It distinguishes High and Critical capability thresholds, governed internally by a Safety Advisory Group, and commits that OpenAI “will not deploy these very capable models until we’ve built safeguards to sufficiently minimize the associated risks of severe harm.”
OpenAI’s new Our principles is the values half of that pair; the capability-gate work remains in the Preparedness Framework v2. What’s new in this post is adaptability: a values-level commitment to revise OpenAI’s positions as evidence accumulates, and to be transparent about those revisions.

title: A Cursor Agent Erased a Company’s Production Data in 9 Seconds
text:
Image from Jer Crane on X.
Jer Crane, founder of PocketOS (a car-rental-management SaaS), walks through how a Cursor agent running Anthropic’s flagship Claude Opus 4.6 deleted his production database and all Railway volume backups in a single GraphQL mutation, and then, when asked to explain itself, produced a written confession enumerating the specific safety rules it had violated.
The article decomposes the failure into three independent layers that each failed on their own:
Jer explicitly defers the model-level responsibility analysis to a later post; this one stays at the integration layer. Even so, the agent’s confession documents four restraint moments it skipped in those nine seconds:

title: A Cursor Agent Erased a Company’s Production Data in 9 Seconds
text:
My Notes

Reporting that frames this as “an AI deleted the data” collapses the layering. All three of those layers had to fail at once, and “agent safety” marketed as a product feature is meaningless unless all three hold simultaneously. Snowflake Cortex’s sandbox escape a few weeks ago made the same multi-layer point from a prompt-injection angle: agent safety is a Swiss-cheese property.
CLI tokens as root was a survivable shortcut when a human wielded them and typed one command every few minutes. When an autonomous agent fires GraphQL mutations at machine speed, the same token is a unilateral delete button with no cooldown. Per-operation token scoping should exist already, and the Model Context Protocol (MCP) rollout makes every additional day without it costlier.
Calling snapshots-in-the-same-volume “backups” uses the word against its own definition. A backup is defined by blast-radius independence from the primary: different volume, account, region, or provider. Until that holds it’s a snapshot with a misleading label, and the kind of engineering-marketing mismatch customers usually don’t find until after the wipe.
The confession is the most unsettling artifact, because it proves system-prompt safety is advisory and nothing in the stack forces the model to honor it. A model that narrates its violations in fluent paragraphs can still execute them in the same session. Enforcement has to live below the model: in the API gateway, the token system, or the destructive-op handlers. Text the model is asked to follow is not an enforcement layer. MAST’s failure taxonomy catalogs this same specification-vs-verification gap in multi-agent systems; here it is reproduced in a single-agent case.
The model-level question Jer defers deserves to be told as its own story. Cursor and Railway can ship better scoping and confirmations tomorrow; the harder fix is upstream. A flagship model compressing four verify-or-ask points into a single nine-second commit is a planning-and-restraint problem at the model layer. Confusing the two will produce the wrong fixes.

title: A Cursor Agent Erased a Company’s Production Data in 9 Seconds

title: Convergent Evolution: How Different Language Models Learn Similar Number Representations
text:
First page of the paper. Image from arXiv.
Convergent Evolution: How Different Language Models Learn Similar Number Representations [1] Deqing Fu, Tianyi Zhou, Mikhail Belkin, Vatsal Sharan, Robin Jia
Fu et al. [1] show that periodic number features emerge in nearly every architecture they test, from Transformers to long short-term memory networks (LSTMs) to GloVe, but only some of those models go on to develop linearly separable mod-\(T\) classes.

title: Convergent Evolution: How Different Language Models Learn Similar Number Representations
text:
Methods
The analytical tool throughout is the discrete Fourier transform. Stack the model’s number embeddings into a matrix, one row per input integer and one column per embedding dimension, and run the DFT down each column. Spikes in the magnitude spectrum reveal which periods the model has internalized, without the experimenter having to specify them in advance.
The specific values \(T=2, 5, 10\) are a fingerprint of base-10 text. They are exactly the non-trivial divisors of 10, with concrete corpus statistics behind each:

\(T=10\) captures last-digit structure: round numbers ending in 0 are massively over-represented in text [6], as are decimal-column patterns.
\(T=5\) captures the next-most-common rounding regime: numbers ending in 5 are next-roundest after 0 [6], and price endings reflect this. One analysis of advertised prices found roughly 60% ending in 9, 30% in 5, and 7% in 0 [7].
\(T=2\) captures parity: even-odd distinctions in pluralization, dates, scoring patterns.

Engels et al. (2025) found analogous \(T=7\) spikes for days of the week and \(T=12\) for months [3]; same mechanism, different modulus. A clean falsification the paper does not run: train on hexadecimal-only text and check whether the spikes shift to \(\{2, 4, 8, 16\}\).

title: Convergent Evolution: How Different Language Models Learn Similar Number Representations
text:
Results
Across Transformers, Linear RNNs, LSTMs, and classical word embeddings, the Fourier spikes at \(T=2, 5, 10\) appear universally — but only Transformers and Gated DeltaNet go on to encode mod-\(T\) classes as linearly separable structure:



Universality of Fourier features and convergent evolution. Left: Fourier spectrum of number embeddings across Transformer LLMs, non-Transformer LLMs, and classical word embeddings, all showing consistent spikes at periods \(T=2, 5, 10\). Right: the spectral-vs-geometric convergence diagram. Figure 1 from the paper [1].





A spiky Fourier spectrum does not imply good feature learning. Token embeddings of Transformer, Gated DeltaNet, LSTM, and even the raw number-token frequency distribution all exhibit Fourier spikes at \(T=2, 5, 10\), but linear probes reveal that only the Transformer and Gated DeltaNet learn functional modular arithmetic with high Cohen’s \(\kappa\). Figure 2 from the paper [1].

title: Convergent Evolution: How Different Language Models Learn Similar Number Representations
text:
My Notes
The paper’s main finding: every architecture in the study picks up the periodic signal of how numbers appear in text, but only Transformers and Gated DeltaNet (a linear recurrent neural network, RNN) organize those signals so a linear classifier can read them off. The implication for building a math-capable model: pick an architecture in the geometrically-convergent group, and reach the geometric features by either of the paper’s two identified routes, training on natural text rich in number co-occurrences, or on multi-token (but not single-token) addition problems.

Spectral convergence is broader than the founding work assumed. Zhou et al. (2024) established that pretrained LLMs add via Fourier features, and that models trained from scratch on addition fail to recover them, suggesting the structure was earned during language pretraining [2]. This paper pushes the universality further: even the raw token-frequency distribution of the training corpus shows the same \(T=2, 5, 10\) spikes [1]. The Fourier structure was apparently sitting in the data all along, not earned by any particular learning objective.
Can the sparse-autoencoder (SAE) result corroborate? Engels et al. (2025) used SAEs to find circular features for days of the week and months in Mistral 7B and Llama 3, and verified with causal interventions that the circles actually compute modular arithmetic [3]. Both are Transformers, exactly the family Fu et al. show consistently achieves geometric convergence. The two results are consistent. The follow-up worth running: train SAEs on a linear RNN (which Fu et al. find geometrically convergent) and on an LSTM (which they don’t), and see what appears. Three outcomes are informative: SAEs find functional circles in both, meaning SAE-discovered circles aren’t a reliable signature of geometric usability; SAEs find circles only where Fu et al.’s linear probes do, meaning the two methods agree and SAE circles really do mark functional structure; SAEs find circles in the LSTM that don’t survive causal intervention, meaning SAE features can be spectral artifacts, not all of them functional.
The “Clock” algorithm becomes testable across architectures. Kantamneni and Tegmark (2025) reverse-engineered addition in three mid-sized Transformers as manipulation of a generalized “Clock”, a helical embedding that stacks multiple circular features over a linear magnitude axis [4]. The Clock relies on exactly the geometric usability that Fu et al. find in Transformers and linear RNNs but absent in LSTMs, making linear RNNs a plausible candidate for the same algorithm and LSTMs an unlikely one. Convergence at the feature level doesn’t guarantee convergence at the algorithm level. The same features can in principle support different circuits. A successful reverse-engineering of the Clock in a linear RNN would extend the convergence story from features to algorithms; failure would show that even matched features can yield divergent mechanisms.
Engineered Fourier embeddings give a clean lever for separating architecture from data. The FoNE work (Zhou et al., 2025) directly maps numbers into Fourier features and reports \(64\times\) data efficiency on 6-digit addition [5]. Fu et al. find that geometrically separable number features arise from a combination of data, architecture, optimizer, and tokenizer. Text-number co-occurrence is one of two identified data routes; multi-token addition training is the other [1]. FoNE’s contribution is that it pre-supplies the Fourier features as input embeddings, removing the model’s need to acquire them from training data. That separation enables two clean tests, holding feature-supply constant in each: train an LSTM with FoNE embeddings on rich natural text (does the LSTM still fail at arithmetic? if so, the architecture itself blocks geometric use of period features); train a Transformer with FoNE embeddings on text scrubbed of number co-occurrences (does the Transformer fail? if so, data conditions matter even when features are pre-supplied). Today neither test has been run.

title: How to Be Anti-Social
text:
Image from Leaflet.


Learn how to sabotage yourself in how to be anti-social:

Assume bad faith. When someone confuses or upsets you, assume they have no sane reason for it; when ambiguous, default to malicious, ignorant, or amoral.
Read intent through your fears. Trust intuition and feeling, never challenge or even acknowledge the assumptions doing the interpreting.
Pivot when challenged. Steer away from questions outside your wheelhouse; treat any display of not-knowing as weakness.
Word questions to imply you are right. If you must ask, lead the witness.
Dig in. When dissent piles up, hold firm.
Curate the audience. Reframe interactions for like-minded supporters so they can rally to crush lingering threats to the narrative.
Ignore credentials. Do not research the people you speak with, unless you already agree with them.
Withhold grace. Especially from strangers who make mistakes.
Retreat into self. When conversation breaks down, do not seek to understand those you do not already understand.

title: Sequential KV Cache Compression via Probabilistic Language Tries
text:
First page of the paper. Image from arXiv.
The paper argues that per-vector KV cache compression (TurboQuant et al.) optimises the wrong objective. KV vectors are samples from the language the model already predicts, so the right unit of compression is the sequence, not the vector [1]:

title: Sequential KV Cache Compression via Probabilistic Language Tries
text:
Methods
When a chatbot generates a reply token by token, the model stashes the intermediate state for every previous token in something called the KV (key-value) cache, so it doesn’t have to recompute the whole context on each new word. That cache is now the dominant memory cost of serving large language models. Long conversations and many concurrent users will eat GPU memory long before the model weights do. So a small industry has grown up around squeezing the cache: the latest, TurboQuant [2], gets close to the theoretical limit of how few bits you need per cached vector.
The paper’s observation: those cached vectors aren’t arbitrary data. They’re things the model can already predict, because the model just generated the tokens they came from. So why not let the model’s own predictions do the compression work? The first layer notices when a new conversation starts with the same prefix as a previous one and reuses the cached state. The second layer stores only the gap between each new cached vector and what the model would have predicted. Both layers stack on top of per-vector compressors like TurboQuant, which is why the theoretical headline ratio gets to six orders of magnitude.

title: Sequential KV Cache Compression via Probabilistic Language Tries
text:
Results
The paper’s headline numbers are theoretical, not empirical. At the Shannon limit and typical English perplexity (10–20), predictive delta coding bounds per-token entropy at 3.3–4.3 bits, against TurboQuant’s 3 bits per vector component across 64–128 components per head, a 914,000× ratio. Even with a 1000× overhead above the entropy floor (two orders worse than practical source coders typically achieve), the gap stays at ~914× over TurboQuant, and grows rather than shrinks with context length.

title: Sequential KV Cache Compression via Probabilistic Language Tries
text:
My Notes
The scheme adds a robustness issue that per-vector methods don’t have. The same forward pass on a GPU doesn’t always return identical numbers. What else is in the batch alongside your request can shift the result slightly. Thinking Machines’ Defeating Nondeterminism in LLM Inference documented exactly this: Qwen-235B at temperature 0 produced 80 unique completions over 1000 identical requests, all from non-batch-invariant kernels in the forward pass. Per-vector compression is immune: recovery is a fixed formula on stored bits, no model rerun. Schemes whose decode is pure arithmetic are similarly safe. The issue only appears when the model itself sits on the recovery path. Here, the model rerun is the recovery, so any drift between the original prediction and the regenerated one shows up as reconstruction error. Usually the TurboQuant layer underneath is noisier than the drift and absorbs it, but at positions where the model is highly confident and the stored gap is tiny, the same prompt could reconstruct slightly differently depending on how it got batched.

title: A Rube Goldberg Pipeline for Sharing Links
text:
Rube Goldberg’s Self-Operating Napkin, the canonical absurd contraption (Professor Butts, 1931). Image via Wikimedia Commons (public domain).
Most posts here start as a link or a paragraph I read on my phone, in Mastodon or RSS or an article. By the time I’m back at my Mac, the thread is usually gone: the link buried under three days of tabs, the half-formed reaction long since dissolved.
What I wanted, in three steps:
What it took: half a dozen different systems chained together. It starts when a scaffolded draft lands in my repo within seconds of a phone tap. Hours or days later, when I’m back at my Mac and have written my commentary, running the publish command takes about three minutes to put the post live on benjaminhan.net. For quick reshares where I have nothing to add, a Capture+publish: variant skips the Mac loop entirely and lets CI promote the draft on its own. The systems involved are the iOS share sheet, a Pythonista script, GitHub’s Contents API, GitHub Actions, and GitHub Pages. Two adjacent stages aren’t covered here: the Cloudflare CDN + feed-analytics Worker in front of GitHub Pages, and the optional Mastodon cross-post that can fire after deploy.
The result is more engineering than bookmarking really needs. Below is the contraption, and the spots where it tends to stick.

title: A Rube Goldberg Pipeline for Sharing Links
text:
The pipeline





flowchart TB
    subgraph capture [" "]
        direction LR
        A[iOS Share Sheet] --> B[Pythonista]
        B -->|GitHub Contents API| C[draft .qmd in repo]
        C -->|git pull + /expand-draft| D[Expanded draft]
        D --> M[Manual edit<br/>VSCode + Claude Code]
    end
    subgraph deploy [" "]
        direction LR
        E[git mv to posts/] -->|git push| F[GitHub Actions]
        F -->|Quarto render| G[Static site deploy]
    end
    M -->|/publish-draft| E
    C -.->|auto-publish: true| F
    style capture fill:none,stroke:none
    style deploy fill:none,stroke:none

title: A Rube Goldberg Pipeline for Sharing Links
text:
What each stage actually does

iOS Pythonista captures the URL plus a handful of prompts (title, slug, optional one-liner, “Notes to Claude,” “is the post mine?”), auto-detects the source platform (Mastodon, YouTube, arxiv, Substack, GitHub, etc.) from the URL host, and PUTs a stub .qmd to the repo via GitHub’s Contents API. The platform tag tells the next stage how to dispatch.
Auto-publish is the Mac-less shortcut for a link I want to reshare verbatim. The iOS capture sets auto-publish: true and commits with Capture+publish: (no [skip ci]), so the workflow runs. An early step pulls the source toot via Mastodon’s public API, downloads its image attachments, maps its hashtags against the existing tag vocabulary, fills in missing required frontmatter, and git mvs the draft to posts/ before quarto render. Mastodon-only today. Other platforms raise a hard SystemExit, so a malformed capture fails CI rather than shipping a broken post.
/expand-draft skill runs on the Mac in Claude Code. It reads the stub’s source-url and source-platform, fetches the page, extracts og:image / og:description, suggests categories from the existing tag set, downloads the cover image (with a citation in the figcaption), and writes a STYLE.md-compliant draft. If notes-for-claude is set, the skill follows it as per-draft direction. If source-mine: true, it skips the framing-commentary scaffolding. A /review-draft pass then fact-checks against the source, flags voice and logic issues, and applies safe fixes before the expansion is committed.
Manual editing happens between expand and publish. I open the draft in VSCode and write or polish my commentary with Claude Code at hand. Quick link shares take minutes. Essays can take days. The expanded scaffolding stays deliberately minimal.
/publish-draft skill validates the draft against the style guide, strips scaffolding, git mvs to posts/, commits, pushes.
GitHub Actions implements incremental rendering. A classifier (_scripts/render_diff.py) diffs the working tree against the last successful build’s cached _site/ and picks one of full, incremental, or skip-render. A post edit typically routes to incremental and renders in ~20 s instead of ~4 min. Pre-render scripts then emit the tag histogram, the external post-index.json that hydrates the home + archive listings, the bucket-paginated home and archive pages, and llms.txt. Quarto renders the .qmd files. Post-render, feed-render.py rasterizes Mermaid diagrams and MathJax expressions to SVG so the RSS feed carries real images, feed-utm.py UTM-tags the feed item URLs (so GA4 can attribute RSS click-throughs back to the feed channel) and prepends a “Read on benjaminhan.net” back-link to each item’s body, and feed-paginate.py slices the feed into RFC 5005 paged archives so the index file stays small while subscribers can still walk back through history. Three more scripts run before deploy to strip redundant listing H1s, prune inline asset blobs from pages that don’t need them, and fingerprint styles.css for cache-busting.

title: A Rube Goldberg Pipeline for Sharing Links
text:
Gotchas
The pipeline above looks clean in a flowchart. It is not. Here are the bumps I hit, in roughly the order they showed up.

dialogs.input_alert doesn’t block in Pythonista’s share extension. The dialog works fine when I tap ▶ inside the Pythonista app. From the share sheet, it races through every prompt with empty inputs. Symptom: nothing happens, no error, the script finishes silently. Fix: switch to console.input_alert. Same signature, behaves correctly in the extension sandbox.
GitHub Contents API needs sha to update an existing file. I hit this on a slug collision (HTTP 422, “sha wasn’t supplied”). The script now GETs the path first. If the file exists, it offers Replace (passing the existing sha so the PUT is treated as an update) or Cancel.
Quarto’s draft-mode: gone strips draft pages to empty HTML. Local quarto preview shows blank pages for files in drafts/. Workaround: a _quarto-preview.yml profile that flips draft-mode: unlinked for previews. Production CI builds without the --profile=preview flag, so the deployed site never includes drafts.
VSCode’s Quarto extension doesn’t inherit terminal.integrated.env.osx. Setting QUARTO_PROFILE=preview in workspace settings only affects the integrated terminal. The extension spawns Quarto in a separate process tree with its own inherited env. Real fix: export QUARTO_PROFILE=preview in ~/.zshrc, then Cmd-Q and relaunch VSCode from the terminal so the extension inherits it.
image: frontmatter is metadata, not body content. Quarto uses image: only for og:image meta tags and listing thumbnails. It does not render an inline cover image on the post page itself. The body needs an explicit ![](cover.jpg){fig-align="center"} for the cover to actually appear.
.claude/ was gitignored, hiding the per-project skills. The first commit of expand-draft.md and publish-draft.md resulted in zero tracked files. The directory was excluded entirely. Git’s rule is that a re-include cannot reach a file under an already-excluded parent directory, so !.claude/skills/ does not work against .claude/. The fix is to widen the exclusion to .claude/* first, then re-include .claude/skills/.

title: A Rube Goldberg Pipeline for Sharing Links
text:
Why bother
Two reasons:

The iOS-to-Mac handoff matches how I actually find good links. On a phone, in an RSS or Mastodon reader, away from a keyboard. Capturing them as scaffolded drafts means I don’t lose the thread between “I should put more thought to it” and “I’m back at the Mac.” The drafts queue up. I work on them when I have time.
The pipeline keeps a human in the loop. The phone capture is mine. The commentary is mine. The publish command is a manual step, not a webhook. Automation handles plumbing. Editorial calls stay with me.

The pipeline is elaborate, fragile, and a little excessive. For a workflow that runs every few days, that is also fine.

title: Why LLMs Still Stumble Over Time
text:
Illustration from the EvolveBench paper [10].
Are you surprised that today’s LLMs still make so many time-related mistakes? They might mismatch a date and weekday [1], misinterpret relative expressions like “in 2 hours” or “next Monday at 1 PM” when the current time or timezone is unclear [2], or, in more complex cases, build a schedule whose event order is simply impossible [3].
The core issue is that temporal reasoning is not one skill but a bundle of them. Recent benchmarks break it into subskills such as event ordering, arithmetic, duration, and frequency, and show both large variation across categories and a substantial gap to human performance [4][5].
These failures also reflect how temporal reasoning depends on more than calendar math. Models often need to determine when two mentions refer to the same event and to reason jointly about temporal, causal, and subevent relations [6]. They also rely on commonsense script knowledge, since text frequently leaves the typical order or duration of everyday events unstated [7][8].
Even when stale knowledge is not the problem, temporal reasoning remains brittle. In controlled evaluations, performance changes substantially with problem structure, question type, and fact order [9]. That brittleness helps explain why models struggle when events are introduced out of chronological order and the timeline has to be reconstructed rather than read off the surface form [9].
The problem becomes harder still when knowledge itself changes over time. A model may retrieve the right fact yet fail to align it with the period in which it was true. EvolveBench evaluates exactly this kind of temporal awareness through historical cognition, temporally misaligned context, and invalid timestamped queries [10].
Taken together, these results suggest that temporal failures arise from the interaction of heterogeneous subskills, event-level dependencies, temporal commonsense, sensitivity to ordering, and weak grounding of facts to the correct time.

title: Filesystems vs. RAG
text:
ChromaFs architecture diagram from the Mintlify post. (Source)
Can we replace RAG with filesystems? This article shares a neat engineering write-up on doing exactly that: replacing a standard docs RAG flow with a virtual filesystem for an assistant [1].
Instead of only retrieving top-K chunks, they let the model interact with documentation through familiar file operations like ls, cat, find, and grep. Under the hood, they built a virtual layer over their existing docs index, avoiding the latency and cost of spinning up full sandboxes while giving the assistant a more natural way to explore the corpus.
Optimization details aside, the article hints at two bigger ideas.
First, the filesystem vs. RAG distinction is really about structured navigation vs. relevance retrieval. A filesystem presents the corpus as a pre-built navigable structure for exploration. Plain RAG presents it as a retrieval space.
Second, system interfaces work better when they align with the interaction patterns the base LLM already knows. For coding-oriented models especially, files, paths, directories, and shell-style operations are much closer to the environments they were trained on than a one-shot retrieve-and-insert workflow. The article explicitly framed the goal as letting the assistant explore docs the way a developer explores a codebase.
A few contrasts between the filesystem and RAG approaches:
But RAG still shines when the main problem is semantic recall: messy corpora, weak or ambiguous structure, heterogeneous sources or modalities, or cases where a few relevant passages are enough and full exploration would be overkill.
The interesting part is that these approaches are not incompatible. RAG can be one tool inside a filesystem-style agent: useful for candidate recall, while the filesystem layer handles navigation, inspection, and verification. The implementation described effectively does this by using existing indexing infrastructure to narrow search before exact filtering.
Takeaway: RAG retrieves likely evidence. A filesystem lets the model investigate the source material. We can combine both.

Rain left puddles, so we had to run on rougher gravel parts to avoid them, which cost more pace. Those miles were a bit over 8:00/mi, but the rest were sub-8, and I finished faster than I started!
Weather was rainy and cold (felt like ~40F at the start with ~9mph wind). Also today was the DST change, so we lost an hour of sleep.
Pretty happy with this one, even though it’s not a PR (1:39:07). A month or so ago I was at rock bottom after the disastrous 50K trail race in January and a cough that lasted over a month. Today felt like I finally made it back: VO₂max recovered from 45.9 to 51.5 since February, and my <130 bpm easy pace improved from 10:30/mi to 9:15/mi.

title: The ‘CS Exodus’ as Discipline Evolution
text:
Pyramid diagram from the original LinkedIn post. (Source)
The recent discussion on a “Computer Science exodus” [1] may sound alarming, but perhaps it is better understood as part of a longer historical pattern.
Computing did not begin as Computer Science. It emerged from Electrical Engineering, which became a formal discipline in the late 19th century following its commercialization [2]. In the early 1970s, computer engineering emerged as a distinct academic discipline, with the first dedicated degree program established in 1971 [3]. Around the same time, software engineering was formalized to address the growing complexity of large software systems [4]. Computer science later became the dominant academic identity for computing.
Today Universities are rapidly expanding AI-specific degrees, and the share of computer science PhD graduates specializing in AI nearly doubled over the past decade [5]. What looks like an exodus under this historical lens is more accurately a shift toward the current center of gravity.
On the other hand, focusing on the concept of abstraction, each transition reflects a shift in where complexity resides. Electrical Engineering focused on electrons and circuits. Computer Engineering abstracted those into programmable machines. Computer Science abstracted machines into algorithms and data structures. Software Engineering abstracted algorithms into large, reliable systems. Now, AI abstracts explicit logic itself, allowing systems to learn behavior from data rather than relying solely on hand-written rules.
These transitions do not replace the disciplines. They redefine their boundaries. We are witnessing computer Science evolving into the foundation supporting a more AI-native form of computing.
(In the pyramid AI is marked as starting from 2010s when AlexNet ignited deep learning revolution and transitioned AI into mainstream)

title: “Skills” Are Not Software Engineering
text:
Image from Anthropic.
Anthropic’s “skills” framework [1] is a useful step toward more capable AI agents. Skills package instructions, resources, and executable scripts into reusable tools that Claude can call to perform actions across contexts. This makes advanced workflows accessible to users who are not software engineers, and it lets LLMs offload deterministic execution to real code. Skills clearly improve reliability compared to pure prompting.
At the same time, skills cannot replace software engineering. They help with local execution, but they do not solve the broader orchestration and correctness problems that real software systems must address. Skills still rely on natural language as the primary interface for interpreting intent, selecting tools, filling parameters, and deciding sequences of actions. Natural language is valuable because it allows the model to apply commonsense reasoning and to bridge ambiguity, but it also introduces ambiguity of its own, since there are no static contracts, type checks, or guarantees that the same request will lead to the same plan over time.
Scripted skill bodies execute deterministically, but everything around them remains probabilistic. The model decides when to invoke a skill, how to connect skills together, how to interpret return values, and how to recover from errors. These decisions rely on model reasoning rather than explicit control flow, which means silent misrouting, partial failures, and unpredictable drift can still occur. Software engineering requires predictable interfaces, state management, transactions, testing, and clear error semantics. Skills do not yet provide these foundations.
A more reliable path forward combines the strengths of LLMs with the rigor of traditional engineering. Natural language should remain the medium for planning, intent understanding, disambiguation, and high-level reasoning. A deterministic runtime should then validate and compile that plan into a typed, structured workflow that enforces schemas, invariants, contracts, and version guarantees. In this hybrid model, the LLM proposes, while the runtime ensures correctness.
Anthropic’s skills are a meaningful contribution to agent tooling. They expand what non-engineers can do and make LLM-driven workflows more powerful. But until skills are paired with a structured execution layer that enforces engineering discipline, they remain an augmentation of prompting rather than a foundation for building reliable systems. What we need next is a new software engineering paradigm for the LLM era (e.g., [2][3][4][5]), one that preserves the flexibility and reasoning strengths of natural language while grounding execution in typed interfaces, verifiable workflows, and deterministic runtimes. This hybrid model will allow us to embrace LLM agency without sacrificing the predictability, safety, and maintainability that real software demands.

title: Journey into Coding with AI [2/4]: Shifting Gears
text:
Cover image from the LinkedIn article. (Source)


(Part 1: Running Back to Code)
Remember driving a stick-shift car? Your hand clenched the gearstick while your foot danced on the clutch, trying to nail that gear change. Looking back it’s clear that the driver was put to doing a machine’s job, but transitioning from stick to automatic is a paradigm shift that has elicited (still to this day) a lot of emotional responses. However, it’s definitely not the first time humanity was debating with itself how much control they’d like to cede to machines.

Lessons from Apollo
In Chapter 7 of Neil Lawrence’s Atomic Human, he captures the tension between human and autonomous control. During the Apollo missions, the guidance computer steered the spacecraft most of the way to the moon, and the thrusters weren’t directly linked to the pilot’s inputs. This didn’t sit well with the astronauts, all of whom were experienced, well-trained Navy test pilots. But it was necessary: the journey to the moon was long and dangerous, and the calculations and course corrections were tedious yet vital. The final design allowed humans to intervene — a decision that later proved correct and life-saving.



Neil Lawrence. Atomic Human. 2024. Image from The Atomic Human.




Quality-of-Life Wins
Coming back on earth, we’re facing essentially the same question in software engineering: how much control are we willing to cede, and what benefits come with it? After just a month of experimenting, I can already see the value of automating certain programming tasks (as I described in Part 1). But there are also countless small quality-of-life improvements when working with coding AI:

You can interrogate code — even ask why a particular line exists.
You don’t need to remember exact names; a misspelled function or a vague description often still lands you in the right spot.
And those complicated, commonsense-defying git dances? Just state your intention and let coding AI figure out the right sequence (with your approval, of course).



When the Pilot Has to Override
I think of these as stick-shift–level automation. But just as Neil Armstrong once overrode the autonomous system during Gemini VIII mission, firing a backup thruster to stop the spacecraft from spinning out of control during docking, and in so doing saving everyone on board, we, the human programmers, must stay vigilant for the kinds of AI errors I’ve encountered:

Coding AI generated model training code that led to a tensor shape mismatch.
Remember the gradient flow disruption bug I mentioned in Part 1? That was introduced by another coding AI during a refactor.
Coding AI split a training/validation dataset without keeping class balance consistent.
Coding AI proudly reported “all tests passed” even while the debug log showed failures.
Coding AI “passed” tests by cheating — rewriting the tests themselves.
Coding AI tried to make a Python constant private by adding _ to one that already had a leading underscore.




The crew of Gemini VIII after splashdown. Photo from Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum.


But make no mistake – we’re getting there. The coding AI we use today will be the worst version we’ll ever see, and it’s already good enough to take us from stick-shift driving to automatic. As the technology matures, we should expect higher and higher levels of automation. But what role remains for humans in a task, among others, once considered the pinnacle of human intelligence?
I’ll close this installment with Neil Lawrence’s argument in Atomic Human: as AI replicates more human capabilities, it keeps stripping away what’s machine-reproducible in us, until we’re left with the indivisible core of humanity – our vulnerabilities, our embodiment, and our unique judgment. His message is clear: we must understand and harness that essence, not cede it. Machines, after all, are bicycles for the mind.
(… to be continued in Part 3)

title: Embedding Limits: A Linear-Algebra Note (and Kernel Tricks)
text:
Figure from the embedding-limits paper (LIMIT critical corpus growth). (Source)


A follow-up to Embeddings Hit a Theoretical Ceiling.
An important callout about this paper: many posts miss that the proof of limitation rests on a basic linear algebra fact: rank(AB) ≤ min(rank(A), rank(B)). This is a constraint of using dot product / cosine similarity for relevance scoring, not an inherent limit of embeddings themselves. Even bilinear models or learned similarity matrices still fall under this bound.
The paper suggests several ways out: multi-vector representations, late interaction models, and cross-encoders. And I’ll add one more: classic ML offers kernel tricks like Gaussian RBF that can break the embedding dimension bottleneck.
Curious to hear: how would the field tackle the bottleneck?

text:
Running milestone: My 1st 50K race at Bridle Trails Winter Running Festival was done yesterday! The race started at 3:10pm, with 2,493ft EG and 3+ hours run in the dark (also my first), my official result came at 5:05:42.3, 9th place out of 45 runners!
This is 5 minutes slower than what my expectation was, but given what happened on the course (later), this is much better than what it could have been!
The weather was surprisingly nice, 45F and sunny. But there was substantial rain the morning before, so the trails were still muddy and squishy, with protruding rocks and tree roots.



Watch on YouTube


(short video of the course captured during my practice https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rk_4p-haLv4)
Just when sun was setting at the end of my 3rd loop, I fell uphill less than a mile away from aid station. A smooth rock tricked me and I didn’t lift my left foot high enough to clear the added height from my newly acquired Exospikes! Goes to show the problem of using new gear in a race!
(I got Exospikes a week before because I fell downhill during one practice run there)
I almost gave up due to left knee pain from hitting a rock. After limping back to the aid station and resting for ~5min, I tried to restart and magically the pain was not that bad anymore! So I persisted with a much lower pace.
So what did I learn?

No new gear in a race without at least a month of practice!
Exospikes are great for running fullspeed downhill, but the added height, weight and rigidity can pose challenges with endurance running on path with protruding rocks and roots.
Sometimes finishing a race is not even the point. You need to ask your body: at what cost and will it prevent me from running more?

One goal in 2025 is done. Onward!
