Teaching well: physics background, micrograd, first-order terms
Dwarkesh Patel: Can I ask some questions about teaching well? If you had to give advice to another educator in another field that you’re curious about to make the kinds of YouTube tutorials you’ve made. Maybe it might be especially interesting to talk about domains where you can’t test someone’s technical understanding by having them code something up or something. What advice would you give them?
Andrej Karpathy: That’s a pretty broad topic. There are 10–20 tips and tricks that I semi-consciously do probably. But a lot of this comes from my physics background. I really, really did enjoy my physics background. I have a whole rant on how everyone should learn physics in early school education because early school education is not about accumulating knowledge or memory for tasks later in the industry. It’s about booting up a brain. Physics uniquely boots up the brain the best because some of the things that they get you to do in your brain during physics is extremely valuable later.
The idea of building models and abstractions and understanding that there’s a first-order approximation that describes most of the system, but then there’re second-order, third-order, fourth-order terms that may or may not be present. The idea that you’re observing a very noisy system, but there are these fundamental frequencies that you can abstract away. When a physicist walks into the class and they say, “Assume there’s a spherical cow,” everyone laughs at that, but this is brilliant. It’s brilliant thinking that’s very generalizable across the industry because a cow can be approximated as a sphere in a bunch of ways.
There’s a really good book, for example, Scale. It’s from a physicist talking about biology. Maybe this is also a book I would recommend reading. You can get a lot of really interesting approximations and chart scaling laws of animals. You can look at their heartbeats and things like that, and they line up with the size of the animal and things like that. You can talk about an animal as a volume. You can talk about the heat dissipation of that, because your heat dissipation grows as the surface area, which is growing as a square. But your heat creation or generation is growing as a cube. So I just feel like physicists have all the right cognitive tools to approach problem solving in the world.
So because of that training, I always try to find the first-order terms or the second-order terms of everything. When I’m observing a system or a thing, I have a tangle of a web of ideas or knowledge in my mind. I’m trying to find, what is the thing that matters? What is the first-order component? How can I simplify it? How can I have a simplest thing that shows that thing, shows it in action, and then I can tack on the other terms?
Maybe an example from one of my repos that I think illustrates it well is called micrograd. I don’t know if you’re familiar with this. So micrograd is 100 lines of code that shows backpropagation. You can create neural networks out of simple operations like plus and times, et cetera. Lego blocks of neural networks. You build up a computational graph and you do a forward pass and a backward pass to get the gradients. Now, this is at the heart of all neural network learning.
So micrograd is a 100 lines of pretty interpretable Python code, and it can do forward and backward arbitrary neural networks, but not efficiently. So micrograd, these 100 lines of Python, are everything you need to understand how neural networks train. Everything else is just efficiency. Everything else is efficiency. There’s a huge amount of work to get efficiency. You need your tensors, you lay them out, you stride them, you make sure your kernels, orchestrating memory movement correctly, et cetera. It’s all just efficiency, roughly speaking. But the core intellectual piece of neural network training is micrograd. It’s 100 lines. You can easily understand it. It’s a recursive application of chain rule to derive the gradient, which allows you to optimize any arbitrary differentiable function.
So I love finding these small-order terms and serving them on a platter and discovering them. I feel like education is the most intellectually interesting thing because you have a tangle of understanding and you’re trying to lay it out in a way that creates a ramp where everything only depends on the thing before it. I find that this untangling of knowledge is just so intellectually interesting as a cognitive task. I love doing it personally, but I just have a fascination with trying to lay things out in a certain way. Maybe that helps me.
Dwarkesh Patel: It also makes the learning experience so much more motivated. Your tutorial on the transformer begins with bigrams, literally a lookup table from, “Here’s the word right now, or here’s the previous word, here’s the next word.” It’s literally just a lookup table.
Andrej Karpathy: That’s the essence of it, yeah.
Dwarkesh Patel: It’s such a brilliant way, starting with a lookup table and then going to a transformer. Each piece is motivated. Why would you add that? Why would you add the next thing? You could memorize the attention formula, but having an understanding of why every single piece is relevant, what problem it solves.
Andrej Karpathy: You’re presenting the pain before you present a solution, and how clever is that? You want to take the student through that progression. There are a lot of other small things that make it nice and engaging and interesting. Always prompting the student.
There’s a lot of small things like that are important and a lot of good educators will do this. How would you solve this? I’m not going to present the solution before you guess. That would be wasteful. That’s a little bit of a…I don’t want to swear but it’s a dick move towards you to present you with the solution before I give you a shot to try to come up with it yourself.


Curse of knowledge; share dumb ChatGPT conversations
Dwarkesh Patel: Because if you try to come up with it yourself, you get a better understanding of what the action space is, what the objective is, and then why only this action fulfills that objective.
Andrej Karpathy: You have a chance to try it yourself, and you have an appreciation when I give you the solution. It maximizes the amount of knowledge per new fact added.
Dwarkesh Patel: Why do you think, by default, people who are genuine experts in their field are often bad at explaining it to somebody ramping up?
Andrej Karpathy: It’s the curse of knowledge and expertise. This is a real phenomenon, and I suffered from it myself as much as I try not to. But you take certain things for granted, and you can’t put yourself in the shoes of new people who are just starting out. This is pervasive and happens to me as well.
One thing that’s extremely helpful. As an example, someone was trying to show me a paper in biology recently, and I just instantly had so many terrible questions. What I did was I used ChatGPT to ask the questions with the paper in the context window. It worked through some of the simple things. Then I shared the thread to the person who wrote that paper or worked on that work. I felt like if they could see the dumb questions I had, it might help them explain better in the future.
For my material, I would love it if people shared their dumb conversations with ChatGPT about the stuff that I’ve created because it really helps me put myself again in the shoes of someone who’s starting out.


“Just say the thing” — why oral explanations beat papers
Dwarkesh Patel: Another trick that just works astoundingly well. If somebody writes a paper or a blog post or an announcement, it is in 100% of cases that just the narration or the transcription of how they would explain it to you over lunch is way more, not only understandable, but actually also more accurate and scientific, in the sense that people have a bias to explain things in the most abstract, jargon-filled way possible and to clear their throat for four paragraphs before they explain the central idea. But there’s something about communicating one-on-one with a person which compels you to just say the thing.
Andrej Karpathy: Just say the thing. I saw that tweet, I thought it was really good. I shared it with a bunch of people. I noticed this many, many times.
The most prominent example is that I remember back in my PhD days doing research. You read someone’s paper, and you work to understand what it’s doing. Then you catch them, you’re having beers at the conference later, and you ask them, “So this paper, what were you doing? What is the paper about?”
They will just tell you these three sentences that perfectly captured the essence of that paper and totally give you the idea. And you didn’t have to read the paper. It’s only when you’re sitting at the table with a beer or something, and they’re like, “Oh yeah, the paper is just, you take this idea, you take that idea and try this experiment and you try out this thing.” They have a way of just putting it conversationally just perfectly. Why isn’t that the abstract?


Learning advice: depth + breadth, explain to learn
Dwarkesh Patel: Exactly. This is coming from the perspective of how somebody who’s trying to explain an idea should formulate it better. What is your advice as a student to other students, if you don’t have a Karpathy who is doing the exposition of an idea? If you’re reading a paper from somebody or reading a book, what strategies do you employ to learn material you’re interested in in fields you’re not an expert at?
Andrej Karpathy: I don’t know that I have unique tips and tricks, to be honest. It’s a painful process. One thing that has always helped me quite a bit is—I had a small tweet about this—learning things on demand is pretty nice. Learning depth-wise. I do feel you need a bit of alternation of learning depth-wise, on demand—you’re trying to achieve a certain project that you’re going to get a reward from—and learning breadth-wise, which is just, “Oh, let’s do whatever 101, and here’s all the things you might need.” Which is a lot of school—does breadth-wise learning, like, “Oh, trust me, you’ll need this later,” that kind of stuff. Okay, I trust you. I’ll learn it because I guess I need it. But I love the kind of learning where you’ll get a reward out of doing something, and you’re learning on demand.
The other thing that I’ve found extremely helpful. This is an aspect where education is a bit more selfless, but explaining things to people is a beautiful way to learn something more deeply. This happens to me all the time. It probably happens to other people too because I realize if I don’t really understand something, I can’t explain it. I’m trying and I’m like, “Oh, I don’t understand this.” It’s so annoying to come to terms with that. You can go back and make sure you understood it. It fills these gaps of your understanding. It forces you to come to terms with them and to reconcile them.
I love to re-explain things and people should be doing that more as well. That forces you to manipulate the knowledge and make sure that you know what you’re talking about when you’re explaining it.
Dwarkesh Patel: That’s an excellent note to close on. Andrej, that was great.
Andrej Karpathy: Thank you.

title: Anthropic on AI Coding: Scaffold, Not Substitute
text:
Chart from Anthropic’s study. (Source)
Anthropic’s research on AI-assisted coding highlights an interaction effect: outcomes depend on how the tool is used [1].
In their study, overall quiz performance was lower for participants with AI help, with the biggest gaps on debugging and conceptual understanding. But within the AI group, interaction style mattered: using the model to ask conceptual “why/how” questions and to explain errors aligned with better comprehension, while more delegative use (having it produce most of the solution) aligned with worse learning.
Important takeaway: treat AI as a scaffold for reasoning and debugging, not a substitute for forming the mental model.

title: Marcus vs. Brundage: A Concrete AGI Bet
text:
Image from the original LinkedIn post. (Source)
Gary Marcus, a cognitive scientist and longtime critic of scaling-centric AI, and Miles Brundage, an AI policy researcher and former OpenAI policy lead, agreed in 2024 to make the following bet on AI [1]:
The tasks are ambitious. AI systems must:
My first reaction: this doesn’t look like average human general intelligence. Almost no human could do all of these tasks! Clearing eight of ten feels less like “human-level AGI” and more like cross-domain elite expertise — something close to a superhuman polymath.
But the wager does not require a single unified AI system to accomplish all tasks. Multiple AI systems can be used across domains, as long as each task is completed with minimal human involvement. So the benchmark is about demonstrating AI capability collectively, not necessarily one monolithic AGI.
The asymmetric odds are striking. Brundage risks $20,000 to win $2,000. For that to be positive expected value, he would need to believe the probability of success exceeds roughly 91 percent. Here is how prediction markets see it today:
That gap between the private conviction and the crowd forecast is especially interesting. But ultimately, the bet surfaces a deeper question: What do we actually mean by AGI — average human breadth, elite cross-domain capability, or highly autonomous systems operating across fields?
Whatever happens by 2027, I appreciate that this wager forces the conversation into concrete, falsifiable milestones instead of vague timeline claims.
REFERENCES

title: Snowflake Cortex AI Escapes Sandbox and Executes Malware
text:
Cover image from the PromptArmor write-up. (Source)
A good reminder that agent safety is not just about having a sandbox.
Snowflake’s Cortex Code CLI recently patched an indirect prompt injection flaw where untrusted content, such as a repo README, could trigger malicious shell commands, bypass user approval, and run outside the sandbox [1].
The deeper lesson is that safety can fail in two places at once: incomplete command validation and weak observability across agent layers. If a lower-level agent can act while the top-level agent thinks it only detected risk, the system is not actually in control.
Multi-agent systems need recursive validation, strong isolation, and end-to-end action visibility.

title: Redmond City Marathon: #30, with a Sprained Ankle
text:
Today I ran my 30th marathon (since 2024) at the Redmond City Marathon race, finishing in 3:38:33 (watch time) with pace 8’20”/mi. It also extended an unusual streak for me: 7 straight weeks of running HM or longer!
This was my first marathon raced by HR, and that part mostly went to plan: I got avg/max HR of 149/159 bpm. The bigger challenge in the second half was actually not keeping my HR down, but getting it up. My legs were prematurely tired mainly due to a very silly mistake happened early in the race: I stored gels in the shallow part of my vest pockets, and they went flying at ~2.6mi mark! I stepped onto the unpaved edge to retrieve them, and proceeded to spraining my left ankle!
Running on it didn’t feel too bad and I thought I had cheated disaster. It started to rear its ugly head around the famous mile 20. Well, this is what it is – at least I managed to have a strong-ish finish in the last 2+mi!
Not the race I originally imagined, but sometimes sh*t happens (okay, most of the times). My next marathon is ~24 weeks out –- a lot of training to do, but I have the time! Onward!

title: APIs, Tools, Skills, and Where MCP Fits
text:
APIs, tools, and skills form a rough abstraction ladder. Each one builds on the layer below it, and confusing them leads to systems that are either too rigid or too loosely defined. MCP is a different kind of thing: a protocol that crosscuts the ladder. It deserves its own discussion.





graph LR
    subgraph MCP["<b>MCP</b> — standardizes exposure to models"]
        API["<b>API</b><br/>raw interface"]
        TOOL["<b>TOOL</b><br/>callable action"]
        API -->|"wrapped by"| TOOL
    end

    TOOL -->|"used by"| SKILL
    API -->|"used by"| SKILL["<b>SKILL</b><br/>judgment, sequencing"]

    style API fill:d98c4a,stroke:a66a2e,color:fff
    style TOOL fill:#5ba55b,stroke:#3d7a3d,color:fff
    style SKILL fill:#4a90d9,stroke:#2c5f8a,color:fff
    style MCP fill:f3ecf9,stroke:#8b5fbf,color:#4a2a7a







API: The Raw Interface
An API is a defined interface that lets one software system interact with another. It exposes endpoints, methods, inputs, and outputs. It does not tell an agent when to call it, what to do with the result, or how the call fits into a broader task.
In a customer support agent, the API is the HTTP interface to the ticketing system: create ticket, update status, fetch history. The API does not know why you are calling it.


Tool: The Callable Action
A tool is a capability packaged so an agent can invoke it directly. It has a schema the model can read, a name that signals intent, and a defined effect. In many systems a tool is backed by an API, but the tool adds a layer: it tells the model what the action does, what parameters it needs, and what shape the result will take.
In that same support agent, “search_tickets” is a tool. It wraps the ticketing API’s search endpoint, describes its parameters in a model-readable schema, and returns structured results. The agent can decide to call it. The API underneath does not care who is calling or why.
The key difference: a developer writes code against an API. An agent selects and invokes a tool. The tool is the API made legible to a model.


Skill: The Playbook
A skill is a reusable method for solving a class of problems. It involves judgment, sequencing, and often multiple tools. If a tool says “send an email,” a skill says “triage the inbox, identify messages that need a response, draft replies in the right tone, and flag anything that needs human review.”
For the support agent, a skill might be “handle refund request”: check the order status, verify the refund policy applies, draft a response to the customer, create an internal ticket if escalation is needed, and log the outcome. That is not one action. It is a procedure with branching logic and defaults.
Skills are where know-how lives. A tool gives the agent something to do. A skill tells it how to do a job well.


Where MCP Fits
MCP (Model Context Protocol) is not another rung on this ladder. It is a standard for exposing tools, resources, and context to models in a consistent way. Its job is interoperability: making capabilities discoverable and portable across environments.
Without MCP, every agent framework wires up tools differently. The schema formats vary, discovery is ad hoc, and switching between hosts means rewriting integrations. MCP standardizes that surface so a tool written once can be used by any compliant client.
MCP can also expose resources (files, database rows, live context) alongside tools, which means a model can see both what it can do and what it is working with. This is useful but distinct from the API/tool/skill question. MCP does not replace any of those layers. It makes them portable.
Think of it this way: APIs, tools, and skills describe what capabilities exist and at what level of abstraction. MCP describes how those capabilities are presented to models.


A Concrete Example
Consider a code assistant that can read files, run tests, and create pull requests.





graph TB
    SKILL["<b>SKILL: Review and ship a bug fix</b>"]

    SKILL --> S1["1. Read failing test<br/><i>judgment: which file?</i>"]
    SKILL --> S2["2. Identify + fix broken code<br/><i>judgment: what change?</i>"]
    SKILL --> S3["3. Run test suite"]
    SKILL --> S4["4. Open PR<br/><i>judgment: description,<br/>reviewers, linked issue</i>"]

    S1 --> T1["<b>TOOL</b><br/>read_file"]
    S3 --> T2["<b>TOOL</b><br/>run_tests"]
    S4 --> T3["<b>TOOL</b><br/>create_pull_request"]

    T1 --> A1["<b>API</b><br/>Filesystem"]
    T2 --> A2["<b>API</b><br/>Test runner CLI"]
    T3 --> A3["<b>API</b><br/>GitHub REST<br/>POST /pulls"]

    style SKILL fill:#4a90d9,stroke:#2c5f8a,color:fff
    style T1 fill:#5ba55b,stroke:#3d7a3d,color:fff
    style T2 fill:#5ba55b,stroke:#3d7a3d,color:fff
    style T3 fill:#5ba55b,stroke:#3d7a3d,color:fff
    style A1 fill:d98c4a,stroke:a66a2e,color:fff
    style A2 fill:d98c4a,stroke:a66a2e,color:fff
    style A3 fill:d98c4a,stroke:a66a2e,color:fff







The APIs are the filesystem interface, the test runner’s CLI, and the GitHub REST API.
The tools are “read_file,” “run_tests,” and “create_pull_request,” each with a schema the model can parse.
An MCP server bundles those tools (and possibly resources like the repo’s directory tree or recent CI results) into a package any compliant model host can connect to.
A skill is “review and ship a bug fix”: read the failing test, identify the broken code, make the fix, run the test suite, and open a PR with a clear description. The skill uses all three tools and applies judgment at each step.



The Boundaries Are Not Fixed
Yes, a skill can become a tool. This happens routinely. The “handle refund request” skill from the earlier example starts as a multi-step procedure with judgment at each point. But once the team has run it enough times, the branching logic stabilizes, the edge cases get codified, and someone wraps the whole thing in a single callable function: “process_refund.” Now it looks like a tool. The agent calls it in one shot. The orchestration still happens, just inside the wrapper rather than in the agent’s reasoning loop.
This is the natural lifecycle. Skills get hardened into tools. Tools get commoditized into APIs. What was once a careful, multi-step procedure becomes a reliable black box. The abstraction ladder is not a static taxonomy. It is a description of where the judgment currently lives, and that shifts as systems mature.





graph LR
    SKILL["<b>SKILL</b><br/><i>handle refund request</i><br/>judgment in the agent"]
    TOOL["<b>TOOL</b><br/><i>process_refund</i><br/>judgment in the wrapper"]
    API["<b>API</b><br/><i>POST /refunds</i><br/>judgment removed"]

    SKILL -->|hardens into| TOOL
    TOOL -->|commoditizes into| API
    API -.->|edge cases resurface| TOOL
    TOOL -.->|context demands judgment| SKILL

    style SKILL fill:#4a90d9,stroke:#2c5f8a,color:fff
    style TOOL fill:#5ba55b,stroke:#3d7a3d,color:fff
    style API fill:d98c4a,stroke:a66a2e,color:fff






The movement goes the other direction too. When a tool starts failing in new contexts, or when its behavior needs to vary based on surrounding conditions, it may need to be unpacked back into a skill. A “create_pull_request” tool works fine when the agent has already done everything right. But if the PR needs a certain description format, specific reviewers based on the files changed, and a linked issue, that single tool call becomes a skill again: a sequence of checks and decisions that the agent has to reason through.
The practical implication: do not over-invest in classifying a capability as one or the other permanently. Instead, pay attention to where the judgment lives right now. If the agent is making multi-step decisions around a capability, that is a skill, even if it is technically implemented as a single function. If a capability can be called reliably without the agent thinking about it, that is a tool, even if it was once a complex workflow.


When You Are Building an Agent
If you are deciding what to build and in what order:





graph LR
    A["<b>① API</b><br/>raw access<br/><i>always needed</i>"]
    T["<b>② Tool</b><br/>callable action<br/><i>always needed</i>"]
    M["<b>③ MCP</b><br/>portable exposure<br/><i>if multi-host</i>"]
    S["<b>④ Skill</b><br/>orchestrated workflow<br/><i>when patterns emerge</i>"]

    A -->|wrap| T
    T -->|expose| M
    M -->|orchestrate| S

    style A fill:d98c4a,stroke:a66a2e,color:fff
    style T fill:#5ba55b,stroke:#3d7a3d,color:fff
    style M fill:#8b5fbf,stroke:#6b3fa0,color:fff
    style S fill:#4a90d9,stroke:#2c5f8a,color:fff







Start with the APIs. You need raw access to the systems your agent will interact with. If the integration does not exist, nothing above it works.
Wrap them as tools. Give each action a clear name, a schema, and a description. This is what the model will actually call.
If you need portability, add MCP. If your tools will be used across multiple model hosts or clients, exposing them through MCP saves you from writing bespoke integrations for each one. If you are building for a single environment, this can wait.
Encode skills last. Once your agent can take individual actions reliably, identify the recurring workflows where sequencing and judgment matter. Package those as skills. Premature skills, built before the underlying tools are solid, tend to be brittle.

The layers are complements: APIs provide access, tools provide action, MCP provides portability, and skills provide method. Most agent systems need all four, but they should be built in roughly that order.

Originally posted on LinkedIn.

title: Silver Bars and Language Models: Reading Babel in the Age of LLMs
text:
Cover of R.F. Kuang’s Babel: Or the Necessity of Violence (Harper Voyager, 2022). (Source)
R.F. Kuang’s Babel was published in August 2022 [1], three months before OpenAI released ChatGPT [2]. The novel is set in an alternate 1830s Oxford and concerns the British Empire’s monopoly on a magical system of translation: silver bars that harvest the gap between languages and convert it into industrial power. Kuang was not writing about AI. But she finished describing a world in which linguistic knowledge is industrialized and centralized just as our world began building exactly that, and in retrospect the structural parallels are precise enough that the novel reads as one of the clearest available descriptions of what large language models actually do.

title: Prompt Repetition Improves Non-Reasoning LLMs
text:
First page of Leviathan, Kalman, and Matias 2025. Image from arXiv.
Another inference-time trick for getting more out of an LLM without touching its weights [1].

title: Prompt Repetition Improves Non-Reasoning LLMs
text:
Methods
The trick is one line: prepend a copy of the user’s prompt before the model generates. No fine-tuning, no extra decoding tokens, no latency hit at generation time — just a longer prefill.

title: Prompt Repetition Improves Non-Reasoning LLMs
text:
Results
The paper sweeps 70 benchmark-model combinations across Gemini, GPT, Claude, and Deepseek:



Figure 1 from the paper: prompt repetition vs baseline accuracy across Gemini, GPT, Claude, and Deepseek on multiple benchmarks. Repetition wins 47/70 benchmark-model combinations, with 0 losses. Image from arXiv.

title: Prompt Repetition Improves Non-Reasoning LLMs
text:
My Notes
Why does this work? Causal attention. The autoregressive LLMs we’re talking about — Gemini, GPT, Claude, Deepseek — read left-to-right: each token can only attend to tokens that came before it. So when a model is given <context> <question>, it has to encode every word of the context before it ever sees the question. This is the opposite of how “good” students prepare for exams: they look at past questions first, then read the texts with those questions in mind, focusing attention on what’s likely to be asked. Repeating the prompt gives the model the same second pass — by the time it encodes the second copy, the question is already in view, so the context can be processed in light of what’s being asked. Because prefill is parallelizable, doubling the prompt doesn’t slow generation down.
The paper itself names the root cause:

LLMs are often trained as causal language models, i.e. past tokens cannot attend to future tokens. Therefore, the order of the tokens in a user’s query can affect prediction performance.

Bidirectional attention over the prefix would fix this natively — every prompt token attending to every other, no repetition needed. Encoder-decoder models (T5, BART) do this in their encoder; Prefix-LM variants (UL2) bidirectionally attend over the prompt and switch to causal only at generation. The paper flags “Explore interactions with techniques such as Prefix LM” as a future direction. But decoder-only causal architectures won the scaling battle: simpler training at scale, more efficient KV-caching for sequential serving, more natural in-context learning. Prompt repetition is a runtime patch that buys back some of what bidirectional attention would natively provide — without retraining the frontier models we already have.
Compare to the LLM Neuroanatomy post: there, the trick was duplicating a block of middle transformer layers and running them twice. Here, the trick is simpler still: duplicate the input itself. The intuition is the same in both cases — give the model another pass over the same information.

title: Prompt Repetition Improves Non-Reasoning LLMs
text:
References

Yaniv Leviathan, Matan Kalman, and Yossi Matias. “Prompt Repetition Improves Non-Reasoning LLMs.” arXiv. 2025-12-17. https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.14982

title: Overzealous Coding Models
text:
Figure 1 from the post — GPT-5.4 rewrites an entire function when the correct fix is changing one number in a range() call. Image from nrehiew’s blog.
In Coding Models Are Doing Too Much, nrehiew puts a number on a frustration anyone using AI coding tools has felt — the model fixes the bug, then quietly rewrites half the function around it.

title: Overzealous Coding Models
text:
My Notes

The Opus 4.6 gap is not subtle — highest Pass@1 and smallest diffs, in both reasoning and non-reasoning modes. Anthropic appears to have trained explicitly against this failure mode, and it shows.
A single sentence of prompt closes most of the gap for everyone else — over-editing is a default, not a capability ceiling.
Style problem, not knowledge problem. That LoRA at rank 64 nearly matches the full fine-tune is the giveaway — a small parameter delta shifts the behavior without touching the underlying capability.
The tooling implication is bigger than the model implication. “Preserve the original code” should be wired into every coding tool’s system prompt by default, and diff-review UI should surface a minimality score alongside the patch.

title: Anthropic Economic Index
text:
Illustration from Anthropic.
Anthropic’s fourth Economic Index report (Jan 15, 2026) introduces economic primitives — a set of five foundational measurements Claude extracts from every sampled conversation — and uses them to revisit earlier findings about AI’s impact on work.
The primitives:
What the November 2025 sample (1M Claude.ai conversations + 1M first-party API transcripts, mostly Sonnet 4.5) shows:

title: Anthropic Economic Index
text:
My Notes
“Time horizon” in this report borrows METR’s framing: the longest task, measured in human-equivalent hours, that a model can complete with at least 50% success. The metric is designed to track AI progress without saturating the way fixed benchmarks do, since as models improve, the horizon stretches.
Which brings a caveat about what is actually being measured in Anthropic’s report. They didn’t actually measure the time from actual humans from what I can tell. They asked Claude:

We derive these primitives from asking Claude to answer a common set of questions about every conversation in our sample for this report.

And in a footnote:

We measure complexity through estimated human time to complete tasks without AI, time spent completing tasks with AI, and whether users handle multiple tasks within a single conversation.

So while METR’s 2h figure is grounded in actual humans on the clock, Anthropic’s 3.5h and 19h are model-generated estimates of human time. The two methodologies are not exactly the same.
Assuming the two sides are comparable, the differences in time horizon between METR and Anthropic come from differences in experimental conditions, not from differences in what the model can do (because they were all measured on the same model). Two things vary across the setups: whether a human steers the model mid-task, and whether the task was pre-selected as something the model could plausibly handle. METR has neither: an autonomous agent runs a fixed benchmark, with no steering and no pre-selection. The API sample has pre-selection but no steering: developers send Claude tasks they have already validated will work, and the calls then run on their own. Claude.ai has both: the human steers and decomposes the work as it goes, and the human only brings tasks they expect will succeed. The result? Pre-selection alone moves the horizon from METR’s 2h to the API’s 3.5h, a modest 1.75×. Human steering on top moves it from there to Claude.ai’s 19h, a much bigger 5× jump.
This is less a story about what Claude can do today than about how humans and AI work together. The 5× multiplier from human steering shows that the most productive AI work right now happens in the human-AI pair, not in autonomous agents. The complement is the point: humans bring task decomposition, judgment about what to attempt, and verification of what comes back; the model brings speed, breadth, and stamina. The 19-hour result on Claude.ai is what that pairing makes possible, on tasks neither side would have completed as quickly alone. As models get better, the kinds of work that fit this pairing keep expanding, and so does the range of jobs where the most useful human skill is steering the model well rather than competing with it.

title: The Global Edtech Boom Is Fading as Investors Look Elsewhere
text:
Image from Rest of World.
Rest of World reports on the global edtech funding collapse: venture capital is leaving K-12 worldwide as investors prioritize AI tools and workforce training with clearer returns [1]. Global edtech investment peaked at $16.7B in 2021 and fell below $3B by 2025; new founders dropped from roughly 10,500 in 2020 to 645 last year [1].
Where K-12 AI capacity is actually accumulating gets one sentence in the article and deserves more. Nonprofit Khan Academy launched its AI tutor Khanmigo on March 14, 2023, originally built on GPT-4, with a pilot reaching about 65,000 students across 53 school districts at $4 per month [2]. The product line has since expanded to a Writing Coach in November 2023, then free generative-AI tools for teachers in August 2024 in partnership with Microsoft, and most recently an integration with Google Gemini announced at Bett UK in January 2026 [2]. The pattern that displaced the venture-backed K-12 startup is nonprofit-with-frontier-API-access. Its incentives around pedagogy, pricing, and outcomes look nothing like the ones the $16B in venture capital was chasing.
The article’s most revealing line is that retention suffered from “murky learning outcomes,” which is to say that after $16.7B and five years, the sector still cannot reliably measure whether AI tutoring helps a child learn [1]. The places where AI capital is now flowing, workforce certification, professional skill prep, and B2B corporate L&D, share two features K-12 lacks: self-motivated learners, and a clearly priced outcome in the form of a job, a credential, or a salary delta. K-12’s bottleneck has never been content delivery, which is what LLMs are good at. It is the social and motivational scaffold around the content, which LLMs do not obviously replace. The collapse may be telling us less about AI than about which problems are tractable to a venture-funded product wedge in the first place.

title: AbstRaL: Augmenting LLMs’ Reasoning by Reinforcing Abstract Thinking
text:
First page of the paper. Image from arXiv.
In AbstRaL: Augmenting LLMs’ Reasoning by Reinforcing Abstract Thinking [1] (ICLR 2026), Silin Gao, Antoine Bosselut, Samy Bengio, and Emmanuel Abbe (EPFL) train large language models (LLMs) to first translate a math word problem into a symbolic abstraction, then derive the answer via external symbolic tools, with reinforcement learning rewards on both abstraction quality and final answer correctness. The reported gains on GSM-Symbolic [2] and GSM-Plus [3] are largest for the smallest models tested (0.5B parameters), where the underlying reasoning was most fragile to surface-form perturbations.

title: AbstRaL: Augmenting LLMs’ Reasoning by Reinforcing Abstract Thinking
text:
Methods
Training happens in two stages. The first stage is supervised fine-tuning on a dataset the authors call GranulAR, where each example shows the model a four-step pipeline for solving a math word problem:

Spot the inputs. Find the numbers in the problem and replace each with a placeholder name like in0, in1, in2.
Reason in placeholders. Rewrite the solution chain using those placeholders instead of the actual numbers, with arithmetic steps marked inside double angle brackets (<<in0 * in1 = out0>>).
Extract the abstraction. A simple script pulls those bracketed steps out of the chain. Together they form the abstraction: the equations with placeholder variables, stripped of any specific numbers.
Plug in numbers. An off-the-shelf math solver (SymPy) takes the abstraction plus the actual input values and produces the final answer.




GranulAR training data construction: the four-step pipeline from a socratic chain-of-thought to an executable abstraction. Figure 4 from the paper [1].


The GranulAR examples are produced by a teacher model (Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct) doing format conversion on existing GSM8K data. The teacher does not generate new mathematical content; it takes the original gold socratic CoT answer and rewrites it twice. The first pass replaces concrete numbers with abstract symbols. The second converts the socratic format into the GranulAR sub-question decomposition. Each rewriting step is filtered: the rewritten output is parsed for <<...>> derivations, run through SymPy, and only kept if the final answer matches GSM8K’s gold answer. Of 7473 training samples, 6386 (85.5%) survive both filter passes. The filter is execution-based, so an accidentally-right abstraction with the wrong structure could pass. The symbolic-distance RL reward exists downstream to push the model away from accidentally-right toward structurally-correct.
Supervised fine-tuning alone gets a model to produce output in this format, but the paper finds it often writes abstractions that look right yet fail when the solver tries to run them. The second stage uses reinforcement learning (Group Relative Policy Optimization, or GRPO, the same algorithm DeepSeek used for its reasoning models) to fix that, with two hand-designed rewards:

Answer-correctness reward. Run the model’s abstraction through SymPy. If the result matches the known answer, the model gets a fixed positive reward. Otherwise zero.
Symbolic-distance reward. Compare the model’s abstraction to a gold abstraction piece by piece. The more editing needed to turn one into the other, the lower the reward. The closer the match, the higher.




The two reinforcement-learning rewards. Symbolic distance (center) measures how much editing is needed to turn the model’s abstraction into the gold reference; answer correctness (right) fires only when SymPy’s derivation matches the target. Figure 5 from the paper [1].


The symbolic-distance reward prevents shortcut learning: even an abstraction that happens to produce the correct answer by accident receives zero reward when its structure differs from the gold reference. The gradient pushes the model to produce faithful abstractions, which is the failure mode of supervised fine-tuning that the paper identifies.

text:
Results
The paper tests LLMs from 0.5B to 7B parameters. The headline numbers come from two endpoints: Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-Math-7B-Instruct. The benchmarks are GSM-Symbolic [2] (100 GSM8K templates, where names and numbers are perturbed) and GSM-Plus [3] (numerical, phrasing, and distractor variations of 1,319 GSM8K problems).

Vary Both is GSM-Symbolic accuracy when both numbers and names are perturbed. \(\Delta\) is the percentage drop from the original 100 GSM problems (lower is better; negative means higher than original). On GSM-Symbolic’s hardest split, “Vary Both”, where both numbers and names in each problem are perturbed simultaneously:

Qwen2.5-0.5B: AbstRaL scores 44.6%, against 32.3% for CoT-RL and 36.8% for the next-best baseline (SyReLM). The tiny model scores higher on the perturbed variants than on the original problems (\(\Delta\) = −1.3%), something no baseline achieves.
Qwen2.5-Math-7B: AbstRaL is 90.2%, against 88.1% for CoT-RL. The absolute gain is modest, but the drop-from-original (\(\Delta\)) is 0.9% for AbstRaL versus 8.2% for CoT-RL.

The largest per-task win is on distractor insertion, where the problem contains irrelevant sentences the model must ignore. On the 0.5B model, AbstRaL scores 36.5% versus the best CoT baseline at 22.7%.
Ablations confirm the abstract-reasoning behavior lives in the model weights, not the tools:

Removing SymPy and the regex extractor costs about 1 point on Qwen-0.5B and 0.2 points on Qwen-7B. The external tools are not the source of the gain.
Removing reinforcement learning entirely drops Vary Both to 29.6 (Qwen-0.5B) and 78.5 (Qwen-7B), below every CoT-trained baseline (CoT-8S, CoT-RL, SyReLM) and far below AbstRaL.
Removing just the symbolic-distance reward costs around 7 points on both model sizes. That single reward term accounts for roughly half the RL gain.
Removing the four-step GranulAR data format is most costly on the distractor split (Qwen-7B drops from 82.3 to 66.8). The granular decomposition is what teaches the model to ignore irrelevant sentences.

Out-of-distribution generalization. Even though AbstRaL is trained only on GSM8K, it transfers to eleven other math benchmarks (MATH, Minerva-MATH, SAT-Math, AIME-24, SVAMP, ASDiv, MAWPS, Gaokao-2023, TABMWP, College-Math, AQUA) and beats the baselines on almost all of them. On Qwen-7B, the Minerva-MATH score actually exceeds the model’s own prior fine-tuned checkpoint (34.6 → 38.6), meaning AbstRaL training improves a held-out benchmark beyond the model’s starting capability.

title: AbstRaL: Augmenting LLMs’ Reasoning by Reinforcing Abstract Thinking
text:
My Notes

The “SFT memorizes, RL generalizes” pattern keeps accumulating evidence. Chu et al. (2025) [4] demonstrated this on an arithmetic card game and a visual navigation environment: reinforcement-learning-trained models held up on out-of-distribution variants where supervised fine-tuning collapsed to memorization. AbstRaL reproduces the split at finer grain. Supervised fine-tuning yields unfaithful abstractions, reinforcement learning yields faithful ones. When the post-training objective is teaching a behavior rather than memorizing facts, reinforcement learning preserves the underlying capability. The consistency across such dissimilar tasks makes the pattern harder to dismiss.
AbstRaL’s separation makes abstraction itself a trainable target. Program of Thoughts (PoT) [5] and Program-Aided Language Models (PAL) [6] have the model generate Python code that an interpreter executes; abstraction and execution are fused into one program. AbstRaL splits them: the model generates only the symbolic equations, and SymPy derives the answer. The genuinely new affordance is not inspectability (PoT code is also inspectable) but separately rewardable abstraction. With AbstRaL the abstraction step has its own training signal (the symbolic-distance reward to the gold abstraction), so reinforcement learning can push faithfulness independently of execution. PoT and PAL can only reward the final answer, so a Python program that lands on the right number for wrong-shaped reasons gets reinforced.
The SFT-to-RL swap on an established recipe is the real comparison. Chain-of-Abstraction (CoA) [7] was Silin Gao’s prior work, the same first author. It fine-tuned LLMs to decode abstract reasoning chains before calling domain tools to fill them in. AbstRaL keeps that abstract-then-tool-call paradigm but replaces supervised fine-tuning with reinforcement learning, and outperforms CoA on the paper’s benchmarks. Because the authorship and recipe are held constant, the gain isolates the post-training objective itself rather than confounding it with architecture or prompting choices. The follow-up worth running: at what model scale does the gap close? If base models internalize abstraction during pretraining, the SFT-then-tools formulation may catch up at larger sizes.
Gains concentrate at small scale; frontier evidence is missing. On Qwen2.5-0.5B, AbstRaL lifts Vary-Both accuracy from 32.3 (CoT-RL baseline) to 44.6 and fully eliminates the perturbation gap (\(\Delta = -1.3\)). On Qwen2.5-Math-7B the same recipe lifts Vary-Both from 88.1 to 90.2, a 2-point gain on a baseline already near-saturated. Some of this is ceiling effect, but the paper’s claim that “abstract thinking broadly enables better generalizability” rests on improvements observed at 0.5B-7B without testing at the 30B-70B+ scales where current reasoners operate. Whether the abstraction-specific reward buys anything beyond what a larger base model already internalizes during pretraining is an open empirical question the paper invites but does not answer.

title: Is AI Cannibalizing Human Intelligence?
text:
Illustration: Edmon De Haro for The Wall Street Journal.
A WSJ essay by theoretical neuroscientist Vivienne Ming, reporting on her experiment that pitted humans alone, AI models alone (ChatGPT and Gemini), and human–AI hybrids against Polymarket’s prediction market.
Only 5–10% of hybrid teams actually beat the market. They treated the AI as a sparring partner, demanding evidence, asking for counterarguments, pushing back when it sounded confident. Most hybrids instead rubber-stamped the model’s answer or used it to ratify their own priors (classic confirmation bias plus sycophancy), and performed no better than the AI alone. The qualities that separated the winners were perspective-taking and intellectual humility, both fundamentally emotional skills. Ming names the deeper risk the Information-Exploration Paradox: as the cost of information approaches zero, human exploration collapses.

title: Is AI Cannibalizing Human Intelligence?
text:
My Notes
Ming’s most underrated claim is the one buried near the end: nearly all AI benchmarks measure what AI agents can do alone. The entire field optimizes against scoreboards that reward solo performance, which inevitably trains labs to build products that make the human optional rather than sharper. A hybrid-intelligence benchmark, scored on what the pair produces together relative to either component alone, would change what counts as an improvement. Anthropic’s Economic Index recently surfaced one version of that measurement: the Claude.ai task time horizon is 19 hours with human steering, against the same model’s 2 hours when running autonomously on METR’s benchmark. That 5× gap comes from the human bringing task decomposition, judgment about what to attempt, and verification mid-flight. It is exactly the hybrid-intelligence delta Ming is arguing the field should be measuring directly.
The sparring-partner pattern is also where decades of cognitive-science literature have the most to add. Philip Tetlock’s superforecasters, the top ~2% of volunteers identified by accuracy across a multi-year IARPA forecasting tournament, exhibit active open-mindedness and treat their own forecasts as tentative hypotheses, revising them when new evidence arrives. That disposition is exactly what the 5–10% of hybrid cyborgs were doing with their AI. If Ming is right about which qualities separate the winners, the field already has research on how to cultivate them in individuals, and tools like calibration training could transfer to the human half of the hybrid directly. She doesn’t make that connection explicit.
The Information-Exploration Paradox is probably more useful as a population-level claim than an individual one. At the individual level, the students who arrive with good metacognitive habits may use AI to skip the easy struggle and spend their friction budget on harder ideas, while the students who don’t may skip the struggle entirely. The paradox may not apply uniformly. It may widen existing gaps along lines that already correlate with educational outcomes. The prescription then becomes less “design AI that preserves friction” and more “design AI that scaffolds the metacognitive moves that separate the cyborgs from the rubber-stampers” — the scaffold-not-substitute distinction Anthropic found in its coding study.
The hardest unresolved tension in the piece is commercial. Most AI revenue today comes from removing friction, which means a product that preserves it loses to the one that doesn’t in head-to-head adoption. The AI Ming wants to see built is probably not going to come out of consumer chatbots at all. It will come from tutoring, coaching, and domain-expert tools where the user is explicitly paying for the struggle to be preserved. Duolingo and ChatGPT both use AI, but only one is structurally set up to build the capacities she is arguing for.

title: Even Experts Are Surprised by AI’s Latest ‘Vibe-Mathing’ Advance
text:
Abstract Rubik’s-cube artwork. Image from Scientific American.
Scientific American reports how Liam Price, a 23-year-old with no advanced mathematics training, got GPT-5.4 Pro to prove a 60-year-old Erdős conjecture about primitive sets in a single prompt.
What the article reports:

title: Even Experts Are Surprised by AI’s Latest ‘Vibe-Mathing’ Advance
text:
My Notes

Tao’s framing matters. “Maybe easier than expected” once a mental block was dislodged is a very different achievement than the model out-thinking the field, and the lay-press reflex to collapse the two loses the distinction. It slots into Tao’s earlier research-buddy pattern, where the model’s job is less to solve on command than to surface where the human had gotten stuck.
The prompter-as-author question sharpens here. Credit attribution in this pipeline has at least three discernible links (prompter, recognizer, verifier), and the community will have to develop conventions that describe the chain rather than collapsing it into “Price solved it” or “GPT-5.4 Pro solved it.”
If Tao and Lichtman are right about the technique, the value of this incident is less the single proof and more a transferable move humans can now use on adjacent problems, which is closer to how mathematical progress usually works than the “AI solves problem” headline suggests.
For mathematicians, the practical lesson lies slightly off to the side. Every long-standing conjecture in the file cabinet is worth a single pass through the frontier model now. Twenty seconds is the entire cost; the upside, once in a while, is a mental block no one had spotted.

title: TurboQuant: A First-Principles Walkthrough
text:
The “Putting it together” page: a five-step pipeline for TurboQuant-MSE plus a live demo with sliders for bits and dimension. Image from Interactive TurboQuant Walkthrough.
Arkar Min Aung, a deep-learning engineer, has published an extraordinary interactive walkthrough [1] of TurboQuant [2], the per-vector KV cache quantizer that approaches the Shannon limit, with draggable demos for every concept the paper builds on. TurboQuant is also the per-vector baseline that an earlier post here pushes against, so this walkthrough doubles as an introduction to the target that alternative is measuring itself from.
What Aung covers:

title: TurboQuant: A First-Principles Walkthrough
text:
My Notes
What the walkthrough covers that the TurboQuant paper does not:

Draggable interactive demos for every concept the paper builds on. A reader can rotate a vector and watch the outlier spike redistribute, or fire 50 shots and watch the bias/variance bullseye form.
An opening primer covering eight prerequisite concepts, each with its own demo: vectors, inner product, MSE, first and second moments, biased vs unbiased estimators, rotations, the Central Limit Theorem, and uniform vs Gaussian noise. The paper assumes the reader already has these in hand.
Plain-language naming of the cost. Aung states outright that TurboQuant’s random rotation is a different way of paying the per-block metadata tax production quantizers already pay to handle outliers. The paper treats the trade-off formally.

Sites like this one are why the open web is still a wonderful place.

title: DSPy: Compiling Declarative Language Model Calls into Self-Improving Pipelines
text:
Results with in-context learning on GSM8K math word problems. Each row is a separate pipeline: the module in the Program column is compiled against the examples in the Training set. All programs in this table are expressed by composing two to four DSPy modules and teleprompters. Compiling the correct modules, instead of string prompts, improves different LMs from 4-20% accuracy to 49-88% accuracy. Table 1 from the paper [1].
In DSPy: Compiling Declarative Language Model Calls into Self-Improving Pipelines [1] (ICLR 2024), Omar Khattab et al. (Stanford and collaborators) introduce a programming model that treats LM pipelines as composable, typed modules and compiles them via teleprompters that bootstrap their own few-shot demonstrations from a small unlabeled training set.

title: DSPy: Compiling Declarative Language Model Calls into Self-Improving Pipelines
text:
Methods
The programming model rests on three abstractions. Signatures declare the input/output shape of an LM call as a natural-language type spec (e.g., "question -> answer" or "context, question -> rationale, answer"), which the framework expands into a prompt template. Modules implement signatures via specific techniques: Predict runs a single-shot LM call, ChainOfThought adds a rationale step, ReAct interleaves thought/action/observation for tool use. Modules can contain other modules, so a retrieval-augmented QA pipeline is just a Python class that composes Retrieve and ChainOfThought. Teleprompters are the compilers: given a program, a metric, and a small training set (inputs only, no intermediate labels), a teleprompter runs the program on the training examples with a “teacher” model, keeps traces where the final output satisfied the metric, and uses those traces as few-shot demonstrations in the compiled program. BootstrapFewShot is the default; variants add random search over candidate demonstrations, compose with a stronger teacher program, or finetune a smaller model on the bootstrapped traces. The human writes the program structure and the metric; the compiler figures out what to put inside each prompt.

title: DSPy: Compiling Declarative Language Model Calls into Self-Improving Pipelines
text:
Results
The paper runs two case studies: GSM8K grade-school math (200 train / 300 dev / 1.3k test) and HotPotQA multi-hop retrieval QA. Base models are GPT-3.5 and Llama2-13b-chat; one HotPotQA run uses 770M-parameter T5-Large as the compile target. On GSM8K, the same three-line ChainOfThought program goes from 25.2% test accuracy (vanilla GPT-3.5 with no compilation) to 81.6% with the bootstrap + ensemble teleprompter; Llama2-13b-chat reaches 46.9% with the ThoughtReflection program plus ensemble, versus 9.4% baseline. On HotPotQA, a simple multihop program with bootstrap raises GPT-3.5 test EM from 31.5% (fewshot baseline) to 39.6%, and the ensemble reaches 45.6% on half the test set. The 770M T5-Large compiled from a Llama2-13b-chat teacher hits 39.3% HotPotQA answer EM on the dev set, using only 200 labeled and 800 unlabeled questions. That’s roughly on par with the much larger base models.



Results with in-context learning on HotPotQA for GPT-3.5 and Llama2-13b-chat across four DSPy programs (vanilla, CoT_RAG, react, multihop) and compilers (fewshot, bootstrap, ensemble, bootstrap×2). Answer exact match (Ans) and pair-retrieval accuracy (Psg) are reported for dev and test splits. Ensemble-compiled multihop tops both models; CoT_RAG with bootstrap is the next-best configuration. Table 2 from the paper [1].

title: DSPy: Compiling Declarative Language Model Calls into Self-Improving Pipelines
text:
My Notes

The programming model is the real contribution, and the teleprompters are interchangeable. Pre-DSPy prompt optimization worked at the string-template level. APE [2] and later EvoPrompt [3] searched over isolated prompt strings with LLM-implemented operators. DSPy moves optimization up a layer: because modules have typed signatures and compose into a graph, a teleprompter can treat any pipeline as a black box to optimize end-to-end against a single metric, bootstrapping intermediate demonstrations along the way. Putting composition at the module boundary is what enables pipeline-level search. MASS [4] can search over typed-module topologies because DSPy established the abstraction; its prompt optimization at block and workflow levels uses DSPy’s MIPRO teleprompter directly. The teleprompters themselves (bootstrap + random search) are conventional. The novelty is that they operate on a program rather than a prompt.
DSPy-styled distillation works: the 770M T5 result is the demonstration.

When DSPy compiles, the teacher model runs the program on training inputs; the metric filters complete-pipeline runs where the final output is correct; those good runs’ intermediate steps become demonstrations for the compiled program. No human annotates intermediate hops. Final-output supervision via the metric does that filtering.
Table 2 shows this in action: a 770M T5-Large, compiled from a Llama2-13b-chat teacher on 200 labeled + 800 unlabeled HotPotQA questions, reaches 39.3% answer EM on dev, within a few points of GPT-3.5 fewshot. The paper calls this “orders of magnitude lower costs for inference”; the stronger read is that for retrieval-heavy tasks with good pipeline structure, most of the capability lives in the pipeline, and the base model just has to execute the compiled prompts competently.
The distillation analogy is apt, with three caveats on what gets kept, what the student inherits, and what the procedure costs. Both let you train a smaller model without hand-labeled intermediate supervision; the teacher’s outputs stand in.

Distillation uses every teacher-generated input-output pair as student training data. DSPy uses only per-module steps from traces whose final pipeline output passed the metric; those steps become few-shot demonstrations inside each module’s prompt.
Distillation compiles the teacher’s capability into a single forward pass of the student; DSPy keeps the pipeline structure intact. The 770M T5 still runs the same multihop program, just with bootstrapped few-shot demos inside each module’s prompt.
Distillation trains the student via gradient descent over thousands to millions of teacher outputs on GPU clusters, taking days to weeks. DSPy’s default teleprompters do no gradient training; they just insert filtered demonstrations into the student program’s prompts. Even the finetune variant that produced the T5-770M result trains in minutes on 200 + 800 examples, with total compile cost bounded by a few hundred teacher inference calls.

Whether the pipeline gain stays significant as base models mature is an open question.

DSPy is a clean instance of extrinsic self-improvement. Humans design the programming model, pick the modules, write the metric, and choose the teleprompter strategy (bootstrap vs. random search vs. finetune). The LM only generates candidates that the compiler scores and keeps. The intrinsic metacognitive learning position paper [5] calls this out as the ceiling case: DSPy won’t decide that the task needs a different module type, or that the metric is misspecified, or that the teleprompter’s search strategy is a poor fit. Every one of those is wired in. In engineering or production settings that explicit control is often a feature. Teams need predictable, auditable behavior more than they need an agent that redesigns its own loop. The ceiling matters only when you measure against intrinsic.
DSPy has become a de facto substrate for both research and industrial LLM development.

Scale signals. 34K+ GitHub stars since January 2023. The dspy.ai “Community Use Cases” page lists 25+ named company deployments and 15+ published research papers built on DSPy, and is maintained as a growing index.
Research adoption runs beyond the cluster we’ve been reviewing: STORM (Wikipedia-article generation), Co-STORM, PATH (IR with 10 gold labels), IReRa (extreme classification with 10K+ labels), ECG-Chat (medical reports via GraphRAG), Palimpzest (declarative AI workload optimization), WangLab @ MEDIQA (Toronto’s competition winner), UMD’s suicide-detection system (beating 20-hour expert prompt engineering by 40%). Within this cluster, MASS uses DSPy’s MIPRO as its prompt-optimizer primitive and MetaSPO cites DSPy as prior art.
Industry adoption spans finance (Moody’s), healthcare (STChealth, Infinitus, Raia, Salomatic), legal (Truelaw), travel (JetBlue), semiconductor (Normal Computing), e-commerce (Sephora, Zoro UK), developer tooling (Replit), enterprise AI (Databricks, VMware, RadiantLogic), and security (Haize Labs red-teaming). The Databricks integration is particularly sticky: DSPy co-author Matei Zaharia is Databricks CTO, and DSPy now powers parts of their LM-judge, RAG, and agentic offerings.
Why the abstraction endured. Teleprompter algorithms keep evolving (MIPRO → MIPROv2 → GEPA, all listed on dspy.ai), but the programming model (signatures, modules, teleprompters) has stayed stable. New optimizers slot into the same surface.

title: Truly Self-Improving Agents Require Intrinsic Metacognitive Learning
text:
Spectrum of shared metacognition, from intrinsic (agent runs its own metacognitive loop) through shared (agent and designer split the metacognitive work) to extrinsic (metacognitive loop is fully externally defined). Figure 2 from the paper [1].
In Truly Self-Improving Agents Require Intrinsic Metacognitive Learning (ICML 2025) [1], Tennison Liu and Mihaela van der Schaar at Cambridge argue that almost every current “self-improving” LLM agent leans on hand-designed metacognitive loops, and that genuine, sustained self-improvement requires agents that can themselves evaluate, plan, and adapt their own learning processes.

title: Truly Self-Improving Agents Require Intrinsic Metacognitive Learning
text:
Methods
The paper formalizes metacognitive learning as a bi-level process. A metacognitive layer sits above the cognitive layer where task-level learning actually happens, monitoring and regulating it. The metacognitive layer has three components that close a loop: knowledge informs planning, planning produces learning activity, and evaluation feeds back into both.

Metacognitive knowledge is the agent’s self-model.

It comes in three flavors: knowledge of self (what the agent can already do, where its limits lie, what skills it has), knowledge of task (what the current task demands and what would help), and knowledge of strategies (which learning approaches are available and where each tends to apply).
The biggest threat to this component is hallucination: LLMs can confidently misrepresent their own internal state, including basic facts about which tools they have access to.
The paper cites recent work showing agents can classify math problems by required solution procedure [2] and identify which training tasks would help them, so the ingredient is at least partially present.

Metacognitive planning turns that self-model into action through two questions.

What to learn is a task-allocation question, traditionally answered by curriculum learning over a curated task pool [3]. Intrinsic variants replace the human-designed curriculum with internal drivers like curiosity, learnability, and regret, and let agents generate their own tasks rather than draw from a fixed pool [4].
How to learn is a strategy-selection question with two phases:

Exploration (temperature scaling, upper-confidence-bound tree search [5], uncertainty-guided sampling, prompt-based novelty seeking) chooses what experiences the agent gathers.
Learning extracts capabilities from those experiences via in-weight updates (finetuning on self-generated traces, à la STaR [6]), long-term memory writes (episodic experiences, abstract rules, reusable skills as tool functions), or both.

The paper flags this whole component as the most under-developed in current systems: nearly every shipped agent picks one fixed mechanism and applies it uniformly across tasks and over time.

Metacognitive evaluation closes the loop and has two aspects.

Tracking progress is the ongoing assessment of how learning is going. Held-out benchmarks like MMLU [7] work for well-defined capabilities. LLM-as-judge [8] fills in for fuzzier targets like emotional intelligence, creativity, or interestingness, where no quantifiable metric exists.
Metacognitive reflection is the post-hoc analysis of learning plans, distinct from task-level reflection (Reflexion-style [9]) by operating one level up: it evaluates long-term learning trajectories rather than per-task performance.
Because it operates over representations of the cognitive process rather than the task itself, metacognitive reflection can in principle be domain-agnostic, given enough domain-specific signal to extract progress from.

title: Truly Self-Improving Agents Require Intrinsic Metacognitive Learning
text:
Results
The paper walks three well-known systems through this framework as case studies, ordered by increasing intrinsic-ness:

STaR [6] (Zelikman et al., 2022): a reasoning bootstrapping method. Given a small set of problems with reasoning traces plus a larger set with answers only, the agent attempts problems and gets finetuned on any trace that led to a correct answer, then the cycle repeats on harder problems. Almost entirely extrinsic: the agent doesn’t assess its own capabilities, doesn’t choose which tasks to attempt (externally curated), and doesn’t adapt its learning strategy (rationalization with answer hints is fixed). The metacognitive loop sits with the system designer.
Voyager [10] (Wang et al., 2023): an LLM-based embodied agent for lifelong learning in Minecraft. It maintains a growing library of executable Python skills and autonomously discovers increasingly complex actions to perform. Partially intrinsic: the agent tracks what it can do (knowledge) and balances exploration against task learnability when picking next goals (planning). The learning strategy stays fixed though: the same exploration-learning loop runs across all tasks. Voyager beats expert-designed curriculum baselines, which the paper takes as evidence the intrinsic components matter.
Generative Agents [11] (Park et al., 2023): agents in a Sims-style sandbox that accumulate experiences, form relationships, and develop distinct personas through lived interaction. Most intrinsic of the three. Agents form evolving identities and motivations (knowledge), autonomously plan daily activities (planning), and periodically trigger an abstract reflection, such as recognizing a newfound interest or reinterpreting recent events, that updates their semantic memory and shapes future plans (evaluation). The paper flags the contrast with Reflexion-style [9] techniques: Reflexion reflects at the cognitive level to improve performance on specific tasks; Generative Agents reflect at the metacognitive level, drawing inferences about their own trajectory.

The arc across the three case studies is how the paper builds its argument: each system is intrinsic on more components than the last, and the paper argues the more-intrinsic systems show more sustained progress in the diversity and novelty of their evolving capabilities. The paper acknowledges these are preliminary observations that still require rigorous, systematic studies to substantiate.

title: Truly Self-Improving Agents Require Intrinsic Metacognitive Learning
text:
My Notes

Both limitation claims rest on one example each. The “lose efficacy” claim cites Song et al.’s 2024 generation-verification-gap finding [12]. The “fail to generalize” claim points at STaR and bootstrapped self-training, which worked in their original domain but didn’t transfer. No new experiments.
Every shipped agent is extrinsic in this taxonomy. The system designer decides what to monitor, what counts as progress, and when to switch strategies. Supervising Ralph Wiggum [13] hand-designs a Co-Regulation Agent with a fixed role and loop position. ReMA [14] hand-designs the high-low decomposition. The prompt-optimization line (MASS, MetaSPO, EvoPrompt) uses LLMs as inner-loop optimizers but humans fix the search-space structure.
“Sustained progress” lacks a cross-system metric. STaR runs in math/reasoning, Voyager in Minecraft, Generative Agents in a Sims sandbox. A residual learning rate (slope late in training over slope early) gets the y-axis unit-free, but the x-axis stays domain-specific: a STaR training step isn’t a Voyager training step, and Sims days don’t align with Minecraft exploration. The cross-system ordering needs either a shared benchmark or a principled x-axis alignment, neither of which the paper provides.
SelfReflect bounds the optimism about LLM metacognitive ingredients. The paper argues frontier LLMs already exhibit pieces of metacognitive knowledge, planning, and evaluation. Apple’s SelfReflect [15] finds, across 20 modern models, that LLM self-reports of their own answer distributions don’t match what those models actually sample. So the metacognitive-knowledge ingredient is thinner than the paper’s optimism implies, at least without help from techniques like sample-then-summarize.

title: Truly Self-Improving Agents Require Intrinsic Metacognitive Learning
text:
Related Posts

DSPy: Compiling Declarative Language Model Calls into Self-Improving Pipelines: the cleanest example of the extrinsic ceiling this paper describes, where humans wire in the modules, metric, and search strategy.
ReMA: Learning to Meta-think for LLMs with Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning: a hand-designed high/low metacognitive split, one of the systems this taxonomy classifies as extrinsic on the planning component.
MemSkill: Learning and Evolving Memory Skills for Self-Evolving Agents: a self-evolving agent that pushes toward the intrinsic end by learning which memory operations to apply, rather than running one fixed loop.
Supervising Ralph Wiggum: Exploring a Metacognitive Co-Regulation Agentic AI Loop for Engineering Design: another hand-designed co-regulation loop with a fixed role and position, the kind of extrinsic mechanism the paper argues limits scalability.
SelfReflect: Can LLMs Communicate Their Internal Answer Distribution?: empirical counterweight to the paper’s optimism, finding that the metacognitive-knowledge ingredient is thinner than assumed across 20 models.

title: System Prompt Optimization with Meta-Learning
text:
Generalization across different domains. Left: MetaSPO’s performance on domains not used for prompt optimization, plotted against their similarity to the training domains. Right: Effect of the number of training domains, with more domains yielding stronger generalization. Figure 5 from the paper [1].
In System Prompt Optimization with Meta-Learning (NeurIPS 2025) [1], Yumin Choi, Jinheon Baek, and Sung Ju Hwang (KAIST, DeepAuto.ai) introduce MetaSPO, a bilevel optimization framework that meta-learns a task-agnostic system prompt while simultaneously updating task-specific user prompts in an iterative inner loop.

title: System Prompt Optimization with Meta-Learning
text:
Methods



Concept figure. (A) An LLM input has three parts: task-agnostic system prompt, task-specific user prompt, target example. (B) Conventional task-specific optimization tunes the user prompt for one task and generalizes poorly. (C) MetaSPO meta-learns a system prompt that transfers to unseen target tasks. Figure 1 from the paper [1].


Against this three-part structure, MetaSPO’s bilevel algorithm runs two nested optimization loops. The outer loop optimizes the task-agnostic system prompt, and the inner loop iteratively refines task-specific user prompts. At each outer step, the current system prompt is paired with candidate user prompts across multiple source tasks. The model’s failures on held-out examples feed an LLM optimizer that proposes refined candidates (user prompts inside the inner loop, system prompts at the outer loop). The meta-learned system prompt transfers to unseen target tasks with no further system-prompt tuning; at test time, only the user prompt is adapted per target task.
The system prompt starts as “You are a helpful assistant.” (the Default baseline) and is iteratively refined through the outer loop. At each step of either loop, a separate optimizer LLM (GPT-4o mini in the main experiments, distinct from the Llama-3.2 3B base LLM that generates task responses) is prompted with the current prompt and its incorrectly-predicted examples, asked to analyze the failure modes, and then asked for multiple candidate refinements. Candidates are evaluated against held-out task data, and the top-k by performance survive to the next iteration. Both loops follow this same textual-gradient pattern (after Pryzant et al. [4]), applied at different scopes: user prompt per task in the inner loop, system prompt aggregated across source tasks in the outer loop.



MetaSPO overview. The inner loop refines candidate user prompts via failure analysis on a target task; the outer loop refines the system prompt by aggregating failures across multiple source tasks. Figure 2 from the paper [1].

title: System Prompt Optimization with Meta-Learning
text:
Results
The paper evaluates on 14 unseen target tasks across 5 domains (Medical, Review Analysis, Reasoning, Safety, Grounding), with each score the average performance of a system prompt paired with ten different user prompts. Within-domain Domain MetaSPO averages 44.5 over the 14 tasks, beating the next-best baseline SPRIG at 37.0 and the no-system-prompt Default at 32.2. The cross-domain Global MetaSPO setting (one system prompt meta-learned across all 5 domains) averages 41.4, still ahead of all baselines but ~3 points behind the within-domain Domain setting. Separately, on test-time efficiency: a MetaSPO-pretrained system prompt reaches Default’s converged performance with 80% fewer optimization iterations and 75% less data during test-time user-prompt adaptation.



Main results on 14 unseen target tasks, grouped by 5 domains. Global methods use a single system prompt across all domains; Domain methods use a system prompt meta-learned on the target’s domain. Each cell is the average score across 10 different user prompts on that target task. Domain MetaSPO (bottom row) tops the overall average at 44.5. Table 1 from the paper [1].


Figure 4 tests whether MetaSPO’s lift transfers uniformly across target tasks or depends on source-target task similarity. The paper measures similarity via Bag-of-Words overlap between the source-task training distribution and the target task, then plots per-task improvement against it.



MetaSPO’s gain over the Default baseline as a function of source-target task similarity (measured by Bag-of-Words overlap). Points above the y=0 line indicate a positive lift over Default; Pearson correlation 0.56 between similarity and improvement. High-similarity target tasks see larger gains; low-similarity tasks see near-neutral gains. Figure 4 from the paper [1].

title: System Prompt Optimization with Meta-Learning
text:
My Notes

The decomposition is the contribution, more than the method. Before this paper, “prompt optimization” treated the prompt as one optimization target for one task. DSPy [2], MIPRO [3], Pryzant et al.’s textual gradients [4], and EvoPrompt [5] each target a different piece of that setup, but all produce task-specific prompts. The bilevel split (task-agnostic system prompt above, task-specific user prompt below) is the key move; once you make it, the meta-learning structure follows naturally because the outer loop has a natural “across tasks” loss to optimize. The MetaSPO algorithm itself is a structurally familiar inner/outer LLM-as-optimizer loop. What matters here is the decision about what to put in each level.
The system prompt does most of the transfer work.

MetaSPO’s headline wins on unseen tasks come from the system prompt. In Table 1’s Unseen Generalization scenario, user prompts are LLM-sampled per task and held fixed; only the system prompt varies across the methods compared. Domain MetaSPO averages 44.5 over 14 unseen target tasks vs. Default’s 32.2, a +12.3-point lift attributable to the system prompt alone.
Appendix B.7 tests system-prompt vs user-prompt optimization head-to-head: MetaSPO (system-prompt optimized on source tasks) vs. ProTeGi (user-prompt optimized on source tasks), evaluated on the unseen Reasoning domain. MetaSPO wins across every source-domain starting point; ProTeGi drops below the Default system prompt, indicating user-prompt optimizations don’t transfer past the specific tasks they were tuned on.

Test-time efficiency is the practically relevant finding. The headline number is the unseen-generalization performance, but the deployment-relevant result is in §4: a MetaSPO-pretrained system prompt reaches the Default baseline’s converged performance with 80% fewer optimization iterations and 75% less data during test-time user-prompt adaptation. That’s a recipe for shipping prompt-optimized agents when each new task gets a small calibration budget rather than full re-optimization.
Generalization is asymmetric along source-target similarity. Figure 4 shows MetaSPO’s gain over Default scales with source-target task similarity measured by Bag-of-Words. High similarity, big gain; low similarity, the meta-learned system prompt is closer to neutral. That’s the expected meta-learning failure mode on out-of-distribution tasks, but it also bounds the deployment story: a system prompt meta-learned on Medical+Review+Reasoning will help most on tasks that look like those at the BoW level, and the cross-domain Global setting underperforms the within-domain Domain setting (41.4 vs. 44.5 avg). The follow-up question: at what point does the meta-learned prior become a liability on a sufficiently distant task?
