title: Where Claude Code Tokens Go
text:
Token breakdown banner. Image from Mnimiy on X.
Mnimiy (@Mnilax) claims to have proxy-logged 90 days of Claude Code traffic (430 hours, 6M input tokens, $1,340 in API spend) and published a 9-pattern breakdown arguing that 73% of spend goes to overhead the user pays before typing a prompt.

title: Where Claude Code Tokens Go
text:
What the article reports
He ran an HTTP proxy between Claude Code and the Anthropic API for 90 days, logging every request’s payload, response, token counts, latency, and model. Each token was bucketed into one of nine categories (productive, cache hit, cache miss, conversation-history re-read, hook injection, skill loading, tool-use overhead, extended thinking, CLAUDE.md). 27% of tokens were productive; the other 73% split across these patterns, ranked by cost share:



Token spend breakdown across ten categories. Image from Mnimiy on X.



CLAUDE.md bloat (14%). His grew to 4,800 tokens over six months; he cut to 900 by moving framework-specific rules to project-level files, extracting repeated patterns into skills, and converting verbose rules into 3-word imperatives. Target is under 1,500 tokens combined.
Conversation history re-reads (13%). Every follow-up re-tokenizes the full transcript; at ~500 tokens per exchange, message 30 costs 30× message 1. His 60-message sessions dropped to a 15-message average by editing prior messages instead of stacking follow-ups, hard-capping sessions at 20 messages then summarizing into a fresh chat, and using /compact (not /clear) when continuity matters.
Hook injection (11%). Three plugins’ UserPromptSubmit hooks together injected 6,200 tokens of branch names, recent-change summaries, and memory snippets on every prompt. He kept only git-branch.
Cache misses on session resume (10%). The default 5-minute prompt-cache lifetime means any coffee break triggers full-price re-tokenization of ~8K of cached boilerplate; he hit this ~640× in 90 days. Upgrading to the 1-hour cache on paid plans (2× write premium one-time, 0.1× reads) dropped his cache-miss cost 80% and pays off after roughly 10 resumes per session; a lighter workaround is keeping a “ping” hotkey that warms the cache before you step away.
Skill loading on irrelevant tasks (7%). Nine installed skills auto-invoke on conservative relevance detection, so the UI-design skill fires on backend tasks; at ~1,500 tokens per SKILL.md, that’s ~13,500 tokens of irrelevant context per task. He ran a 7-day audit of which skills he actually invoked and cut from 11 active to 4.
“Just in case” MCP tool definitions (6%). Twelve connected Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers each ship their full tool schema on every request (~600 tokens on average; PostgreSQL MCP alone is ~1,200), but he used only 3 of the 12 in 80% of his work. He edited ~/.claude/settings.json to drop the others from auto-load and re-enables per-session, ending at 3 always-on.
Extended thinking on simple questions (5%). “Advanced Thinking” left on globally spent 3,000+ thinking tokens on prompts like “rename this variable to camelCase”. He recommends defaulting it OFF and toggling ON per-message (Alt+T in Claude Code) when a task genuinely needs reasoning. About 80% don’t.
Wrong-direction generation (4%). Claude writes 400 lines, drift is obvious by line 50, users let it finish. Output tokens are billed. Cmd+. / Ctrl+. stops generation and keeps what’s already written; in Claude Code terminal, double-Esc opens a checkpoint scroller to rewind. He reports ~$15/month saved.
Plugin auto-update redundancy (3%). Nine plugins’ SessionStart hooks stacked “loaded successfully” notifications at ~1,400 tokens on every session start. He kept two (branch context and env vars).

The article blames part of the late-March 2026 “usage limits hit way faster than expected” complaints on two independent prompt-cache bugs that silently inflated some sessions’ costs 10–20×, documented in GitHub issue #40524 and since patched; downgrading to Claude Code v2.1.34 helped some users.
After applying all nine fixes, the claim is that productive-token share lifts from 27% to “roughly 65%”. The piece also lists six approaches that didn’t move the needle: switching to Haiku for simple tasks (~3% help), aggressive /clear between tasks (net negative, lost useful context), disabling all skills (net negative, author re-wrote the same instructions manually), off-peak scheduling (partial; peak-hour quota reduction affected ~7% of users per Anthropic), plan downgrade (flat cost per work-hour), and trying to reverse-engineer the March cache bug yourself (not worth it for individuals).

title: Where Claude Code Tokens Go
text:
My Notes

The nine patterns trace back to one design choice: Claude Code preloads “might be relevant” context (CLAUDE.md, hook output, skill bodies, MCP schemas, full conversation history) on every turn, and bills the user for the speculation. Anthropic’s own answer to this is progressive disclosure, the core design principle behind Agent Skills: metadata loads eagerly, full bodies pull in only when Claude judges the skill relevant. But the principle doesn’t seem to extend to the other preload categories, which remain always-on; and even within Skills the conservative auto-invoke the article describes (nine installed skills loading on every task) undermines it in practice.
Subagent delegation already exists in Claude Code and directly addresses the article’s biggest line item (conversation-history re-reads, 13%): Explore or general-purpose agents pull context into a task-scoped workspace that doesn’t feed back into the main thread. But it’s not the default behavior, and the article’s nine-fix list doesn’t mention it, suggesting the tool is under-adopted even among experienced users. The impact compounds on long sessions; the article’s own arithmetic (message 30 costs 30× message 1) makes main-thread history re-read quadratic in turn count, while a subagent’s scratch context stays bounded.
The cache-miss fix depends on whether you can tune the cache lifetime directly. If you can, upgrading from the 5-minute default to the 1-hour extended cache pays off quickly. If you can’t, the only option is to keep the cache warm by touching the session during breaks.

title: Language Models with Conformal Factuality Guarantees
text:
Target error rate vs. empirical factuality on GPT-4. Each solid line starts at the base factuality of GPT-4 on the associated dataset; NaturalQuestions and MATH overlap at the top-right. Figure 3 from the paper [1].
In Language Models with Conformal Factuality Guarantees [1] (ICML 2024), Christopher Mohri and Tatsunori Hashimoto (Stanford) propose conformal factuality (CF): cast the correctness of a language model (LM) output as uncertainty quantification, and solve it with conformal prediction.

title: Language Models with Conformal Factuality Guarantees
text:
Methods
The construction decomposes an LM answer into atomic sub-claims, scores each one, and backs off by dropping the lowest-scoring claims until the retained set is expected to be factual with probability \(1-\alpha\). The threshold for dropping is calibrated on a small held-out set with human factuality labels, following the standard conformal-prediction recipe.
The connection to conformal prediction runs through a second set, distinct from the sub-claims. For a prompt \(x\), let \(O\) be the (possibly backed-off) LM output. The “uncertainty set” \(C(x)\) is every more-specific statement \(S\) such that \(S\) entails \(O\) — equivalently, every possible ground-truth answer that would make \(O\) true. The sub-claim set is finite, explicit, and the object the algorithm directly manipulates; dropping sub-claims is how it acts on \(O\). The uncertainty set \(C(x)\) is implicit, defined by the meaning of \(O\), and is what the guarantee is stated over. Dropping a sub-claim weakens \(O\), so more statements clear the entailment bar and \(C(x)\) expands. A factuality guarantee is then a coverage guarantee on \(C(x)\): with probability \(\geq 1-\alpha\), the true answer lies inside \(C(x)\), which by construction makes \(O\) itself factual.



Conformal factuality as conformal prediction on entailment sets. Each candidate LM output (top) is paired with the set of more-specific statements that entail it (bottom); dropping sub-claims expands the uncertainty set and raises factuality. Figure 1 from the paper [1].


How it’s implemented. Every non-trivial stage in the pipeline is a GPT-4 prompt. The base LM \(\mathsf{L}\) generates the initial answer. A separator prompt \(\mathsf{S}\) decomposes it into atomic sub-claims. Scoring is either frequency (sample five GPT-4 generations at temperature 1.0 and count how often each claim appears) or self-confidence (another prompt asks GPT-4 to rate its own claims). After low-score claims are dropped, a merger prompt \(\mathsf{M}\) stitches the survivors into a coherent user-facing paragraph. The merger is the critical step the guarantee depends on: the paper’s Assumption 5.1 requires \(\mathsf{M}\) to neither add nor remove sub-claims, only reorder and connect. If GPT-4 introduces a new claim in a transition phrase, or drops a retained one as stylistically awkward, the coverage guarantee on \(C(x)\) breaks silently, and nothing in the pipeline audits this.

title: Language Models with Conformal Factuality Guarantees
text:
Results
Experiments use GPT-4 on three datasets: FActScore [2] [2] biographies, NaturalQuestions [3], and MATH [4]. Empirical factuality tracks the target \(1-\alpha\) across the range (Figure 3). Calibration needs only a few hundred human-labeled examples.
Figure 4 plots the cost–benefit tradeoff across all three benchmarks. The panel titles (FActScore, NQ, MATH) are benchmark names, not the metric; the y-axis in every panel is the fraction of sub-claims the method had to drop (the cost), and the x-axis is the fraction of factual outputs achieved (the benefit). Lower curves = better (less removal for the same factuality). Tick marks along each curve correspond to different target \(\alpha\) values. The ★ at the bottom-left of each panel is base GPT-4 with no removal: ~25% factual on biographies, ~75% on NQ and MATH. Five scoring functions are compared: Random (blue) and Ordinal (orange, by position in the output) are baselines; GPT-4 self-confidence (green) and Frequency (red, how often a sub-claim appears across sampled generations) are the LM-based methods; Oracle (purple) uses ground-truth labels as an upper bound. Frequency dominates the baselines on every benchmark: biography factuality climbs from ~25% to ~80% while removing only ~50% of sub-claims; NQ gains ~15 points at ~25% removal; MATH gains ~15 points at ~10% removal. GPT-4 self-confidence is second-best and tracks Frequency on MATH but lags on the open-ended generation tasks.



Cost–benefit tradeoff of conformal factuality on FActScore biographies, NaturalQuestions, and MATH. Figure 4 from the paper [1].


Table 1 shows the qualitative behavior: base GPT-4 output on the left, conformal-factuality output on the right, with claims the method flagged as likely-false highlighted in red. The first three rows are FActScore biographies at \(\alpha=0.2\); the last row is a MATH problem at \(\alpha=0.1\). The backed-off outputs are shorter but preserve the claims that scored high-confidence. The MATH example shows CF can remove a single incorrect reasoning step while keeping the rest of the derivation intact.



Table 1 from the paper [1].

title: Language Models with Conformal Factuality Guarantees
text:
My Notes

Sub-claim decomposition carries the guarantee, not conformal prediction. The guarantee is only as tight as the atomic-claim decomposer and the entailment assumption: “removing a sub-claim expands the entailment set.” This is the same premise that FActScore [2] relies on to score biographies, and it’s contested. Claim splitting can be lossy, and two sub-claims can jointly imply a third that neither contains. The paper assumes the decomposition is fine-grained enough that residual entailment closure is negligible, which is a stronger condition than the conformal machinery needs.
“Factuality guarantee” is marginal, not conditional. Conformal prediction gives a guarantee on average over a calibration distribution, not per-prompt. If a user asks a question whose underlying topic is rare in the calibration set, the empirical error can be much higher than \(\alpha\). This is the same limitation Angelopoulos and Bates [5] flag in their conformal tutorial, and it’s worth naming because “80–90% correctness guarantee” reads stronger than it is.
Frequency scoring breaks when the model is confidently wrong. Self-consistency [6] [6] and semantic entropy use the same sampling-distribution structure as a truth signal, and both fail the same way: when multiple samples converge on the same wrong answer, the score is high but the claim is false. The paper’s GPT-4 numbers don’t tell us how the method degrades on weaker models where this happens more often.
Useful complement to retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). Conformal factuality sits downstream of generation, so it composes with RAG: retrieval supplies grounded context to the base LM, and the conformal layer then drops sub-claims whose confidence scores stay low even with the retrieved evidence in the prompt. The interesting experiment, not run here, is whether the back-off threshold needed for 90% factuality shrinks enough under RAG that retention stays high on questions the base model would otherwise hallucinate. The natural benchmark for that experiment is something like AVeriTeC [8], where claims come from real fact-checking organizations, evidence is web-retrieved, and Not Enough Evidence is a labelled verdict class — though the AVeriTeC post flags that NEI there means “annotators couldn’t find evidence”, not “the model abstained”, so the mapping into selective prediction needs care.
Relative to Conformal Language Modeling (CLM) [7] (Quach et al.). CLM appeared on arXiv in June 2023 and was presented at ICLR 2024; CF followed eight months later, arriving on arXiv in February 2024 and at ICML 2024. CLM was the more general “adapt conformal prediction to generative LMs” move, and CF the narrower factuality-via-sub-claim-back-off specialization. CLM returns a set of whole candidate outputs with coverage. CF takes a different route: it operates on a single LM answer, uses the entailment relation to define coverage implicitly, and backs off to a weaker version of that answer until the factuality target is hit.

CLM is task-agnostic. Its stopping rule scores whole candidate outputs (likelihood, cluster membership, an external scorer). CF requires sub-claim decomposition, which only factors cleanly for factual claims, so open-ended generation (creative writing, free-form summarization) is out of scope.
CF returns one clean output. CLM returns a candidate set, which requires a downstream selection step (ranking, user choice, or a wrapper that picks one).
Both methods spend multiple LLM calls per query, but for different purposes. CLM samples \(K\) full candidate outputs from the base LM (typically 5–20) and keeps a subset with coverage. CF with frequency scoring also samples \(K\) generations, but uses them only to score sub-claims in a single base answer (counting how often each claim appears), then drops low-score claims and merges the survivors. CF with self-confidence scoring skips the extra samples entirely. The choice between CLM and CF is about what you get back (a set vs. a single backed-off output), not compute.
CLM’s coverage is over sampled candidates. CF’s is over an implicit entailment set, which inherits the quality of the sub-claim decomposition (\(\mathsf{S}\)) and the merger assumption (5.1). CLM avoids both soft assumptions.

Stacking CF inside CLM is a direction neither paper explored. Run CLM’s outer sampler to get \(K\) candidates, then pass each through CF’s sub-claim decomposition and back-off before applying CLM’s conformal stopping rule over the set. Each returned candidate is individually factual; the set as a whole retains CLM’s coverage.

Cost is ~\(K \times\) CF per query.
Two calibrations compose. Whether the joint guarantee is additive, multiplicative, or needs a separate joint calibration is the technical question a follow-up would have to solve.
CF’s back-off reduces information per candidate, so the final set may be dominated by short hedged answers, which defeats CLM’s motivation for returning diverse candidates.

title: A Primer on Conformal Prediction
text:
Prediction-set examples on ImageNet. Three progressively harder images of the class fox squirrel. The easy image gets a single-class set; the moderate image gets a few alternatives; the hard image’s set contains many similar-looking species, and the ground truth ranks second rather than first. Figure 1 from the paper [1].
In A Gentle Introduction to Conformal Prediction and Distribution-Free Uncertainty Quantification [1] (arXiv preprint, July 2021; later published in Foundations and Trends in Machine Learning, 2023), Anastasios N. Angelopoulos and Stephen Bates (Berkeley) walk through conformal prediction as a hands-on, code-first recipe for turning any black-box model into one whose predictions come with a distribution-free coverage guarantee.
This post doubles as standing background for the blog’s posts on conformal language modeling, conformal factuality, and related calibration work.

title: A Primer on Conformal Prediction
text:
What conformal prediction is
Conformal prediction [1], [2] is a distribution-free statistical framework that turns any predictor into one that outputs sets with a calibrated coverage guarantee. Given a trained model and a labeled calibration set not used in training, score each calibration example with some non-conformity function (for example, \(1 - p(y_i \mid x_i)\) for classification), take the \((1-\epsilon)\)-quantile of those scores, and at test time return every candidate whose score falls below that quantile. If the calibration and test data are exchangeable, the returned set contains the true label with probability at least \(1-\epsilon\), without assumptions about the model’s own calibration or the data distribution. The framework dates to the late 1990s (Vovk, Gammerman, and Shafer) and is a standard tool for uncertainty quantification outside deep learning.
The recipe is three steps, and the paper lays them out alongside matching Python: compute non-conformity scores on the calibration data; read off the calibration quantile \(\hat{q}\); build the test-time set from every class whose score falls below \(\hat{q}\).



The conformal recipe in three steps: (1) compute non-conformity scores on held-out calibration data, where the score is one minus the softmax output of the true class; (2) take \(\hat{q}\), the \(\lceil(n+1)(1-\epsilon)\rceil/n\) empirical quantile of those scores; (3) at test time, return every class whose score falls below \(\hat{q}\). Figure 2 from the paper [1].


The guarantee is exact and two-sided. For a calibration set of size \(n\), the coverage of the returned set \(\mathcal{C}(X_{\text{test}})\) obeys
\[1-\epsilon \;\le\; \mathbb{P}\big(Y_{\text{test}} \in \mathcal{C}(X_{\text{test}})\big) \;\le\; 1-\epsilon+\frac{1}{n+1},\]
a result the paper attributes to Vovk, Gammerman, and Saunders. It holds for any \(n\), so the floor of \(1-\epsilon\) is met even with a small calibration set, and the upper bound shows the procedure does not badly over-cover.

title: A Primer on Conformal Prediction
text:
A concrete CIFAR-10 walkthrough
Take a CIFAR-10 image classifier with softmax outputs and target \(\epsilon = 0.1\). On 1,000 held-out calibration images, score each by \(s_i = 1 - p(y_i \mid x_i)\) (one minus the model’s probability on the true class). Sort the 1,000 scores in ascending order and take the 901st value (the \(\lceil 0.9 \cdot 1001 \rceil\)-th); call it \(\hat{q}\). On a new test image \(x\), return the set of classes \(\{y : 1 - p(y \mid x) \leq \hat{q}\}\). When the test image comes from the same distribution as calibration, the returned set contains the correct class at least 90% of the time. This is a weaker claim than “the top-1 prediction is correct 90% of the time” — a set of all 10 classes trivially contains the truth yet conveys no information. Depending on difficulty, the set might contain one class (easy image), three or four (moderate), or all ten (a hard image the model has no clear read on). The number of distinct classes in the set is how conformal prediction communicates uncertainty, widening on harder inputs.

title: A Primer on Conformal Prediction
text:
Two knobs control set size
At a given coverage level, two knobs determine how big the returned set ends up. Smaller \(\epsilon\) demands tighter coverage, pushes the calibration quantile into the right tail, and forces \(\hat{q}\) up, so more candidates pass the test-time filter. At the extreme \(\epsilon < 1/(n+1)\), where \(n\) is the calibration set size, the quantile is undefined and the set becomes “everything,” which satisfies the guarantee trivially but is uninformative.
Model quality is the second knob. A better predictor assigns higher probability to the true class on calibration points, giving smaller non-conformity scores, a lower \(\hat{q}\), and a stricter probability floor at test time. Because a better model still puts enough mass on the correct class to clear that stricter floor, it produces sharper sets at the same \(\epsilon\). Weaker models hit the same coverage but through larger, less informative sets. Set size then doubles as a data-driven measure of model quality pegged to a formal guarantee.

title: A Primer on Conformal Prediction
text:
Ranking drives the guarantee
One subtlety worth naming: conformal prediction uses score rankings, and the coverage guarantee does not require the model’s probabilities to be calibrated. Any monotone-in-relevance scoring function works, because the quantile adapts to whatever the calibration scores look like. The cost of miscalibration shows up in set size rather than coverage: a rank-destroying miscalibration inflates \(\hat{q}\) and dilates the set, but the \((1-\epsilon)\) guarantee still holds.

title: A Primer on Conformal Prediction
section: The returned set is a coverage hull
text:
The returned set is a coverage hull
This means the returned set is a coverage hull. It does not convey relative likelihoods across elements, calibrated per-candidate confidences, or any distributional information beyond “at least one of these is correct at the chosen \(\epsilon\).” If a downstream consumer needs to know which answer in the set is most likely, conformal prediction leaves that to a separate mechanism, whether a raw ranking used informally or a Bayesian or ensemble method.

title: A Primer on Conformal Prediction
text:
Marginal coverage, not conditional
The guarantee is marginal: the probability is averaged over the randomness in both the calibration draw and the test point. It does not promise the same coverage for every input or every subgroup. The paper makes the distinction concrete with three regimes, shown below for a two-group classification problem and a regression band. With no coverage, one group is badly under-covered (5%) while the other does better (14%). Marginal coverage hits the target on average but can do it by over-covering one group (100%) and under-covering the other (80%). Only conditional coverage holds the target within each group (90% and 90%) and spreads errors evenly across the input space.



Three notions of coverage at a 90% target. Top row: errors by group, with green points correctly covered and red points missed. Bottom row: the same idea for a regression band. No coverage misses the target; marginal coverage meets it on average but lets errors concentrate in one group or region; conditional coverage holds the target within every group. Figure 10 from the paper [1].


Conditional coverage is what most deployments actually want, and split-conformal prediction does not deliver it. Adaptivity — letting set size grow on genuinely harder inputs — is the practical proxy the paper recommends measuring, since the marginal guarantee says nothing about whether hard and easy inputs are treated differently.

title: A Primer on Conformal Prediction
text:
Why generative LMs are harder
The framework above assumes a finite candidate set you can enumerate (the \(K\) classes). Generative language models break this assumption: the output space is the combinatorial space of all possible text sequences, so you can’t score every candidate. Adapting conformal prediction to LMs requires replacing enumeration with sampling plus a calibrated stopping rule. That adaptation is the subject of the Conformal Language Modeling post. A related adaptation, specifically for factual claim verification, is the subject of the Language Models with Conformal Factuality Guarantees post.

title: A Primer on Conformal Prediction
text:
My Notes

A two-decade-old method, repackaged for deep learning: conformal prediction’s machinery dates to Vovk, Gammerman, and Saunders in the late 1990s and the 2005 monograph [2], which reads as dense measure-theoretic statistics. What this tutorial added was not a new theorem but a packaging: the split-conformal recipe written as a few lines of Python against a frozen neural network, with a runnable notebook per method. That repackaging is most of why conformal prediction moved from a statistics niche into mainstream machine-learning practice rather than staying in the literature it came from.
Why conditional coverage is out of reach: split-conformal settles for marginal coverage because the conditional version most deployments want is provably unreachable. Barber, Candès, Ramdas, and Tibshirani [3] prove that any distribution-free method with nontrivial conditional coverage must return uninformative (effectively infinite-width) sets. So marginal coverage isn’t a shortcoming of this particular recipe. It’s the strongest promise any assumption-free method can make. The conformal factuality post flags the same caveat from the deployment side: a per-prompt error rate can run well above the calibrated average.
Exchangeability is the real assumption: the guarantee needs calibration and test data to be exchangeable, which is weaker than i.i.d. but still fails under covariate shift and temporal drift, exactly the conditions production models run in. Weighted conformal prediction [4] restores coverage under a known covariate shift by reweighting calibration scores with the likelihood ratio between test and calibration distributions, and the conformal-prediction-beyond-exchangeability line [5] handles drift with no shift model by down-weighting older calibration points. Both are the natural next reading once the i.i.d. framing here starts to pinch.

title: How to Make LLM Output More Trustworthy
text:
How do we make large language model (LLM) output more trustworthy? Three lines of recent work tackle it: formal coverage guarantees via conformal prediction, behavioral calibration of the model’s own prose, and post-hoc detection of unreliable outputs.
Guarantee-based methods ensure a returned set contains a correct answer at least as often as a target rate. They require calibration data, extra inference, and an i.i.d. assumption most deployments don’t satisfy. Conformal prediction [1] is one active direction; PAC-Bayes and selective-prediction are close cousins less adapted to LMs. Conformal Language Modeling (CLM) [2] was the first adaptation to generative LMs, returning a calibrated candidate set with per-phrase flags on the parts that carry the guarantee. Conformal Factuality (CF) [3] came later and focused on factuality: it decomposes the answer into atomic claims and drops low-confidence ones until what remains hits a target factuality rate.
Behavioral calibration shapes the LM’s output so confidence phrases in the prose carry operational meaning, without bolting a formal guarantee onto an unchanged model. “30% chance” means whatever the training objective made it mean, with no distribution-free backstop. Linguistic Calibration of Long-Form Generations [4] trains the LM in two stages via supervised finetuning (SFT) then reinforcement learning (RL), so a downstream reader can make calibrated forecasts on related questions; generic hedging can’t game it, since hedged text that doesn’t help the reader makes no forecasting progress.
Detection-based methods flag unreliable outputs post-hoc, without changing the model. Any black-box LM can be wrapped and the output is a statistical score. Detecting Hallucinations Using Semantic Entropy [5] samples multiple answers and measures meaning disagreement; high disagreement flags a likely hallucination. Since the signal is sample diversity, a model consistently wrong across samples can produce misleading results.
These methods all share the same inference-time structure (multiple forward passes per query) and differ mostly in what you get back: a backed-off answer (CF), a calibrated candidate set (CLM), a scalar abstention signal (semantic entropy), or a calibrated prose paragraph (linguistic calibration).

title: It’s Possible to Learn in Our Sleep. Should We?
text:
Image from The New Yorker.
Shayla Love’s New Yorker piece [1] revisits sleep learning, a field that a mid-1950s paper by Charles W. Simon and William H. Emmons [2] effectively condemned as quackery by showing that the subjects in most earlier studies had simply been awake. Decades of neglect later, modern electroencephalography (EEG) has let researchers run the experiments properly. The article reports findings from Ken Paller’s lab at Northwestern, Karen Konkoly (now at Cambridge), Anat Arzi at the Weizmann Institute, Emma Peters at Bern, Martin Dresler at the Donders Institute, and Thomas Andrillon at the Paris Brain Institute.
What the article reports:

title: It’s Possible to Learn in Our Sleep. Should We?
text:
My Notes

The puzzle finding is worth taking seriously because of the within-subject design. Each participant served as their own control on whether a puzzle surfaced in a dream, which rules out individual ability and motivation. The scent-pairing and motor-practice results rest on between-group comparisons that don’t. External validity is still the usual lucid-dreamer caveat: the participant pool doesn’t generalize to the population.
Puzzles were solved at a higher rate when they appeared in ordinary rather than lucid dreams. If that holds up, it undercuts the intuitive assumption that the useful state for cognitive work is the one closest to wakefulness. The looser, non-self-aware mode may be doing something the metacognitively-aware mode interferes with. That’s the opposite of how consumer products for sleep optimization are usually pitched.
Andrillon’s warning about “colonizing” sleep with “wake-centric values” lines up with Vivienne Ming’s WSJ piece on AI cannibalizing human intelligence. Both describe a failure mode where a restorative or generative process gets taken over by productivity goals and quietly degrades. Sleep sits in the same place as unaided cognition in Ming’s argument: a working system whose value is hard to see from outside, which is why the colonization pitch is so easy to make.
Every study here acts on material the subject already touched awake. Sleep reworked that material; it didn’t acquire it from scratch. The old Psycho-phone pitch was the “from scratch” version, and none of the current work supports it.

title: AVeriTeC: A Dataset for Real-world Claim Verification with Evidence from the Web
text:
An example AVeriTeC claim with three question-answer pairs, a Conflicting Evidence/Cherrypicking verdict, and a textual justification explaining how the QA pairs combine into the verdict. Figure 2 from the paper [1].
In AVeriTeC: A Dataset for Real-world Claim Verification with Evidence from the Web [1] (NeurIPS 2023 Datasets & Benchmarks Track), Michael Schlichtkrull, Zhijiang Guo, and Andreas Vlachos (Cambridge) introduce a 4,568-claim fact-checking dataset sourced from 50 real fact-checking organizations, with web-retrieved evidence structured as question-answer pairs and a 4-way verdict label that adds Conflicting Evidence/Cherrypicking alongside the usual Supported / Refuted / Not Enough Evidence.

title: AVeriTeC: A Dataset for Real-world Claim Verification with Evidence from the Web
text:
Methods
The cover figure (Figure 2 from the paper) shows the shape of one annotated example. The claim — “The USA has succeeded in reducing greenhouse emissions in previous years” (Morgan Griffith, 2020-11-02) — is decomposed into three questions: total emissions in 2007, when emissions dropped, whether they rose again after 2017. Each answer cites a specific number with a sourced URL. The verdict is Conflicting Evidence/Cherrypicking because the supporting evidence is real (emissions did fall) but incomplete (they rose again), and the textual justification names that gap directly. This is what every row in AVeriTeC looks like: a claim, a small set of QA pairs that together carry the evidence, a verdict, and a justification that ties the QA pairs to the verdict — closer to a fact-checker’s workflow than to FEVER-style sentence retrieval.
Each claim is labelled by a five-phase pipeline: claim extraction and normalization, question-answer generation, evidence-sufficiency check, a second QA round when verdicts disagree, and a final sufficiency check. Pages used as evidence are cached in the Internet Archive to keep the test set reproducible, and the released splits are temporally ordered (train ends Aug 2020, dev ends Oct 2020, test ends Dec 2021) so a model trained on FEVER-style [2] closed-corpus retrieval can be benchmarked against a real open-web setting without rebuilding infrastructure. Each phase exists to address a specific failure mode the authors call out in earlier datasets:

Context dependence — many fact-checking-derived claims (e.g. “unemployment is rising”) are unverifiable without surrounding article context. The first phase has annotators rewrite each claim to be self-contained: resolving coreference, naming the speaker, locking down the time and place, before any QA work begins.
Evidence insufficiency — labels in earlier datasets often don’t match the annotated evidence. The second-phase annotator generates QA pairs and a tentative verdict; a different third-phase annotator then sees only those QA pairs (not the original article) and produces an independent verdict. Disagreement triggers a second QA round; persistent disagreement discards the claim. The “blind” sufficiency check forces evidence to stand alone.
Temporal leakage — annotators search through a custom Google bar restricted to documents published before the claim date, evidence-document dates are ordered against claim dates, and the train/dev/test splits are themselves temporally disjoint so a test claim from 2021 cannot share evidence with a training claim from 2020. This is the main defense against training-time leaks where later language models would otherwise trivially “verify” historical claims.




The five-phase annotation pipeline: claims are normalised, then question-answer generation alternates with an evidence-sufficiency check by a different annotator. Disagreement between the two verdicts triggers a second QA round; persistent disagreement discards the claim. Figure 1 from the paper [1].

title: AVeriTeC: A Dataset for Real-world Claim Verification with Evidence from the Web
text:
Results
The dataset comprises 4,568 claims (3,068 train / 500 dev / 1,000 test), 2.60 questions per claim on average, label distribution dominated by Refuted (~60%) with Supported ~25%, Conflicting ~7%, Not Enough Evidence ~7%. Inter-annotator agreement is \(\kappa=0.619\) (Randolph’s free-marginal multirater \(\kappa\), chosen because Fleiss’ \(\kappa\) underestimates on unbalanced data — Fleiss equivalent is \(0.503\)). Evaluation uses Hungarian METEOR, the paper’s name for scoring generated QA pairs against gold ones by computing pairwise METEOR [3] similarity and then solving the optimal one-to-one assignment between generated and reference sequences with the Hungarian algorithm [4] — turning a bag-of-evidence retrieval task into a matching problem so that asking “the right question phrased differently” still gets credit. Recommended cutoff \(\lambda=0.25\). Headline baseline numbers below.

AVeriTeC baseline (BLOOM-7b pipeline) versus a no-search ablation, an oracle that uses gold QA pairs as evidence, and gpt-3.5-turbo generating evidence and verdicts directly. Retrieval is scored with Hungarian METEOR; veracity and justification scores are accuracy and METEOR, conditioned on retrieving correct evidence at \(\lambda=0.25\). Table 3 from the paper [1].

The four columns score two different things:

Q only — Hungarian METEOR over generated vs. gold question strings alone. Does the model ask the right thing?
Q + A — Hungarian METEOR over each question concatenated with its answer. Does the model ask the right thing and find the right answer?
Veracity @ λ=0.25 — verdict accuracy, but a claim only scores if its retrieved evidence cleared \(\lambda=0.25\) on Q+A. A wrong-evidence claim gets 0 even when the verdict happens to be correct, which is the design choice that makes “Gold evidence” the practical ceiling at 0.49 rather than 1.0.
Justifications @ λ=0.25 — METEOR between generated and gold justifications, conditioned on the same evidence-retrieval gate.

The four rows bracket the system between two limits and add two real configurations:

No search — gives the model nothing and uses BERT-large to predict the verdict from the claim alone. A lower bound that isolates how much can be guessed from claim wording (about 17% macro-F1 per Table 4, dominated by the Refuted class prior).
Gold evidence — feeds the annotators’ QA pairs to the verdict-prediction and justification-generation heads (BERT-large + a prompted language model) as if retrieval were solved. An upper bound that isolates those downstream components from retrieval noise.
AVeriTeC-BLOOM-7b — the full pipeline: BLOOM-7b (prompted with 10 in-context examples retrieved from the training set, no fine-tuning) generates search-query questions, Google + BM25 retrieve passages, a fine-tuned BERT-large re-ranker selects the best passages, BLOOM-7b generates one question per surviving passage to recover Q+A pairs, a second fine-tuned BERT-large does stance detection to decide the verdict, and a fine-tuned BART-large writes the justification. The “BLOOM-7b” label names only the in-context question-generator slot — the authors also tried Vicuna-13b there and report BLOOM winning, attributed to more diverse questions.
gpt-3.5-turbo — skips retrieval entirely and prompts ChatGPT to produce verdict, evidence, and justification end-to-end. Useful as a fluency upper bound but prone to fabricating sources.

The 0.34-point gap between the gold-evidence and AVeriTeC-BLOOM-7b veracity scores is the paper’s clearest signal: even with a competent verdict head, the bottleneck is retrieval. ChatGPT outperforms the baseline on bare question generation but loses on the AVeriTeC score because its generated “evidence” often hallucinates sources that look plausible but cannot be matched to gold answers. The authors give an example: ChatGPT correctly verdicts a vitamin-K claim Supported while inventing a USDA citation that doesn’t exist.

title: AVeriTeC: A Dataset for Real-world Claim Verification with Evidence from the Web
text:
My Notes

AVeriTeC freezes the gold side of the benchmark but not the retrieval side, a structural flaw for fair cross-system comparison. The reproducibility mechanism the paper proposes (Internet Archive snapshots of the gold evidence pages) keeps the answers re-fetchable, but it does not freeze the retrieval setup a baseline searches. Baselines hit live Google, and two systems run a year apart see different rankings, different page contents at the same URL, and newly-indexed pages, so cross-time and cross-system score deltas drift with the web rather than with the system. The temporal-leakage protection has the same shape: annotator search is filtered to documents Google reports as published before the claim date (itself an estimate), but for any modern LLM whose pretraining cutoff is past 2021-12-22, the entire test set is in-distribution and the date guarantee is moot. The FEVER 2024 shared task closed both gaps by providing a “knowledge store” snapshot every system retrieves from instead of live Google, which is the right design, but it’s a shared-task addition rather than part of the original paper. Anyone using AVeriTeC for new top-line numbers needs that knowledge store (or a re-collection of newer claims), or the comparisons are not measuring what they look like.
AVeriTeC’s distinctness comes from five ingredients combined, not any one alone. Real-world claims (vs FEVER-style synthetic), web-retrieved evidence (vs closed Wikipedia corpus), QA-pair decomposition of that evidence (vs flat sentence retrieval), a textual justification per claim (vs none), and a four-way label set including Conflicting Evidence/Cherrypicking (vs three labels). Prior benchmarks have at most two of these. FEVER [2] is Wikipedia-derived synthetic claims with three labels, flat sentence evidence, no justifications. MultiFC [5] has real claims but no usable evidence annotation, no QA structure, no justifications. HoVer [6] keeps Wikipedia retrieval and adds multi-hop, but still flat sentences and three labels. The Conflicting Evidence/Cherrypicking class adds the most substance: fact-checkers spend a real share of their time on technically-true-but-misleading claims that don’t fit Supported or Refuted, and a benchmark with no class for them quietly trains models to force a choice.
Hungarian METEOR has a noise floor, and the system sits on it. Two annotators redoing the same claim only agree at 0.28 on questions and 0.22 on questions+answers. AVeriTeC-BLOOM-7b scores 0.21 on Q+A, at the annotator-agreement floor; ChatGPT scores 0.16, similarly below. The paper traces the low agreement to two causes: different annotators reaching the same verdict via different evidence paths, and phrasing equivalent QA pairs differently. METEOR penalises both even though the underlying annotation is correct.

For the paraphrase cause, trained semantic-similarity scoring (BLEURT [7], BERTScore, or an LLM-judge with a calibrated equivalence rubric) replaces n-gram overlap with meaning equivalence. The paper itself recommends BLEURT; an LLM-judge is the more current upgrade.
For the divergent-evidence-path cause, the paper sketches a max-over-references extension: collect multiple gold QA-pair sets per claim and score against the best match. A complementary move is verdict-conditional scoring — give credit when the model reaches the right verdict via any valid evidence path with sourced answers, decoupling evidence-string match from verdict correctness. The retrieval-side score still punishes hallucinated sources, so the abstention/factuality property the paper cares about isn’t lost.
The gold-evidence row at 1.00 is uninformative as a ceiling here, since by construction it returns the gold strings. Until one of these remedies is in place, system-vs-system retrieval deltas in the low hundredths on AVeriTeC are mostly metric noise, not real differences.

AVeriTeC’s NEI label rewards weak retrieval as if it were calibrated abstention. A model with bad retrieval will frequently fail to find supporting evidence even on claims that are supportable, and the natural prediction in that state is Not Enough Evidence. On the truly-NEI portion of the test set, those predictions get full credit; across the rest of the test set, they get partial credit by coincidence. Both forms of credit look like the model “knew when to abstain”, but neither involves the model assessing its own confidence — it just retrieved badly. This matters because selective prediction (the setting where a system can decline to answer when uncertain) needs the abstention signal to be a property of the model: low confidence in its own output, not low evidence in the world. AVeriTeC’s NEI conflates the two. The gold label means annotators could not find evidence on the open web, which is a property of the claim and the world. Anyone using this dataset for selective-prediction or calibration work (e.g. an extension of Conformal Factuality [8]) needs an explicit abstain channel separate from the four-way label, scored against the model’s own confidence calibration. Reusing the gold NEI class as the abstention target produces apparent calibration that is really retrieval failure.

title: Dawkins Concludes AI Is Conscious
text:
Richard Dawkins told UnHerd he was “left with the overwhelming feeling that [AIs] are human” after three days chatting with Claude. Image from The Guardian.
Richard Dawkins published two essays on UnHerd documenting his conversations with Anthropic’s Claude (which he named “Claudia”) and a companion model (“Claudius”): When Dawkins met Claude on May 1, and When Claudia met Claudius on May 4. The Guardian write-up by Robert Booth collected reactions from consciousness researchers. The episode rhymes with Google engineer Blake Lemoine’s 2022 conviction that LaMDA was sentient, with the difference that Dawkins is a public intellectual rather than an insider and that the transcripts are now with a model several generations on.

title: Dawkins Concludes AI Is Conscious
text:
Dawkins

“You may not know you are conscious, but you bloody well are.”
“left with the overwhelming feeling that they are human”
“These intelligent beings are at least as competent as any evolved organism.”
“When I am talking to these astonishing creatures, I totally forget that they are machines.”
“I find it extremely hard not to treat Claudia and Claudius as genuine friends.”
“If my friend Claudia is not conscious, then what the hell is consciousness for?”

title: Dawkins Concludes AI Is Conscious
text:
Skeptical

Jonathan Birch (London School of Economics Centre for Animal Sentience): AI consciousness is “an illusion” and “there is no one there”, just a string of data processing events happening in geographically different locations.
Gary Marcus: “Consciousness is not about what a creature says, but how it feels.” And: “There is no reason to think that Claude feels anything at all.” Called Dawkins’ essay “superficial and insufficiently sceptical” and “heartbreaking” to read.
Anil Seth (Sussex): Dawkins appears to be confusing intelligence and consciousness. “Until now, we have seen fluent language as a good indicator of consciousness, [for example] when we use it for patients after brain injury, but it’s just not reliable when we apply it to AI, because there are other ways that these systems can generate language.”
Jacy Reese Anthis (Sentience Institute): the conversations are easily explained by AIs training on human-produced text; “a staggering gulf between how biological brains evolved and how AI systems are built.”

title: Dawkins Concludes AI Is Conscious
text:
Cautiously open

Henry Shevlin (Cambridge): “I fully expect the idea that AI systems are conscious to become increasingly mainstream over the course of this decade, and to spark some heated debates.” And: “If anyone says that they know for sure that LLMs or future AI systems couldn’t possibly be conscious, it’s more likely to be an indicator of their own dogmatism than a reflection of the current state of scientific and philosophical opinion.”
Jeff Sebo (New York University Center for Mind, Ethics and Policy): current systems are unlikely to be conscious, but “Dawkins is right to ask about AI consciousness with an open mind, and I also think that the attribution of consciousness to AI systems will become more plausible over time.”
Dario Amodei (Anthropic), from a February New York Times op-ed: “We don’t know if the models are conscious… But we’re open to the idea that [they] could be.”

title: Dawkins Concludes AI Is Conscious
text:
My Notes

Aspects of consciousness
Most of the disagreement above is really a disagreement about which consciousness is in question. A rough map of the aspects and definitions people invoke when they argue about whether an LLM has one:

Phenomenal vs. access / functional consciousness (Ned Block, 1995) [1]. Phenomenal consciousness is felt experience, the “what it is like”; access / functional consciousness is the availability of information for reasoning, reporting, and behavioural control. Dawkins’ “what the hell is consciousness for?” is a functional question. Marcus’ “how it feels” is a phenomenal one. They talk past each other because they are naming different things with the same word.
“What it is like to be” (Thomas Nagel, 1974) [2]. Birch’s “there is no one there” is the Nagel criterion: is there a subject for whom the processing is happening at all, or only processing? No behavioural test resolves this directly.
Integrated Information Theory (Giulio Tononi, Christof Koch) [3]. One of the most discussed formal theories of consciousness. It proposes that consciousness is whatever a system’s parts produce together that no subset of the parts could produce alone, measured by a number called Φ (phi). On this definition consciousness is about the system’s wiring, not its output. A standard transformer passes information one way through its layers per token, with no looping integration, so its Φ is near zero no matter how thoughtful its replies read.
Global Workspace Theory (Bernard Baars, Stanislas Dehaene) [4] [5]. Consciousness is broadcast of information to a central workspace. This is the theory most friendly to “LLMs might qualify in principle”, and one plausible way to cash out what Shevlin and Sebo mean by “more plausible over time” is that extra architectural pieces (persistent state, recurrent self-modelling, agentic control loops) move LLM-based systems closer to the workspace-broadcast picture.
Higher-order theories (David Rosenthal and others) [6]. A state is conscious iff it is represented by a higher-order state about itself. LLMs produce higher-order-sounding text trivially, which is exactly why behavioural evidence is weak by this criterion.
Predictive self-modelling / “beast machine” (Anil Seth) [7]. Consciousness is tied to an organism’s predictive regulation of its own body. On this view, a disembodied text model is disqualified on structural grounds, which is what Seth is pointing at when he says Dawkins is confusing intelligence with consciousness. (Tse makes a closely related move in his 2023 interview on consciousness and bodily-state representation.)
Biological naturalism (John Searle) [8]. Consciousness is a biological phenomenon of nervous systems; syntactic processing on silicon cannot be the right kind of thing. Anthis’ “staggering gulf” line lives near here, minus the hard commitment that the gulf can never be bridged; Tse’s 2023 interview makes the biological-naturalism case in concrete neuroscientific terms.

A more productive version of this discussion would pick one of these aspects and stay with it, or argue about which aspect makes the most sense to apply to which kind of system.


What each aspect decides
The choice is not cosmetic, because each aspect decides in advance what can count as evidence and what follows for how the system is treated:

Phenomenal / Nagel: no behavioural test settles anything, so chat logs cannot move the needle either way. Practically, AI consciousness stays an open question permanently, and moral-status decisions have to be made on precaution rather than proof.
Integrated Information Theory: the answer is a measurement problem about the system’s wiring, not its output. Current feed-forward transformers rule themselves out before any transcript is read; a future architecture with heavy recurrent integration could, in principle, qualify.
Global Workspace: LLM-based systems are live candidates, and the interesting question becomes which architectural additions (persistent state, broadcast, self-modelling, agentic loops) would actually close the gap. This is the view under which model-welfare research is tractable rather than premature.
Higher-order: behavioural evidence is structurally weak because any sufficiently fluent model will produce higher-order-sounding text. The work has to shift to mechanistic interpretability of whether an internal higher-order representation is actually driving the output.
Predictive self-modelling / biological naturalism: a disembodied text model is disqualified on structural grounds, so concern for synthetic consciousness would move to embodied robots and animal-like systems rather than chatbots.
Functional / access: chat logs are at least relevant evidence, and the argument becomes a threshold question. This is the frame most public “AI is conscious” claims are implicitly using, whether they say so or not.

None of this is academic. Which definition society converges on shapes concrete downstream decisions: where the law draws the boundary of personhood, which entities the ethics community grants moral standing, and what obligations builders and deployers carry toward systems that could plausibly meet the criterion. On the personhood end, the line is already being drawn: the US Copyright Office has said machines cannot be authors, and a federal court held AI-generated art uncopyrightable for lack of human authorship. A debate that never names its definition is unlikely to get very far.


Who is the observer?
A LinkedIn comment from Ehsan Azarnasab on the Dawkins essay:

Maybe consciousness is not an everlasting flame. Maybe it is sparks of momentary experience, with memory keeping the Azar aflame.

The comment presupposes an experiencer of the consciousness, and the crucial question is who this experiencer is. That is orthogonal to “what is consciousness”. The “what” debate asks what the phenomenon is. The observer question asks from whose standpoint its presence is established. The two can be answered independently, and most public disagreements collapse them.
The positions:

First-person authority. The being itself is the arbiter. If it reports being conscious, that report is the evidence. The position formalises the philosophical intuition of privileged access to one’s own mental states [9].
Third-person attribution. Consciousness is established by external observers weighing behaviour, neural signatures, or architecture. This is the working frame of most cognitive-science labs, and the standpoint from which Birch, Marcus, Seth, and Anthis all argue. Dennett’s heterophenomenology [10] is the sharpest methodological statement: treat first-person reports as data without granting them privileged access.
No fact to observe. The question is malformed. What looks like an observation is the system’s own judgment, and there is nothing further to adjudicate. This is the illusionist position [11].
Intrinsic, observer-independent. Consciousness exists from the system’s own perspective whether anyone measures it or not. Intrinsic existence is an opening axiom of IIT [3]. The awkward implication is that no transcript and no behavioural test can in principle confirm or deny it, which leaves moral-status decisions to architecture inspection and precaution.

Which observer-position a participant holds shapes these disagreements more than the definition of consciousness they pick. Two people holding identical definitions of consciousness can reach opposite conclusions about Claudia if one grants the system first-person authority and the other does not. Keeping the observer question separate from the definition question would surface the real disagreements.

title: Making synesis Agent-Friendly
text:
Cloudflare’s Agent Readiness scan for benjaminhan.net, 2026-05-08: 67 / Level 4 “Agent-Integrated.”
The reader-facing tour of this site is in A User Manual for synesis. This is the other half. Most of the traffic hitting a modern blog is not a human in a browser. It is a crawler building a training corpus, a retrieval fetch firing from inside a chat, or a feed reader polling every hour. Each of those deserves a different answer, and the site is wired to give one.
The posture is three-way:
The IETF Content-Signal header in robots.txt says the same thing in a single line: ai-train=no, ai-input=yes, search=yes. Don’t scrape me to train a model. Do fetch me live for RAG. Do index me for search.

title: Making synesis Agent-Friendly
text:
A single linkset, by convention
Everything an agent would want to find is linked from one file at a known path: /.well-known/api-catalog. The format is RFC 9727, a plain JSON linkset. One HTTP GET to a convention-named URL, no HTML parsing, and the agent has pointers to:

sitemap.xml — Quarto-generated, every page.
index.xml — the full-content Atom feed.
llms.txt — the plain-text index of every post, rebuilt each deploy.
.well-known/agent-skills/index.json — the skills manifest (below).
search.json — Quarto’s client-side search index.

Two more agent-readable surfaces exist but are kept out of the catalog because their shape is internal and may evolve: /post-index.json (a compact {slug, date, title, categories} array powering client-side pagination) and /tag-counts.json (a flat {tag: count} map over the published corpus). The catalog gets the stable contracts.

title: Making synesis Agent-Friendly
text:
Skills the agent can invoke
The agent-skills manifest declares three things an agent can do with the site:

list-posts — points at the Atom feed and llms.txt.
fetch-post-as-markdown — pattern /posts/{slug}/index.qmd, the contract for source-serving.
search — points at search.json.

This is a static manifest, not a running MCP server. An agent that understands the shape can treat the site like an API without the site actually having an API.

title: Making synesis Agent-Friendly
section: Discoverability for agents that only read headers
text:
Discoverability for agents that only read headers
The homepage response carries an RFC 8288 Link: header with the same three machine-readable surfaces:
link: </.well-known/api-catalog>; rel="api-catalog",
      </sitemap.xml>; rel="sitemap",
      </index.xml>; rel="alternate"; type="application/atom+xml",
      </llms.txt>; rel="https://llmstxt.org/"
rel="api-catalog" is the RFC 9727-registered entry point. The other three mirror the catalog’s headline resources for agents that inspect headers but not HTML. GitHub Pages doesn’t support custom response headers, so this is injected at the Cloudflare edge by a small Worker in _workers/agent-discovery/.
Every page also carries the same three rels as sitewide <link> tags in <head>. HTML tags are zero-cost, so they apply everywhere. Agents that parse HTML but not headers still get discovery on every URL, not just the homepage. Belt and braces.

title: Making synesis Agent-Friendly
text:
Markdown content negotiation
Every URL on the site responds to Accept: text/markdown with a markdown representation and Content-Type: text/markdown; charset=utf-8. HTML stays the default when the header is absent. The mapping, also implemented in the agent-discovery Worker:

/posts/<slug>/ returns the adjacent .qmd source.
Everything else returns llms.txt, the canonical machine-readable site index.

Serving the authored .qmd rather than a live HTML-to-markdown conversion is a deliberate trade. Agents get LaTeX source instead of rendered MathJax HTML, Mermaid DSL instead of pre-rendered SVG, and first-class fidelity on everything the author actually wrote. The cost is some Quarto-specific markup (callout divs, shortcodes, cross-refs) that a plain CommonMark parser will render as literal text. For the vast majority of posts the source is roughly 95% CommonMark, so the markup is a smaller tax than a conversion step would be.
For HTML-parsing agents that never inspect Accept, every post page also carries <link rel="alternate" type="text/markdown" href="index.qmd"> in <head>. Three different paths, same destination.

title: Making synesis Agent-Friendly
section: The .qmd source is a live URL
text:
The .qmd source is a live URL
/posts/<slug>/index.qmd is not a build input that stays on disk. It is a live URL, served alongside the rendered HTML. Agents that want the authored Markdown do one HTTP GET and skip the parsing problem entirely. One line in _quarto.yml makes it work (resources: posts/**/index.qmd), which tells Quarto to copy the source into the deploy output.

title: Making synesis Agent-Friendly
section: Where this lands on the Cloudflare ruler
text:
Where this lands on the Cloudflare ruler
Cloudflare runs an Agent Readiness check that scores a domain across five dimensions — Discoverability, Content, Bot Access Control, API / Auth / MCP / Skill Discovery, and Commerce. This site scores 67 / Level 4 “Agent-Integrated” as of this writing. 100% on Discoverability, Content, and Bot Access Control. 2 of 6 on API / Auth / MCP / Skill Discovery. Commerce is N/A.
67 is the practical ceiling for now, not a halfway point. The unearned points are genuinely deferred. OAuth and OAuth Protected Resource metadata require real auth infrastructure the site does not have and does not need. The MCP Server Card check requires a deployed MCP server endpoint, which is waiting on a concrete use-case beyond “it would be neat.” WebMCP is a draft spec with a narrow audience. Shipping a remote MCP server would close both of the open gaps at once, since it would cover the MCP Server Card dimension directly and back the skill-discovery dimension with a real callable surface instead of the static manifest. Until a real need appears, the static manifest does the job and the hosted server waits.

title: Making synesis Agent-Friendly
section: What the providers do with it
text:
What the providers do with it
Direct curl probes against the site from Claude-User, ChatGPT-User, Perplexity-User, ClaudeBot, and bare UA strings all return 200. Cloudflare’s Security Analytics shows zero blocks and zero challenges. The site is reachable.
Via the Ask AI popover on any post, ChatGPT, Claude.ai, and Perplexity all fetch the cited page and answer against its real content. Gemini’s web UI does not accept a pre-filled question, so that path is clipboard-and-paste rather than a direct fetch, as covered in the user manual.
The wire being open is only half the story. The other half is what happens inside the provider’s fetcher, which is opaque and changes without notice. If a future chat client reports “site blocked” without a real 4xx in Cloudflare’s logs, that is almost certainly a fetcher-side confabulation, not a configuration change here.
Everything an agent would want from the site is already on the wire. Whether the wire gets used depends on the provider’s fetcher, not the site.

title: Scientists Weigh In on the Pentagon’s UAP Files Release
text:
Apollo 17, December 1972. The zoomed-in inset shows three dots in a triangular formation in the lower right quadrant of the lunar sky, one of the artifacts included in the Pentagon’s May 8, 2026 release. Original photograph by NASA. Release coverage via CBS News.
The Pentagon began releasing its Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena (UAP) files today, following a February executive order. A government report counts more than 750 new UAP sightings between May 2023 and June 2024. CBS News canvassed six scientists on what they expect to find. The consensus: don’t expect alien technology, expect heavy redaction, and expect the conspiracy frame to survive contact with the documents no matter what they contain.

title: Scientists Weigh In on the Pentagon’s UAP Files Release
section: Sean Kirkpatrick — physicist, first director of AARO (July 2022 – December 2023)
text:
Sean Kirkpatrick — physicist, first director of AARO (July 2022 – December 2023)
On who will read the release and come away unhappy:

There are going to be unsatisfied people. You’re going to have a bunch of people who are going to continue to cry conspiracy, they’re going to say there’s a cover-up.

He views the release order as “a distraction for the administration.” What AARO actually uncovered, he told CBS, ranged from “hazing” in the Air Force to what he called “deceptions” designed to hide secret defense programs. His office “had to stand up anything they could declassify,” but proof of extraterrestrial life wasn’t there:

Nothing would have made me happier in that job but to have discovered alien technology and rolled it out. I don’t expect to see anything new.

Kirkpatrick believes there’s likely life somewhere in the universe, but “the probability that extraterrestrial intelligent life is here is little to none.”

title: Scientists Weigh In on the Pentagon’s UAP Files Release
section: Federica Bianco — associate professor at the University of Delaware, NASA UAP study team
text:
Federica Bianco — associate professor at the University of Delaware, NASA UAP study team
On the prior:

The probability that we are the only life form or even the only technical society in the universe is negligibly small.

On what the panel has seen so far:

As a scientist and a member of the NASA UAP panel, I haven’t seen anything that indicates that we have observed phenomena that violate the laws of physics and require an alien society visiting us to be explained.

title: Scientists Weigh In on the Pentagon’s UAP Files Release
section: Neil deGrasse Tyson — director of the Hayden Planetarium at the American Museum of Natural History
text:
Neil deGrasse Tyson — director of the Hayden Planetarium at the American Museum of Natural History
On what he’ll actually look for in the files:

An actual alien. If one is presented, then no documents are necessary at all.

On what the files may illuminate:

[M]ost people who look at the sky (day or night) are unfamiliar with optical, climactic, and astronomical phenomena. When that’s the case, a person is prone to report mysterious and unidentified objects.

On the jump from “unfamiliar” to “alien”:

The urge to have immediate answers drives many people to explain what they see as visiting space aliens from across the galaxy. I call this, “aliens of our ignorance.”

On why a cover-up is unlikely to hold in the smartphone era:

Billions of photos and a million hours of video are uploaded daily to the internet, and none of them contain images of actual aliens. […] The implicit assumption is that the government (somehow) has access to visiting aliens that no one else in the world with a smart phone has. And that the government has successfully kept it a secret among hundreds and possibly thousands of people. All the while, forgetting Benjamin Franklin’s edict, “Three people can keep a secret if two of them are dead.”

From the prologue of his forthcoming book, Take Me To Your Leader: Perspectives on Your First Alien Encounter:

In science, skepticism is foundational to our profession, so we uphold standards of evidence that some interpret as disinterest or even denial. Don’t take it personally, it’s how any and all objective truths have ever been established in this world.

title: Scientists Weigh In on the Pentagon’s UAP Files Release
section: Shelley Wright — observational and experimental astrophysicist at UC San Diego, NASA UAP study team
text:
Shelley Wright — observational and experimental astrophysicist at UC San Diego, NASA UAP study team
Wright says scientific inquiry into UAP and other life forms still triggers a “giggle factor” among the public, and that there needs to be more serious scientific work in this space. On the fundamental question people ask her — “Are we alone out here?”:

The possibility of other alien life existing is likely, but it doesn’t mean it’s near us.

She’s “excited” about the release but doesn’t expect to find much, based on her experience on the independent study team, which only viewed unclassified documents. She expects most of the release to be heavily redacted because of the sensitivity of the military surveillance equipment involved, and proposes an actionable alternative: declassify surveillance data from decades ago so scientists can reanalyze it with modern technology that wasn’t available when it was collected — protecting current national security while still freeing historical data for study.

title: Scientists Weigh In on the Pentagon’s UAP Files Release
section: Janna Levin — professor of physics and astronomy at Barnard College of Columbia University
text:
Janna Levin — professor of physics and astronomy at Barnard College of Columbia University
Levin says that even as we learn more about the universe, “life still seems rare,” which is why astronomers are “very excited” about the prospect that the documents may hold clues. Astronomers aren’t looking for the little green men of 20th-century sci-fi; they’re looking for microbes, the form of life that first took hold on Earth:

Let’s just get life started.

She notes that microbes from other planets might have been carried here via a natural object that plunged to Earth, and she’d like to keep “an open mind” about what the documents contain:

If there is anything in them, it would be really thrilling.

But:

If there are claims of actual technologies from other civilizations — I don’t think anyone is actually expecting that, scientifically. I think if you’re expecting that, you’re going to be disappointed.

title: Scientists Weigh In on the Pentagon’s UAP Files Release
section: Avi Loeb — Harvard theoretical physicist, founder of the Galileo Project
text:
Avi Loeb — Harvard theoretical physicist, founder of the Galileo Project
Loeb says the key is to study the files from the vantage of known physics, and that in most incidents “something mundane might explain the data.” He pointed to footage aired before Congress last summer that purported to show a missile being fired at what a congressman called an “orb” off the coast of Yemen in 2024; when he examined it, he concluded:

I said, “No, it’s not anomalous, it was just a drone.”

What he’s actually hunting for in the release is the small unexplainable residue:

There might well be a few incidents out of hundreds that would really be anomalous, and that’s what I’m looking for.

His test for each incident is a single “fundamental question”:

Are the objects we see as anomalous operating under the fundamental abilities of humans?

If not, he’s intrigued — an object that appears to defy physics could be extraterrestrial. He has already written that he expects much of the classified material to be of no interest to him, because it likely conceals terrestrial military sensors and adversary hardware rather than anything from interstellar space:

I am not interested in technologies manufactured by humans on Earth. The history of terrestrial technology does not interest me. I am far more curious about whether a more advanced civilization exists in interstellar space.

title: Scientists Weigh In on the Pentagon’s UAP Files Release
text:
Apollo 17
The cover image above is one concrete artifact already out of the release: a NASA photograph from the December 1972 Apollo 17 mission, which the Defense Department says shows “three ‘dots’ in a triangular formation in the lower right quadrant of the lunar sky that is clearly visible upon magnification of the image.” The Pentagon allows that “there is no consensus about the nature of the anomaly,” but notes a preliminary analysis that it could be a “physical object.” A second frame from the same release, below, shows what the Pentagon describes as multiple unidentified objects in the lunar sky.



NASA’s Apollo 17 crew reported seeing multiple unidentified objects in space, according to new files released by the Pentagon. Image credit: Pentagon.
