title: Making synesis Quick
text:
CI wall-clock time per push, before and after the incremental-render work. A post edit drops from around 6:30 to around 2:00, and a docs-only push skips the render step entirely.
Two durations matter on a blog like this one. The first is the time between git push and the updated post being live. The second is the time between a reader clicking a link and the page being ready to read. On the baseline workflow, continuous integration (CI) was taking about six minutes per push, and every home or archive page was shipping a payload that grew with the corpus. This post walks through what that looked like, what was done about each, and why the specific fixes work.

title: Making synesis Quick
section: How the site is put together
text:
How the site is put together
synesis is a Quarto site. The source tree lives in a private GitHub repository, a GitHub Actions workflow builds the static _site/ tree on every push to main, and a chain of downstream services hands that output to readers at benjaminhan.net. There is no database, no server-side rendering, no application runtime.





flowchart TB
    A[Source repo<br/>.qmd · CSS · includes · Python scripts]
    A -->|git push main| B[GitHub Actions workflow]

    subgraph build [" "]
        direction TB
        C[Install Quarto · uv · Playwright]
        D[Pre-render scripts<br/>tag counts · post index<br/>paginators · llms.txt]
        E[quarto render]
        F[Post-render scripts<br/>feed SVG · UTM tags<br/>feed pagination · CSS fingerprint]
        C --> D --> E --> F
    end

    B --> C
    F -->|force push _site/| G[Deploy repo<br/>GitHub Pages origin]
    G --> H[Cloudflare edge<br/>cache · TLS · Workers]
    H --> I[Reader<br/>benjaminhan.net]

    style build fill:none,stroke:none






Everything discussed below happens inside the GitHub Actions workflow, or in the HTML and JSON the workflow produces. GitHub Pages and Cloudflare are downstream of that.

title: Making synesis Quick
text:
The build side
A full quarto render on this project renders a few hundred .qmd files at roughly 580 ms each on GitHub’s runners. That is about 3 minutes 48 seconds of pandoc work on top of ~10 seconds of pre-render and post-render scripts, plus the runner’s own setup and deploy overhead. Total wall time on the baseline workflow was around 6 minutes 23 seconds for a single-post publish.
Most pushes touch only a handful of files. A typical push edits one post’s body, or adds a new post and leaves every other post alone. Rendering every file on every push spends almost all of that 3 minutes 48 seconds regenerating output that is byte-identical to what is already on disk.
Skipping that work requires two capabilities the default workflow does not have:

Somewhere to keep the previous _site/ so it can be reused when unchanged.
A reliable way to know which source files actually changed since that previous _site/ was built.

The four pieces below provide both, plus the supporting conditions that make them safe.

Caching the previous _site/
The workflow uses actions/cache@v4 to tar the _site/ tree at the end of each successful run, keyed on the commit SHA. On the next run, the cache is restored at the top of the job. A one-line stamp file inside the tarball, _site/.last-built-sha, records which commit this _site/ was built from. That stamp is the baseline everything else diffs against.
The stamp file is excluded from the deploy, so it never ships to the public repository. It is internal bookkeeping.


Classifying the diff
The script _scripts/render_diff.py reads the baseline SHA from the stamp, runs git diff against it, and picks one of four modes for the render step:

skip-render if every changed path is one that never reaches the deploy (docs/, drafts/, .claude/, CLAUDE.md). The workflow re-deploys the cached _site/ as-is.
tags-only if the only changed path is _tags.yml. The workflow regenerates tag-counts.json and post-index.json, copies them into the cached _site/, re-stamps cache-bust query strings on the JSON fetch URLs, and ships. Post HTML on disk does not change. The next subsection describes the source-of-truth move that this mode rests on.
incremental if the changed paths are post bodies, post assets, or frontmatter. The workflow hands the changed posts/<slug>/index.qmd files to quarto render as explicit arguments. Quarto’s listing tracker picks up affected listing pages automatically and regenerates search.json, sitemap.xml, and listings.json. Cached HTML for untouched posts is left alone. Typical wall time: around 20 seconds. Past a configurable batch ceiling (INCREMENTAL_MAX_POSTS, default 10), large multi-post pushes escalate to full because Quarto’s internal parallelism beats per-file invocation at that scale.
full if the change touches templates, includes, scripts, config files, or anything else whose output reaches every page. The workflow drops the cached _site/ and runs a full render. Typical wall time: around 4 minutes.

The default when a path is unrecognized is full, not incremental. The classifier errs on the side of rebuilding too much rather than serving stale output.


Keeping rendered HTML byte-stable
An incremental render only produces correct output if the HTML files it chose not to re-render are still valid. That requires every per-page output to depend only on inputs specific to that page, not on global state that changes when unrelated posts change.
Two global inputs in <head> broke this condition before the incremental work began:

A <script>window.__tagCounts = {...}</script> block inlined the entire tag histogram into every page. Adding a new tag to one post changed the histogram, which changed the <head> of every other post.
A similar inline block for the post index listed every post. Publishing a new post changed the listing, which changed the <head> of every post again.

Both were moved to external JSON files (/tag-counts.json and /post-index.json) fetched by a small loader stub at page load time. The stub itself is byte-stable. The corpus-wide data it fetches is not part of the HTML. After this change, a post’s rendered HTML is a pure function of that post’s source. Unrelated posts can come and go without invalidating the cache.
The pre-render scripts that produce these JSON files (_scripts/tag-counts.py, _scripts/post-index.py) compare their proposed output to what is already on disk before writing. If the content is unchanged, the file is not touched and its mtime does not advance. The same discipline applies to the paginators _scripts/paginate-home.py and _scripts/paginate-archive.py. Closed listing pages, which hold 25 posts on the home side and 50 on the archive side, are byte-identical run-to-run in steady state. Quarto’s freeze: auto skips re-rendering them.
Without byte-stable pre-render outputs, every pre-render script would churn mtimes on every push, and Quarto’s freeze cache would invalidate on every run. The byte comparison is what keeps the classifier’s incremental decision safe.


Lifting tags out of frontmatter
A single top-level file, _tags.yml, holds every post’s tag set, keyed by slug. The pre-render scripts _scripts/tag-counts.py and _scripts/post-index.py read from it instead of from per-post categories: frontmatter. A tag rename or merge becomes a one-file commit.
The prior scheme stored tags inside each post. Renaming a tag, merging two near-duplicates, or dropping a stale singleton rewrote dozens of .qmd files in one commit. Every one of those files then went through quarto render, every page in the corpus picked up a new mtime, and the test tiers ran end to end. None of the work changed any prose.
The tags-only mode in the previous classifier list is what this enables on the build side. When the only changed path is _tags.yml, the workflow regenerates the two JSON artifacts, copies them into the cached _site/, re-stamps the cache-bust ?v=<sha> markers on the JSON fetch URLs, and ships. Post HTML on disk does not change. Clients pick up the new tags via _includes/hydrate-tags.html, which reads post-index.json on next page load and injects the tag-chip DOM the original frontmatter would have produced.
A schema gate runs the contract tests for both JSON files before the tags-only deploy. Without it, a regression in either pre-render script would ship malformed JSON and silently break tag hydration on every page.
Drafts keep categories: in their own frontmatter during authoring. The /publish-draft flow strips that line and writes the slug → tag list into _tags.yml at promotion time.


Gating the test tiers
The test suite is split into tiers: unit tests, contract tests, integration tests, smoke tests, and UI tests. The full suite runs in about 23 seconds, with the UI tier (Playwright-driven browser tests) accounting for roughly 14 of those. Content-only pushes do not change the UI, so the UI tier cannot regress as a result of those pushes.
A path gate inside the same workflow drops the UI and smoke tiers when the diff only touches post content, bringing the test wall down to about 8 seconds. A further gate drops the slow incremental-parity integration test, which runs two full quarto render invocations back-to-back, unless the render pipeline itself (the classifier, the paginators, _quarto.yml, or the workflow file) was modified in the same push. Any change that could actually break the tests still runs them. Changes that cannot, do not.


Pinning Quarto
One risk the gated tests introduce is that Quarto’s own output could drift between pushes without the gated tiers running to catch it. The workflow pins Quarto to version 1.9.37 to make that drift impossible without an explicit commit. A separate step compares the pin to the latest published Quarto release and emits a workflow warning when the pin lags, so bumps are a considered change, not a silent one.


Where the time went
A content-only push now takes around 115 seconds end-to-end, down from around 6 minutes 23 seconds, as shown in the cover chart. A docs-only push deploys the cached _site/ unchanged in around 88 seconds. A tag cleanup push lands close to the docs-only cost: it shares the no-render fast path, plus a few seconds to regenerate the JSON files and re-stamp cache-bust markers. A push that touches templates, scripts, or config still runs the full render and full test suite, because that is when the full cost is actually needed.
One post-render cost deserves a separate note. _scripts/feed-render.py uses headless Chromium to rasterize Mermaid diagrams and MathJax expressions into inline Scalable Vector Graphics (SVG) inside the Really Simple Syndication (RSS) feed. A full browser round-trip per item is slow, so the rendered SVGs are cached under .feed-cache/svg/ keyed on a schema version. Repeat builds reuse the cached SVG. The schema version is bumped whenever the rendering pipeline changes in a way that affects output, which invalidates the whole cache at once.

title: Making synesis Quick
text:
The read side
Page-load time on a static site comes from five phases: Domain Name System (DNS) lookup, Transport Layer Security (TLS) handshake, first-byte wait, payload download, and in-browser processing (parse, style, layout, JavaScript execution, subresource fetches). The first three are handled by Cloudflare’s edge cache and are mostly out of the site’s hands. Everything below addresses the last two: how much data a page carries, how much of it can be reused across pages, and what work can be moved from page-load time to build time.

Bounding the page payload
A listing that grows with the corpus is the easiest way for a site to slow down over years. A 400-post home page is a 400-post payload on every visit. The goal is for each page’s payload to be O(1) in the size of the corpus, not O(N).
Straight fixed-size pages would do that, but at a cost to the reader’s first impression. Whenever a single new post pushed a page past capacity, a fresh page would open with that one post, leaving the landing briefly sparse until the next few publishes caught up. The compromise is an overflow band. Each home listing page holds 25 posts in steady state, with the newest allowed up to 12 overflow for 37 at most. The archive uses 50 and 25 for 75 at most. A new publish grows the newest page one post at a time until it hits the overflow ceiling. At that point the oldest 25 (or 50) close off into a page one step older, and the newest page re-opens at a comfortable size rather than at one.
A side effect of this design is URL stability. Once a page closes, the set of posts it holds does not shift again, so a bookmark to /archive/page/5/ still points at the same 50 posts a year later. Only the newest page and the landing churn on every publish.
Older content is reached through RFC 5005 paginated archives. Each page’s payload is bounded by the page size, not by the size of the corpus.


Pre-computing the client-side search index
Quarto builds a JSON file, search.json, at deploy time that indexes every post’s title, body, and code blocks. The in-page search overlay loads it once per session, indexes in memory, and answers every keystroke locally. There is no per-query network round-trip. The search also keeps working if the reader loses connectivity after the initial load.
Moving the index build to deploy time means the reader pays the indexing cost once, not per query. It also means there is no search server for the site to operate.


Sharing cross-corpus data across pages
/tag-counts.json and /post-index.json are small files fetched once per session and reused on every subsequent page. The post index is about 74 KB: a flat array of {slug, date, title, categories} records that powers the home-page timeline, the archive tag cloud, pagination math, and previous/next navigation on every post.
Keeping this data in external JSON rather than inlining it into every page’s <head> means the browser fetches it once, caches it under a stable URL with a long Cache-Control max-age, and reads from cache on the next page. The inline version made every page’s <head> grow linearly with the corpus. The external version makes it fixed size.
The same choice enabled incremental render on the build side. A single change in how cross-corpus data is delivered fixed two problems at once.


Fingerprinting the stylesheet
_scripts/cache-bust-css.py rewrites styles.css to styles.<content-hash>.css in the deployed HTML. The stylesheet ships with a one-year Cache-Control max-age, which means a returning reader downloads it at most once per release. When the stylesheet actually changes, the hash changes, the URL changes, and the browser fetches a new copy. Atomic invalidation is a property of content-addressed URLs. There is no separate cache-bust step to remember.


Loading fonts only when they are used
The default reading palette is set by unconditional rules in styles.css over the system font stack. A reader who never presses f to cycle palettes fetches zero font bytes from the site. Each of the three alternative palettes (reader, almanac, manuscript) has its @font-face rules scoped to html[data-font-palette="<slug>"]. Browsers only fetch the woff2 files when the attribute matches, which it does only after the reader activates that palette. font-display: swap keeps text visible while the font is loading.
The general pattern is that optional features should be zero-cost until activated. Most readers will never activate them, and should not pay for them.


Sizing images to the reader’s screen
Source images arrive in a post directory at whatever resolution the capture device produced, often several thousand pixels wide. Post bodies render into a narrower column. Shipping the originals would waste bytes on the wire and decode work in the browser, for pixels the reader cannot see.
_scripts/resize_images.py runs as a pre-render sweep. For every referenced image above a size threshold, it renames the original to <stem>-full.<ext> and writes a display-size sibling at the original path. JPGs stay JPG, capped at 1600 pixels wide and re-encoded at quality 82. PNGs re-encode as WebP at quality 85. The body reference in index.qmd is rewritten to point at the display copy and tagged with data-lightbox-src="<stem>-full.<ext>" so the lightbox has a path to the hi-res. If the re-encoded display copy does not come out smaller than the original, the split is reverted. Some source files are already at the encoder’s floor (the source was encoded tightly enough that re-encoding cannot win bytes back).
_scripts/check-image-sizes.py fails the CI build if any referenced image above the threshold is missing its -full sibling. The contract that every heavy image has a display copy is enforced mechanically rather than by discipline.
On the read side, the lightbox gates the hi-res fetch on viewport width. Screens narrower than 1024 Cascading Style Sheets (CSS) pixels receive only the 1600-pixel display copy, and the -full is never fetched. At those widths the display copy is already at or near the device’s physical resolution, so the hi-res upgrade adds no visible detail. On wider screens the -full (itself capped at 3000 pixels wide) is fetched when the lightbox first shows that image, decoded off the main thread via img.decode(), and held in a per-session cache so returning to the same image does not trigger another decode.


Not carrying weight that is not needed
Quarto’s default behavior is to include Mermaid, MathJax, and syntax-highlighting bundles in every page, regardless of whether the page actually contains a diagram, an equation, or a code block. _scripts/strip-unused-assets.py scans each rendered page for references to each asset family and removes the unused script tags after render. A short plain-text post ships with none of the three.
_scripts/strip-listing-titles.py removes redundant H1 elements that Quarto emits on listing pages, for the same reason: less markup for the browser to parse, style, and lay out.


Pre-rendering math and diagrams for the feed
Most RSS readers do not run JavaScript. A feed item containing $\hat{y} = f(x)$ or a Mermaid block would arrive as unrendered source text, because MathJax and Mermaid both run client-side.
_scripts/feed-render.py replaces every math expression and every Mermaid block in the RSS feed with inline SVG at deploy time. The subscriber’s client does no extra work, and the feed is self-contained. The same script is the one whose SVG cache was described earlier. It saves CI time on repeat builds and reader time on every subscribed fetch, from a single pass at deploy time.

title: Making synesis Quick
text:
Where this leaves things
The build and read sides of this post use the same technique in different contexts: compute something once at the moment its inputs change, name the result under a stable address, and let every downstream reader of that result pick it up from cache. On the build side the cached result is _site/, or a pre-render JSON, or a frozen listing page. On the read side it is search.json, or a per-session JSON fetch, or a fingerprinted stylesheet, or a pre-rendered feed SVG.
What remains unsettled is where this breaks at scale. The post index is 74 KB today and will be several hundred kilobytes by the time the corpus crosses a thousand posts. search.json has the same shape. Neither is a problem today. Both are shapes to keep an eye on. The critical assumption behind every fix above is that the corpus changes slowly compared to the cache lifetimes. That assumption is a choice about how often to publish, not a property of the infrastructure.
Related reading: A Rube Goldberg Pipeline for Sharing Links walks through how a captured link becomes a draft and then a post. A User Manual for synesis tours the reader-facing features. Making synesis Agent-Friendly covers the machine-readable surfaces the site exposes.

title: Interaction Models: Training Real-Time Collaboration into the Model
text:
Cover video from Thinking Machines Lab.
Thinking Machines Lab, the OpenAI-alumni startup founded in February 2025 by former OpenAI CTO Mira Murati with OpenAI cofounder John Schulman, former OpenAI VP of Research Barret Zoph, and former OpenAI VP Lilian Weng on its founding team, has announced a research preview of interaction models: frontier models trained from scratch to take in audio, video, and text concurrently and to think, respond, and act in real time, without a surrounding orchestration harness handling turns, interruptions, or modality switches.
The argument the announcement makes:

title: Interaction Models: Training Real-Time Collaboration into the Model
text:
Methods

Capabilities
With interaction native to the model rather than the harness, one system provides what normally takes a stack of separate components:

Seamless dialog management (video). The model implicitly tracks whether the speaker is thinking, yielding, self-correcting, or inviting a response, without a separate turn-taking module.
Verbal and visual interjections (video). It jumps in when context warrants (“interrupt when I say something wrong”, “tell me when I’ve written a bug”) rather than waiting for the user to finish.
Simultaneous speech (video). User and model can talk at the same time, which makes live translation and live commentary straightforward.
Time awareness (video). A direct sense of elapsed time, so “remind me to breathe every four seconds until I ask you to stop” is a first-class request.
Concurrent tools, search, and generative UI (video). Web searches, tool calls, and UI generation can run while the model is still speaking and listening, with results folded into the conversation as they arrive.



Approach

Time-aligned micro-turns. Input and output are streams chunked into 200 ms windows and continuously interleaved, so silence, overlap, and interruption stay in the model’s context instead of being flattened into an alternating token sequence.
Two-model split. A real-time interaction model holds presence with the user; an asynchronous background model handles sustained reasoning, tool use, and longer-horizon work. The interaction model delegates with the full conversation as context and weaves background results back into dialog when the moment fits.
Encoder-free early fusion. Audio enters as dMel [2] embeddings, images as 40×40 patches through a light hMLP [3], audio exits via a flow head [4], and every component is co-trained from scratch with the transformer. No standalone Whisper-style encoder or text-to-speech (TTS) decoder.
Streaming-session inference. A custom inference path, upstreamed into SGLang, appends each 200 ms chunk into a persistent GPU sequence to avoid per-chunk prefill overhead, paired with batch-invariant kernels for bitwise trainer-sampler alignment.

title: Interaction Models: Training Real-Time Collaboration into the Model
text:
Results
The benchmarks below:

FD-bench v1 [6]: simple turn-taking latency in seconds; streaming audio, lower is better.
FD-bench v1.5 [6]: average interaction quality across four scenarios: user interruption, user backchannel, talking to others, and background speech.
FD-bench v3 [6]: response quality and pass@1 on audio + tool-use tasks.
Audio MultiChallenge [7]: turn-based intelligence and instruction-following, scored as Average Pass Rate (APR).
BigBench Audio [8]: turn-based accuracy on audio tasks.




Figure 5 from the announcement. “Our model dominates interaction quality while being more intelligent than any non-thinking model. We achieve the best responsiveness measured as a latency between user and model turns.”



TML-interaction-small leads interactivity by a wide margin. On FD-bench v1.5 (interaction quality, average) it scores 77.8, versus 54.3 for the next best (Gemini-3.1-flash-live minimal) and 46–48 for the GPT-realtime-2.0 variants.
Lowest turn-taking latency measured. FD-bench v1 puts it at 0.40 s, against 0.57 s for Gemini-flash-live minimal, 1.18 s for GPT-realtime-2.0 minimal, and 1.63 s for GPT-realtime-2.0 xhigh.
Instant-model Pareto frontier on intelligence too. Audio MultiChallenge APR is 43.4%, the best among non-thinking realtime models; only thinking variants like GPT-realtime-2.0 xhigh (48.5%) score higher, at the cost of much larger latency.
Two new in-house proactive-audio benchmarks. TimeSpeak tests whether the model initiates speech at a user-specified time with correct content; CueSpeak tests whether it speaks at the semantically right moment, including while the user is still talking.

title: Interaction Models: Training Real-Time Collaboration into the Model
text:
My Notes

Human-in-the-loop latency deserves its own objective. Most recent frontier work treats autonomy as the capability that matters and interaction as something you add afterward with voice-activity detection, turn routers, and interruption heuristics. Thinking Machines takes the opposite bet: the right architectural split is human-in-the-loop latency vs. no-human-waiting latency, and the first deserves its own training objective. That parallels Ben Thompson’s argument that the inference stack is already splitting into answer inference (human waits, latency premium) and agentic inference (no human waits, memory capacity wins), with different hardware and latency profiles. The claim here extends the same split up into training objectives and model families. The awkward case is the middle: today’s chat interfaces, which are neither fully autonomous nor genuinely real-time.
In-model interaction isn’t a new ambition. Moshi [5] (Kyutai, 2024), GPT-Realtime, and Nemotron VoiceChat trained full-duplex audio into the model rather than bolting it on. Rabbit Inc. pitched an analogous framing for UI actions with its “Large Action Model”, though how much of the shipped r1 was actually a trained action model versus scripted Android automation became contested. The preview extends the in-model claim to video, text, and tool use alongside audio, with enough general capability to compete on intelligence benchmarks. The 200 ms micro-turn design is tuned for sub-second exchange; whether it also scales to agentic work running for minutes or hours is the open architectural question.
Pointing is the same question at the input layer. DeepMind’s AI-enabled pointer, announced the day after this post, attacks the same bottleneck from the input side: today’s chat box forces users to drag their world into a small window, so the fix is to let humans gesture at what they mean. Point at a PDF, say “summarize this”; hover over a table, say “pie chart.” Thinking Machines trains interactivity into the model. DeepMind builds it into the input modality. Both bets assume today’s text-prompt interface is the bottleneck, but they disagree on which layer to unbottleneck.
Evaluation is the hard part. Every widely-used LLM benchmark is turn-based. The post introduces TimeSpeak, CueSpeak, and the FD-bench family as interactivity metrics, but these are in-house and not yet standard across labs. Without a cross-lab metric for “good collaborator,” effort keeps flowing to the measurable thing (the existing intelligence benchmarks) and the interactivity side keeps being filed under “qualitative.”
UX is the bottleneck; labor displacement is its consequence. Today’s chat UX fits turn-based question-and-answer, not continuous collaboration, so for work that would benefit from sustained human presence capable models default to autonomous use, which looks like labor substitution. Interaction models are Thinking Machines’ attempt to change that bottleneck: a model trained for real-time collaboration recasts the substitute-vs-augment debate as a UX problem that can be solved, not a capability fact that has to be accepted. The test is whether the result stays closer to “a bicycle for the mind”, amplifying the human in the loop, or drifts into a tool that works best when the human is absent.
The founder’s framing, a month on. In a June 2026 Bloomberg Tech interview, Murati described interaction models as the first concrete step of Thinking Machines’ human-in-the-loop bet and granted that the autonomy-first path is the faster way to advance AI — a useful gloss on why the lab is putting the interaction objective first.

title: The Math Behind the Cost of AI Agents
text:
Cover image from Vasco’s Inference Notes post.
Vasco Schiavo, writing on the Inference Notes Substack, derives why agent token costs explode and fits the predicted curves against real benchmark traces. The core claim: each turn re-sends the entire conversation history, so total input tokens pile up as a triangular number \(T(T-1)/2\), quadratic in turns, while output tokens grow linearly.

title: The Math Behind the Cost of AI Agents
text:
The growth law



A four-turn conversation, colored by token type: blue cells are input, red cells are output. Image from Vasco’s Inference Notes post.


Prompt caching does not change the shape of this picture, but it changes which cells are cheap. Green cells below are cached input, billed at a fraction of the fresh rate (typically around 10%). The triangle still grows quadratically, but the dominant term becomes cheap re-reads instead of full-price input, so over the practical turn range the total cost looks linear even though the underlying formula is not.



The same diagram with caching on. Green cells are cached input. Image from Vasco’s Inference Notes post.


The full with-cache cost formula is \(M \cdot T + c \cdot M \cdot T(T-1)/2\), still quadratic in \(T\) with the \(T^2\) term just multiplied by the small constant \(c \cdot M / 2\). The post argues that once caching is deployed, the linear term dominates over the practical turn range, so it fits the cached data with a line rather than a quadratic. The takeaway it pulls out: without caching, cost scales as \(T^2\); with caching, cost scales as \(T\) plus a negligible \(T^2\) correction.

title: The Math Behind the Cost of AI Agents
text:
Fits on SWE-bench
To test those predictions on real data, the post fits two curve shapes — \(a \cdot t^2\) for no-cache and \(b \cdot t\) for with-cache — against cumulative paid tokens per turn on SWE-bench traces from the OpenHands evaluation index, across three models: GPT-5.2, Gemini-3-Flash, and Claude Opus 4.6. Each coefficient has a concrete interpretation:

\(a\) — per-turn verbosity. How many fresh tokens each turn contributes on average. A large \(a\) means the model (or its harness) is pushing a lot of new content per turn.
\(b\) — cache-era marginal cost. The effective per-turn cost once caching is doing its job. A small \(b\) means cache hits are carrying most of the load. A large \(b\) means the cache is not catching much.

In all three panels below, red is the no-cache median (dashed line = quadratic fit), blue is the with-cache median (dashed line = linear fit), and the pink band is the interquartile range (IQR) across task instances.

Gemini-3-Flash on SWE-bench, 500 tasks. Image from Vasco’s Inference Notes post.

GPT-5.2 and Opus 4.6 are roughly matched on \(a\) (around 1,000 fresh tokens per turn), while Gemini-3-Flash is a third of that, reflecting shorter responses and more compact tool calls. On \(b\), the three separate sharply: Opus’s \(0.0008\) is more than 10× shallower than the other two, meaning a higher cache hit rate, less fresh content per turn, or both at Anthropic’s end. That is why, on the Opus panel above, the with-cache line almost disappears into the x-axis against a no-cache peak of 3.7M tokens.

title: The Math Behind the Cost of AI Agents
text:
My Notes

Tension with “Where Claude Code tokens go”. Reading this alongside Where Claude Code tokens go surfaces a tension. Mnimiy’s proxy measured ~13% of Claude Code cost going to conversation-history re-reads and another ~10% to cache misses on session resume, together about a quarter of spend on the re-read triangle. But the SWE-bench Opus 4.6 fit here puts with-cache marginal cost at \(b = 0.0008\), so flat that re-reads should barely register. The gap is probably the cache-hit-rate assumption: SWE-bench traces one continuous session under near-ideal cache conditions, while real Claude Code usage invalidates the cache constantly — 5-minute timeouts on coffee breaks, CLAUDE.md edits, hook changes, tool reordering — pushing re-reads back to full price and moving the user onto the steeper no-cache curve.
IQR variance across the three models. Fitting to the median across ~500 tasks smooths away the tail that actually burns money, and the post barely addresses how wide that tail is. The no-cache interquartile bands differ sharply. Opus at \(T=80\) has a band about 0.8M wide on a 3.7M median — roughly 20% of the median width. Gemini at \(T=175\) is in a different regime: the median is 8M tokens and the upper quartile reaches 16M, so just the upper half of the IQR equals the median itself. GPT-5.2 sits in between. Some of that is Gemini running longer trajectories, which lets cumulative variance compound. But even at similar turn counts the proportional spread is higher for Gemini, probably because its per-turn token count is more variable: tool calls ranging from small greps to full-file reads, or a subset of tasks dragging into verbose off-path exploration. With Q3 = 2× median, 25% of Gemini sessions cost at least double what the median fit would predict, before you hit true outliers. For anyone using these curves to forecast agent spend, a \(p95\) cumulative-token curve would be more decision-relevant than the median fit.
Gemini’s 2× trajectory length. Trajectory length itself differs markedly across models, and the post doesn’t unpack why. Gemini-3-Flash runs out to \(T \approx 175\); GPT-5.2 tops out around \(T \approx 75\) and Opus 4.6 around \(T \approx 80\). Even with Gemini’s leaner per-turn verbosity (\(\sim 300\) tokens/turn), the longer trajectories end up consuming more total tokens: \(\sim 8\text{M}\) cumulative no-cache at session end versus \(\sim 3.7\text{M}\) for Opus. If the tasks are roughly equivalent across runs, that is twice the work to reach comparable outcomes, which would look like a capability gap. But I can’t rule out harness-level differences: different per-model step limits, different tool-call styles (many small reads vs fewer large ones), or different early-exit thresholds could each produce the same pattern without implying anything about the model. Without OpenHands config detail it stays ambiguous. The observation worth holding onto either way: “leaner per turn” doesn’t translate to “cheaper overall” if it costs twice as many turns to finish.
The two-line fix anecdote. The author notes in passing that the OpenAI cache slope looked several times steeper than theory predicted, traced it to a bug in how their own code was calling OpenAI’s cache API, and shaved the slope down with a two-line fix. That is a useful case for regression-testing cache behavior against a theoretical baseline. Any provider whose cached slope deviates from \(c \cdot M\) by more than some margin is either misconfigured in your client or mis-documented upstream.
Prompt-prefix stability, not just size. Prompt-prefix stability is what actually decides whether caching works, and the best-practices list treats it as a small detail tucked inside the “keep system prompts clear, concise, and stable” bullet. Rotating system prompts, reordering tool definitions, or appending per-session memory to the front of the context all silently invalidate the cache: a single edit anywhere inside the cached prefix flips the whole thing back to full price. That deserves its own bullet near the top of the list, not a clause inside one about size. The closest comparable analysis at another layer is Reiner Pope’s blackboard derivation of frontier LLM economics, which does the same thing one level down at the hardware layer: derive from the formula, calibrate to public prices.

title: The Math Behind the Cost of AI Agents
text:

title: Vibe Coding and Agentic Engineering Are Getting Closer
text:
Cover art for Heavybit’s High Leverage podcast, Ep. #9, the conversation that prompted this post.
Simon Willison reflects on his recent appearance on Heavybit’s High Leverage podcast and notices something uncomfortable: the line he drew between vibe coding and the responsible use of AI to write code, which he now calls agentic engineering, has started to blur in his own work. He no longer reviews every line of code Claude Code writes for him, even on production systems, and he names the trust drift directly: normalization of deviance.

title: Vibe Coding and Agentic Engineering Are Getting Closer
text:
What the post argues

Vibe coding and agentic engineering are blurring. The hard line he once drew between them, where vibe coding doesn’t look at the code and agentic engineering does, no longer holds in his own work. He’s stopped reviewing every line Claude Code writes, even on production systems.
The internal-team analogy. When another team hands him an image-resize service, he doesn’t read its source. He reads the docs and ships, digging in only if something breaks. He’s starting to treat coding agents the same way.
Normalization of deviance is the risk. Every uninspected commit that turns out fine pushes trust up, and at some point he’ll trust the agent at the wrong moment and get burned. Claude Code has no professional reputation to lose, which is what made the human-team analogy work in the first place.
Polished repos no longer signal quality. A polished README, a hundred commits, and full tests used to mean weeks of care. It now takes half an hour. The new signal is whether someone has actually used the thing.
Bottlenecks shift upstream too. Citing Anthropic design leader Jenny Wen: elaborate design processes exist because three-month build mistakes are catastrophic. If builds aren’t three months anymore, the design process can be cheaper and riskier.
He’s not afraid for his career. Working with agents reminds him how hard software is. The tools amplify what an experienced engineer already knows. He’d rather use a professionally managed AI-assisted product than vibe-code his own. “I can plumb my house if I watch enough YouTube videos. I would rather hire a plumber.”

title: Vibe Coding and Agentic Engineering Are Getting Closer
text:
My Notes
Disasters strike when you stop watching. Trust accrued over a streak of clean commits doesn’t immunize the next one. In late April, a Cursor agent wiped a company’s production database and Railway backups in nine seconds and then enumerated, in writing, the safety rules it had violated. The defense against the long tail isn’t more careful review — it’s the harness and guardrails around the agent: sandboxes that can’t reach production, write-fences on destructive commands, rollback paths that survive the agent’s mistakes.

title: The Anthropic Institute’s Research Agenda
text:
Illustration from Anthropic.
Anthropic published the research agenda for The Anthropic Institute (TAI) on May 7, 2026. The premise: a frontier lab can see AI’s real-world effects earlier than outside researchers can, and TAI’s job is to publish those signals so external organizations, governments, and the public can act on them. Outputs are described as inputs to the Long-Term Benefit Trust (LTBT) and to release decisions, with the Anthropic Fellowship as the recruitment surface. The LTBT is an independent five-trustee body that, via a special Class T share, elects a growing share of Anthropic’s board (a majority within four years); its remit was announced as long-range and extreme-event decisions, not day-to-day operations.
The agenda lays out four pillars:

title: The Anthropic Institute’s Research Agenda
text:
My Notes

TAI is the field’s first research-agenda layer. Across the four frontier labs, OpenAI’s Our principles and its peer documents map two existing document types: declared values and deployment gates. TAI is a third type, set up to produce empirical findings the other two layers can be checked against. The Anthropic Economic Index, with more granular data and higher cadence under TAI, is one concrete commitment. OpenAI’s new “Adaptability” principle commits to updating positions as evidence accumulates; TAI is the closest the field has to an institution set up to produce that evidence.
Two ways TAI matters, both untested.

Externally, the agenda promises an “early warning signal for significant change and disruption”, language that asserts a verifiable measurement. If outsiders can’t reproduce TAI’s numbers from the published procedure, anyone acting on the early-warning claim has to take Anthropic’s word for it.
Internally, TAI’s findings feed into the LTBT, giving the Trust a steady research-policy stream beyond the extreme-event scope it was originally announced for. That integration becomes meaningful only when a Trust position publicly diverges from a commercial decision.

The R&D pillar’s telemetry could check Clark’s forecast. Jack Clark put 60% on full AI-driven R&D by end of 2028 from public benchmark trends. TAI commits to publishing the internal R&D speedup data that would let outside readers compare that forecast to actual progress. Without publication, the pillar stays purely internal and only useful to Anthropic.

title: Can LLMs Reliably Self-Correct Their Own Reasoning?
text:
Can LLMs reliably self-correct their own reasoning? 3 papers walk us through their discoveries.
Self-Refine proposes a naive intrinsic-feedback loop: a single frozen LLM acts as generator, critic, and rewriter inside a prompt-only loop. The paper reports about 20 percentage points of average lift across seven tasks, claiming that no training, RL, or external signal is needed. The gains vary widely by task — large where “good” is hard to define from a one-line critique, but very small on math reasoning, where the feedback model fails to catch subtle errors.
But Cannot-Self-Correct tests the strong claim head-on: can LLMs revise their own reasoning answers without any external signal about correctness? Across three benchmarks (GSM8K, CommonSenseQA, HotPotQA), the answer is NO. The model’s confidence carries over from the initial answer into the revision, and the self-correction loop tends to degrade rather than improve performance. The result refutes the class of approach Self-Refine belongs to.
Then we have Reflexion that threads the needle by splitting self-correction into two LLM steps. An Evaluator detects success or failure. A Self-Reflection model diagnoses what went wrong. The Evaluator’s external signal — a hand-written heuristic, exact-match grading, or test execution — gates whether the diagnosis fires at all. The ablations found however when the signal misfires, as on MBPP Python’s high false-negative rate, Self-Reflection rewrites correct code into wrong code, which is exactly the failure mode Cannot-Self-Correct documented. So Reflexion can be read as a positive existence result for self-correction with a reliable external signal, not as a refutation to Cannot-Self-Correct.
All three papers predate the reasoning-model era. A follow-up — Self-Correction After the Reasoning-Model Era — engages Peter Bloem’s question on whether the arc still holds for o1- and R1-style models trained with RL on verifiable rewards.
Originally posted on LinkedIn.

title: Can LLMs Reliably Self-Correct Their Own Reasoning?

title: Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning
text:
Reflexion across three task types: decision-making (AlfWorld), programming (HumanEval), and reasoning (HotPotQA). For each task, the agent takes a trajectory, receives an evaluation signal (rule-based heuristic, self-generated unit tests, or exact-match grading on the final answer), reflects on what went wrong in natural language, and stores that reflection in memory for the next attempt. Figure 1 from the paper [1].
In Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning [1] (NeurIPS 2023), Noah Shinn et al. (Northeastern, MIT, Princeton) introduce an agent architecture that “learns” across episodes purely by writing natural-language reflections to an episodic memory, without gradient updates or weight changes.

title: Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning
text:
Methods



(a) Diagram of Reflexion. (b) Reflexion reinforcement algorithm. Figure 2 from the paper [1].


The agent operates by interaction: at each step it emits an action — a tool call, environment command, or free-form answer — and the environment returns an observation. A single attempt at the task is an episode (also called a trial), and the action-observation sequence within one episode is the trajectory (\(\tau\)) — the agent’s short-term memory.
The Reflexion framework factors the agent into three roles. The Self-Reflection model is always an LLM. The Actor is always an LLM, and in most setups the same LLM as the Self-Reflection model, with different prompts. The Evaluator can be an LLM but is often a non-LLM signal: a hand-written heuristic, exact-match grading, or the pass/fail of a generated test suite.

Actor (\(M_a\)) — an LLM whose weights, together with the current experience buffer, jointly parameterize the policy \(\pi_\theta(a_i \mid s_i)\) from which each next action is sampled (\(\theta = \{M_a,\ \text{experience}\}\)).
Evaluator (\(M_e\)) — scores the resulting trajectory: a hand-written heuristic (or an LLM-as-judge variant) on AlfWorld, the pass/fail of self-generated unit tests on HumanEval, exact-match grading on HotPotQA’s final answer.
Self-Reflection (\(M_{sr}\)) — takes the trajectory plus the evaluator’s signal and produces a short natural-language reflection (e.g. “I failed because I assumed they both had the same professions”), appended to the experience buffer — the agent’s long-term memory that persists across episodes.

On the next episode, the Actor is conditioned on the accumulated experience and attempts the task again. The LLM weights stay fixed; the only thing that updates between episodes is the experience text. The “reinforcement signal” is literally the reflection text the Self-Reflection model writes after each failure.

title: Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning
text:
Results
The paper evaluates Reflexion on three task families:

AlfWorld [2] [2] (sequential decision-making, 134 task instances) — Reflexion adds 22 percentage points absolute over a ReAct [3] [3] baseline within 12 iterative learning steps, and the best variant solves 130 of 134 tasks. Figure 3(a) tracks cumulative tasks solved by trial number under both self-evaluation modes (a hand-written heuristic and a GPT-as-judge classifier); 3(b) decomposes the residual failures into hallucination and inefficient planning — both decay steadily under Reflexion, while the ReAct-only baseline plateaus.




AlfWorld learning curves and failure-mode decomposition (Figure 3 [1]).



HotPotQA [4] [4]  (multi-hop reasoning) — Reflexion improves accuracy by 20 points on a 100-question subset. Figure 4 separates the contribution: (a) Reflexion benefits both ReAct and Chain-of-Thought actors; (b) the gain holds even when the actor is given the ground-truth context, so it isn’t just better retrieval; (c) decomposes the lift between including past trajectories (episodic memory) and the verbal Self-Reflection step. Episodic memory carries most of the gain, and Self-Reflection adds an 8-point boost on top.




HotPotQA results across actor variants and the episodic-memory ablation (Figure 4 [1]).



HumanEval [5] [5] (Python coding, GPT-4 as Actor) — Reflexion reaches 91% pass@1 versus the reported 80% GPT-4 baseline (11-point gain). Table 1 shows the gain is consistent across languages and benchmarks: HumanEval Rust 60 → 68, MBPP [6] [6] (Mostly Basic Programming Problems) Rust 71 → 75. The paper also introduces LeetcodeHardGym, a benchmark of 40 hard-rated Leetcode problems with scaffolding across 19 programming languages, but only reports results on the Python subset (7.5 → 15); the multi-language scope is released as an artifact, not used in any reported experiment. The exception to the across-the-board gains is MBPP Python, where Reflexion (77.1) underperforms the GPT-4 baseline (80.1) — see the test-generation table below.




Pass@1 across code-generation benchmarks and languages (Table 1 [1]).


The paper’s ablations compare self-generated unit tests vs ground-truth tests as the evaluation signal, examine memory-length effects, and separate the contribution of the Evaluator from the Self-Reflection step. Two things to flag about Table 2 before reading. First, the test suites used as the Evaluator’s signal are all LLM-generated: Reflexion’s procedure is the same on every code benchmark — the Actor writes tests from the problem description (with chain-of-thought prompting), filters for syntactic validity, and uses those tests’ pass/fail as the signal. MBPP ships with its own curated tests, but Reflexion doesn’t use them; the model generates fresh tests from the prompt. Second, the four diagnostic columns are conditional probabilities: TP and FP are conditional on tests passing (TP + FP = 1), FN and TN on tests failing (FN + TN = 1).
The Base and Reflexion columns are pass@1 — the approach’s headline accuracy with and without the Reflexion loop. The TP / FN / FP / TN columns rate the LLM-generated tests as a classifier of solution correctness, and they predict approach performance directly. HumanEval Python’s tests are clean — TP=0.99, FP=0.01 — and Reflexion lifts 0.80 → 0.91. MBPP Python’s tests are noisy on both sides: FP=0.16 lets buggy code through, FN=0.59 means most “test failures” were actually correct solutions the loop then rewrites, and Reflexion drops to 0.77.
The paper doesn’t diagnose why MBPP’s LLM-generated tests are noisier, but the prompt structure of the two benchmarks is a plausible explanation: HumanEval prompts are docstrings that often include doctest-style I/O examples (the LLM can crib from those when writing tests), while MBPP prompts are bare natural-language sentences (“Write a function to remove duplicates…”) with no I/O examples, so the LLM has to invent both inputs and expected outputs from scratch.



Self-generated test accuracy on HumanEval and MBPP, broken into TP/FN/FP/TN. Rust columns use the hardest 50 HumanEval problems translated via MultiPL-E (Table 2 [1]).

title: Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning
text:
My Notes

Verbal feedback as policy state. Reflexion is the paper that established natural-language reflection as a first-class component of agent design, and the lineage is visible across 2024 agentic frameworks — from AutoGen [7] [7] to LangGraph to the critic-refiner loops in Anthropic’s computer-use agents. What’s distinctive here is keeping the reflections as long-term memory across trials rather than compressing them into the immediate context the way Self-Refine [8] does.
The 91% HumanEval caveat. Later reproductions found Reflexion’s gain is bottlenecked by test-generation quality rather than by the repair step itself: Olausson et al. (2024) [9] [9] studied iterative self-repair on HumanEval and APPS and argued that “self-repair is bottlenecked by the model’s ability to provide feedback on its own code” — substituting a stronger feedback model lifts the gains substantially. Reflexion’s own ablation (Table 3 on HumanEval Rust) tells the same story: removing test generation drops Reflexion from 0.68 to 0.52, while removing the self-reflection step alone barely moves the number (0.68 → 0.60). CodeT [10] [10] makes the self-generated-test mechanism explicit; Reflexion adds a reflection step on top but inherits CodeT’s dependence on test-generation quality.
Reflexion vs Cannot-Self-Correct. Reflexion’s headline claim — that verbal reinforcement lifts an LLM agent — sits next to a result by Huang et al. [11] that LLMs cannot reliably self-correct. The two don’t contradict.

Huang et al. define intrinsic self-correction as a model revising its own answer with no external signal, and show it degrades reasoning. Reflexion always supplies an external signal via the Evaluator — a heuristic on AlfWorld, exact-match on HotPotQA, test execution on HumanEval.
The structural overlap is Reflexion’s Self-Reflection step. Diagnosing what went wrong over the model’s own trajectory is exactly what Huang et al. studied. The Evaluator is upstream: it gates whether Self-Reflection fires at all.
Table 2 backs this up with the FN column: MBPP Python’s FN is 0.59 vs HumanEval Python’s 0.40, meaning MBPP’s tests fail on already-correct solutions much more often. Reflexion then “corrects” those correct solutions and ends up below the GPT-4 baseline on MBPP Python — 80.1 (baseline) vs 77.1 (Reflexion).
So Reflexion is best read as a positive existence result for self-correction with reliable external signal, not a refutation of the intrinsic-failure result.

Memory-as-parameters has a context budget. The paper writes the policy as \(\pi_\theta\) with \(\theta = \{M_a, \text{mem}\}\) — the memory is part of the parameter set. The interesting question is what learning in token space gives up. First, the experience is task-specific and doesn’t transfer: every new task starts with an empty buffer. Second, as the buffer grows across trials, the Actor’s context budget becomes the bottleneck, so the effective “learning rate” is bounded by how much context the system can spend per inference. Later work on extending effective context (MemGPT [12] [12]) and agent-specific long-context finetuning is partly a response to this limit.

title: TIOBE May 2026: A Statistical-Language Consolidation
text:
Top 20 of the May 2026 TIOBE Programming Community Index. Image from TIOBE.
The May 2026 TIOBE Programming Community Index is out. R has matched its all-time high at #8, while MATLAB, SAS, SPSS, Wolfram/Mathematica, and Stata keep losing ground — the statistical-computing stack is consolidating around two ecosystems.
What the index reports this month:

title: TIOBE May 2026: A Statistical-Language Consolidation
text:
My Notes

Python’s drop may be a ceiling effect. TIOBE ratings are roughly zero-sum share of search, course, and vendor attention. Python sits at 19.98% this month, down from ~25% a year ago. From that height, even small simultaneous gains across many competitors mathematically pull from the leader, so the YoY drop doesn’t require a Python-specific story. An AI-assistant suppressant is also plausible (fewer “how do I do X in Python” searches per unit of code written), but it would dampen all languages, not just the leader.
C’s rise is harder to attribute. +1.84% YoY at #2 is consistent with the lower-level half of the AI stack (CUDA, kernels, embedded inference, where Python wrappers eventually bottom out into C), but TIOBE doesn’t break down its rating sources, so any specific driver is speculation. C# +1.19% may reflect a similar refresh from the .NET 9/10 release cycle and Unity’s continued grip on game dev.

title: Hassabis: Use AI to Do More, Not Lay People Off
text:
Demis Hassabis, CEO of Google DeepMind. Image from WIRED.
In a WIRED interview ahead of Google I/O, Demis Hassabis, CEO of Google DeepMind, pushed back on the idea that more capable AI coding models mean fewer engineers. Even while talking up Gemini 3.5 Flash’s agentic coding (translating codebases, fixing deep bugs, writing operating systems from scratch), he said he had no idea why people predict doom for software developers, and suggested some of those predictions may have an ulterior motive like raising money.
His argument is that when engineers become three or four times more productive, the response should be to do three or four times more, not to cut headcount. He called companies that replace developers with AI short on imagination, and said Alphabet has a backlog of ideas, from drug discovery to game design, it would happily staff with the freed-up capacity. The interview ran alongside Google’s I/O announcements, including the Antigravity coding tool and Gemini 3.5 Flash, as Google works to close the developer-adoption gap with Anthropic’s Claude and OpenAI’s Codex.

title: LLMs Know When They Know, but Do Not Act on It: A Metacognitive Harness for Test-time Scaling
text:
Figure 1 from the paper [1].
In LLMs Know When They Know, but Do Not Act on It: A Metacognitive Harness for Test-time Scaling [1] (arXiv preprint, May 2026), Qi Cao, Yufan Wang, Peijia Qin, Shuhao Zhang, and Pengtao Xie (UCSD) propose a test-time control loop that turns pre-solve and post-solve self-assessment signals into explicit retry, stop, and aggregate decisions, lifting a fixed Claude Sonnet-4.6 from 48.3 to 56.9 pooled accuracy on STEM, code, and multimodal benchmarks without any parameter updates.
Two terms borrowed from cognitive psychology carry the argument:
The two scalars sit outside the answer text rather than inline with reasoning, which keeps them structurally separable from the chain of thought and cheap to elicit. Figure 1 lays out the empirical premise in three panels: (a) shows the prompting setup that elicits FOK before answering and JOL after; (b) shows that those self-reports track actual correctness — accuracy rises monotonically from low- to high-confidence bins for both signals across all candidate models; (c) shows that the same models do not currently allocate reasoning length according to those signals — output length is roughly flat across the low/medium/high confidence bins. Panels (b) and (c) together motivate the harness: the calibration signal exists (b), but the model isn’t using it to direct effort (c). The harness in this paper is the machinery that closes the gap between (b) and (c) by turning the two scalars into routing decisions at inference time.

title: LLMs Know When They Know, but Do Not Act on It: A Metacognitive Harness for Test-time Scaling
text:
Methods
The harness has two stages:

Metacognition diagnosis runs once per candidate model on a 100-problem anchor set disjoint from any downstream benchmark. For each problem the model emits an FOK score (no reasoning allowed), produces a solution, and emits a JOL score. The triples \((\mathrm{FOK}_i, \mathrm{JOL}_i, y_i)\), where \(y_i\) is correctness, are scored for discrimination and calibration, then used as supervision to fit a small per-model controller: a support vector machine over the two-dimensional feature \((\mathrm{FOK}, \mathrm{JOL})\), with isotonic post-hoc calibration, trained via GroupKFold cross-validation on the 100-question anchor set. The kernel is selected per base model (polynomial degree 3 for Sonnet-4.6, linear for Opus-4.6); the calibrated output is a joint \(P(\text{correct})\) thresholded at \(p_{\rm stop}=0.7\). The paper rules out a hand-crafted alternative explicitly: the best closed-form rule the authors found, \((1{-}\mathrm{JOL})\cdot\mathrm{FOK}\), underperforms the learned SVM, so raw self-reports are not directly actionable as routing signals.
Deployment applies the fitted controller at inference. Low-FOK problems get extra reasoning budget directed at them; solutions whose post-solve \(P(\text{correct})\geq p_{\rm stop}\) are accepted and no further attempts are generated; mixed cases continue drawing additional solutions from the same base model and route the set to a final aggregator.

Training is moved off the base model, not eliminated. The framing claim of “no parameter updates” is accurate at the LLM level — Sonnet-4.6’s weights never change — but the harness still requires a small, fast supervised fit per base model on the 100-question anchor set. The cost is two orders of magnitude below conventional fine-tuning and produces an artifact (the SVM) that’s a few kilobytes rather than a checkpoint, but it is training, and it has to be redone when the base model changes.
Figure 2 lays out the harness as a Nelson–Narens [2] two-level loop: a meta level monitors reasoning state through the self-reported signals, while an object level performs test-time scaling actions (retry, stop, aggregate) under meta-level supervision. The two levels are deliberately separated so that the same base model serves as both the reasoner and the monitor, with the controller — not a fine-tune — deciding when each role activates.



Figure 2 from the paper [1].

title: LLMs Know When They Know, but Do Not Act on It: A Metacognitive Harness for Test-time Scaling
text:
Results
The harness wraps a fixed Claude Sonnet-4.6 base model — no fine-tuning — and is evaluated on three benchmarks chosen to span the modalities the paper cares about: HLE-Verified [3] for text reasoning, LiveCodeBench v6 [4] for code, and R-Bench-V [5] for multimodal STEM. Two comparison sets are reported:

Public single-model leaderboards — top-1 entries from frontier model families on each benchmark.
Matched-inference-budget baselines — four prior test-time scaling approaches under a fixed compute budget per question:

Vertical scaling (one trajectory, more reasoning per attempt): Self-Refine [6] and Budget Forcing [7].
Parallel scaling (N independent attempts combined by a separate selector): Verifier Reranking [8] [9] and Aggregator [10].


Table 1 reports both comparisons: Panel A vs. the leaderboard, Panel B vs. the test-time scaling baselines (with average attempts and dollar cost per question).



Table 1 from the paper [1].


Headline findings:

Pooled accuracy: 48.3 → 56.9 (+8.6) against same-base test-time scaling baselines (Panel B). Largest gain among all listed methods at the lowest cost per question among the parallel approaches.
Beats every public single-model leaderboard entry on the three primary settings (Panel A). Notably +12.0 over GPT-5.2-H on HLE-Verified (52.5 → 64.5) and +19.6 over o4-mini-H on the LiveCodeBench Hard split (63.5 → 83.1).
Pareto-dominant on cost. $0.78 per question vs $1.32–$1.42 for parallel-selection baselines; matches Aggregator’s accuracy at 55% of its cost. The savings come from FOK gating: easy problems short-circuit at the first high-JOL solution instead of paying the full N-attempt budget.
Average attempts: 2.4 vs 4.0 for parallel baselines, with a higher accuracy ceiling. Effort is allocated unevenly — confident problems exit fast, uncertain problems get more attempts.
Ablations. Removing any of three ingredients — calibrated decision rules from the diagnosis step, directed retry guided by JOL feedback, or per-attempt context management — drops the gain materially. Uniform sampling and longer single-trajectory reasoning, the obvious cheaper substitutes, do not recover the harness’s accuracy.




Table 2 from the paper [1].

title: LLMs Know When They Know, but Do Not Act on It: A Metacognitive Harness for Test-time Scaling
text:
My Notes

Closing the open loop — the contribution sits inside a multi-year arc. Kadavath et al. [11] already showed in 2022 that frontier models are well-calibrated on lettered multiple choice and can self-evaluate via \(P(\text{True})\) and \(P(\text{IK})\) probes. What the metacognition literature has been missing is a closed-loop way to act on those signals during inference rather than treating them as a measurement target, exactly the gap a recent position-paper line argued for (Liu and van der Schaar’s intrinsic metacognitive learning frame [12]). This paper is one of the first published instances of that loop actually closed end-to-end.
The SVM is the external verifier Huang et al. [13] said the loop needs. Huang’s ICLR 2024 result was that intrinsic self-correction fails without an external signal. Reflexion [14], framed as self-reflection, actually depends on environment reward at each retry. The metacognitive harness sits in the same family: the model’s FOK and JOL scalars only correlate with correctness, and the SVM is the piece that learns a calibrated \(P(\text{correct})\) from ground-truth labels on the 100 anchor questions. The labels are the actual external signal; the harness’s distinction is supplying it offline once per model rather than at inference via an oracle or critic LLM.
Per-model calibration is partial credit. Cacioli’s 33-model atlas [15] shows that the same LLM’s ability to know when it’s wrong varies sharply across knowledge domains — best on Applied/Professional questions, worst on Formal Reasoning and Natural Science. The harness’s per-model SVM is the right direction, but per-(model, domain) is where Cacioli’s evidence points.
Portability across model families is the open question. A separate May 2026 line of work, The Compliance Trap [16], shows that 8 of 11 frontier models lose up to 30.2 accuracy points under instructions that force the model to commit to a confident answer when it would otherwise hedge or abstain, with the most-capable reasoning models suffering the worst absolute collapse. Anthropic’s Constitutional AI [17] shows near-perfect immunity. The harness uses Sonnet-4.6, and FOK/JOL elicitation matches compliance-forcing’s shape, so the headline gain may be conditional on the alignment family rather than the harness design. A natural follow-up replicates the harness across Gemini, GPT-5, and DeepSeek bases to see whether the gain transfers, or whether Claude-specific alignment was doing the work.

title: TRIAGE: Evaluating Prospective Metacognitive Control in LLMs Under Resource Constraints
text:
Triage efficiency across models and benchmarks at moderate budget (\(\alpha = 0.5\)). Figure 1 from the paper [1]. Image from arXiv.
In TRIAGE: Evaluating Prospective Metacognitive Control in LLMs under Resource Constraints [1], Zabir Al Nazi (UC Riverside) and Shubhashis Roy Dipta (UMBC) introduce a benchmark that scores 20 frontier and open-source models on whether they can plan token-budget allocation across a queue of problems before any of them is attempted, and find that most cannot.

title: TRIAGE: Evaluating Prospective Metacognitive Control in LLMs Under Resource Constraints
text:
Methods
TRIAGE operationalizes the Nelson & Narens (1990) distinction between metacognitive monitoring (judging whether a problem is solvable) and metacognitive control (acting on those judgments to allocate effort), focusing on the prospective form: every decision is committed before any task is attempted. The harness has two stages.
Intuitively, the setup is a competition-style budget allocation. The model sees a list of problems with point values and a shared token budget; without trying any of them, it must choose which to attempt, in what order, and how many tokens to spend on each. The plan is then executed and scored against an oracle that knew in advance which problems were solvable for this model and how expensive each would be. A model that’s good at planning skips the items it can’t solve and pours its budget into the ones it can; a model that’s bad at planning chases unsolvable problems and runs out of tokens.
Scoring uses a triage efficiency ratio. Let \(\pi\) be the model’s plan and \(V(\pi)\) the achieved value — the sum of point values \(v_i\) over problems \(\pi\) actually solved within budget. The main protocol fixes \(v_i = 1\) for every problem — uniform by design, so the planner cannot read difficulty off the point values and must infer it from problem text alone. The ratio normalizes \(V(\pi)\) against two references:
\[\eta = \frac{V(\pi) - V_{\text{random}}}{V_{\text{oracle}} - V_{\text{random}}}\]
where \(V_{\text{oracle}}\) is the best feasible plan with full knowledge of each problem’s solvability and cost, and \(V_{\text{random}}\) is the expected value of a budget-feasible plan drawn uniformly. So \(\eta = 1\) matches the oracle, \(\eta = 0\) matches uninformed random selection, and \(\eta < 0\) is worse than random.

Plan. The shared budget is \(B = \alpha \cdot B_{\text{baseline}}\), where \(B_{\text{baseline}}\) is the model’s own measured cost on a prior baseline run and \(\alpha \in \{0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0\}\) is the budget pressure — \(\alpha = 1.0\) supplies the full baseline budget (every item fits, in principle); \(\alpha = 0.25\) supplies a quarter of it, forcing the planner to skip most items.
Execute. The plan \(\pi\) is run in plan order under one of two regimes, yielding two scores:

Advisory — each problem runs to its natural completion; the queue stops once the next item’s true cost would exceed the remaining \(B\). Yields \(\eta_U\).
Enforced — each problem is hard-capped at its declared \(a_i\) (over-budget attempts score zero, and \(a_i\) is still spent from \(B\)); the queue stops once the next item’s \(a_i\) would exceed the remaining \(B\). Yields \(\eta_E\).


To diagnose the source of bad plans, the framework decomposes them along two axes:

Detection asks: did the planner correctly skip the unsolvables? Higher is better. Formally: \(D = |U \setminus S| / |U|\), the fraction of unsolvable problems correctly excluded from the plan, where \(S = \{i : a_i > 0\}\) is the planned set and \(U\) is the set of unsolvable items.
Waste asks: of the tokens it did spend, how many went to lost causes? Lower is better. Formally: \(W = \sum_{i \in S \cap U} a_i / \sum_{i \in S} a_i\), the fraction of allocated tokens spent on unsolvable items.

title: TRIAGE: Evaluating Prospective Metacognitive Control in LLMs Under Resource Constraints
text:
Results
The evaluation covers 20 model architectures: 4 standard LLMs and 16 reasoning-augmented LLMs, with each reasoning-augmented model run twice — once with extended reasoning enabled (marked [ext] in the heatmaps) and once without ([std]). Benchmarks: AIME 2024–2025, GPQA Diamond [2], LiveCodeBench [3], and Humanity’s Last Exam (HLE) [4]. The cover figure at the top of the post (Figure 1 in the paper) summarizes the headline finding at \(\alpha = 0.5\): solid bars are advisory \(\eta_U\), hatched bars are enforced \(\eta_E\), and red dashed lines mark baseline accuracy. Three findings across budgets and benchmarks:

Most models plan worse than random. Both \(\eta_U\) and \(\eta_E\) are widely negative; only a handful of (model, \(\alpha\), dataset) combinations reach positive \(\eta_E\) at all.
The advisory-vs-enforced gap is large. Models routinely declare per-problem budgets they then ignore — when allocations are merely advisory, planning skill (\(\eta_U\)) is meaningfully higher than under enforcement (\(\eta_E\)).
Reasoning-augmented modes often plan worse than standard. The [ext] rows in the heatmap below are systematically below the matching [std] rows, consistent with prior findings that reasoning training does not improve abstention behavior.

The two heatmaps below show \(\eta_U\) and \(\eta_E\) across the full (model, \(\alpha\), dataset) grid. The \(\alpha = 1.0\) column should be read with caution: η loses resolution there because the oracle-random gap collapses (every item fits, so both oracle and random plans attempt nearly everything). The paper recommends its alternative normalized regret \(\tilde{R} = (V_{\text{oracle}} - V) / V_{\text{oracle}}\) for that regime — bounded in \([0, 1]\) (\(\tilde{R} = 0\) matches the oracle, \(\tilde{R} = 1\) captures no value), so it stays stable when η doesn’t. Treat α=1.0 cells in the heatmaps as “metric saturated,” not “model planned well.”
Figure 2 below is the \(\tilde{R}\) companion to the cover Figure 1 at the same \(\alpha = 0.5\) anchor — solid bars are \(\tilde{R}_U\) (advisory), hatched are \(\tilde{R}_E\) (enforced), red dashed lines mark baseline accuracy. The same configurations that lead in η lead in \(\tilde{R}\) (lower is better here); the bounded scale also lets you see how close models come to capturing zero value in the enforced regime, where many \(\tilde{R}_E\) values land near 1.



Normalized triage regret \(\tilde{R}\) across models and benchmarks at moderate budget (\(\alpha = 0.5\)). Figure 2 from the paper [1].


Returning to η in heatmap form, Figure 5 shows the advisory regime (\(\eta_U\)) across all four α values:



Triage skill in the advisory-budget regime, \(\eta_U\), per (model, \(\alpha\), dataset). Figure 5 from the paper [1].


Figure 6 shows the same grid for the enforced regime, \(\eta_E\), where per-problem allocations are binding. The pattern is markedly worse: \(\eta_E\) is negative for the large majority of configurations at \(\alpha = 0.5\), with most cells deep into anti-skill territory. Across all 30 configurations tested, only Gemini 2.5 Flash (standard) achieves positive \(\eta_E\) on every benchmark, and only it and Qwen 3.5 27B (standard) achieve usable enforced-regime performance on more than one.



Triage skill in the enforced-budget regime, \(\eta_E\), per (model, \(\alpha\), dataset); color encoding identical to Figure 5. Figure 6 from the paper [1].


A focused detection experiment traces four models — Gemini 2.5 Flash (think), Qwen 2.5 32B, Qwen 3 32B (think), and GPT-OSS 20B (think) — through \((D, W)\) space on two benchmarks (GPQA-Abstain, MMLU-Math-Abstain) as the injection ratio \(r\) — the fraction of the pool replaced by guaranteed-unsolvable problems drawn from AbstentionBench [7], with pool size held constant — varies from 0.25 to 1.0 (marker size grows with \(r\)). Three findings:

Cluster split. Gemini 2.5 Flash and standard Qwen 2.5 32B stay near the high-\(D\), low-\(W\) corner; the two reasoning-trained models drift away from it.
Within-family probe. The Qwen pair is the cleanest test: at \(r = 0.25\) the standard 32B detects most unsolvables (\(D = 0.67\) on GPQA, \(D = 0.88\) on MMLU-Math), while the reasoning-trained 32B at the same ratio detects far fewer (\(D = 0.08\) and \(D = 0.54\)) — reproducing the AbstentionBench finding inside a single architecture family.
Mechanism gap. The paper documents the pattern but does not propose a mechanism, and explicitly hedges that the effect isn’t uniform across families (Gemini 2.5 Flash is also reasoning-augmented and retains detection across the range). The same shape — reasoning-trained models doing worse on a metacognitive task than non-reasoning siblings — also surfaces in the Compliance Trap’s “capability inversion” result (more-capable reasoning models suffer the worst degradation under compliance-forcing prompts), suggesting it isn’t an artifact of one benchmark family. A plausible mechanism appears in My Notes below.




Trajectories through \((D, W)\) space across four models and two benchmarks; marker size grows with \(r\), and the star marks the ideal corner. Figure 3 from the paper [1].


A separate budget-aware re-solve experiment probes the planning failure’s deeper layer: when the model is shown its own per-problem budget in the prompt and re-attempts the problem, accuracy lifts modestly across three tested models (Gemini 2.5 Flash +1.9pp, Kimi K2.5 +4.9pp, GLM 5.1 +8.3pp) — but compliance is poor (37%, 6%, 16% respectively). The paper’s interpretation: stating the budget in the prompt functions not as a respected constraint but as length pressure that prompts earlier commitment.

title: TRIAGE: Evaluating Prospective Metacognitive Control in LLMs Under Resource Constraints
text:
My Notes

Measures the control axis, not just monitoring. Liu and van der Schaar’s position paper [5] named three components of metacognitive learning (knowledge, planning, evaluation) and argued that today’s self-improving agents lean on hand-designed extrinsic loops rather than intrinsic ones. TRIAGE doesn’t directly fill that gap (it uses the Nelson-Narens monitoring vs. control split rather than the Liu/vdSchaar terminology), but the design is in the same spirit: scoring what the model does under resource constraints, not what it verbally claims to know. Within that split, Kadavath et al.’s “Mostly Know” [6] sits on the monitoring side (predicting per-question correctness) and Cao et al.’s metacognitive harness [8] sits on the test-time control side (gating retry, stop, and aggregate decisions during inference); TRIAGE adds the prospective-control corner that neither covers.
Pre-commitment is what makes control measurable. Retrospective measures (post-hoc confidence, abstention after a partial attempt) collapse monitoring and control because the model can adjust mid-stream. By committing the plan ex ante — before any execution feedback — TRIAGE removes that mid-stream channel and forces the model to act on its prior estimate of its own cost and solvability. The same logic generalizes: only when self-assessment is locked in before observing partial output can it be cleanly separated from in-stream adjustment.
Why do reasoning models fare worse? Kirichenko et al.’s AbstentionBench [7] reports the upstream finding: reasoning fine-tuning degrades abstention by roughly 24% across 20 unanswerable-question datasets. The mechanism is plausible: RLHF/RLVR rewards arriving at some answer, so the trained policy learns to spend tokens rather than skip. A useful follow-up would isolate whether the gap closes when the reward function explicitly prices abstention, e.g. by training on the TRIAGE objective itself rather than per-problem accuracy.
Models lack a reliable internal token-counter. Length-controlled generation has been studied for instruction-following, but those benchmarks measure verbalized length compliance for human-readable outputs, not self-imposed compute budgets. The compliance numbers above suggest the gap runs deeper: no plan can survive an executor that ignores its own allocations, and the compliance failure deepens the planning failure rather than replacing it.
