Kadavath, S., Conerly, T., Askell, A., Henighan, T., Drain, D., Perez, E., Schiefer, N., Hatfield-Dodds, Z., DasSarma, N., Tran-Johnson, E., et al. “Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2207.05221), July 11, 2022. https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.05221
Kirichenko, P., Ibrahim, M., Chaudhuri, K., & Bell, S. J. “AbstentionBench: Reasoning LLMs Fail on Unanswerable Questions.” NeurIPS 2025 Datasets and Benchmarks Track (arXiv:2506.09038), June 10, 2025. https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.09038
Cao, Q., Wang, Y., Qin, P., Zhang, S., and Xie, P. “LLMs Know When They Know, but Do Not Act on It: A Metacognitive Harness for Test-time Scaling.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2605.14186), May 13, 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.14186

title: TRIAGE: Evaluating Prospective Metacognitive Control in LLMs Under Resource Constraints
text:
Related Posts

AbstentionBench: Reasoning LLMs Fail on Unanswerable Questions: the upstream finding TRIAGE draws its unsolvable problems from and reproduces — reasoning fine-tuning degrades the model’s ability to skip lost causes.
LLMs Know When They Know, but Do Not Act on It: A Metacognitive Harness for Test-time Scaling: the test-time control approach TRIAGE extends, gating retry/stop/aggregate during inference, where TRIAGE adds the prospective pre-commitment corner.
Truly Self-Improving Agents Require Intrinsic Metacognitive Learning: names the planning component TRIAGE operationalizes, scoring what the model does under resource constraints rather than what it verbally claims.
Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know: the monitoring-side anchor TRIAGE pairs against control, predicting per-question correctness without acting on it.
The Compliance Trap: How Structural Constraints Degrade Frontier AI Metacognition Under Adversarial Pressure: shares the capability-inversion result, where more-capable reasoning models do worse on a metacognitive task than their non-reasoning siblings.

title: Yann LeCun on What Comes After LLMs
text:
Thumbnail for Jacob Effron’s Unsupervised Learning episode with Yann LeCun. Watch on YouTube.
In the May 15, 2026 episode of Jacob Effron’s Unsupervised Learning podcast, Yann LeCun — Turing Award winner and former Chief AI Scientist at Meta — lays out the technical thesis behind his new company, AMI Labs, and his reasons for leaving Meta after twelve years of building FAIR. The 1h 21m conversation moves from his core claim that LLMs are not a path to human-level intelligence, through the JEPA [1] architecture he is scaling, his sovereign-AI project Tapestry, why he diverged from Geoffrey Hinton and Yoshua Bengio starting in 2023, and a remarkably candid account of his actual role at Meta — which, contrary to the public narrative, included zero technical contribution to Llama.
The main points, each linking to the supporting passage in the transcript:
I’ve built an enriched transcript at the bottom of this post — the YouTube auto-caption transcript, sliced into chapter and topic subsections, with inline hyperlinks, acronym expansions, and editor’s-note callouts. See the preamble of that section for details.
YouTube chapters (jump to the enriched transcript below, or watch on YouTube):

title: Yann LeCun on What Comes After LLMs
text:
Transcript
What’s here is the YouTube auto-caption transcript, reorganized into a reader-friendly form. The dialog itself is verbatim — no words added, cut, or reworded — but five layers of editorial structure have been added on top:

Chapter + topic outline. 13 YouTube chapters, each linking to its timestamp, sliced into ~30 fine-grained topic subsections. The subsection titles are editorial summaries of the topic being discussed, not verbatim speaker quotes. The full outline is in the right-hand sidebar.
Inline hyperlinks. First mention of every salient acronym, concept, paper, product, person, or company links to the most authoritative source.
Bracketed acronym expansions. Where an acronym appears for the first time without being expanded in speech, the expansion is inserted in [square brackets] (e.g. JEPA [joint embedding predictive architecture]) to mark the addition as editorial.
Editor’s notes in blue callout boxes flag claims that are verifiable and slightly off, heuristics the speaker himself qualifies as ballpark, or unsourced numbers.
Numbered references. Every paper or book cited has a [[N]](#ref-N) cite linking to the References block at the bottom.

YouTube auto-captions ship without punctuation, capitalization, or paragraph breaks — those are editorial. Obvious ASR mishearings of proper nouns and technical terms were corrected silently: JEPA (variously transcribed as “Jeter”, “Japa”, “JPA”), Llama (“Lama”), Yann LeCun (“Yan Lun”), Geoff Hinton (“Jeff”), Andrew Bosworth (“Dub Bosworth”/“Andrew Budworth”), Joelle Pineau (“Joel Pino”), Jürgen Schmidhuber (“Jurgen Schmidber”), Randall Balestriero (“Randall Bistriero”), VICReg (“VC rag”), LeWorldModel (“L world model”), NeurIPS (“Nurips”), MAE (“ME to encoder”), and GenAI (“geni”/“ji”).

0:00:00 — Intro

Cold-open teaser clips
Jacob Effron: You’re one of the godfathers of AI. What’s your kind of view of the path of progress here?
Yann LeCun: Five years, complete world domination.
Yann LeCun: [Different clip.] The best way to get breakthrough research is you hire the best people, you get the [bleep] out of the way. Pardon my French.
Jacob Effron: You share the Turing Award with two others. When did your views start diverging?
Yann LeCun: In 2023.
Jacob Effron: How do you know it was time to leave Meta? It sounds like you were thinking through some of these things over a period of time.
Yann LeCun: Here’s a big misconception about my role, my relation to Alex, and how AI was run at Meta.
Jacob Effron: What’s like one thing you’ve changed your mind on in the last year?
Yann LeCun: I mean, the whole idea of, uh —


Jacob’s framing intro
Jacob Effron: Yann LeCun is one of the godfathers of AI. He’s an absolute legend in the field. Someone I’ve admired for a long time, and so it was such a treat to get him on Unsupervised Learning.
He’s been a noted skeptic of LLMs in many ways, and so we dug into what LLMs can do, what they can’t do, some of the limitations he sees, and why he ultimately decided to pursue a different architecture.
We also talked about his time at Meta — you know, the things he’s proud of in setting up FAIR, how the last few years proceeded, and what ultimately led him to spin out and start his own company, AMI.
I think it’s just fascinating to get Yann’s thoughts on everything happening in the AI ecosystem today — this tension between basic research and then pushing LLMs forward, and how that’s happening in a bunch of organizations today, as well as his thoughts on just where the whole space is headed. He’s just an absolute giant in the field, and when I started this podcast I hoped we’d get guests like him. So it is just such a treat. I think folks will really enjoy hearing the conversation we had.
Without further Yann — this is such a pleasure. You’re one of the godfathers of AI. I feel like when I started doing this podcast years ago, I was really hoping we might one day get someone like you on.
Yann LeCun: You know, I don’t like that term, because I live in New Jersey. When you’re a godfather in New Jersey, it doesn’t mean the same thing.



0:01:45 — Why LLMs Aren’t the Path to Intelligence

The opening provocation: AMI as the technical thesis
Jacob Effron: Very fair. Very fair. You know, obviously, your bet on neural nets when everyone doubted them is legendary. And I feel like today you’re making a similar bet in many ways against LLMs and the kind of predominant generative architectures that so many believe in.
You’ve recently started a new company behind this theme. Our goal today in the conversation is to leave our listeners with a lot more information about AMI, what you’re doing there, some of your work at Tapestry. You know — why you think the rest of the field is pointed in the wrong direction around some of these generative models, and then also just get your reflections on the way the field’s unfolded, your time at Meta, and all that. So, you know, modest goals for a single podcast episode.
I figured it’d be great to start with the meat, because the company feels like the clearest statement of your technical thesis going forward. You recently launched the company. It’s focused on world models and scaling the JEPA architecture, which you obviously pioneered over at Meta. And so I’m wondering if you could talk a little bit about the origins of that architecture and the extent to which you drew inspiration from the human brain and the way that works.


“There’s nothing wrong with LLMs — they’re just not a path”
Yann LeCun: So first of all, I want to say there’s nothing wrong with LLMs in the sense of LLM. You know, LLMs are the basis for a lot of very useful AI products that all of us use, including me. They’re great, okay, for what they do. They’re just not a path towards human-level or human-like intelligence, or even animal-like intelligence. So that’s my claim, okay? I’m not saying they are useless. I’m just saying they’re not a path towards human-level intelligence.
Jacob Effron: I mean — you helped build some of the first major open-source ones, right?
Yann LeCun: Absolutely.


What AMI stands for: AI for the real world
Jacob Effron: So what is AMI?
Yann LeCun: AMI really stands for advanced machine intelligence, and the kind of subtitle, the motto if you want, is “AI for the real world.” So basically, a lot of AI techniques that people know about today are good for language manipulation — either human language, or computer code, or mathematics, or legalese, which barely qualifies as human language. Unfortunately a lot of human language used for it —
Jacob Effron: Right, sadly.
Yann LeCun: You know, language is very special in a way, and it’s particularly well suited for the type of architectures that have been so successful recently — large language models, GPT-style architectures. But what about the real world? What about understanding the physical world? Turns out reality is way more complicated than language, because it’s high-dimensional, it’s continuous, it’s noisy, it’s messy. And training a system to understand the real world is much, much harder.
So that’s really what we’re after. That’s what I’ve been after for most of my career, and really kind of working on in an accelerated fashion over the last five, six years or so, and making significant progress over the last two years. And so it made sense to really do a startup around it and sort of go into high gear in pushing that.
And it became clear by the end of last year that Meta was really not the right place for that. So that’s why I left and started AMI Labs.


Two modes of R&D: exploratory research vs. product engineering
Jacob Effron: I think it’s an interesting trend that we’re seeing across the board, where it feels like there’s many folks spinning out of either some of the large companies or research labs that have a particular direction of research they’re excited about. You’d have such an interesting vantage point of this from your time at FAIR.
This almost tension that exists between go pursue as many different research directions as possible in these companies versus, hey, something’s really working, this is the thing that we’re going to sell for the next 6 to 12 months, like go focus on that. I’m curious your thoughts on that and what you’ve kind of seen in the industry at large.
Yann LeCun: Well, it’s a strange trade-off. There’s really two modes of R&D. There’s a lot of exploratory research, a lot of research directions. And sometimes something kind of seems to work, and you need to push it further, and it’s not research anymore. I mean, the people working on it are researchers, or they’re called researchers at least in the press, but really it’s becoming more engineering and pushing for products.
So that happened a number of times at Meta because of things that started at FAIR. Such a thing happened in early 2023 essentially, when Llama — which was developed at FAIR, Llama 1 — was very promising, and Meta created a whole organization, GenAI, to turn it into something real and a series of products, and produced Llama 2, Llama 3, Llama 4, which was a bit of a disappointment.
And because Mark Zuckerberg was disappointed by it, he kind of rebooted the entire organization, reorganized it, and hired new people, etc.






Note



Editor’s note. “Llama 4 was a bit of a disappointment” reflects the widely-reported reception of the April 2025 Llama 4 release (Scout and Maverick models, with Behemoth pre-announced). Reviews flagged degraded reasoning relative to Llama 3.1 on real-world tasks despite leaderboard wins, and the Behemoth release slipped. Meta restructured its AI org in mid-2025 around the new “Meta Superintelligence Labs” (MSL) led by Alexandr Wang after the Scale AI investment.


But what also happened over the last year is that basically the company, Meta, realized that they had fallen behind a little bit, and so that kind of refocused the strategy on trying to catch up with the industry. And the sad side effect of it is that a lot of the exploratory research was basically not given high priority anymore.
I mean, it didn’t concern the stuff I was working on — all the JEPA and world models, because Mark himself, and Andrew Bosworth the CTO, and a bunch of other people in the company were really interested in that project and really believed in the long-term impact. But the rest of the company was just totally, entirely focused on LLMs, and made it clear to me that Meta was really not the right place to push for that project anymore.
And then we started to have good results, and so it was clear that we had to kind of make that transition between research and actually developing the technology, scaling it up and building products out of it.
And we realized also that most of the applications were probably for things that Meta was not particularly interested in. A lot of applications of the kind of stuff that we’ve been working on is in industry — like manufacturing industry and stuff like that.



0:07:51 — AMI and World Models

Comparing JEPA against generative world-model approaches
Jacob Effron: Obviously you’re pursuing world models in that broader world, and I think there’s other people that have come at the world-model space from a more generative approach. And so I think you’ve got the Google folks in Genie and the video models. You’ve got folks building VLAs on the robotic side. You’ve got Fei-Fei Li and World Labs and kind of like the 3D spatial models.
As you think about the body of evidence that got you excited about the JEPA models and how you compare them to what the generative folks have done — where do you think we are today in terms of comparing these architectures and approaches?
Yann LeCun: Okay, so “world model” is quickly becoming a buzzword, right now, certainly in research but also in industry to some extent. And then there are two factions if you want.


Why VLA “is now seen as a failure”
I’m not going to talk about VLA, because VLA is clearly now being seen as not going anywhere. Like, it’s really not working.
So VLA is, you know, vision-language-action models, right? To basically use the LLM technology to train a system to produce actions for controlling a robot or something like this. So you have vision in, language in, action out, maybe language out too.
And that’s pretty much now seen as a failure. Not being reliable enough, requiring too much training data, things like that.






Note



Editor’s note. Calling VLA “a failure” is stronger than the field consensus. As of 2026, VLA architectures (e.g. Physical Intelligence’s π0/π0.5, Google’s RT-2 and successors, NVIDIA GR00T N, Figure Helix) remain the dominant paradigm for general-purpose robot foundation models, and several have shown impressive zero-shot generalization. LeCun’s stronger objection is data efficiency and reliability, which he develops in the next chapter; the “failure” framing is his characterization, not a settled judgment.




Defining a world model: predicting consequences of actions
Okay. Then there is world models. So what is a world model? A world model at a very general level is something that allows an agentic system to anticipate the consequences of its own actions — predict the consequences of its own actions.
From my point of view, I cannot imagine how you can even think of building an agentic system without that system having the ability to predict the consequences of its actions. I mean, that’s pretty essential, right?
When we act in the world, we have this ability, and when we take an action without thinking about the consequences, we are taking a big risk. And very often, you know, other people think we’re an idiot.
We have plenty of examples on the international political scene at the moment of people who have complete, you know, ability to predict the consequences of their actions.
So that’s the world model. That’s all it is — ability to predict the consequences of your own actions. If you have this ability, then you can plan a sequence of actions to accomplish a task, to satisfy a goal. And you do this by planning, reasoning, by a process of search and optimization. You don’t do this by predicting one action after the other autoregressively. You do this by searching for a sequence of actions that will accomplish the task you set for yourself.
So the blueprint for this is completely different from what LLMs can do at the moment. LLMs do not have the ability to predict the consequences of their actions, and they do not have any planning abilities, because inference is by predicting the next token, right? It’s not by search.


Two characteristics of intelligent behavior, plus a third on the level of prediction
Okay, so right there you have the two characteristics that I think are essential for intelligent behavior. Ability to predict consequences of your actions, and second, ability to plan by optimization, by search — find a good sequence of actions that will produce the correct outcome. And then there is a third characteristic which is: how do you predict the consequences of your actions?
Okay, so if I have a water bottle in front of me — I realize some people would just listen to this and not have the picture. So I have an open, uncapped water bottle in front of me. If I push at the bottom, it’s going to slide on the table. If I push near the top, it’s probably going to flip.
We can’t predict exactly how the bottle will fall, in which direction. We can’t exactly predict how it’s going to slide, you know, how the water will spill, whether the table is tilted in one way and the water will kind of flow in one direction or another. There’s no way we can predict this at a pixel level. And so our mental model of the world predicts, but at an abstract —



0:12:07 — The JEPA Architecture Explained






Note



Editor’s note. For a from-scratch primer on JEPA — the three-component architecture, the latent-prediction objective, the three families of collapse-prevention fixes, and what V-JEPA / V-JEPA 2 demonstrate — see What Is JEPA? on this blog.



Cognitive science System 1 vs. System 2 as motivation
Jacob Effron: — level of representation. So as you were working on this architecture, was a lot of it inspired by the human brain? I mean, obviously the way you’re articulating things — exactly how we do things.
Yann LeCun: Right, or at least by, you know, cognitive science. Whether you can sort of translate this into a neural architecture and things like this — there’s a big gap there.
Okay, so certainly cognitive science was a bit of a motivation, or what psychologists call System 2, which is this idea that the way you behave in sort of deliberate, reflective behavior is that you do imagine, predict the consequences of your actions, and you plan accordingly — contrary to System 1 where you just act reactively and instinctively.
So yeah, there is an inspiration. But also there is a lot of empirical evidence that you don’t want to generate pixels.


Five-year-old epiphany: every successful representation method is non-generative
Okay, I’ve been really interested in that problem of learning models of the world by prediction for a very long time, and then had an epiphany about five years ago realizing that all of the architectures that have been successful to learn representations of images and videos are non-generative architectures, and all the generative ones basically have been failures.
Right? So VAEs [2] — variational autoencoders — or autoencoders more generally. It’s kind of a natural way to think about learning abstract representations of inputs. So you put an image at the input of a neural net and then you train it to just reproduce the input on its output.
Now, with a big neural net — if you just do it this way, your neural net will not do anything interesting. You just learn the identity function.
Jacob Effron: Yeah.
Yann LeCun: Completely uninteresting. It doesn’t work. Like if you train a VAE to learn representations of images, you get something, but it’s really not that great. Same with sparse autoencoders.


Denoising and masked autoencoders: another disappointment
Then you have another set of techniques, and it’s kind of a derivative of something called the denoising autoencoder. Masked autoencoder [3] is a version of this. BERT [4] is a version of this for NLP.
So you take the image, you corrupt it in some way, and then you train this big neural net to recover the original image. There’s a huge project at FAIR on this called MAE — masked autoencoder. It was very disappointing. A lot of computation, and not really great satisfying results.


JEPA: joint-embedding predictive architecture
Simultaneously, some of the same people working on MAE and some other people in Paris and in New York were working on other techniques using non-generative architecture — joint embedding architecture. So take an image, corrupt it in some way, and then run the two images through encoders, and then try to predict the representation of the original image from the representation of the corrupted one. That’s JEPA [1].
Jacob Effron: Yeah.
Yann LeCun: Okay. So JEPA means joint-embedding predictive architecture, right? So you have one encoder that observes — makes an observation — another encoder that makes a different observation. You try to predict the representation of the first one from the second one with a predictor.
And those techniques turned out to work much better for representing images and video. So things like DINO [5], DINO V1, V2, V3 [6] — projects that are still going on at FAIR in Paris. Projects like I-JEPA [1], and then V-JEPA [7], and then before that there were like SimCLR [8] and MoCo [9], and like a whole bunch of different techniques, mostly from Meta. There was a bunch of others from other groups.
But that turned out to be a much better way of learning representations of images than predicting pixels.
Jacob Effron: Yeah.
Yann LeCun: And so it just clicked in my mind, but, you know, not just mine, that this was the way to go and predicting pixels was kind of a losing proposition.



0:15:55 — Problems with Robotics Models Today

Imitation learning is brittle and data-hungry
Jacob Effron: You know, it feels like there’s all these robotics demos that are released from some of the model companies that feel increasingly impressive and maybe seem to resemble things like planning and reasoning when, you know, they maybe haven’t seen a room or a specific version of a task before, and are still able to execute that task.
What would you say to our listeners that observe that stuff and feel like, ah, it feels like we’re trending toward some real progress with some of the generative approaches?
Yann LeCun: Well, there is real progress, and some of those demos are really impressive. But they are trained with enormous amounts of data, collected either from teleoperation or from just human action with things you hold in your hand that look like —
Jacob Effron: Grippers.
Yann LeCun: Grippers, that you collect the data for. Or just tracking hands and fingers of a person, and then translating this into commands for a robot. And so those things are trained with imitation learning mostly, and a little bit with reinforcement learning to fine-tune, mostly in simulation.
So the issue with this is that you need a lot of data to train those systems with imitation, and it becomes expensive. And it’s a little brittle, in the sense that you need to collect lots of data for every task you want the robot to solve.
Whereas if the system had a world model that allowed it to predict the outcome of an action, it would just plan an action to solve a new task without actually having to be trained to accomplish this task. So the degree of generalization you would get with a world-model-based system is much, much larger — you know, kind of wider spectrum of tasks with less training data than would be required by a system trained with imitation learning and fine-tuning.


Zero-shot generalization, and the 17-year-old driver
Jacob Effron: No doubt those approaches require more data, and I guess this question of generalization really is the big question, right? Some folks have shown some results around getting better at task A helps with task B, but that obviously feels like still the big unanswered question around those architectures.
Yann LeCun: I mean, you get this synergy between tasks. So the more tasks that you train the system to solve, the more tasks it’s going to be able to acquire with a small amount of data, regardless of what technique you use.
But the hope with world models is that the system can solve much zero-shot, which humans are completely capable of doing, right? And many animals as well. So that’s really the hope — solving a lot more problems with either a small amount of training data, or no training data at all, and just a little bit of maybe RL-style fine-tuning.
Yeah. Like, how is it that a 17-year-old can learn to drive in like a dozen hours, or maybe 20 hours? We have millions of hours of training data of people driving cars. We still don’t have level-five autonomous cars, right? So imitation learning obviously doesn’t work, even for just the task of autonomous driving.


Why scaling synthetic video data isn’t the answer
Jacob Effron: Yeah, I guess it’ll be a race between the ability to develop some of those capabilities — which may take time and lots of data — versus this kind of architecture.
I feel like there’s this dream of using video models to just generate tons of synthetic data for simulation. And, you know, even if it’s not perfect, these video models from a physics perspective are like helpful enough to improve robotics and the underlying physical world.
What have you made of some of those approaches? Obviously I think a lot of the Veo work has been focused there. Google seems to be going down that road.
Yann LeCun: I’m sort of asking again the question — why can a 17-year-old learn to drive in 20 hours? You don’t need millions of hours of demonstration, and you don’t need synthetic data. You don’t need any of that. So I want a system that can learn as fast as that. If we crack that, then we don’t need generated data. I mean, we might need to train a system in simulation, but not with the same amount of time or trials as current systems require. It’s really a question of data efficiency.
Jacob Effron: You know, I interviewed Jerry Tworek on the podcast, as he was at OpenAI and spun out to start his own lab, and you could sense a similar tension where I think he actually might even agree that, you know, if you continued scaling RL the way we’re scaling, you get more — you continue getting very impressive results — but I think he felt, god, there’s just got to be some way more efficient way to do this.
And it’s an interesting tension, because you could imagine if you’re OpenAI and you know something is going to continue — like, you could continue scaling it and it will keep getting better — there’s not a ton of incentive necessarily from a business perspective —



0:20:37 — Silicon Valley Herd Behavior

“Everybody is digging the same trench”
Yann LeCun: Right. There’s no incentive for the other companies to do anything different either, because they’re all chasing the same thing — they can’t afford to fall behind the others, right? So they all work on the same thing.
Jacob Effron: Yeah.
Yann LeCun: And there’s a bit of this sort of, you know, kind of herd behavior, mostly in Silicon Valley, where everybody is digging the same trench.
Jacob Effron: Yeah.
Yann LeCun: So I purposely set up the headquarters of AMI Labs in Paris.
Jacob Effron: Yeah.
Yann LeCun: The American office being in New York, not Silicon Valley.
Jacob Effron: It’s really interesting because I think it points to a tension that exists in the broader ecosystem today, where you could imagine the other side being: sure, maybe there are more data-efficient methods out there, but like almost who cares, because we can keep scaling what we have to better and better results.
And then obviously I think from both new things you can accomplish from these models, as well as just the joy of being a researcher and finding these new things, I get why there’s such an attraction to these other architectures as well.
Yann LeCun: And it’s a bet, but you know, we’re pretty confident, because we have results already.


Where AMI is pointed: domestic robots, industry, healthcare
Jacob Effron: As you think about the kind of initial spaces you’re most excited about for the AMI technology — where do you think the technology goes, and what are you most excited about?
Yann LeCun: Well, I mean, AI for the real world. Where is your domestic robot? Where is your level-five self-driving car?
Jacob Effron: Yeah. When am I going to get a domestic robot? I’m excited about this.
Yann LeCun: Well, so this is several years down the line, okay. Despite the fact that there is like a huge number of companies building robots, none of those companies actually has any idea how to make them smart enough to be useful, right?
Jacob Effron: Or trust it around with a baby in the house or something.
Yann LeCun: Certainly not that. But even for relatively narrow manufacturing tasks, right? None of them really knows how to do this reliably, other than for, by imitation learning, for a small number of tasks. So how do we make those things useful? That’s a relatively long-term objective.
Shorter term, there is a huge amount of applications in industry, where you need to have an intelligent system that has the ability of predicting what’s going to happen if I change this control variable on this complex system, be it a jet engine, a chemical plant, a power plant, some manufacturing line, a patient, a human cell.
Those are systems that are sufficiently complex that you can’t model their behavior with a small number of equations. The traditional way of modeling does not work. And what you need to do is train a neural net deep learning system to model the dynamics of that system from data.
And what you get at the end is a phenomenological model of that process, of that system. And if it’s action-conditioned, then you get basically a world model of that system that allows you to control it optimally for whatever purpose you have. And I think the number of applications of this in industry is mind-boggling.






Note



Editor’s note. “Phenomenological” here is in the deep-learning sense — a data-driven neural surrogate for a system whose dynamics you can’t write down in closed form — not the stricter physics sense of “merely correlational.” The action-conditioning is what makes the surrogate predictive of consequences, which is what fits LeCun’s earlier definition of a world model. The unstated caveat: action-conditioning trained on observational data doesn’t automatically yield causal validity under novel interventions — if the historical operating data didn’t span the action space, the surrogate will mispredict on policies it hasn’t seen, the classic confounding-by-policy problem in off-policy reinforcement learning. Industrial deployments typically close that gap with exploration data, simulation, or careful experimental design layered on top of the surrogate.




“Five years, complete world domination”
Jacob Effron: Where do you think we’ll be with JEPA models over the next couple years? Are there milestones you’d point to, or what’s your view of the path of progress here?
Yann LeCun: Okay, a couple of years is a little short. Like, five years, complete world domination essentially.
Jacob Effron: Okay, so somewhere on the path to world domination in five years.

Jacob Effron: Yeah.
Yann LeCun: Two of the authors of Llama basically created Mistral with another —



1:00:26 — Reflections on FAIR

Mistral genesis, GenAI conservatism, Llama 4 reboot
Yann LeCun: Guy from Google. And, you know, a few people kind of left and did other things. This was not a kind of a happy time at Meta for various reasons.






Note



Editor’s note. The two Llama authors who co-founded Mistral are Guillaume Lample and Timothée Lacroix, both ex-FAIR and listed on the original Llama paper. The “guy from Google” is Arthur Mensch, who came from Google DeepMind and is Mistral’s CEO. Mistral incorporated in Paris in April 2023.


And so there were a bunch of people kind of left, and then the GenAI organization, which kind of took over Llama 2 to some extent and Llama 3 and 4, was under so much short-term pressure that they became very conservative. And it’s a combination of disparity of the groups, but pressure from the leadership.
And I mean, there’s many ways things can go wrong, and you can’t blame anyone in particular, killer. But yeah, that’s kind of what happened.


Are research labs like the old FAIR still possible inside the industry?
Jacob Effron: I mean, it feels like a lot of these organizations obviously are under short-term pressure right now because there’s just an incredible race going on. And so I’m curious like, obviously this FAIR setup you had — and there’s a similar one at Google for many years, and certainly many researchers running around OpenAI, Anthropic trying many different things — do you think that is still possible going forward, or like, is one of the only paths to leave and do your own company?
Or are there still places within the industry that you think have this original ethos of FAIR even amidst the race dynamics that are happening?
Yann LeCun: I think there are a few places within Google Research and DeepMind where people actually do research. But increasingly the industry has become more closed. I mean, Google certainly clammed up, and Meta and FAIR is kind of going a bit in the same direction.
There are restrictions on publication now — more restrictions — and so it’s less appealing for people who really want to do breakthrough research. They don’t get as much resources, and if they do something that is relevant in medium term, they’re told not to talk about it. And so it’s not a good atmosphere for breakthrough.
It’s not conducive. The best way to get breakthrough research of the type that we were getting in the early days of FAIR, and at Bell Labs in the good days, in Xerox PARC, is you hire the best people — and those are people who have a good nose to know what to work on, what projects to attack — you give them the means to succeed, and you get the [bleep] out of the way. Pardon my French.


Yann’s actual role at Meta: director of FAIR (2014–2018), then chief AI scientist
Jacob Effron: Yeah. I’m curious what impact it then ends up having on the broader research communities. Obviously one of the legacies of FAIR is you trained so many researchers, and they’re all throughout the ecosystem.
And it feels like now the maybe equivalent of those people that came in younger in their careers at FAIR, you know, they’re joining these labs with maybe shorter-term priorities and focus. And I guess I’m wondering, in this current ecosystem where it feels like a lot of younger people getting into the field are thrust much more into these short-term dynamics, does that change anything about the way the ecosystem evolves?
Yann LeCun: Well, I mean, the people who tend to want to work with me are generally people who are sufficiently crazy to do it first.
Jacob Effron: Very fair.
Yann LeCun: And, or kind of subscribe to the whole idea that in academia and during your PhD, you should work on the next generation of AI systems. You shouldn’t work on the current generation.
Yeah. Like, if you work on LLMs in academia now, it’s incredibly boring. At least to me, it’s boring. It’s basically studying how and why LLMs work and explaining why they work, or what the limitations are.
It’s like descriptive science. It’s really not creative. Very creative. Like, I don’t find that particularly interesting. It’s useful.
Jacob Effron: Yeah.
Yann LeCun: And, you know, if you really want to show how to do new things with LLMs, you’re not going to have the GPUs you need for that.
Jacob Effron: Totally.
Yann LeCun: So like, forget that. Like, don’t work on LLMs if you’re doing a PhD, like, there’s no point. You cannot contribute.


Stepping down as FAIR director in 2018; designing the AMI architecture
Jacob Effron: How do you know it was time to leave Meta? It sounds like you were thinking through some of these things over a period of time. Was there a moment that it crystallized?
Yann LeCun: Well, it was a combination of things. So first of all, you have to understand — a lot of people have completely wrong idea about what my role at Facebook was. So I joined in late 2013, really kind of started early 2014.
The first four and a half years, I was director of FAIR. So I built the FAIR organization, set up the culture, hired the key people, sort of managed it. And after four and a half years I stepped down from that role for a number of reasons, and I became chief AI scientist.
The reason is, I was getting close to turning 60 — first of all, 58 — and I just don’t want to do management. I mean, I was ready to do it for a while to get the organization started, but I’m just not good at it. It’s not the thing — I’m more like a scientific or technical visionary and engineer and scientist.
So other people are much better at management than I am. So I basically stepped down. Two other people, Joelle Pineau and Antoine Bordes, took over the directorship of FAIR, and I became chief AI scientist.
So I was reporting to the CTO, and had goals of basically restarting a research project that I thought was necessary, because the ambition of FAIR was always to build intelligent systems.
Jacob Effron: Yeah.
Yann LeCun: Right. And I thought — I put my own research in parenthesis while I was running FAIR. I just didn’t have the time. And I thought it was important to design the architecture of human-level, human-like AI systems.
And I had come up with the concept that this was going to be based on self-supervised learning, and on prediction from sensory signals like video, things like that. I mean, these are old ideas, and world models.
I actually gave a keynote at NeurIPS in 2016 where I said this is the way AI research should go — like world models, predict consequences of your actions and plan. And I said RL is not the thing that will take us there because it’s too inefficient. Supervised learning has shown its limits. And so the future is self-supervised learning and world models.
So how do we do self-supervised learning and world models? I started a few projects on this with a few avenues that didn’t pan out, some projects on video prediction and stuff like that.
And then came up with this concept that you could train self-supervised learning from video, but you have to train the system to make predictions in representation space. So that’s the idea of JEPA.
And if you have JEPA, you can turn it into a world model by making it action-conditioned, and then you can use it for planning.






Note



Editor’s note. “Action-conditioned” is doing a lot of work in one phrase. The mechanism: in a vanilla JEPA, an encoder maps inputs (frames, image patches) to latent representations \(z_t\), and a predictor learns to map \(z_t \to z_{t+1}\) — pure observation dynamics with no notion of agency. To turn this into a world model, the predictor is given an additional input: the action \(a_t\) the agent takes at time \(t\). It now learns \((z_t, a_t) \to z_{t+1}\) — a forward dynamics model in latent space. The encoder is still trained self-supervised (no action labels needed for representation learning); the action input enters only at the predictor. Once trained, planning means searching over candidate action sequences \(a_t, a_{t+1}, \ldots\) and rolling out the predictor to score which sequence reaches a goal state. LeWorldModel [19] is exactly this design — encoder + action-conditioned predictor + SIGReg [17] on the encoder outputs to keep representations from collapsing.




The 2022 vision paper and the AMI initiative inside FAIR
So I had this idea around 2020. And in 2022 I wrote a long vision paper [11]. I said, I’m just going to write a paper with my entire vision. Spill all my secrets, like I don’t care. But maybe they will rally a bunch of people to that vision.
And boy, did it work. Because not only did I rally a bunch of students who came working with me at NYU or in Paris because they wanted to work on this, but also a whole team at FAIR who said, “this sounds great, that’s what we want to work on.”
And then Joelle Pineau said, “well, maybe this should be a major mission of FAIR.” And we called it advanced machine intelligence. That was the internal name of —
Jacob Effron: Interesting.
Yann LeCun: The park.
Jacob Effron: And they let you leave with it.
Yann LeCun: And now it’s the name of the company. And, you know, Mark Zuckerberg kind of read that paper and knew what it was about and subscribed to the project.
And Andrew Bosworth, the CTO, also. And Mike Schroepfer, the previous CTO. Chris Cox, who was my direct manager, chief product officer, also loved the idea. So there was a lot of support in the leadership about this project that we internally called AMI.


Why it didn’t work out: applications were industrial, Meta wasn’t interested
And it started really kind of working for video. But the company kind of refocused all of its effort on LLMs. Despite support from Mark and Andrew Bosworth — Boz, we call him Boz — the layers below didn’t see the point, I think. And so politically it sort of became a little difficult.
The applications of JEPA world models — there are applications in wearable agents and stuff like that, and robotics, but Meta chose to get rid of its entire robotics AI group, that was led by Jitendra Malik, who is now at Amazon. And so clearly it wasn’t the right environment anymore.
Most of the applications were in industry that Meta had no interest in. FAIR was increasingly getting pressure to basically help Meta Superintelligence Labs with LLMs.






Note



Editor’s note. The “Gita Matalatic” in the auto-caption is Jitendra Malik — the Berkeley computer-vision pioneer who served as research director and site lead of Facebook AI Research Menlo Park from 2018, leading the team’s vision, ML, and robotics work, and has since moved to Amazon.


So it made it clear. And, you know, that throughout, my reasoning worked really well with investors too — because when I had to raise money for AMI, everybody knew my story, and many investors and staff at various VCs that read my paper or had listened to my talks had bought my story. They were realizing LLMs had limitations, and were kind of interested by the idea of building the next-generation AI systems.


Did the Scale AI acquisition catalyze the LLM focus?
Jacob Effron: I guess, was the Scale acquisition like part of this catalyst of the pure LLM focus internally?
Yann LeCun: Yeah, definitely. I mean, there’s probably some other reasons to it. I don’t have any inside information to comment on this, but it’s possible that Mark sees in Alex kind of a potential successor to himself, like a younger version of himself.


The biggest misconception: zero technical contribution to Llama
Jacob Effron: Yeah, I feel like a lot of the popular narrative in the media has been like, oh, like, you know, when Alex comes in, it then gets harder to run a research organization. I don’t know if to the extent you felt that, or —
Yann LeCun: Well, okay. So here’s a big misconception about my role, my relation to Alex, and how AI was run at Meta. I had zero technical contribution to Llama. Like, none whatsoever.
My one contribution to Llama was to argue for open-sourcing Llama 2, because there was a big internal debate whether we should open-source. The legal department was against it, the policy department was kind of against it, the comms department was for it, all the engineering side was for it — like Boz was for it.
So there was enormous internal discussions at a very high level — 40 people from Mark Zuckerberg down, every week for two hours, for months. So really it was a big debate internally.
And I really, really, really argued for the fact that — and Boz also was very vocal about it — that the safety risks were basically overblown. The opportunities to create an industry were extremely strong. And that we were going to jumpstart the AI industry by open-sourcing Llama 2. And in fact that’s exactly what happened.
So I had zero contribution to Llama, positive or negative. Like, I didn’t do anything to stop it or slow it down or anything. There was a lot of people working on LLMs within FAIR and it was fine. I never said anything against it — other than saying, this is not a path to human intelligence, but it’s fine. It’s useful. Same thing for speech recognition, translation, right?
And particularly since 2018, when I stepped down from being director of FAIR, I didn’t have any direct influence on what people were working on, other than basically publishing my vision and then rallying people around my project. But they were working with me because they wanted to, not because I was their boss. I wasn’t telling them to work with me.
So I had no positive or negative influence on LLMs within Meta. And I had some influence on the strategy, but it was more like the long term and how you maintain a research lab and things like this.
And in the last year — starting maybe early 2024, and certainly in 2025 — the direction in which FAIR was being moved and managed basically did not correspond to what I thought was necessary to preserve innovation, research and breakthrough, and preserve the good people. Like, a lot of good people have left already.
Jacob Effron: Yeah. And I guess a lot of, you know, you probably was harder to get people to work on the stuff you were working on internally. And I’m sure there was pressure for you yourself to work on a lot of the LLM stuff.
Yann LeCun: Yeah, no, but a lot of other people also have left, right?
Jacob Effron: No, it’s fascinating.



1:12:11 — Advice for PhD Students

What changed: self-supervised learning succeeded — for language, not video
Jacob Effron: I mean, one thing I’m struck by throughout our whole conversation is, I feel like you’ve had a remarkably consistent point of view in the space for a long time. And you can go back to a bunch of the earlier talks you referenced. Obviously it is a fast-moving space, and a ton of interesting things have happened in the last year. What’s like one thing you’ve changed your mind on in the last year?
Yann LeCun: I mean, the whole idea of what we used to call unsupervised learning that we now call self-supervised learning. Until about 2003, the whole idea of unsupervised pre-training, where you get a good representation for the input data and then you either fine-tune the model with a little bit of supervised label data — and it sort of gives us some evidence that this whole technique could work.
I tried to apply this to video, because ultimately what I wanted to do is train a system to understand how the world works by just watching the world go by. Yeah. Right? I mean, that’s the basic idea.
I sort of started to argue for this in the early 2010s. Did some work on simple video prediction. We didn’t have GPUs.
And then sort of doing this more seriously after the creation of FAIR, by doing pixel-level video prediction, realizing that wasn’t working, but then arguing for self-supervised learning.
Okay, this whole idea of training a system generically not to solve a task, but to basically just predict, and then using the representation that is learned this way as input to a downstream task that you can train supervised or reinforcement or whatever.
So that was a bit of the topic of my second half of my keynote at NeurIPS in 2016. It was still called NIPS at the time.
Jacob Effron: Yeah, of course.
Yann LeCun: In 2016. And then I kept pushing for this idea, and tried to discover some methods to get that to work. And what surprised me is that that became incredibly successful — but not for video. For language. LLMs basically are a blindingly successful example of self-supervised learning.
Jacob Effron: No, that they are.


The closing technical lecture: why representation collapse is the JEPA problem
Well, I feel that’s almost like the perfect note to end on, but I want to make sure to leave the last word to you. I feel like all our listeners are very familiar with you, but I want to at least give you the mic to point them to anything that you think they should check out with some of the new stuff you’re doing, or any of your work you want to point to. The mic is yours.
Yann LeCun: Okay. Let me tell you one thing. An LLM works because when you have a sequence of discrete symbols, making predictions is easy — because there’s only a finite number of possible symbols in your language, 100,000 possible tokens or something like that, right?
And you can have your neural net produce a probability distribution over all possible tokens. And then you can sample from that distribution, shift the token into the input, and then produce the next token, and you can do autoregressive prediction. Okay, so that’s a special case.
If you have the real world, you can’t use a generative model. So now you have to train a system that learns a representation and makes predictions in the representation space.
There’s a big issue with this — which I didn’t think until about five years ago was easily solvable, even though I invented one technique to solve it decades before that. And it’s the problem that, if you take two inputs — let’s say the initial segment of a video and the continuation of that video, or you take one image and a corrupted version of it — you run them both through an encoder, and you train a predictor to predict the representation of one from the representation of the other, there’s a very simple solution where the system basically predicts a constant representation.
In other words, the prediction problem becomes trivial. That’s called a collapse — representation collapse.






Note



Editor’s note. A useful intuition for why this is JEPA’s defining problem: the JEPA training signal measures agreement between two encoded representations, not their content. Concretely, take two related inputs (e.g., a video frame \(x_t\) and a future frame \(x_{t+k}\)). Pass each through the encoder: \(z_t = E(x_t)\), \(z_{t+k} = E(x_{t+k})\). Train a predictor \(P\) to map \(z_t \to \hat{z}_{t+k}\). The loss is \(\| P(z_t) - z_{t+k} \|^2\).
Now suppose the encoder degenerates so that \(E(x) = c\) — the same constant vector — for every input. Then \(z_t = c\) and \(z_{t+k} = c\) for any pair of frames. The predictor is only ever queried at one input, \(c\), so its output is some fixed vector \(p = P(c)\) — whatever it happens to be. Gradient descent then jointly drives \(c\) and \(p\) to coincide, and the loss \(\|p - c\|^2\) reaches zero. Perfect minimization, zero learning. The two representations agree because the entire encoder-predictor pair has collapsed to a trivial fixed point, not because the model has discovered anything about the inputs.
Generative models (autoregressive LLMs, VAEs, diffusion) don’t have this failure mode because they have to reconstruct the input from the representation, which anchors it — a constant encoder would make every input’s reconstruction the same, blowing up the loss. JEPA has no reconstruction term; only the consistency signal, which the trivial solution kills perfectly.
Concretely, a collapsed encoder is downstream-useless — every input maps to \(c\), so the model can’t distinguish anything. The three fix families LeCun describes next each kill the trivial fixed point in a different way: contrastive methods force pairs of different inputs apart with explicit negative samples; distillation/EMA methods (BYOL [15], DINO [5]) break the symmetric gradient path that would otherwise drive both encoders to a constant; and information-content regularizers (VICReg [18], SIGReg [17]) directly penalize low-entropy representations.


So the big question of self-supervised learning for JEPA, for the joint-embedding architecture, is: how do you prevent collapse?


Three families of fixes: contrastive, distillation, and regularizer methods
Jacob Effron: Yeah.
Yann LeCun: The solution that I came up with many years ago — 1993 — is contrastive learning [12]. So basically you have examples of things that should be predictable from one another, and an example of things that should not be predictable from one another. It turns out this method works, but it doesn’t scale with dimension. It doesn’t scale very well.
There’s another technique that was actually invented by Geoff Hinton and Suzanna Becker in the late 80s — late 80s, I’m sorry — where you have those two networks and you try to maximize the mutual information between them [13].
Jürgen is mad at me, because he also came up with a version of this in 1992 [14], and he says that’s JEPA. It’s not JEPA. It’s just another way of preventing collapse of a joint-embedding architecture. Which is fine, but it’s not, you know, it’s a particular way of doing it, which I don’t think is particularly good.
Okay. So now you have this JEPA architecture. You have to come up with a good way of preventing collapse, and there is a couple ways. So as I already said, contrastive methods I think is not a good approach. There’s another set of methods that are kind of called distillation methods, and they do prevent collapse — we don’t know why. So a good example of that is DINO.
Jacob Effron: Yeah.
Yann LeCun: That’s a joint-embedding method using the distillation method. Basically, one of the encoders trains the other one, is used as a teacher for the other encoder. The encoder that is being trained, you do backprop to. The one that is not being trained, you don’t do backprop, but you share the weights with the other one with some exponential moving average.
It’s a collection of recipes. There’s a paper from DeepMind about it called Bootstrap Your Own Latent (BYOL) [15], which uses this trick. That trick is derived from some intuition from reinforcement learning, and somehow it prevents collapse, but we don’t know why. There are a few theoretical papers on it that explain why it possibly might work in some simple cases, but it’s not satisfactory.






Note



Editor’s note. The two most-cited theoretical analyses of why BYOL avoids collapse without negative samples are Tian, Chen, and Ganguli 2021 [20] — which analyzes the eigenstructure of the predictor + stop-gradient combination under linear-network and isotropic-data assumptions — and Wen and Li 2022 [21], which characterizes the role of the prediction head specifically. Both confirm collapse is avoided in simplified settings, but neither closes the gap that LeCun flags here: the loss the optimizer actually descends isn’t the loss you can monitor in training, so practitioners can’t tell from the loss curve whether collapse is happening.


The cost function you think you’re minimizing — you’re not actually minimizing. And so you can’t monitor it. It actually goes up when you train. So we don’t like this method, but it works.
And some of the models we’ve trained, large-scale video representation learning systems — V-JEPA, V-JEPA 2 [16], V-JEPA 2.1 — they train using this method. JEPA also. But we’re moving away from this.


The third family: information-content regularizers (VICReg, SIGReg) and LeWorldModel
And now we have a few papers that came out recently on an explicit regularizer to prevent this collapse, which basically tries to maximize the information content coming out of the encoder. So it’s in the same family as the Becker and Hinton from ’89 and the Schmidhuber 1992, and a bunch of others since then, and to some extent also contrastive techniques — although it’s not sample-contrastive.
And then the question is, how do you measure information content? How do you maximize the information content coming out of a neural net?
The problem is, if you want to maximize the quantity, you either need to be able to measure it, or you need to have a lower bound on it.






Note



Editor’s note. The intuition behind the regularizer family: collapse is the limit case where the encoder outputs carry zero information about the input — every input maps to the same \(c\), so the entropy of the representation distribution is zero. If you can force the encoder’s output distribution to have high entropy — i.e., spread across the latent space rather than concentrated on a single point — collapse is mechanically excluded. No need for negative samples (contrastive) or asymmetric architectural tricks (BYOL/DINO); the regularizer term in the loss does the work directly.
The technical obstacle LeCun flags is that differential entropy of a continuous distribution isn’t easy to estimate from samples — you can only construct upper bounds (estimators that overstate true entropy). Maximizing an upper bound isn’t a guarantee, so practitioners maximize a tractable proxy and hope the bound is tight enough.
The two methods named here implement that proxy differently:

VICReg [18] is three terms — Variance (each feature dimension must have at least unit variance, so no dimension can collapse), Invariance (paired views agree on their representations, the original JEPA consistency signal), and Covariance (off-diagonal terms of the feature covariance matrix are pushed to zero, decorrelating features so they don’t all encode the same information). Spread + decorrelate.
SIGReg [17] is one term: project the encoder output onto many random 1-D directions and run a normality (Epps–Pulley) test on each projection. Aggregating the test statistics pushes the joint distribution toward an isotropic Gaussian. Why an isotropic Gaussian? Under fixed variance, the Gaussian distribution has maximum differential entropy — so matching that target is equivalent to maximizing information content under a unit-variance constraint. The LeJEPA paper [17] proves the isotropic Gaussian is the optimal target distribution for JEPAs.



Jacob Effron: Yeah.
Yann LeCun: Information content, we only have upper bounds. We cannot measure it. We can only come up with upper bounds. And so we take an upper bound and we cross our fingers. Okay. And it kind of works.
So the latest one is called SIGReg [17] — that means Sketched Isotropic Gaussian Regularization. We had a previous one called VICReg [18] — variance-invariance-covariance regularization. And the SIGReg stuff is really cool.
This is some work by Randall Balestriero, who was a postdoc with me, is an assistant professor at Brown University now. And it basically consists in forcing the distribution of variables coming out of the encoder to be jointly Gaussian, essentially — sort of maximize information, if you want, just a very different way of doing it than what Jürgen Schmidhuber and Suzanna Becker and Geoff Hinton were doing.
So this is super promising, in my opinion. And we have variations of it — one that can produce sparse representations, another one that can produce isotropic representations but not necessarily Gaussians.
And we have a paper with Randall — student at Mila — where we train a world model with this. It’s still small scale, but I think it’s super promising.
So if you want to read one paper, read that paper. It’s LeWorldModel [19].






Note



Editor’s note. When LeCun says “a paper with Randall — student at Mila,” he conflates two people. Randall Balestriero is the assistant prof at Brown; the student at Mila is Lucas Maes, lead author of LeWorldModel [19].


Jacob Effron: Awesome. We’ll definitely link to it too.
Yann LeCun: Yeah, I’m not responsible for the name. Randall picked it up.
Jacob Effron: Amazing. Well, Yann, seriously, thank you so much. It is such a privilege to get to spend the last bit of time with you, and really appreciate you coming on the podcast.
Yann LeCun: Thanks for having me. That was fun.


Outro: Jacob’s signoff
Jacob Effron: I’m Jacob Effron, and this has been Unsupervised Learning, a podcast where I get to talk to the smartest people in AI and ask them tons of questions about what’s happening with models and what it means for businesses in the world. As I hope is clear, I have a ton of fun doing this. It’s a nights-and-weekends project in addition to my day job as an investor at Redpoint.
But our ability to get these incredible guests on really comes from folks like you subscribing to the podcast, sharing it with friends. It’s really what ultimately makes this whole thing work. And so please consider doing that. And thank you so much for your support and listening. We’ll see —

title: Improving Metacognition and Uncertainty Communication in Language Models
text:
Figure 3 from the paper [1].
In Improving Metacognition and Uncertainty Communication in Language Models [1] (arXiv preprint, September 2025), Mark Steyvers, Catarina Belem, and Padhraic Smyth (UC Irvine) show that supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on consistency-derived confidence targets raises both calibration and discrimination of verbalized LLM confidence (within domain, across new domains, and across two different metacognitive task formats), but only when the training data covers both formats jointly.

title: Improving Metacognition and Uncertainty Communication in Language Models
text:
Methods
The authors define two metacognitive tasks that probe the same underlying ability — verbalizing internal uncertainty — through different output formats:

Single-question confidence (S) — the model emits an answer plus a numeric confidence (e.g. “my confidence is 0.75”). Scored with two metrics: Expected Calibration Error (ECE), the bin-weighted average gap between predicted confidence and empirical accuracy (11 bins of width 0.1), and Area Under the Curve (AUC), the probability that the model assigns higher confidence to a correct answer than to an incorrect one.
Pairwise confidence comparison (C) — given two questions, the model picks which one it is more likely to answer correctly. Scored with two AUC variants: AUC\(_c\) (does the selection match the question with the higher consistency-derived reference confidence?) and AUC\(_a\) (does the selection match which question the model actually answers correctly?).

Both formats are illustrated side-by-side in Figure 1.



Figure 1 from the paper [1].


Training labels are derived from the model’s own behavior, not human annotations. For each training question the authors sample the model multiple times, compute a consistency score across samples and the modal answer, then build two parallel training sets:

Single-question targets — each training question gets two targets: an answer target and a confidence target. The answer target is the modal answer — the answer that appears most often across the multiple samples drawn from the model. The confidence target comes from a calibration mapping that does use ground-truth correctness:

Across the labeled training-set questions, the authors compute consistency scores, bin questions by score, and record the empirical accuracy (fraction actually correct, using ground truth) in each bin — yielding a curve \(a(s)\) that maps consistency \(s \to\) accuracy.
For each training question with consistency \(s\), the confidence target is \(a(s) + \varepsilon\) (small noise added to prevent the model from memorizing the discrete bin boundaries) — i.e., “questions whose samples agree this much come out right this often, on average.”

Pairwise targets — each training example is a pair of questions and gets a single selection target: which of the two the model should claim higher confidence on. The supervision label is whichever question has the higher consistency score (the ranking is what matters here, so the raw consistency score is enough — no calibration-curve lookup needed).

The full pipeline — sample, score, look up calibrated target, build training set — is laid out in Figure 2.



Figure 2 from the paper [1].


They fine-tune two base models (GPT-4.1-mini via OpenAI’s SFT API and Llama-3.1-70B locally) under three training conditions — S (single-question targets only), C (pairwise targets only), or C+S (both jointly, the multitask condition) — on three within-domain corpora: MMLU-PRO (M), GSM8K (G), and TriviaQA (T), plus the M+G+T mixture. Held-out evaluation uses both within-domain test splits and three out-of-domain corpora: TruthfulQA, MetaMedQA, and LegalBench. Significance is assessed with a paired bootstrap over 1,000 resamples.

title: Improving Metacognition and Uncertainty Communication in Language Models
text:
Results
Evaluation covers six datasets across two base models, two task formats (single-question S, pairwise C), three training conditions (S, C, C+S as defined above), and three generalization tiers (within-domain, across-domain, across-task). ECE measures calibration error (lower is better); AUC measures discrimination (higher is better). One thing to keep in mind for interpreting the deltas: the SFT loss never sees ground-truth answer labels directly — training tuples pair each question with the model’s own modal answer and a confidence scalar. Ground truth enters the pipeline only offline to fit the consistency-to-accuracy curve that produces those scalars. The recipe is therefore not aimed at improving factual accuracy, and Appendix Table A3 reports that accuracy is in fact similar before vs. after fine-tuning across all conditions. Pre/post deltas in ECE and AUC can therefore be read primarily as changes in confidence behavior, not in answer quality.
The cover figure (Figure 3) shows the within-domain calibration curves at a glance: baselines (cyan) sit below the diagonal, with confidence values clustered in [0.85, 0.95] but actual accuracy much lower at those points — overconfidence; the fine-tuned curves (pink) hug the diagonal across the full [0, 1] range. Table 1 quantifies the effect across all three generalization tiers.



Table 1 from the paper [1].


The findings:

Within-domain SFT works on the trained format (Table 1 rows 1–6, Table 2 rows 1–6). On the format the model is trained on, ECE collapses and AUC lifts substantially across all three corpora. Multi-domain training (M+G+T) does not interfere with per-domain gains.
Cross-domain transfer holds for the trained format (rows 7–9). Single-task SFT trained on M+G+T improves both metrics on TruthfulQA, MetaMedQA, and LegalBench — except on TruthfulQA, where ECE actually rises because the baseline was already well-calibrated there.
Across-task transfer fails — and can backfire (rows 10–12). Pairwise-only SFT worsens single-question calibration on the already-calibrated domain and yields no AUC gain. Single-task SFT tested on the pairwise format shows the symmetric failure. Format isn’t a free transfer.
Multitask SFT (C+S) recovers and adds (rows 13–15). Joint training lifts AUC and drops ECE on the out-of-domain evaluations, beating single-task SFT alone — except again on TruthfulQA, where the already-calibrated-domain regression persists.
Llama-3.1-70B partially diverges. Single-question gains mirror GPT-4.1-mini, but multitask fine-tuning fails to lift Llama’s out-of-domain pairwise discrimination relative to comparison-only training. The “multitask helps both formats” headline is GPT-specific.




Figure 4 from the paper [1].


Figure 4 plots the OOD calibration curves under multitask SFT — the diagonal-hugging gain is largest on LegalBench, where the baseline was most overconfident.

title: Improving Metacognition and Uncertainty Communication in Language Models
text:
My Notes

The “self-consistency only” framing is overstated: the paper says “the model is not trained using ground-truth correctness signals” (§2.1). True at the loss level: the SFT loss doesn’t reference per-question GT labels. But the confidence target \(\hat c = a(s) + \varepsilon\) depends on \(a(s)\), the empirical accuracy at consistency \(s\), computed by comparing modal answers to ground truth (§4.3.2). The recipe inherits the label dependency of any supervised calibration method.
What this paper actually adds: consistency-based SFT is prior art (the authors cite three earlier works). The contribution is the 3×3×3 grid (training condition × generalization tier × test domain), which documents three failure modes: across-task transfer fails, well-calibrated domains regress under joint training, and Llama doesn’t inherit the multitask benefit on the comparison task. Does semantic entropy [2] or the verbal-confidence work in Kadavath et al. [3] have similar transfer failures? Their evaluations don’t run this grid.
S and C may be separable abilities: the paper concludes single-question (S) and pairwise (C) tasks are “distinct metacognitive routines, not interchangeable manifestations of a single uncertainty signal” (§2.3). The evidence: training only on S doesn’t improve C performance, and training only on C doesn’t improve S (Table 1 rows 10–12, Table 2 rows 10–12). Open question: is the underlying uncertainty signal also format-specific, or does the split only emerge at verbalization? AbstentionBench [4], metacognition atlas [5], and compliance-trap [6] each catalog one uncertainty failure mode (abstention, monitorability, prompt-regime collapse); this paper adds format-specific transfer. None has measured them together.
Calibration cost on already-calibrated domains: on TruthfulQA the baseline ECE is already 0.10; multitask SFT raises it to 0.13. A training intervention that helps most domains can hurt a well-behaved one. The Cacioli atlas [5] showed monitorability varies by 0.3+ AUC across MMLU subjects from the same base model; this paper adds that an SFT intervention’s sign can flip with domain. Evaluate the target domain’s pre-SFT calibration before deploying.
Compare to the test-time SVM harness: a recent metacognitive harness for Sonnet-4.6 [7] solves the same problem at the inference layer instead of via SFT. The harness leaves the model untouched and fits a small external SVM mapping \((\text{FOK}, \text{JOL}) \to P(\text{correct})\), where FOK is the model’s pre-solve confidence rating and JOL is the post-solve rating. Inference flow: model emits FOK; if low, allocate more reasoning budget; model solves and emits JOL; SVM gives \(P(\text{correct})\); if \(\geq 0.7\), accept, else draw more attempts and aggregate. Both methods need GT correctness offline (this paper to fit \(a(s)\), the harness to fit the SVM on a 100-question anchor set). Trade-off: the harness needs only ~100 labeled questions per base model and produces a tiny artifact but refits per model; this paper needs a larger labeled set and full SFT but produces a self-contained model that emits a calibrated confidence number from one sample at inference.
Practical alternative to abstention-from-prompting: the compliance-trap result [6] showed structural prompt constraints degrade frontier abstention by up to 30 accuracy points. This paper offers a weight-level analogue: train calibration into the model directly, so the prompt has less to override at inference. Follow-up: rerun compliance-trap on a model fine-tuned with this recipe; does the 8–30 point drop shrink?

title: ProgramBench: Can Language Models Rebuild Programs From Scratch?
text:
ProgramBench evaluates models on their ability to write software projects from scratch. Given a program (e.g. an executable) and its documentation, a software engineering agent must produce source code and a build script that reconstructs the original program’s behavior. Figure 1 from the paper [1].
In ProgramBench: Can Language Models Rebuild Programs From Scratch? [1], John Yang, Kilian Lieret, Ofir Press, and nine co-authors from Meta, Stanford, and Harvard introduce a 200-task benchmark that asks coding agents to reconstruct an open-source program from its compiled executable and documentation alone.
Each task starts from a real GitHub repository written in a compiled language. The authors compile the project, generate a behavioral test suite by running a software engineering agent (SWE-agent) against the reference executable, then strip the source and tests, leaving only the binary and the docs. The model under test then receives the same starting point and must write source code and a build script whose compiled output passes the hidden tests. The 200 tasks span CLI utilities to large systems including FFmpeg, SQLite, and the PHP interpreter, with no constraint on language, file structure, or build system; every architectural decision is the model’s.
What the paper reports: across nine frontier models from Anthropic, Google, and OpenAI, no task is fully resolved by any model. Claude Opus 4.7 leads on the relaxed “% Almost” metric (≥95% of tests passing) at 3.0% of tasks. Claude Opus 4.6 follows at 2.5% and Claude Sonnet 4.6 at 1.6%. Every other model registers 0% on both metrics. The median test pass rate across all 1,800 leaderboard runs is 32%, but the gap from “partial credit” to “fully resolved” is wide and uniform across models.
Per-task pass rates for the 40 most-starred repositories show difficulty is largely model-agnostic: simpler CLI utilities sit on the left of every model’s row, while complex systems like FFmpeg and the PHP interpreter remain unsolved across the board.
In a separate ablation, the authors gave one model per provider unrestricted internet access and used a 9-judge LM-as-a-judge pipeline to flag trajectories that looked up source code or wrapped the reference executable. Cheating was widespread: 20–36% of tasks flagged for the three stronger models, with source-code lookup accounting for 79–95% of violations. Detection was unreliable too: judges disagreed on 40–57% of tasks. The authors take this as grounds for keeping internet access disabled by default.
The most-quoted analytical finding sits in §5.2: the codebases models produce do not look like the human-written originals. Across trajectories, a single edit accounts for the majority of the final solution, with GPT 5.4 committing a median 96% of its code in one turn.

title: ProgramBench: Can Language Models Rebuild Programs From Scratch?
text:
My Notes

Distance to recursive self-improvement. Recursive Superintelligence’s $4B bet assumes agents that can rebuild and improve their own systems. ProgramBench is a direct test of that capability one rung down: reconstruct one specified program from its executable and documentation, with full architectural latitude. Nine frontier models score 0% fully resolved on 200 mostly small open-source projects, and the cheating ablation suggests part of what looks like reasoning capability in deployed coding agents is source-code retrieval.
From-scratch vs localized repair. Yang and Press were also on the SWE-bench [2] author list in 2024, the bug-fix benchmark where frontier agents now resolve a majority of issues against an existing scaffold. On ProgramBench they resolve zero. Bug-fix benchmarks reward pattern-matching against existing structure, but ProgramBench requires inventing the structure. Headline agent-progress numbers from bug-fix benchmarks don’t extrapolate to from-scratch coding.
Architectural numbers for Faye’s case. Lars Faye argued last week that the orchestrator-with-sub-agents workflow puts growing distance between the engineer and the code, and that catching issues at the architectural level is what a skilled developer is for. ProgramBench supplies numbers from the architectural-quality side: across 1,800 trajectories, models favor monolithic, single-file implementations, and GPT 5.4 commits a median 96% of its lines in one turn (Figure 12).
Agent-fuzzed test suites couple evaluator and evaluated. Each task’s behavioral tests are generated by running a SWE-agent against the reference executable, the same class of system being scored. The paper audits over-specification (§8.3.4) and reports test line coverage comparable to native suites (§5). Neither check isolates the systematic blindspots a fuzzing agent shares with the agent it scores. Whatever a fuzzing agent fails to imagine, such as malformed encodings or unusual flag combinations, is invisible in the score.
