title: AI Assistance Reduces Persistence and Hurts Independent Performance
text:
Experimental design from the paper. Image from the project page.
In AI Assistance Reduces Persistence and Hurts Independent Performance [1] (arXiv preprint, April 2026), Grace Liu at CMU, Brian Christian and Tsvetomira Dumbalska at Oxford, Michiel A. Bakker at MIT, and Rachit Dubey at UCLA run three randomized controlled trials on humans solving math and reading-comprehension problems with and without AI help, and report that brief AI assistance lowers later unaided performance and raises the rate at which participants give up. The project page summarizes the design and findings.
The paper lays out three experiments and one cross-cutting subgroup analysis:
The authors’ headline takeaway. Brief AI-assisted sessions impair subsequent unaided performance and persistence. The impairment is carried by participants who used the AI for direct solutions rather than for hints or clarifications. And the effect generalizes across arithmetic and reading comprehension. Their proposed mechanism is that AI conditions users to expect immediate answers, removing the experience of working through challenges, and persistence (a strong long-term-learning predictor) erodes as a result.

title: AI Assistance Reduces Persistence and Hurts Independent Performance
text:
My Notes

Part of a growing cluster on AI’s cognitive cost. Vivienne Ming’s WSJ essay argued the risk is the quiet outsourcing of judgment in increments too small to notice. This paper supplies the controlled-trial version of that argument with a specific behavioral target (persistence). Together the two pieces make the case from different ends: one from clinical experience, one from RCT data.
Ten minutes is a surprisingly short time. Skill-erosion arguments usually invoke months or years of habituation. This study finds significant post-removal decline after a single ~10-minute session. If the result holds, the next question is the half-life of the effect and whether it persists past one sitting. The paper doesn’t follow participants beyond the session.
Skip-rate is a more alarming result than solve-rate. Solve-rate decline could plausibly reflect transient unfamiliarity with no-AI mode. Skip-rate is a behavioral commitment: the participant chose to give up rather than try. That participants who had AI for ten minutes were more willing to abandon problems is the observation that’s hardest to explain away.
The importance of interaction style is undersold. “AI assistance reduces persistence” reads as a verdict on AI assistance writ large, but the data says the impairment is carried entirely by the 61% who asked for full solutions. Hint and clarification users were indistinguishable from control. The result is consistent with two very different recommendations (limit AI use vs. design AI to push back on direct-answer requests), and the paper’s framing collapses that fork.

title: Claude Code Beyond the Prompt
text:
The opening of Arpan Patel’s Claude Code field guide. Image from Arpan Patel’s blog.
Arpan Patel wrote a long field guide to running Claude Code as a programmable agent instead of a terminal chatbot: the .claude directory, CLAUDE.md the way Boris Cherny writes it, skills, custom subagents, plugins, the underused commands, MCPs, and the workflow habits the Anthropic team actually runs. The author’s badge says it hit #7 on the Hacker News front page.

title: Claude Code Beyond the Prompt
text:
What the Guide Covers
The operating principle. Run Claude Code as an agent that needs guardrails, not a prompt-and-wait chatbot.

Give Claude a way to verify its own work, whether a test, a build, or a grep-able condition, so it keeps iterating until the code runs. Cherny pegs this single move at a 2-3x quality bump.
Drop into read-only plan mode before any change that touches more than one file, so you can review and edit the plan before it turns into code. Skip it for small fixes.
Reference files with @path and pipe errors in with cat error.log | claude, because exact context beats an approximate description.
Write a crisp brief and let Claude run rather than steering it line by line, since the model does better when you delegate than when you pair-program.

The .claude directory. A layered config system, not just a home for CLAUDE.md.

Split config by scope: project files (.claude/, committed) describe the project, global files (~/.claude/) describe you.
Let CLAUDE.md files cascade in a monorepo, so a service folder adds local conventions on top of the root file.
Move folder-specific guidance into path-gated rules/*.md, so it loads only where it applies instead of bloating every session.
Prefer skills over loose commands/*.md, since skills carry supporting files, tool restrictions, and agent overrides.

CLAUDE.md. The file Claude reads at the start of every session, kept as a guardrail rather than a knowledge base.

Keep it short by cutting any line whose removal wouldn’t cause a mistake, because long files bury the rules that matter.
After each mistake, tell Claude to “update CLAUDE.md so you don’t repeat this,” so the file becomes a curated gotcha list in the model’s own phrasing.
Limit it to build commands, run order, single-test invocations, and a Gotchas section of real shipped bugs, and leave out style conventions and codebase tours that go stale.
Commit rules straight from PR-review comments with @claude, so every review becomes a permanent fix (Cherny’s “Compounding Engineering”).

CLAUDE.local.md. A gitignored sibling that loads like CLAUDE.md but never leaves your machine.

Paste recurring PR-review feedback into it as you read it, so it becomes a private rule file tuned to the comments you keep getting.
Keep project feedback and personal habits in separate sections, and prune once something is muscle memory, so the file stays easy to maintain.

Skills. Folders that package reusable expertise as slash commands.

Put a SKILL.md in a folder; the folder name becomes the command, so a repeated workflow turns into something you invoke by name.
Rely on progressive disclosure: only the ~100-token description loads at session start and the full instructions load when the skill fires, which keeps context lean.
Use frontmatter to restrict tools, pin an agent, or require explicit invocation for skills with side effects, so a deploy skill runs only when you type it.
Heuristic: if you’ve typed the same instructions twice, write a skill.

Subagents. Separate Claude instances with their own context and scoped tools.

Hand a fifty-file investigation to a subagent, so it doesn’t crowd the main session’s context.
Keep a reviewer agent read-only, because a reviewer that can patch starts defending its own fixes instead of flagging them.
Give a review agent a “Do NOT flag” section, so its output isn’t drowned in nitpicks.
Add isolation: worktree to run one agent per task across parallel git worktrees.

Plugins. Installable bundles of skills, hooks, subagents, and MCP servers.

Install through /plugin, so a team’s setup travels instead of staying on one machine.
Start with /code-review (parallel agents, confidence-scored findings) and /feature-dev.
Add a language server plugin for symbol-level navigation and on-edit diagnostics, which the team rates the highest-impact install.

Underused commands. What’s past /clear and /compact.

Use /rewind to roll back to a checkpoint instead of typing “that didn’t work,” which only buries the bad attempt in context.
Reach for /branch, /batch, /voice, and /insights to fork a session, fan work out, dictate prompts, and review your usage monthly.
Set /goal to a verifiable completion condition and let Claude grind until it holds.
Force compaction before 300-400k tokens, where context rot starts on the 1M-token model.
For mass edits, generate the task list, hand-check three, tighten the prompt, then loop. That is how he migrated roughly 2,000 component files.

MCPs. A protocol for reaching external systems from inside the session.

Wire in servers like GitHub, Postgres, Sentry, Figma, or Linear through MCP (Model Context Protocol), so the agent reasons about your whole stack, not just the repo.
Install few: every server enlarges the tool list Claude reasons over, and a bloated list degrades decision quality.
Treat an Obsidian vault as three memory tiers: a daily session log (hot), project notes Claude rehydrates at session start (warm), and promoted decisions and reusable notes (cold).

Daily workflow and team habits. How the Anthropic team runs it day to day.

Reproduce a bug with a failing test before asking for a fix, so the fix isn’t a guess.
Run three to five parallel sessions in separate git worktrees, the habit the team rates the single biggest unlock.
Pair a writer session with a fresh reviewer session, so the review carries no implementation bias.
Default to Opus at high effort, since a weaker model that needs correcting is slower overall.
Never let Claude claim success without evidence, because the trust-then-verify gap is the biggest source of bad output.

title: LangChain’s Deep Agents: A Batteries-Included Agent Harness
text:
The Deep Agents harness bundles planning, a virtual filesystem with permissions, subagents, context management, code execution, human-in-the-loop approval, skills, and memory around the core tool-calling loop. Diagram from the Deep Agents documentation.
LangChain has shipped Deep Agents, a standalone library for building agents that plan, spawn subagents, and read and write a filesystem to manage their own context over long runs. It comes in two forms: the deepagents SDK for building your own agents, and Deep Agents Code (dcode), a terminal coding agent built on that SDK in the mold of Claude Code. Both work across any tool-calling model rather than a single provider.
The library matters less than the vocabulary around it. LangChain now describes the agent stack as three layers, and Deep Agents is its bet on the topmost one.
deepagents is built on LangChain’s core and runs on the LangGraph runtime, so the harness inherits durable execution, streaming, and persistence rather than reimplementing them.

title: LangChain’s Deep Agents: A Batteries-Included Agent Harness
text:
What the docs describe
The SDK exposes one constructor, create_deep_agent(model=..., tools=..., system_prompt=...), and bundles a set of capabilities that you would otherwise wire up by hand:

Planning: a built-in write_todos tool lets the agent decompose a task, track progress, and revise the plan as it goes.
Context management: large tool inputs and results are offloaded to a virtual filesystem, and older messages are summarized, so the agent stays within budget across long sessions.
Pluggable filesystem backends: the virtual filesystem can be backed by in-memory state, local disk, the LangGraph store, a composite router, or a custom backend, each governed by declarative read/write permission rules.
Code execution: shell-capable backends add an execute tool. A LocalShellBackend runs on the host, and sandbox backends run it in isolation. A separate JavaScript interpreter lets the agent compose tools and transform data without a full shell.
Subagents: a task tool spawns general or specialized subagents in isolated context windows. Async subagents run in the background with progress checks and cancellation.
Memory, skills, and human-in-the-loop: long-term memory persists across threads via the LangGraph store, skills package reusable workflows, and sensitive tool calls can pause for human approval.
Harness profiles (beta): per-provider or per-model bundles of prompt, tool, and middleware tweaks, so one agent can be tuned for several models declaratively.

Deep Agents Code wraps the SDK as a terminal coding agent. It installs from a curl one-liner, works with any tool-calling LLM, and can switch providers or models mid-session. It carries persistent memory, reads AGENTS.md files for project and subagent configuration, gates file writes and shell commands behind approval (with a --auto-approve escape hatch), loads Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, runs tools in remote sandboxes (LangSmith, Daytona, Modal, Runloop, AgentCore), and exposes itself to IDEs over the Agent Client Protocol. Web search runs through Tavily. It is MIT-licensed.
The docs include a direct comparison with the Claude Agent SDK. At a glance:

title: LangChain’s Deep Agents: A Batteries-Included Agent Harness
text:
My Notes
Most of the comparison with the Claude Agent SDK reduces to “we support more models and we manage deployment for you,” which is a business-model difference. The one substantive architectural difference is where the agent process runs relative to its execution environment. Harrison Chase lays out two patterns: the agent runs inside the sandbox and executes against its local filesystem, or it runs outside on a long-lived server and calls the sandbox as a remote tool. The Claude Agent SDK supports only the first, while Deep Agents supports both. The decoupled pattern is mostly a security and state-ownership argument.

Credentials stay out of the sandbox: running the agent inside means its model API keys live there too, so a prompt injection or container escape can exfiltrate them. With the sandbox as a tool, only code execution happens in isolation, and the keys stay on the agent’s host.
The security boundary wraps the bash tool, not the whole agent: Nuno Campos, who created LangGraph, makes the strongest version of this point in a comment on Chase’s post. With the agent inside, nothing it does can hold more privilege than the bash tool, so any model-generated code inherits the agent’s full network and tool access. With the sandbox as a tool, a web-fetch or database tool can carry more privilege than the model-generated bash, because the isolation wraps execution rather than the agent.
Agent state survives the sandbox: conversation history, reasoning, and memory live with the long-lived process, not the disposable container. A sandbox crash does not lose the run, you can swap providers without touching agent logic, run one agent across several sandboxes in parallel, and pay for sandbox time only while code executes.
This is the harder shape to retrofit: LangChain reads even Anthropic’s own hosted Claude managed agents as decoupled, the direction production is heading, which makes the in-sandbox-only SDK the legacy shape. Build a multi-tenant product on the Claude Agent SDK and you write the per-user sandbox orchestration and the network layer yourself. The decoupled design is what lets Deep Agents hand you per-user isolation, scoped threads, and an auth proxy without that work.

title: Use Boring Languages with LLMs
text:
The xkcd “Python environment” comic the article uses to picture Python’s tooling sprawl. Image from xkcd 1987.
Jacob Young argues that coding agents produce more reliable output in languages and ecosystems with low variance in their training data, and that Go is the best mainstream language for this moment because its conventions, standard library, and one-right-way tooling give an agent fewer ways to go wrong.

title: Use Boring Languages with LLMs
text:
What the article argues
The case, in the order the article makes it:

The core claim: coding agents inherit the variance of their training data. Ecosystems with heavy fragmentation produce the worst agentic output, and the ones with the strongest conventions produce the best.
Inference is a gamble: even when code is cheap, any single generation might install a needless package or reproduce an outdated pattern. The bet is to spend tokens where the model’s weights are most reinforced, which yields median output, and the median program is mostly doing the basics anyway: reading files, serving requests, responding over the network.
JavaScript and Python are the cautionary cases: the 2024 State of JS survey describes a fragmented ecosystem, and Python forces a matrix of choices among pip, Poetry, and uv, sync versus async, Django versus FastAPI. The public corpus reflects every variant in roughly equal weight, so the model has no single idiom to default to.
Ruby on Rails and Go are the counter-cases: Ruby on Rails produces more consistent agentic output because there is essentially one Rails, where JavaScript has a dozen production-grade frameworks covering the same features. Convention over configuration, once a win for human programmers, now helps machines more.
Go gives an agent five specific advantages:

Goroutines avoid the colored-function problem: there is no async-versus-sync split for the model to track.
The standard library carries a large share of real services, net/http and the Google-funded cryptography packages in particular, without reaching for third-party code.
One-right-way tooling (gofmt, go vet, gopls, golangci-lint) enforces a single canonical style and feeds the agent real-time semantic and lint feedback.
Garbage collection gives native-like performance without asking the agent to manage memory, which the article contrasts with Rust’s borrow checker (“a constant fight for agents”) and the memory bugs that fill C and C++ training data.
The set of footguns is small and bounded, unlike Python with arbitrary metaclasses.

What the article concludes: not that Go is the best language, but that this language and toolchain can write the majority of non-visual software, the next CLI, backend server, or agent orchestrator.

title: Use Boring Languages with LLMs
text:
My Notes
The notes below weigh the thesis from both sides, each marked for or against.

Variance may be the wrong variable. Against the thesis. The article credits low corpus variance but never accounts for corpus size, a separate variable. JavaScript and Python are the most fragmented mainstream ecosystems, yet also the most-represented in training data, and code models are strongest on well-represented languages and weaker on low-resource ones like OCaml or Racket [1]. The strongest real-task evidence agrees: on Multi-SWE-bench [3], which extends SWE-bench’s Python tasks to seven more languages (Java, TypeScript, JavaScript, Go, Rust, C, C++), models resolve Python issues at by far the highest rate of the eight, even though Python is one of the most fragmented ecosystems. The authors caution that the agent harnesses were themselves tuned on Python, so part of that lead is tooling rather than training data.




Resolved rate (%) by language on Multi-SWE-bench, across nine models and three agent methods (MagentLess, MSWE-agent, MopenHands). The Python column is the highest in nearly every row, despite Python being one of the most fragmented ecosystems. Table 4 from Multi-SWE-bench [3].



The toolchain advantage isn’t about the language alone. Against the thesis, on its internal logic. The article names two ingredients for good agentic output: a consistent training corpus and “one-right-way tooling for testing and feedback at runtime.” The second is language-independent: deterministic in-loop tooling (gofmt, go vet, gopls, golangci-lint) is a checkable signal the agent can iterate against, and any ecosystem with a strong checker provides one no matter how consistent its corpus is. So only the corpus half supports picking a boring language. The tooling half holds for any language with good tools.
Betting on the median optimizes the cheap part. Against the thesis, on its payoff. The basics the article’s wager targets are also where a competent engineer was already fast, and where an agent’s leverage is smallest. The work that actually costs human time is the non-median part: the unfamiliar API, the awkward edge case, the migration nobody has done before. ProgramBench shows that gap with numbers: asked to rebuild whole programs from scratch with no constraint on language, nine frontier models fully resolve none of 200 tasks, and the failures are architectural rather than matters of language idiom. Picking a boring language makes the agent reliable exactly where reliability was cheapest to get.
The advantage shrinks as harnesses improve. Against the thesis, on its durability. The article cites Claude Code’s “hard-coded some bias for JavaScript frameworks” as proof fragmentation is costly. But that fix lives in the harness, not the language. As harness conventions (system-prompt defaults, convention files, pinned lockfiles) normalize a fragmented ecosystem, the reason to switch languages weakens. The advice is strongest today and weaker with every harness improvement.
The Hacker News thread (228 points, 168 comments) divides on the same fault lines. The salient points, by side.

Against the thesis:

The most common objection is corpus size rather than variance, the point in the first note above. Commenters report the model writes “much better PHP, than Swift” because there is far more open-source PHP to train on, and that the worst results come from GDScript, “python minus the huge corpus of training data.”
The available benchmarks don’t single Go out. A commenter cited AutoCodeBench [2], a 20-language Pass@1 benchmark, for models being “better at writing Elixir than most other languages,” but that benchmark classifies Elixir as low-resource and clusters its four popular languages (Python, C++, Java, C#) within a narrow band, roughly 50 to 54 Pass@1. Go is not in that popular set, and on Multi-SWE-bench’s real issue-resolution tasks [3] it ranks in the middle, ahead of JavaScript and TypeScript but behind Python and Java. No mainstream language stands out.
A large camp argues the property that helps is strictness rather than boringness, and would go the other way toward Rust, OCaml, or Haskell: required Result/Option handling means “if it compiles, chances are higher the code is correct,” which catches more agent errors than a low-variance corpus does.
Goroutines drew specific pushback. Several report agents “trip up a lot on the races and locking” in Go and have moved their agent work to Rust, and note the article gives no evidence for the goroutine claim.
Others argue human familiarity matters more than the model’s preference, since “the bottleneck isn’t what languages the LLM can handle, but what I can handle” coming out of it.

For the thesis:

The feedback-loop point drew the most agreement: compile-time errors and clear compiler messages let the agent iterate, which commenters found true in Elm and Rust as much as in Go.
Anecdotal wins for Go: one reports the code Sonnet “produces for Go is much better than the Python it creates,” another that LLM-assisted Node-to-Go ports came out clean and cut memory roughly tenfold.
“Pit of success” was offered as the better name for the real effect: predictable defaults that are hard to get wrong.

title: Machine-Learning Applications of Algorithmic Randomness
text:
The 2-versus-7 ambiguity that motivates the paper: given a training set of clean 2s and 7s, the smudged middle image should receive much lower confidence than the two flanking it. Figure 1 from the paper [1].
In Machine-Learning Applications of Algorithmic Randomness [1] (ICML 1999), Volodya Vovk, Alex Gammerman, and Craig Saunders at Royal Holloway, University of London unify their earlier transduction work into a single scheme based on the notion of algorithmic randomness — one of the founding papers of what is now called conformal prediction. The complaint that opens the paper is that most learning algorithms output a bare prediction with no measure of how much to trust it, and that the example a classifier is least sure about is exactly the one a user most needs flagged.
The paper rests on two quantities, and the rest of it is about how to compute them. Each candidate label \(Y\) gets a p-value \(p(Y) \in [0, 1]\) measuring how well that labeling fits the training data. The \(p(Y)\) across labels are separate tail probabilities, one per candidate-label hypothesis, not a distribution over labels, and they need not sum to 1. The prediction is the label with the largest p-value, \(\hat{y} = \arg\max_Y p(Y)\):
The pair separates two failure modes that a single probability hides. A prediction can be confident but have low credibility — a signal that the input itself is strange, not just that the label is uncertain.

title: Machine-Learning Applications of Algorithmic Randomness
text:
The abstract

Most machine learning algorithms share the following drawback: they only output bare predictions but not the confidence in those predictions. In the 1960s algorithmic information theory supplied universal measures of confidence but these are, unfortunately, non-computable. In this paper we combine the ideas of algorithmic information theory with the theory of Support Vector machines to obtain practicable approximations to universal measures of confidence. We show that in some standard problems of pattern recognition our approximations work well.

title: Machine-Learning Applications of Algorithmic Randomness
text:
Methods
The construction has three layers, and only the third one runs on a computer.
The ideal, non-computable target. A p-value function, or randomness level, scores how well a data sequence fits the independent-and-identically-distributed (iid) assumption: large when the sequence looks like a typical iid draw, small when it contains a pattern an iid source would rarely produce. (“Random” here is the algorithmic sense of “indistinguishable from a fair-coin sample,” not the colloquial “erratic.”) To classify a test point \(x_{l+1}\), the ideal algorithm tries every candidate label, completes the sequence \((x_1, y_1), \ldots, (x_{l+1}, Y)\), and measures the randomness level \(p(Y)\) of each completion. It predicts the label whose completion has the largest randomness level, \(\hat{y} = \arg\max_Y p(Y)\) — the label that makes the data look most consistent with iid, hence the least anomalous. Credibility is that largest randomness level, \(p(\hat{y})\), and confidence is one minus the second-largest, \(1 - p_{(2)}\).
The second-largest is what matters because the valid prediction set at significance level \(\varepsilon\) is \(\Gamma^{\varepsilon} = \{\,Y : p(Y) > \varepsilon\,\}\), and this is the single label \(\hat{y}\) only when every alternative is rejected. That is an AND across the other labels, so the binding constraint is the largest of their p-values: \(\max_{Y \neq \hat{y}} p(Y) = p_{(2)} \le \varepsilon\). So \(1 - p_{(2)}\) is the highest confidence at which the predictor commits to one label. The error guarantee falls out of validity: each \(p(Y)\) is a genuine p-value, so \(\Pr[\,p(Y) \le \varepsilon\,] \le \varepsilon\) under the hypothesis that \(Y\) is correct, and because a wrong prediction means the true label is the rejected one, it has probability at most \(1 - \text{confidence}\). Credibility plays the complementary role: a small \(p(\hat{y})\) means even the best label is atypical, flagging the input rather than the label.
The trouble is that the universal measures of randomness from Kolmogorov [2] and Martin-Löf [3] are non-computable — they can be approximated from below but never evaluated exactly.
The Support Vector approximation. To get something computable, the paper borrows Vapnik’s Support Vector Machine (SVM) [4]. Solving the SVM’s dual optimization assigns each example a Lagrange multiplier \(\alpha_i\) that grows with how hard the example is to fit. The earlier “Learning by Transduction” paper (Gammerman, Vapnik, and Vovk [5]) turned multipliers into a score with \(f(\alpha) = \operatorname{sign} \alpha\). The companion paper (Saunders, Gammerman, and Vovk [6]) turns them into a p-value by ranking: sort the multipliers in decreasing order, and the p-value of a completion is the rank of the test example’s multiplier divided by \(l+1\). A genuinely strange or mislabelled example earns a large multiplier, ends up near the top of the ranking, and so gets a small p-value.
The experiment. The test bed is United States Postal Service (USPS) handwritten digits (LeCun et al. [7]), each a \(16 \times 16\) image, with a two-class problem separating the digit 2 from the digit 7. The classifier is an SVM with a degree-3 polynomial kernel \(K(x, x') = (x \cdot x')^3 / 256\), trained on 400 examples and evaluated on 100 single-example test sets.

title: Machine-Learning Applications of Algorithmic Randomness
text:
Results

Confidence and credibility separate correct from incorrect predictions (Figure 2, credibility on the vertical axis, confidence on the horizontal). With \(f(\alpha) = \operatorname{sign}\alpha\), the 100 predictions split into two clusters by average credibility: a cluster of 93 correct examples is at credibility 1.0 and average confidence 0.902, while the cluster holding the single error (plus 6 correct examples) is at credibility 0.091. Credibility, not confidence, is what marks the examples the classifier should not be trusted on.
The choice of score function \(f(\alpha)\) matters. The \(f(\alpha) = \operatorname{sign}\alpha\) rule from the transduction paper suffers a “distortion phenomenon” and predicts worse. Switching to \(f(\alpha) = \alpha\) or \(f(\alpha) = \alpha^2\) pushes average confidence above 0.99 on the correct cluster while keeping the error cluster’s credibility low.
The error bound is \(\log(l + 1)\). For a single test example, the randomness deficiency of a wrongly-labelled sequence is at most \(\log(l+1)\), and the paper notes this matches the \(l+1\) denominator in Vapnik’s statistical learning theory and in PAC-style error bounds — the same quantity obtained from the algorithmic-randomness side.




Figure 2 from the paper [1].


The paper closes with a set of impossibility results (Section 6). Under the iid assumption alone:

On-line prediction at every step is impossible (§6.1). If both the data sequence and the stopping time are random, inequality (9) shows that even the wrong labeled sequence has a random continuation under iid — so under iid alone there is no way to rule out wrong predictions at a randomly chosen time. The paper offers this as the technical explanation for why machine learning under iid has stayed in the batch setting. Practical impact: conformal prediction’s coverage guarantee holds at fixed batches, not at adversarially chosen stopping times. Streaming pipelines that need valid coverage at every step need assumptions stronger than iid.
Density estimation in high dimensions is impossible (§6.2). When the input dimension is large compared to the sample size, the unlabelled \(x_i\) are typically all distinct. Under iid, for any generating distribution \(P\) there is a degenerate \(P^*\) that places \(y \mid x\) entirely on \(-1\) or \(+1\) for each \(x\) but is indistinguishable from \(P\) on the sample. So \(P(y_{l+1} = 1 \mid x_{l+1})\) cannot be estimated to anything narrower than \(\{0, 1\}\) without strictly stronger assumptions. Practical impact: conformal prediction returns a prediction set (the true label is among these) rather than a calibrated per-class probability like \(P(\text{class A} \mid x) = 0.73\). The latter is provably out of reach in high dimensions under iid alone.
Regression as conditional-expectation estimation reduces to density estimation (§6.3). Estimating \(\mathbb{E}[y_{l+1} \mid x_{l+1}]\) under iid coincides with density estimation in the binary case, so the §6.2 impossibility transfers. Under a different framing, where \(x_i\) are deterministic and only \(y_i\) are stochastic, even pattern recognition becomes impossible without additional assumptions. Practical impact: conformal regression methods deliver prediction intervals (a calibrated band around \(y\)) rather than calibrated point estimates of \(\mathbb{E}[y \mid x]\), for the same reason.

title: Machine-Learning Applications of Algorithmic Randomness
text:
What came after
The scheme here is transductive — to score a test example it effectively retrains for every candidate label, which is expensive — and the nonconformity signal is tied to the SVM. The work that followed relaxed both.

The general form. Vovk, Gammerman, and Shafer’s Algorithmic Learning in a Random World [8] consolidated the theory into a form where any nonconformity score, not just an SVM multiplier, drives the calibration.
Split conformal prediction. Papadopoulos et al. [9] replaced the per-label retraining with a single held-out calibration set, cheap enough to wrap around any pre-trained model — the form most practitioners use today.
Workarounds for the impossibility results. Each of the §6 impossibilities has a follow-up that recovers what is possible without violating the underlying constraint:

On-line prediction (§6.1): Adaptive Conformal Inference (Gibbs and Candès [13]) updates the conformal threshold over time, holding long-run coverage under distribution shift. The new guarantee is a long-run coverage rate rather than per-step validity, which is why the §6.1 impossibility does not apply.
Density estimation in high dimensions (§6.2): Venn–Abers predictors (Vovk and Petej [11]) output a calibrated probability interval rather than a single number. An interval is what is achievable under iid alone in high dimensions, where the §6.2 impossibility blocks single-number probabilities.
Regression (§6.3): Conformalized quantile regression (Romano, Patterson, and Candès [10]) reformulates the task as quantile estimation and returns calibrated, locally adaptive prediction intervals. The impossibility blocks point estimates of \(\mathbb{E}[y \mid x]\), not interval coverage, so quantile regression sidesteps it.

The deep-learning revival. Angelopoulos and Bates’ tutorial [12] repackaged the framework for deep learning and drove the recent wave of distribution-free uncertainty work — including the conformal factuality and conformal language modeling methods built for language models.

title: Machine-Learning Applications of Algorithmic Randomness
text:
My Notes

The middle layer is the IJCAI companion paper. This paper has three layers (ideal non-computable target, computable SVM approximation, experiment), and the middle layer comes from the same trio’s IJCAI 1999 paper [6] on transduction with confidence and credibility. That paper introduces the SVM-rank-of-multipliers construction standalone, while this one wraps the same construction in algorithmic-randomness theory and adds the impossibility results.
Mapping to LLM prediction. The paper picks the predicted label via \(\hat{y} = \arg\max_Y p(Y)\) and exposes the value at that argmax as credibility, \(\max_Y p(Y) = p(\hat{y})\). LLM token prediction does the same operation, \(\hat{y} = \arg\max_y p_{\text{softmax}}(y \mid x)\), with the max softmax as the value at the argmax. So when an LLM is described as “95% confident in its prediction,” that 95% is colloquially called confidence but is structurally the paper’s credibility. The paper’s confidence (\(1 - p_{(2)}\), one minus the second-largest p-value) is a different number with no common LLM analog. Wrapping conformal prediction around the LLM uses \(1 - p_{\text{softmax}}(y \mid x)\) as the nonconformity score on a held-out calibration set, and the result has the coverage guarantee the raw max softmax lacks.

title: Superintelligence: The Idea That Eats Smart People
text:
The talk’s title slide. Image from Maciej Cegłowski’s talk.
In a 2016 talk at Web Camp Zagreb, Maciej Cegłowski, who runs the bookmarking service Pinboard, argues that belief in machine superintelligence is “the idea that eats smart people”: a chain of individually plausible premises that, followed to the end, turns capable engineers into a quasi-religious movement. He opens with the 1945 worry that the first atomic-bomb test might set the atmosphere on fire, a fear physicists could rule out because the underlying nuclear laws were well understood, and uses it as the foil for the AI version of the same fear: a “runaway reaction” in which a machine reaches and then exceeds human intelligence in a very short span. His target is Nick Bostrom’s Superintelligence, the 2014 book that synthesizes the alarmist case and that Stephen Hawking, Elon Musk, and a raft of Silicon Valley investors found persuasive.
The premises. The talk first lays out the six assumptions Bostrom’s intelligence-explosion argument needs:
The rebuttals. He then attacks the takeoff scenario from about a dozen angles, most named for a memorable image:
The outside arguments. The second half is about what believing all this does to a culture:
His own position: our understanding of the mind is roughly where alchemy was in the 1600s, diligent but missing the key tools, and the pressing risks are mundane, people exploiting people, carelessness baked into automated systems, and surveillance, not a machine takeover.

title: Superintelligence: The Idea That Eats Smart People
text:
My Notes

Ito’s demographic claim held up. The talk quotes Joi Ito on AI being built by a “predominantly male” and “mostly white” group, which in 2016 sounds like an offhand provocation. The measurements that came soon after support it. Nesta’s study of arXiv AI papers found only 13.8% of authors are women, with no improvement in the share of woman-authored papers since the 1990s. The AI Now Institute’s Discriminating Systems report counted women as 18% of authors at major AI conferences and more than 80% of AI professors as men, and put Black workers at 2.5% of Google’s staff and 4% at Facebook and Microsoft. Both are 2019 figures, but because that share had been flat for decades, the imbalance Ito named looks structural rather than a snapshot. More recent workforce counts run somewhat higher, though women remain a clear minority of AI researchers.

title: Advancing Mathematics Research with AI-Driven Formal Proof Search
text:
An agent equipped with AlphaProof working Erdős problem #125: the mathematician supplies a Lean theorem with a sorry placeholder, and the prover reasons informally, calls AlphaProof on individual goals, and decomposes what is left into lemmas. Figure 1 from the paper [1].
In Advancing Mathematics Research with AI-Driven Formal Proof Search [1] (arXiv preprint, May 2026), George Tsoukalas, Anton Kovsharov, Sergey Shirobokov, and 15 colleagues at Google DeepMind and Aarhus University — with Pushmeet Kohli and Swarat Chaudhuri as corresponding authors — report the first large-scale evaluation of LLM-driven formal proof search on open mathematical problems.

title: Advancing Mathematics Research with AI-Driven Formal Proof Search
text:
Methods
AlphaProof Nexus is a framework for agents that query two things in a loop: a frontier LLM that proposes mathematics, and the Lean compiler that checks it. In Lean, definitions, theorems, and proofs are all mechanically verified code. A proof is built from tactics, elementary steps the compiler runs one at a time while tracking the goals still left to prove, and it is complete only when no goals remain. Lean also has a sorry tactic that closes any goal while still passing the type-checker, so proving a theorem reduces to a concrete coding task: rewrite the file until it compiles with no sorry left.
The agent’s input is a proof sketch: a Lean file holding the target theorem, the definitions and library imports it depends on, and sorry where the proof should go. The mathematician can add natural-language context and domain knowledge encoded in Lean, and marks which parts of the file the agent may edit, with EVOLVE-BLOCK regions where it can introduce helper lemmas, definitions, and proof steps, and EVOLVE-VALUE regions enclosing parameters whose values it may change. On success the agent returns a sorry-free proof.
The paper builds four agents on this framework and tests them in four combinations:

(A) Basic generate-and-verify. A set of prover subagents run independently with no shared state. Each is a “Ralph loop”: a sequence of episodes, where an episode is a multi-turn Gemini 3.1 Pro inference loop that reasons step by step and edits the sketch with a search-and-replace tool. After each turn the subagent compiles the sketch. A Lean error message becomes the instruction for the next turn. If an episode ends with a sorry still in the file, the subagent writes a comment summarizing what it learned, and that annotated sketch seeds the next episode.
(B) Basic plus AlphaProof. The prover can hand an unproved goal to AlphaProof, DeepMind’s reinforcement-learning prover for Olympiad-level Lean. AlphaProof returns a proof, which is substituted straight into the sketch, a disproof showing the goal is false, or a failure message. Disproofs and failures are fed back into the prover’s prompt.
(C) Basic plus evolution. Prover subagents draw from and contribute to a shared population of validated sketches, in the style of DeepMind’s AlphaEvolve. Formal proof is pass-or-fail, which leaves an evolutionary search nothing to climb, so a pool of cheaper Gemini 3.0 Flash rater subagents ranks sketches by plausibility, clarity, and novelty: an LLM critic compares them in pairwise matches, the results become Elo scores, and a selection rule from Monte Carlo tree search (P-UCB, which favors high-scoring sketches while still exploring less-tried ones) decides which to evolve next.
(D) Full-featured. Combines AlphaProof and evolutionary search, and is the agent used for the paper’s main results.

A validator checks every result before it counts, confirming that the final sketch compiles and that the agent did not quietly weaken the theorem statement to make the proof easier.



Design of the full-featured agent (D). Figure 2 from the paper [1].

title: Advancing Mathematics Research with AI-Driven Formal Proof Search
text:
Results
The evaluation covers 353 open Erdős problems and 492 conjectures from the On-Line Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences (OEIS), with a focused cost comparison run on six Erdős instances. The metric is solve rate against mean inference cost in dollars, swept over \(K \in \{1, 3, 6, 10\}\) independent attempts. The prover is Gemini 3.1 Pro and the rater Gemini 3.0 Flash. Reported costs exclude AlphaProof’s own inference (estimated around $60 per problem), which the authors note does not change the comparison.
The findings:

Nine of 353 open Erdős problems solved by the full-featured agent (D), including two that had been open for 56 years, at a few hundred dollars per problem.
Forty-four of 492 OEIS conjectures proved.
The basic agent (A) solved all nine Erdős problems too, at higher cost on the hardest ones. On most problems (A) or (B) sat on the cost–performance Pareto frontier, and the full-featured (D) pulled ahead only on the hardest, such as Erdős #125.
Already in use in active research across optimization theory, graph theory, algebraic geometry, additive combinatorics, and quantum optics.




Solve rate versus mean inference cost across six Erdős instances, for the four agents. Annotations mark the number of independent attempts \(K\) grouped together. For the basic agents (A, B), each curve traces a cost–performance frontier with diminishing returns at higher budgets. Figure 3 from the paper [1].

title: Advancing Mathematics Research with AI-Driven Formal Proof Search
text:
My Notes

The base model matters more than the orchestration: the basic generate-and-verify loop (A) solved all nine Erdős problems on its own. Adding AlphaProof (B) mostly matched it within the margin of error, and the full-featured agent (D) beat them only on the hardest instances (#138 and #125, 2–5x cheaper there) while running about twice as expensive on the rest. Standalone AlphaProof and versions of (A) built on smaller Gemini models solved nothing. The capability comes from the frontier prover, not the evolutionary machinery around it, because the Lean compiler already supplies a hard correctness signal. Co-Scientist [2] is the opposite case: with no compiler to check its hypotheses, its Elo tournament is the only quality signal it has, so the same machinery that is optional here becomes essential.
Humans still formalize the problem and digest the proof: the agent only starts once someone has written the conjecture as a Lean theorem, and its output is a machine-checked proof that still has to be read back out (“deformalized”) and understood. It is the split Terence Tao named: generation and verification race ahead while digestion lags. It also revives the older question of what mathematicians are for once a machine can write the proof.
Known answers versus open problems: the Leipzig benchmark [3] graded models on 100 research-level questions that already had known answers, leaving only two unsolved after three rounds. This paper instead targets open problems with no known answer, where a result counts only when the Lean compiler accepts the proof.
A price tag on open problems: a few hundred dollars to settle a question open for decades makes attempting a conjecture a budgeting decision. Progress now has a unit cost, so you can buy more of it, like the broader automation of AI R&D. The bottleneck remains human bandwidth: formalizing the problems and digesting the proofs.

title: Co-Scientist: Gemini Agents That Generate and Rank Hypotheses
text:
Co-Scientist’s system design: a scientist states a research goal in natural language, and a multi-agent system generates, ranks (in a tournament), and evolves hypotheses into ranked research proposals. Figure 1a from the paper [1].
In Accelerating scientific discovery with Co-Scientist [1] (Nature, May 2026), Juraj Gottweis, Wei-Hung Weng, Alexander Daryin, Tao Tu, and five other co-first authors, with senior authors including Vivek Natarajan, Demis Hassabis, James Manyika, Yossi Matias, and Pushmeet Kohli, and roughly 50 co-authors across Google DeepMind, Google Research, Google Cloud AI Research, Stanford University School of Medicine, Houston Methodist, and Imperial College London, introduce Co-Scientist, a Gemini-based system that proposes research hypotheses and ranks them in a tournament that improves the survivors.

title: Co-Scientist: Gemini Agents That Generate and Rank Hypotheses
text:
Methods
Co-Scientist is a compound, multi-agent system built on Gemini, run as a “scientist in the loop”: a researcher states a goal in natural language, sets constraints, and can steer the search or seed hypotheses as it works. The system generates and ranks hypotheses, but the experimental validation stays with people: every proposal passes human expert review and wet-lab assays before it is confirmed.

Six specialized agents under a supervisor. A Supervisor agent parses the goal and assigns six worker agents (Generation, Reflection, Ranking, Evolution, Proximity, and Meta-review) to an asynchronous task queue, all sharing a persistent context memory. The agents are not separate models: they all run on the same base LLM (Gemini 2.0 here) and differ only by their prompts, and the framework is model-agnostic. Every hypothesis must meet default criteria: plausibility, novelty, testability, and safety.
Grounding and critique. The Generation agent drafts hypotheses from literature search and simulated scientific debate. The Reflection agent then reviews them as a peer reviewer would, and its access to web search and specialized AI models is what kept hallucinated, implausible hypotheses down.
Fitness is winning debates. Hypotheses are scored by an internal Elo rating — the chess-style score that ranks competitors, here hypotheses, by who wins pairwise matchups. The Ranking agent stages those matchups as multi-turn scientific debates (single-turn for lower-ranked pairs), judged on correctness, novelty, and testability. A new hypothesis enters at an Elo of 1200 and climbs or falls by its record. The Proximity agent clusters similar hypotheses so the debates pit close rivals against each other.
Evolution reproduces rather than overwrites. The Evolution agent builds new hypotheses from the top-ranked ones: combining the strongest parts of several (the crossover analog), spinning off variants inspired by one or more parents, regrounding them in fresh literature, simplifying them, or forcing deliberately divergent “out-of-the-box” ideas (the mutation analog). It never edits a hypothesis in place, so strong parents survive and every offspring has to earn its own Elo back in the tournament.
It improves without retraining. A Meta-review agent distills recurring weaknesses from the reviews and debates and appends that feedback to every agent’s prompt on the next round, so the system learns by updating its context rather than its weights, with no fine-tuning or reinforcement learning. An asynchronous framework lets it spend more test-time compute on a goal, with the Supervisor tracking progress through periodic summary statistics and deciding when a run hits a terminal state. There is no convergence threshold: quality (Elo) never saturated in the paper’s runs, so they ended on a compute budget rather than because the system stopped improving.




Co-Scientist’s multi-agent architecture: a Supervisor agent parses the research goal and assigns the six specialized agents to asynchronous worker processes over a shared context memory, with the scientist able to feed in goals and feedback. Figure 1b from the paper [1].

title: Co-Scientist: Gemini Agents That Generate and Rank Hypotheses
text:
Results
The paper validates Co-Scientist with automated benchmarks and end-to-end wet-lab experiments in three biomedical areas, all run with experts in the loop. [1]

Quality climbs with test-time compute. Across 203 research goals, both the average and best Elo ratings rose the longer the system reasoned, with no sign of saturation.
Beats frontier reasoning models. On 15 expert-curated goals, Co-Scientist’s Elo eventually surpassed Gemini 2.0 Pro and Flash Thinking, OpenAI o1 and o3-mini-high, and DeepSeek R1.
Experts preferred its output. On 11 goals, Co-Scientist scored an average preference rank of 2.36 and novelty and impact ratings of 3.64 and 3.09 out of 5, and was the top pick of all four LLM judges.




Hypothesis quality rises with test-time compute: best and top-10 average Elo climb across reasoning time (a); on 15 expert-curated goals Co-Scientist’s Elo eventually passes the frontier reasoning models (b); and domain experts rated its hypotheses highest on novelty, impact, and overall preference (c). Figure 2 from the paper [1].



AML drug repurposing. Co-Scientist generated repurposing hypotheses across a curated list of 2,300 approved drugs spanning 34 cancer types. After expert oncologists reviewed and ranked its predictions, five candidates were tested in vitro, and three (binimetinib, pacritinib, cerivastatin) inhibited acute myeloid leukemia (AML) cell viability. Binimetinib, approved for metastatic melanoma, reached a half-maximal inhibitory concentration (IC50, the dose that cuts cell survival in half, so lower means more potent) as low as 2 nM in all AML lines but NOMO-1, while leaving a non-leukemia control line largely unharmed.
Novel single-agent candidates. With no prior preclinical evidence or human feedback, Co-Scientist proposed three wholly new picks: nanvuranlat, KIRA6, and leflunomide. KIRA6, which blocks a cellular stress sensor (the enzyme IRE1α), had an 18-fold safety margin: it killed the stem-cell-like KG-1a leukemia cells at one-eighteenth the dose that affected healthy control cells (an IC50 of 10 nM against 180 nM).




Dose-response curves for the AML repurposing candidates: binimetinib, pacritinib, and cerivastatin against MOLM-13 (a-c), and the wholly novel pick KIRA6 across four AML subtypes and the non-AML TK6 control (d-h). Figure 3 from the paper [1].



Synergistic combinations. Co-Scientist also proposed multi-drug regimens, and of seven it suggested, the two- and three-drug combinations were mostly synergistic in one leukemia line (MOLM-13), meaning the drugs together killed more cells than the sum of each alone, while the harder-to-treat KG-1a line responded inconsistently.




Synergy analysis of Co-Scientist’s proposed combinations: the JNJ-64619178 + selinexor dual combination falls well inside the synergy zone in MOLM-13 and KG-1a (a, b), and excess-effect heatmaps for the JQ1 + olaparib + MSA2 triple show synergy in MOLM-13 but antagonism in KG-1a (c, d). Figure 4 from the paper [1].



Liver fibrosis and antimicrobial resistance. In lab-grown mini-livers (hepatic organoids), Co-Scientist proposed three epigenetic targets (genes that switch other genes on or off), and drugs against two of them reduced scarring without harming the tissue (one, vorinostat, is already an approved cancer drug). For antimicrobial resistance, it worked out in about two days how a family of mobile DNA elements that ferry resistance genes between bacteria (cf-PICIs) jump across species, by borrowing the tail proteins of different viruses, matching an unpublished experiment that was running at the same time.

title: Co-Scientist: Gemini Agents That Generate and Rank Hypotheses
text:
My Notes

Both Nature papers point to the same lesson: grounding beats the raw model. Co-Scientist’s own ablation found that giving the Reflection agent access to external search tools is what prevented hallucinated, implausible hypotheses [1] — the gains came from disciplined literature retrieval rather than a bigger base model. FutureHouse’s Robin [2], in Nature the same week, reached the comparable conclusion automating discovery for macular degeneration. Two independently built systems converging on the same point is the part worth remembering.
The Elo curve is self-evaluated. It is scored by the same model that generates the hypotheses, so a rising Elo means later hypotheses beat earlier ones in the model’s own debates — an internal-consistency signal that can optimize for what the judge likes rather than what is true. The only anchor to real quality is the small human-expert correlation on 11 goals. The wet-lab hits are the harder evidence.

title: Karen Hao on Empire of AI: OpenAI, AGI Believers, and a New Colonialism
text:
Thumbnail for Novara Media’s Downstream episode with Karen Hao. Watch on YouTube.
In a June 2025 episode of Novara Media’s Downstream, Aaron Bastani interviews Karen Hao — the MIT Technology Review and Wall Street Journal reporter who covered OpenAI for years — about her book Empire of AI, built on more than 300 interviews, over 150 of them with current and former OpenAI staff. The conversation runs about 90 minutes and is less a tour of the technology than a structural argument: that a handful of AI labs are behaving like the old corporate empires, and that letting a small group concentrate this much power over data, energy, water, and labor is, in Hao’s word, “structurally unsound.”
A few takeaways, each linking to the supporting chapter below:
With the help of AI, I’ve built an enriched transcript at the bottom of this post — the YouTube auto-captions, content-diarized into speaker turns and sliced into the interview’s chapters and finer topic subsections, with inline hyperlinks, acronym expansions, and editor’s-note callouts. See the preamble of that section for what’s verbatim and what’s editorial.
YouTube chapters (jump to the enriched transcript below, or watch on YouTube):

title: Karen Hao on Empire of AI: OpenAI, AGI Believers, and a New Colonialism
text:
Transcript
What’s here is the YouTube auto-caption transcript, reorganized into a reader-friendly form. The dialog itself is verbatim — no words added, cut, or reworded — but several layers of editorial structure have been added on top:

Speaker attribution and chapter + topic outline. This interview’s auto-captions ship with no speaker markers, so the split into Aaron Bastani (host) and Karen Hao (guest) turns was reconstructed by reading the dialog; a stray line may be mislabeled. The 11 YouTube chapters each link to their timestamp and are sliced into finer topic subsections whose titles are editorial summaries, not verbatim quotes. The full outline is in the right-hand sidebar.
Punctuation is editorial. Auto-captions arrive without reliable punctuation, capitalization, or paragraph breaks; those are added here. Obvious mishearings of proper nouns and technical terms are corrected silently — e.g. Karen How → Karen Hao, Sam Alman/Melman → Sam Altman, Ilas Sutskever/Sudskver → Ilya Sutskever, chat GBT → ChatGPT, Enthropic → Anthropic, Peter Teal → Peter Thiel, Satia Nadella → Satya Nadella, BYU → Baidu, Marate Shake → Marietje Schaake, Angus Hansen → Angus Hanton, Jonathan hate → Jonathan Haidt, dolly → DALL·E, Larry and Jihad → Butlerian Jihad.
Inline hyperlinks. First mention of every salient person, company, product, paper, or concept links to an authoritative source.
Bracketed acronym expansions. Where an acronym appears first without being expanded in speech, the expansion is inserted in [square brackets] to mark the addition as editorial.
Editor’s notes in blue callout boxes flag figures and secondhand claims a reader might want to sanity-check, and add background where the dialog asserts something without explaining it.
Numbered references. The one formal paper cited has a [[N]](#ref-N) cite linking to the References block at the bottom.


0:00:00 — Intro
The episode opens cold on a clip pulled from later in the interview, then Aaron Bastani’s scripted voiceover introduction, before the conversation proper begins.
Karen Hao: I went to school with a lot of the people that now build these technologies. I went to school with some of the executives at OpenAI. I don’t find these figures to be towering or magical. Like, I remember when we were walking around dorm rooms together in our pajamas, and it instilled in me this understanding that technology is always a product of human choices.
And different humans will have different blind spots. And if you give a small group of those people too much power to develop technologies that will affect billions of people’s lives, inevitably that is structurally unsound.
Aaron Bastani: Artificial intelligence is the backbone of some of the biggest companies in the world right now. Multi-trillion-dollar companies can talk about nothing else but AI. And of course, whenever it’s discussed in the media, by politicians and civil society, it’s compared invariably to the steam engine. It is going to be the backbone for a new machine age.
Some people are really optimistic about the possibilities it will bring. They are the boosters, the techno-optimists, the techno-utopians. Others are doomers. They’re down on AI. AGI [artificial general intelligence], it’s never going to happen. And if it does, well, it’s going to look like The Matrix, or maybe even The Terminator and Skynet. We don’t want that, do we?
Today’s guest, however, is not speculating about the future. Instead, they’re very much immersed in the present, and indeed the recent past, of the artificial intelligence industry.
Karen Hao went to MIT. She studied mechanical engineering. She knows the STEM [science, technology, engineering, and mathematics] game inside out. But she made a choice to go into journalism and media, to talk about these issues with a fluency and a knowledge that very few people have.
Rather than speculate, what Karen has done with this book is talk to people in the field. 300 interviews with 260 people in the industry, 150 interviews with 90 employees of OpenAI, both past and present. She has access to emails, company Slack channels, the works.
This is the inside account of OpenAI and the perils of artificial intelligence, big tech, and big money coming after, well, pretty much everything. It’s an amazing story told incredibly well. I hope you enjoy this interview.
Karen Hao, welcome to Downstream.
Karen Hao: Thank you so much for having me, Aaron.
Aaron Bastani: It’s a real pleasure to have you on. Right — we say that to everybody, every guest. But I have to say, and this has had rave reviews, even though I’ve lost the dust jacket — Empire of AI, with this huge poem you’ve written, 421 pages, I think, not including the acknowledgements. Really, really interesting book. It’s about AI, this burgeoning industry in the United States around artificial intelligence. That word has been in circulation since the 1950s, I believe.


0:03:11 — AI, deep learning, and machine learning explained

Why “AI” resists definition: a marketing term from 1956
Aaron Bastani: Yeah. Before we drill down into your book — what is AI, and what do people mean by AI when they talk about it in 2025 in Silicon Valley?
Karen Hao: This is — you would think this is the easiest question, but this is always the hardest question that I get, because artificial intelligence is quite poorly defined.
We’ll go back first to 1956, because I feel like it helps understand a little bit about why it’s so poorly defined today. The term was originally coined in 1956 by this Dartmouth professor, assistant professor John McCarthy. And he coined it to draw more attention and more money to research that he was originally doing under a different name.
And that was something he has explicitly said a few decades later. He said, “I invented the term artificial intelligence to get money for a summer study.” And that marketing route to the phrase is part of why it’s really difficult to pin down a specific definition today.
The other reason is because generally people say that AI refers to the concept of recreating human intelligence in computers. But we also don’t have a scientific consensus around what human intelligence is. So quite literally, when people say AI, they’re referring to an umbrella of all these different types of technologies that appear to simulate different human behaviors or human tasks.
But it really ranges from something like Siri on your iPhone all the way to ChatGPT, which behind the scenes are actually really, really different ways of operating. They’re totally different scales in terms of the consumption of the technologies. And of course they often have different use cases as well.






Note



Editor’s note. McCarthy’s “get money for a summer study” line refers to the 1956 Dartmouth Summer Research Project on Artificial Intelligence, the workshop proposal — co-authored with Marvin Minsky, Nathaniel Rochester, and Claude Shannon — that coined the term. McCarthy was an assistant professor at Dartmouth at the time.


Aaron Bastani: So right now, when OpenAI, Meta, when they use those words “AI” in regards to their products specifically — what are they talking about?
Karen Hao: Most often they are now talking about what are called deep learning systems. So these are systems that train on loads of data, and you have software that can statistically compute the patterns in that data, and then that model is used to make decisions, or generate text, or make predictions. So most modern-day AI systems built by companies like Meta, by OpenAI, by Google are now these deep learning systems.
Aaron Bastani: So deep learning is the same as machine learning is the same as neural networks? These are synonyms?
Karen Hao: Deep learning is a subcategory of machine learning. Machine learning refers to a specific branch of AI where you build software that calculates patterns in data. Deep learning is when you’re specifically using neural networks to calculate those patterns.
So — one of the founding fathers of AI used to call AI a “suitcase word.” Because you can put whatever you want in the suitcase, and suddenly AI means something different.
So we have this suitcase word of AI, and then under that, any data-driven AI techniques are called machine learning, and then any neural-network data-driven techniques are called deep learning. So it’s the smallest circle within this broader suitcase word.
Aaron Bastani: So deep learning and neural networks are kind of interchangeable.
Karen Hao: Not exactly, in the sense that neural networks are referring to a piece of software, and deep learning is referring to the process that the software is doing, right?


The “transportation” analogy: politicians who promise “more AI”
Aaron Bastani: Yeah. Do you get upset when politicians — so in this country we have a prime minister called Keir, you know — and they say, “We think the NHS can save, you know, 20% by using AI applications”? Do you sort of think, “My goodness, these people have no idea what they’re talking about,” because that is such an expansive term? Its political convenience is precisely that it doesn’t mean anything.
Karen Hao: It does frustrate me a little bit. I often use the analogy that AI is like the word “transportation.” I mean, transportation can refer to bicycles, or rockets, or self-driving cars, or gas-guzzling trucks — they’re all different modes of transportation, serve different purposes, different cost-benefit analyses.
And you would never have a politician say, “We need more transportation to mitigate climate change.” You would be like, “But what kind of — what are you talking about?” Or, “We need more transportation to stimulate the economy.”
There is a vagueness around the AI discussion that is really unproductive, and I think a lot of that leads to confusion where people think AI equals one thing, and AI equals progress, and so we should just have all of it.
But actually, if we were to use the transportation analogy — you know, having more bicycles, having more public transit, sounds great. But if someone were actually referring to just using rockets to commute from Dublin to London, and we were like, “Everyone should get a rocket now, that’s going to bring us more progress,” you’d be like, “What are you talking about?” And that’s effectively what these companies are doing with general intelligence.
Aaron Bastani: When you’re giving people tools for free with regards to generative AI to just generate stupid images of nonsense — that’s kind of what we’re doing, right? I presume you would take that analogy to that level. It’s like saying, “Let’s use a rocket to get from Dublin to London to Paris.”
Karen Hao: Yeah, exactly. It’s not fit for the task. And the extraordinary amount of environmental costs for flying that rocket, when you could have flown a much more efficient plane to do the same thing, is like — what are you doing?
And that’s one of the things that people don’t really realize about generative AI: the resource consumption required to develop these models, and also to use these models, is quite extraordinary. And oftentimes people are using them for tasks that could be achieved with highly efficient different AI techniques.
But because we use the sweeping term “AI” to mean anything, people just think, “Oh yeah, right, I’m just going to use ChatGPT for my one-stop-shop solution for anything AI-related.”



0:09:27 — Data centres and resource consumption

Projected energy demand: McKinsey’s “half to 1.2 times the UK’s annual consumption”
Aaron Bastani: So right now, data centers globally, I think, are about 3–3.5% of CO₂ emissions. The data centers for AI are a tiny fraction of that, but obviously they’re growing at an extraordinary pace. Are there any numbers out there with regards to projected CO₂ emissions of data centers globally 5, 10, 15 years from now? Or is it so recent that we can’t really speculate about the numbers involved?






Note



Editor’s note. Estimates vary by what’s being counted. Data centers are usually put at roughly 1–1.5% of global electricity use (the IEA’s figure for 2022 was about 1–1.3%, excluding crypto mining); the higher “2–4%” figures generally refer to the broader information-and-communications-technology sector, not data centers alone. Aaron’s “3–3.5% of CO₂ emissions” is at the upper end of what’s typically cited.


Karen Hao: There are numbers around the energy consumption, which you could then use to try and project carbon emissions. There was a McKinsey report that recently projected that, based on the current pace of data center and supercomputer expansion for the development and deployment of AI technologies, we would need to add around half to 1.2 times the amount of energy consumed in the UK annually to the global grid in the next 5 years.
Aaron Bastani: Wow.
Karen Hao: And most of that will be serviced by fossil fuels. This is something that Sam Altman actually even said in front of the Senate a couple of weeks ago. He said it will most probably be natural gas — so he picked the nicest fossil fuel.
But we’re already seeing reports of coal plants having their lives extended. They were meant to be retired, but they’re no longer being retired, explicitly to power data center development.
We’re seeing reports of Elon Musk’s xAI — the giant supercomputer that he built called Colossus, in Memphis, Tennessee — it is being powered with around 35 unlicensed methane gas turbines that are pumping thousands of toxic air pollutants into that community.
So this data center acceleration is not just accelerating the climate crisis; it’s also accelerating the public health crisis of people’s ability to access clean air as well as clean water.






Note



Editor’s note. The Colossus turbine count traces to reporting by the Southern Environmental Law Center, which used aerial imagery to count roughly 35 gas turbines at the Memphis site, many without the Clean Air Act permits the SELC argued were required. xAI has said it brought turbines on site to meet near-term power needs while grid capacity was built out.




Fresh water for cooling, and the Montevideo drought
Karen Hao: One of the aspects that’s really under-talked-about with this kind of AI development — the OpenAI version of AI development — is that these data centers need fresh water to cool, because if they used any other kind of water it would corrode the equipment, it would lead to bacterial growth. And so most often these data centers actually use public drinking water, because when they enter into a community, that is the infrastructure that’s already laid to deliver fresh water to companies, to businesses, to residents.
One of the things that I highlight in my book is there are many communities that do not have sufficient drinking water even for people. I went to Montevideo, Uruguay, to speak with people about a historic level of drought they were experiencing, where the Montevideo government literally did not have enough water to put into the public drinking water supply. So they were mixing toxic waste water in, just so people could have something come out of their taps when they opened them.
And for people that were too poor to buy bottled water, that is what they were drinking. And women were having higher rates of miscarriages, elderly were having an exacerbation of their chronic diseases. And in the middle of that, Google proposed to build a data center that would use more drinking water.
Aaron Bastani: This is potable water, right? You can’t use seawater, because of the saline aspect.
Karen Hao: Exactly. And Bloomberg recently had a story that said two-thirds of the data centers now being built for AI development are in fact going into water[-stressed areas].






Note



Editor’s note. The figure is from a December 2024 Bloomberg investigation, which found that roughly two-thirds of new data centers built or in development since 2022 are in places with high water stress.




“Unlicensed,” and the erosion-of-democracy thesis
Aaron Bastani: You said a moment ago about xAI’s unlicensed energy generation using methane gas. When you say “unlicensed,” what do you mean?
Karen Hao: As in the company just decided to completely ignore existing environmental regulations when they installed those methane gas turbines. And this is actually one of the things that I concluded by the end of my reporting: not only are these companies really corporate empires, but also that if we allow them to be unfettered in their access to resources and unfettered in their expansion, they will ultimately erode democracy. That is the greatest threat of their behaviors.
And what xAI is doing is a perfect example, at the smallest level — these companies are entering into communities and completely hijacking existing laws, existing regulations, existing democratic processes to build the infrastructure for their expansion. And we’re seeing this hijacking of the democratic process at every level, from the smallest local levels all the way to the international level.
Aaron Bastani: It’s that orthodoxy of “seek permission after you do something” — when you start applying this, this is business as usual for those companies. That’s part of their expansion strategy, which we’ll talk about — and we’re going to talk about the sort of global colonial aspect as well with regards to resource consumption, resource use.



0:14:30 — Who are the major players

The players: US labs, the Chinese ecosystem, and Europe’s “tiddlers”
Aaron Bastani: Just to bring it back to the US again, because at the top of this conversation I want to offer a bit of a primer to people out there who maybe know what AI is, maybe have used ChatGPT — what are the major companies we’re now talking about in this space, particularly in the United States, over the last 5 years?
Who are the people in this race to AGI — allegedly artificial general intelligence, something which either might be sentient (probably not) or capable of augmenting its own intelligence (more plausible)? Who are the major players in that field right now?
Karen Hao: One caveat on AGI is that it’s as ill-defined as the term AI, so I like to think of it as just a rebranding. The entire history of AI has just been about rebranding, and the term “deep learning” was also a rebranding. So, anyway.
But the players: first, OpenAI, of course — they were the ones that fired the first shot with ChatGPT. Anthropic, major competitor. Google, Meta, Microsoft — they’re the older internet giants that are now also racing to deploy these technologies. Safe Superintelligence, which spun out of OpenAI — there are many OpenAI splinters — this was founded very recently by the former chief scientist of OpenAI [Ilya Sutskever]. And Thinking Machines Lab, founded very recently by a former chief technology officer of OpenAI.
And Amazon is now trying to get into the game as well, and Apple is also trying to get in the game. So basically all the older-generation tech giants, as well as a new crop of AI players, are all jostling in this space.
Aaron Bastani: And that’s just the US, right?
Karen Hao: And that’s just the US. The Chinese ecosystem is interesting, because they don’t really use the term AGI. This is a very unique thing about the US ecosystem — that there’s a quasi-religious fervor that underpins the construction of AI products and services, whereas in China it’s much more like, these are businesses, we’re building products that users are going to use.
So if you’re just looking at companies building chatbots that are sort of akin to ChatGPT, then we’re talking about ByteDance, owner of TikTok; Alibaba, the equivalent of Amazon; Baidu, the equivalent of Google; Huawei, the equivalent of Apple; and Tencent — what is the equivalent of Tencent? I guess Meta is the equivalent of Tencent. So they’re also building these things. And there’s similarly a crop of startups moving into the generative AI space.
Aaron Bastani: And in Europe, we’ve got the little tiddlers, like Mistral in France — really not at the races, ’cause we’re Europe.

And I think if everyone can actively play a role in every single part of the supply chain that they interface with — which is quite a lot, most people interface with the data part, many people will now have data centers popping up in a community near them, everyone goes to school at some point, everyone works in some kind of office or community at some point — if we do all of this pushback a hundred-thousand-fold, and democratically contest every stage of this AI development and deployment pipeline, I am very optimistic that we will reverse the imperial conquest of these companies and move towards a much more broadly beneficial trajectory for AI development.


Jonathan Haidt’s worry, and a question about Dune
Aaron Bastani: We’ve had big tech, social media for the last 15, 20 years, and I suppose the question is, is the same set of patterns going to apply to this stuff? And I think when you speak to someone like Jonathan Haidt — when he talks about young people and their consumption now of social media and mobile telephones and so on — his real worry is AI.
Karen Hao: Yeah.
Aaron Bastani: And if there is this lax attitude from policymakers and also, let’s be honest, from civil service, civil society, that there was over the last 15, 20 years — I mean, he’s terrified about the implications. So it’s interesting to see that there’s congruence between what you’re saying and what Jonathan Haidt’s saying. Can I ask you one more question: have you ever read Dune by Frank Herbert?
Karen Hao: I’ve watched the movie, and it’s sitting on my bedside table to actually read the original. And I’m so glad that you asked me this, because this is an analogy that I use all the time now to describe the AI world.
Aaron Bastani: Yeah. The Butlerian Jihad.


True believers and the “ideological black hole”
Karen Hao: So one of the things that was so shocking to me — because we already talked about this quasi-religious fervor within the AI community — I was interviewing people whose voice was quivering when they were telling me about the profound, cataclysmic changes on the horizon. These are very visceral reactions. These are true believers.
And Dune strikes me as a really good analogy for understanding this ecosystem, because Paul Atreides’ mom in the story creates this myth to help position Paul as a supreme leader, and to ultimately control the population. And the people who encounter this myth, they don’t know that it’s a creation. So they’re just true believers. And at some point, Paul gets so wrapped up in his own mythology that he starts to forget that it was originally a creation.
And this is essentially what I felt like I was seeing with my interviews of people in the AI world — because I had the opportunity to start interviewing people all the way back in 2019. I interviewed some people back then, and for the book, to map out their trajectory — and there were non-believers back then that are true believers now. If they were able to stay long enough at that company, they all in the end become true believers in this AGI religion.
And so there’s this vortex — it’s like a black hole, an ideological black hole. I don’t know how to explain it, but people, when they swim too long in the water, it just becomes them.






Note



Editor’s note. For readers who haven’t read Dune: Paul Atreides’ mother, Lady Jessica, belongs to the Bene Gesserit sisterhood, whose “Missionaria Protectiva” had seeded messianic legends across the galaxy — so when the Atreides arrive on Arrakis, the locals are primed to read Paul as the prophesied “Lisan al-Gaib,” the off-world voice. The Butlerian Jihad Aaron mentions is the earlier holy war against thinking machines in Herbert’s backstory, the reason computers are banned in the Dune universe — an apt reach for an interview about AI as religion.


Aaron Bastani: So what you’re saying is, Sam Altman is the Lisan al-Gaib.
Karen Hao: That’s the character, and—
Aaron Bastani: And Paul Graham maybe was the—
Karen Hao: It would seem like that would be the most appropriate character to assign to him. Yeah.
Aaron Bastani: Wow. This has been fabulous. And I have to say, honestly, the book is really, really exceptional — Empire of AI. I read it so much that dust jacket, I think my daughter actually ripped it off. But anyway, it is a sensational book. Sensational journalism, fantastic journalist. We don’t have enough of those in the world.
Karen Hao: Thank you.
Aaron Bastani: Real pleasure to meet you, Karen. Thanks so much for joining us.
