title: Who Will Actually Thrive in the Hybrid AI-Human Work Force?
text:
Illustration by Mario Hugo for The New York Times.
The New York Times Magazine put four people who mostly disagree in a room and asked them a concrete question: if you are a college student today, or any worker watching this happen, how should you prepare for the AI future of work? The full discussion is at the Times (gift link). The panel:
The discussion was moderated by Bill Wasik, editor of the Science desk at the Times. The setting is a season of college commencements where graduates booed speakers who talked up AI, set against entry-level layoffs in the headlines and “learn to code” quietly retired as a guaranteed path.
What follows is a thematic summary of the discussion, with the salient exchanges quoted; the editing and condensing are the Magazine’s.

title: Who Will Actually Thrive in the Hybrid AI-Human Work Force?
section: The “Marcus Chen” problem: how capable, how fast?
text:
The “Marcus Chen” problem: how capable, how fast?
The panel keeps returning to one image, from a habit of Mollick’s: asking the models to describe their own future. The scenario keeps degrading under his questioning: Marcus Chen (a stock chatbot name for a developer) first “goes into the office” to direct his AI agents; asked why he’d commute when the agents do the work, the model retreats to a beach house he checks in from; pressed on why he’d check in at all, it finally settles on “Marcus Chen sits at the beach. …” The joke sets up the real question, which Mollick states plainly:

Mollick: A lot of this comes down to the question of which kind of world we’re in. Is it one where AI is a fairly normal-ish technology and change comes more slowly, or is it a world where AI actually becomes super capable?

His leading example is the one closest to home, programming, where “being a coder” went from “writing good code on a regular basis” to “managing engineering tasks” in the span of months.
Shih takes the beach scenario at face value and asks the obvious follow-up: “He’s on the beach, he’s having a great life. But what about the other workers? It is now faster, more efficient to have fewer cooks in the kitchen.” Acemoglu sharpens it into the question that organizes the rest of the panel:

Acemoglu: How many Marcus Chens can the American economy employ? It’s just not realistic to think that 100 million people will work like Marcus Chen.

The counter-case is Ball’s, and it is a case for slowness. He is bullish on the technology and bearish on the drama:

Ball: The transformation that’s coming is going to take place in the world as it is familiar to us today, and every single day will feel familiar. And there’ll be tiny, tiny changes along the margin. … And 10, 15, 20 years later, we’ll look back and we’ll say, My god, everything is different. But you’ll never notice it happening.

His reasoning is that the jobs everyone worries about are already heavily automated (sending an email, writing code, running a mine), so taking the human out of one more loop is a small slice of the total cost. Acemoglu’s rejoinder targets the central assumption of the agent era:

Acemoglu: The current view is that somehow agents are going to do a lot of the work and we just need to supervise them. I find that very unrealistic. But if it was realistic, it would be a horrible thing.

Shih, who is in the middle of building a startup, splits the difference from experience. The agent tooling let her incorporate, file IRS and California paperwork, and write a privacy policy in days with almost no staff, work that “in the past, we would have needed to hire dozens of people and engage with multiple external law firms” over months. Her verdict is deliberately two-sided: “AI displacement is realistic and real, and it’s both horrible and wonderful.”
Mollick adds the upside (early GPT-4 work that helped Kenyan entrepreneurs) but Acemoglu immediately names the catch: economics’ “excess entry” problem, where cheap access to a profession floods it past the point of being worth anyone’s while. And Mollick closes the section with the practical brake on all the disruption talk: the Walmarts and Coca-Colas of the world have no plan to reorganize around agents, “and that gives us time to react.”






Note



The Kenya study. Mollick is pointing to a field experiment that gave small-business owners in Kenya a GPT-4–based mentoring assistant. The headline finding was uneven: high performers improved while low performers did slightly worse: the assistant amplified existing skill rather than closing the gap.

title: Who Will Actually Thrive in the Hybrid AI-Human Work Force?
section: Which jobs, beyond the tech bubble
text:
Which jobs, beyond the tech bubble
Wasik pushes the panel out of software, and Shih answers with three personas that extend the question beyond tech. First, the shape of the problem, via Amazon: a million-plus workers, a thin “elite group” of coders and supervisors at HQ, and everyone else in the warehouse or driving, “managed to the minute.” Then the two workers nobody puts on a panel:

Shih: Let’s talk about Stacey Smith, a hypothetical health insurance claims adjuster. She and millions of people like her are employed in the U.S. in insurance and banking because of regulatory reasons that those jobs could not be off-shored. But now a lot of those approvals, whether it’s mortgage underwriting or claims adjusting, are easily done by AI agents … What about Bob Johnson? … He is one of three and a half million truck drivers in the U.S. who again make a decent wage. They live in the South … They are the breadwinners for their family. … What happens when the Waymo technology diffuses and we get past regulatory barriers to the Bob Johnsons?

Her point is that the regulatory moat that kept Stacey employed is exactly the kind of barrier agents are built to dissolve, and the geographic concentration means the pain lands hard in specific places.
Ball agrees on the white-collar targets (“consulting, marketing, customer service, entry-level legal work, administrative work … definitely real”) but draws two limits. One is preference, not capability: “I’m kind of doubtful that a humanoid robot’s going to be making you a cocktail at a bar, even if it could. People don’t want that.” The other is that a lot of senior knowledge work is really persuasion and internal politics, which he doubts gets automated away.
Mollick points to a Procter & Gamble experiment where AI didn’t just speed people up, it dissolved the boundary between roles:

Mollick: Business people used to have business ideas, tech people came up with technical ideas. But add AI, and everyone comes up with ideas in between each other.







Note



The P&G study. This is the field experiment written up as “The Cybernetic Teammate”: 776 Procter & Gamble professionals worked real product-innovation tasks alone or in pairs, with or without AI. Individuals with AI matched two-person teams without it, and the commercial/technical role boundary blurred whenever AI was in the loop.


Acemoglu turns the question around to the sectors that actually move the productivity needle (manufacturing, health care, education), and argues each is a bottleneck rather than a quick win. Manufacturing automation “requires a huge amount of engineering services” per step; health care’s last digitization wave (electronic health records) lowered productivity; and education, in his telling, is already the warning: “There’s a nice large-scale study coming out from China … which shows horrible, horrible outcomes from students who use AI.” His fear is that health care repeats the education mistake: “unleashing chatbots in a way that really leads to horrible outcomes.”






Note



The education claim. Acemoglu doesn’t name the study, and “coming out from China” doesn’t correspond to a specific identifiable paper. The closest documented large-scale evidence that unstructured student AI use harms learning is a high-school mathematics randomized controlled trial (RCT) in Turkey: students given GPT-4 without guardrails did worse on later unaided tests, while a guardrailed tutor version avoided the harm [“Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning,” PNAS 2025].


Ball and Mollick push back on the framing itself. Ball: “if all we had were chatbots, I would probably share your pessimism. But … the new coding agents are essentially computer programs that can use computers.” Mollick goes further (“I don’t think we’re talking about chatbots anymore”) and points to AI outperforming doctors on diagnosis in many settings and to evidence that structured AI tutors help even where unstructured use hurts. The disagreement is less about the data than about whether today’s failures are intrinsic or a deployment problem we haven’t solved yet.






Note



Diagnosis and tutoring. On diagnosis: in a randomized study, GPT-4 on its own scored higher on diagnostic reasoning than physicians did with or without it [“Large Language Model Influence on Diagnostic Reasoning,” JAMA Network Open 2024]. On tutoring: a physics RCT at Harvard found students learned more from a well-designed AI tutor than from an active-learning class [“AI tutoring outperforms in-class active learning,” Scientific Reports 2025]. That is the “structured” half of Mollick’s point; the “unstructured use hurts” half is the Turkey RCT in the note above.

title: Who Will Actually Thrive in the Hybrid AI-Human Work Force?
section: Advice for young workers: experience is the scarce input
text:
Advice for young workers: experience is the scarce input
Asked what to tell a young person, the panel produces the predictable answers and then dismantles them. Ball likes “curious generalists” and the skilled trades: “plumbing and electricians and HVAC technicians.” Mollick won’t even grant that: “I also don’t think we can predict well enough to say, Go be a plumber, because then the Plumbot10000 could come out in a couple of weeks.” Acemoglu agrees the trades get more complex and more valuable, with a caveat that doubles as his thesis for the whole panel: “that’s not where the center of gravity of the investments in AI are going.”
Shih reframes it as distribution rather than category. From spending her days with 25-year-olds, she sees “a tale of two cities”: “Those who know how AI works, specifically AI agents, can get their dream job … Those who don’t have those skills, those entry-level jobs are disappearing.” Her concrete prescription is to own a side project end to end, because “it is very difficult to then really understand and stay in control of AI if you don’t learn something end to end.”
Mollick’s concern is why the entry-level rung is the one breaking. Judgment is downstream of experience, and experience is what the bottom rung used to provide:

Mollick: What I really worry about with junior workers is that field experience is often crucial to evaluating work you didn’t create yourself, whether it comes from humans or AI … Daron or I can look at an academic paper instantly and say whether it’s going to be worth an hour of our time to read or not. Dean can scan a piece of AI legislation and spot the loophole. Clara can … look at any bit of code and judge whether it was written by an idiot or an expert. If you have no experience, you can’t do those things.

This is the apprenticeship problem, and Mollick names it as such: the model that built that judgment “worked for 4,000 years” and “all collapsed,” because firms have stopped hiring the juniors who did the grunt work that the assessment depended on. His one structural hope is that universities are “actually quite good at training and assessing” and could extend professional education into the gap AI is opening.
Two qualifications temper the advice. Mollick, who has assigned side projects for a decade, notes they are “not for everyone”: uptake varies sharply by background and socioeconomic status. And Acemoglu rejects the steady state Shih describes as livable. The treadmill of relearning which model does what every quarter just to stay in place is, to him, the tell that something has gone wrong:

Acemoglu: Right now, you have to spend a lot of time learning different models, their capabilities, their shortcomings, and then three months later you have to experiment with lots of different models again in order to just stay where you are. That is absolutely not productive, that’s very dystopian. … To me, that’s a horrible future.

Shih’s answer is the question the rest of the panel is really about: “I said earlier that it’s wonderful and horrible. How do we make it less horrible and more wonderful?”

title: Who Will Actually Thrive in the Hybrid AI-Human Work Force?
section: What to do: coordination versus the Industrial Revolution
text:
What to do: coordination versus the Industrial Revolution
The policy exchange is where the disagreement stops being about forecasts and becomes about values. Ball, who helped draft the White House’s 2025 AI action plan, wants measurement before remedies (“You can’t create policy remedies for a problem you don’t understand”) and is openly hostile to broad consultation:

Ball: Now the pope seems to want us to have a committee of all the AI stakeholders, all the impacted communities. But we didn’t create a stakeholder committee for the Industrial Revolution. It didn’t unfold by show of hands.

Acemoglu takes the analogy and turns it over to show the underside:

Acemoglu: Yeah, there was no committee for the direction of the Industrial Revolution. And what did we get? In the early stages, we got children working to death in coal mines. Conditions in factories became horrible. Wages for many workers fell. Now AI is changing things much faster and affecting many, many sectors at the same time.

Shih answers both at once: “the lesson isn’t that coordination is unnecessary; it’s that skipping it costs us decades of human suffering.” She adds a legitimacy point: policy “that emerges without broad input will not be trusted, as it will be perceived to represent the agenda of big tech, capital or one political faction.”
Ball’s own forecast cuts against his preferred policy:

Ball: I don’t know what the unemployment rate will be in 2028, but I guarantee you that 100 percent of it is going to be blamed on AI.

His worry is that the backlash produces European-style labor rigidity, enacted not in Washington but across “50 different state houses” while everyone pretends to understand what’s happening. Shih reads the same backlash as a reason to act now rather than wait: the Eric Schmidt commencement reaction, a Gallup poll finding a third of Gen Z describe their feelings toward AI as anger, because “these are people we want embracing AI.” and instead “they’re rejecting it on a moral basis.”
Two closing points. Acemoglu’s is a design argument against the whole “automate everything” framing: that AI and human intelligence are simply different kinds of thing.

Acemoglu: When two things are different, the last thing you want is to try to mimic one with the other. … They should work together. And those aren’t the kinds of models we’re trying to develop.

Shih returns to where the panel began:

Shih: The key thing about AI agents is that they all have a goal. And it depends on who deploys it, because whoever deploys it gets to set the goal. … But that’s a choice we can make.

The panel splits on speed, on which jobs, and on whether to coordinate. Its one point of convergence is Shih’s: the goals AI serves depend on who deploys it.

Related Posts

Daron Acemoglu on AI, Jobs, and Liberal Democracy — Acemoglu’s longer-form case for the same position he argues here: today’s AI is pointed at replacing rather than augmenting workers, and the productivity gains aren’t showing up. title: Policy on the AI Exponential
text:
The essay’s title card. Image from darioamodei.com.
Dario Amodei, Anthropic’s CEO, argues that AI capability is racing ahead of the institutions meant to govern it, and uses a new essay to lay out what governments should do across five policy areas before the gap widens. The essay opens with Treebeard, the ponderous tree who takes a full day to say hello while his forest is cut down.
The essay covers five policy areas:
Along with the essay, Anthropic released a legislative proposal on frontier-model testing and a policy framework for job displacement, both with promised financial backing. The essay summarizes the testing proposal in five elements, with the full version published as Anthropic’s Advanced AI Framework:

title: Policy on the AI Exponential
section: The US Suspends Fable 5 and Mythos 5
text:
The US Suspends Fable 5 and Mythos 5
Shortly after the essay, its argument about blocking deployments got a real-world test. On June 12, 2026, the US government issued an export-control directive, citing national security, ordering Anthropic to suspend all access to its newest models, Claude Fable 5 and Mythos 5, for any foreign national inside or outside the country, including the company’s own foreign-national employees. To comply, Anthropic disabled both models for every customer. Its other models were not affected.
The government’s stated concern was a technique for jailbreaking Fable 5. Anthropic says it reviewed the demonstration and found only a few minor, previously known vulnerabilities that other public models, including OpenAI’s GPT-5.5, can find without any bypass. It is complying with the order but disagrees that a narrow jailbreak should justify recalling a model already deployed to hundreds of millions of people, and argues that the same standard applied across the industry would halt frontier deployment altogether.
The essay had argued that the government should be able to block unsafe deployments, but only through a statutory process that is “transparent, fair, clear, and grounded in technical facts.” Anthropic’s statement on the directive says the action “does not adhere to those principles.”

title: How Artificial Analysis Builds Its Intelligence Index
text:
Independent analysis of AI. Image from Artificial Analysis.
Artificial Analysis is an independent benchmarking outfit that ranks language models, and it publishes the full methodology behind its main metric, the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index. The page documents every evaluation in the index, how each is weighted and scored, and the exact testing parameters, down to sampling temperature and retry handling.

title: How Artificial Analysis Builds Its Intelligence Index
text:
How the index works
The Intelligence Index (currently version 4.1) is a single 0–100 score built as a weighted average of nine evaluations across four categories. It is a text-only, English-language suite, and Artificial Analysis estimates a 95% confidence interval of under ±1% on the overall score. The nine weights sum to 100%, and the further benchmarks Artificial Analysis runs (multilingual, visual, mathematical, and several legacy evaluations) are reported separately and not counted in the index.

Four stated principles: every model is run under identical conditions (standardized); answer extraction is built to avoid penalizing valid output variations (unbiased); prompts give instructions without worked examples (zero-shot); and the full method, prompts, and limitations are published (transparent).
The nine evaluations and their weights, grouped by category:

Agents (34%): GDPval-AA v2 (20%), agentic completion of economically valuable tasks across 44 US occupations, with file outputs ranked into an Elo; and τ³-Banking (14%), a fintech customer-support agent built on Sierra’s τ-Knowledge framework that must combine knowledge retrieval with multi-step account changes.
Coding (24%): Terminal-Bench v2.1 (16%), 89 terminal tasks spanning software engineering, system administration, data processing, model training, and security, run through an agent in a sandbox; and SciCode (8%), Python scientific-computing problems scored by unit tests.
Scientific Reasoning (24%): Humanity’s Last Exam (12%), 2,158 open-answer frontier academic questions; GPQA Diamond (6%), 198 graduate-level Google-proof science questions; and CritPt (6%), 70 unpublished research-level physics problems.
General (18%): AA-Omniscience (12%), 6,000 questions over 42 topics scored by an index that rewards correct answers, penalizes hallucinations, and leaves abstentions neutral; and AA-LCR (6%), long-context reasoning over roughly 100,000-token document sets.

Testing parameters: temperature is 0 for non-reasoning models and 0.6 for reasoning models unless a lab recommends otherwise. Non-reasoning models get 16,384 output tokens, while reasoning models get their full disclosed budget. Failed API calls retry up to 30 times, and questions that never succeed are reviewed by hand and dropped.
Scoring and contamination handling: most evaluations use pass@1 averaged over one to five repeats, while GDPval-AA v2 uses an Elo from a three-judge panel, fit with a Bradley-Terry model and anchored to human experts at 1000. Artificial Analysis keeps internal copies of every dataset, and reports cost from provider-side token counts while standardizing performance on a client-side tokenizer.

title: How Artificial Analysis Builds Its Intelligence Index
text:
Current results
As of June 2026, the Intelligence Index (v4.1) is led by Claude Fable 5, Claude Opus 4.8, and GPT-5.5, with a long tail of frontier models close behind.



The Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index (v4.1): the weighted 0–100 score across all nine evaluations. Image from Artificial Analysis.


The single score resolves into different profiles underneath, and Artificial Analysis also publishes category sub-indices. The Agentic Index averages the two agent benchmarks, GDPval-AA v2 and τ³-Banking:



The Artificial Analysis Agentic Index: the average of the GDPval-AA v2 and τ³-Banking agent benchmarks. Image from Artificial Analysis.


The Coding Index averages Terminal-Bench v2.1 and SciCode, and the ranking shifts from the overall order, with GPT-5.5 moving up to second behind Claude Fable 5:



The Artificial Analysis Coding Index: the weighted average of Terminal-Bench v2.1 and SciCode. Image from Artificial Analysis.

title: How Artificial Analysis Builds Its Intelligence Index
text:
My Notes

Closed models lead all three indices: Claude Fable 5, Claude Opus 4.8, and GPT-5.5, all proprietary, take the top three on the overall index and on the agentic and coding sub-indices alike. The strongest open-weight model, GLM-5.2 from Zhipu, reaches fourth on the overall Intelligence Index, about nine points behind the leader. The open weights fall a clearer step behind on the agentic and coding charts, so the gap that has nearly closed on the broad knowledge-and-reasoning mix is still wide on the longer-horizon agentic and coding work.
All four are reasoning models. Beyond that, disclosure differs sharply:

Claude Fable 5 (Anthropic): proprietary weights, no published parameter count or architecture.
Claude Opus 4.8 (Anthropic): proprietary weights, no published parameter count or architecture.
GPT-5.5 (OpenAI): proprietary weights, no published parameter count or architecture.
GLM-5.2 (Zhipu): open weights, 753B total parameters, a sparse mixture of experts (256 routed experts plus one shared, 8 active per token, 78 layers).

The method has limitations:

The weighting is an editorial choice: the index is a weighted average, and the weights reflect a judgment about what matters rather than a measurement. Agents are weighted most heavily, with GDPval-AA v2 alone a fifth of the score, so anyone comparing models on the one number inherits that bet. Ethayarajh and Jurafsky argued years ago that a leaderboard should let each reader set their own weights instead of shipping one ranking for everyone.
Several components are public benchmarks: Humanity’s Last Exam, GPQA Diamond, SciCode, and Terminal-Bench are all openly available, so training-data contamination is a live risk. The defenses are internal copies of every dataset and the evaluations Artificial Analysis built itself, a weaker defense than the post-cutoff, unpublished questions the Leipzig math benchmark used to stay out of the training data.
An LLM panel grades the heaviest evaluation: GDPval-AA v2, the largest single component, scores agentic deliverables by an Elo from a panel of three frontier model judges, anchored to human experts at 1000. The panel reduces the bias any single judge would bring, but the score still measures what frontier models agree is good work, which can differ from what a human expert would rank first.
The compared models are black boxes: the closed leaders disclose neither parameter count nor architecture, so the index ranks delivered capability without controlling for model size, design, or training compute. Only the open-weight entrants publish those details, and cost per task, which Artificial Analysis reports separately, is the nearest proxy for what a score costs to reach.

title: How Artificial Analysis Builds Its Intelligence Index
text:
Related Posts

Utility Is in the Eye of the User: the case that benchmark utility is user-specific and leaderboards should let readers set their own weights, a direct counterpoint to collapsing nine evaluations into one fixed-weight index.
Benchmarks in Leipzig: a benchmark built from fresh, post-cutoff, unpublished questions to resist contamination, the stronger defense the public components of this index lack.
Mapping Global Dynamics of Benchmark Creation and Saturation in AI: the create-then-saturate cycle that explains why an index has to keep swapping in harder evaluations to stay informative.
Anthropic Economic Index: another attempt to measure model capability on economically valuable work, and a reminder that a metric designed not to saturate (time horizon) is a different bet than a fixed-question score.

title: My 84th Half Marathon Through Redmond Watershed Preserve
text:
This Long Run Sunday I ran an accidental HM, and it was my 84th!
My goal was to just run 10mi, because I already ran ~14mi two days ago to Alki beach, and 7mi yesterday including my 103rd parkrun. Plan was simple: 4mi run to a nearby McDonald’s to get my ice cream and iced coffee fix, and then wander around until I hit 10mi!

All told, the damage done was 14.40mi with moving time 2:28:23 pace 10’18”/mi, and EG 1,269ft! And I closed this week with the highest weekly mileage and EG year-to-date: 69.45mi and 3,793ft!
But who cares — those beautiful sights are part of my happy memories now! 🙂
Oh and happy summer and happy father’s day!

title: Dive into Claude Code: The Design Space of Today’s and Future AI Agent Systems
text:
High-level structure of Claude Code: a user prompt enters through the interfaces, the agent loop calls the model and proposes actions, the permission system allows, asks, or denies each one, tools run against the execution environment (files, shell, web, MCP), and state is loaded and persisted around the loop. Figure 1 from the paper [1].
In Dive into Claude Code: The Design Space of Today’s and Future AI Agent Systems [1] (arXiv preprint, April 2026), Jiacheng Liu, Xiaohan Zhao, Xinyi Shang, and Zhiqiang Shen (MBZUAI + UCL) reverse-engineer the published TypeScript of Claude Code and trace its architecture from five stated values down to specific source files.

title: Dive into Claude Code: The Design Space of Today’s and Future AI Agent Systems
section: How the paper reads the code
text:
How the paper reads the code
The paper is a source-level reverse-engineering, not an empirical study. The authors extract the TypeScript of Claude Code v2.1.88 from its published npm package, read it directly, and compare it against OpenClaw, an open-source multi-channel assistant that answers the same design questions in a different deployment context. To keep an analysis of closed, minified code honest, every claim is tagged with one of three evidence tiers:

Tier A (product-documented): drawn from Anthropic’s official documentation and engineering posts.
Tier B (code-verified): tied to specific files and functions in the extracted v2.1.88 source. The paper treats this as its strongest tier.
Tier C (reconstructed): inferred from code patterns, community analysis, or the OpenClaw comparison, and explicitly marked as inference.

The analysis is built around a few recurring design questions put to any agent system: where reasoning lives, how many execution engines run, what the default safety posture is, and what the binding resource constraint is. Claude Code’s answers are traced through source files, then organized into a chain from values to principles to implementation.

title: Dive into Claude Code: The Design Space of Today’s and Future AI Agent Systems
text:
Five values, thirteen principles
The paper reads five human values as motivating the architecture: human decision authority, safety and security, reliable execution, capability amplification, and contextual adaptability. Those values are traced through thirteen design principles to concrete code. Table 1 lists the thirteen, the values each serves, and the design-space question each answers.



Design principles, the values they serve, and the design-space question each answers. Table 1 from the paper [1].


A sixth concern is kept separate from the five, used as an evaluative lens rather than a design driver: whether the architecture preserves long-term human capability. The authors note this is not prominent in Anthropic’s stated values, but flag it because the evidence is real. They cite a “paradox of supervision,” where over-reliance on the agent erodes the skills needed to supervise it, and a study finding developers in AI-assisted conditions score 17% lower on comprehension tests.

title: Dive into Claude Code: The Design Space of Today’s and Future AI Agent Systems
text:
Seven components, five layers
The architecture is deliberately lopsided. Figure 1 (the cover) gives the high-level shape: seven functional components (the user, the interfaces, the agent loop, the permission system, the tools, state and persistence, and the execution environment), with every entry point feeding into one agent loop at the center. The reasoning lives entirely in the model, reached through that single loop, so the loop itself is close to trivial: call the model, run any tools it requests, feed the results back, repeat until it stops asking for tools. Almost all of the code is in the systems wrapped around the loop, which the paper sorts into five layers:

Surface layer: entry points (the interactive and headless CLIs, the Agent SDK, IDE and browser front-ends) and rendering.
Core layer: the agent loop and the compaction pipeline.
Safety/action layer: the permission system and its auto-mode classifier, the hook pipeline, extensibility, built-in and MCP tools, the shell sandbox, and subagent spawning.
State layer: context assembly, runtime state, session persistence, the CLAUDE.md and memory hierarchy, and sidechain transcripts.
Backend layer: execution backends and external resources.




The five-layer decomposition of Claude Code’s architecture. Figure 3 from the paper [1].

title: Dive into Claude Code: The Design Space of Today’s and Future AI Agent Systems
text:
One turn through the loop
A single turn is a fixed pipeline in query.ts, written as an async generator so output streams to the interface while control flow stays single-threaded. The prompt enters through context assembly, the model is called, each tool request passes the permission gate (allow, ask, or deny, with deny feedback looped back to the model), results return, and the loop repeats until a turn produces no tool use and the assistant replies. The paper fills in the mechanics:

Tool dispatch is concurrent-read, serial-write: read-only calls run in parallel as they stream in, state-modifying calls like shell commands are serialized, and results are buffered and returned in the order the model requested them. If one Bash call errors, a sibling abort controller kills the other in-flight subprocesses.
Five context shapers run in sequence before every model call, cheapest first: budget reduction (caps oversized tool results), snip (trims old history), microcompact (fine-grained, cache-aware compression), context collapse (a read-time projection that hides summarized history without deleting it), and auto-compact (a full model-generated summary, fired only if the context still exceeds the pressure threshold after the other four).
Recovery is layered too: escalate the output-token cap up to three times a turn, reactive compaction near capacity, prompt-too-long handling that tries overflow recovery before giving up, a streaming fallback, and a fallback model.
Stop conditions: a turn ends on text with no tool use (the normal case), a max-turns limit, context overflow, a PostToolUse hook halting continuation, or an explicit abort.

The loop is reactive, in the ReAct style: each turn runs one action sequence with no backtracking, trading search completeness for simplicity and latency.



One agentic turn end to end, from user prompt through context assembly, the model call, the permission gate, and compaction, to the assistant response. Figure 2 from the paper [1].

title: Dive into Claude Code: The Design Space of Today’s and Future AI Agent Systems
text:
Permission and safety
Every tool call passes a permission gate before it runs. The default posture is deny-first with human escalation: deny rules override ask rules override allow rules, and an unrecognized action is escalated to the user rather than run silently. Seven permission modes span a graduated autonomy spectrum from plan (approve every plan first) through default and acceptEdits to bypassPermissions. The authorization pipeline runs pre-filtering, a PreToolUse hook, rule evaluation, then the permission handler, and an auto-mode machine-learning classifier adds a two-stage fast filter plus a chain-of-thought safety judgment on each call. Shell commands run in a sandbox. Because reasoning and enforcement sit on separate code paths, a compromised or adversarially manipulated model cannot override the sandbox, the permission checks, or the deny-first rules in the harness.

title: Dive into Claude Code: The Design Space of Today’s and Future AI Agent Systems
section: Four ways to extend the loop
text:
Four ways to extend the loop
The four extension mechanisms attach at different points of the loop and cost different amounts of context:

Hooks: intercept the tool lifecycle (zero context cost).
Skills: inject domain instructions (low cost).
Plugins: bundle components for distribution (medium cost).
MCP (Model Context Protocol): connect external tool servers (high cost).

The paper’s reading is that no single mechanism can span the range from a zero-context lifecycle hook to a schema-heavy tool server without forcing trade-offs on extension authors. The graduated cost ordering lets cheap extensions scale widely while the expensive ones are reserved for cases that genuinely need new tools.

title: Dive into Claude Code: The Design Space of Today’s and Future AI Agent Systems
text:
Context and memory
The context window (200K tokens on older models, 1M on the Claude 4.6 series) is named as the binding constraint, and the memory design is built around it. Figure 6 lays out the sources that converge on the window, grouped into six layers and ordered by how mutable each is and when it loads.



Context construction and the memory hierarchy: sources converging on the context window, by mutability and load time. Figure 6 from the paper [1].


The layers run from a read-only system layer (system prompt, environment info, output styles, MCP tool names) loaded at startup, through hot-reloading project config (the five-level CLAUDE.md hierarchy and path-scoped rules), a memory layer (auto memory and the compact summary that replaces long history), the conversation itself (history and subagent summaries), runtime state appended during the turn (file reads, command outputs, tool results), and a lazy on-demand layer (deferred tool definitions pulled in via ToolSearch only when needed). The window is therefore not fixed at assembly time but grows as the turn runs.
The compaction pipeline has five layers because no single strategy covers every kind of context pressure. Budget reduction targets individual oversized tool outputs, snip handles temporal depth, microcompact reacts to cache overhead, context collapse manages very long histories, and auto-compact does semantic compression as a last resort. Each layer operates at a different cost-benefit point, and the cheaper ones run first.

title: Dive into Claude Code: The Design Space of Today’s and Future AI Agent Systems
text:
Subagents and session storage
A subagent is spawned through the same tool factory as everything else, re-entering the query loop with its own isolated context window and permission scope, optionally inside a git worktree. Only its final response text returns to the parent. The full subagent history never enters the parent’s window, which keeps the parent’s context cheap.
Session storage is append-only (history, sidechains, checkpoints), favoring auditability over query power. Resume and fork restore messages but deliberately not session-scoped permissions, so a resumed session does not silently inherit trust the user granted earlier.

title: Dive into Claude Code: The Design Space of Today’s and Future AI Agent Systems
text:
Claude Code versus OpenClaw
The OpenClaw contrast is the part that generalizes. OpenClaw is a local-first WebSocket gateway daemon that connects roughly two dozen messaging channels (WhatsApp, Telegram, Slack, Discord, Signal, and others) to an embedded agent runtime. Where Claude Code is an ephemeral per-session CLI coding harness bound to one repository, OpenClaw is a persistent control plane for multi-channel personal assistance. Posed the same six design questions, it answers them differently because its deployment context differs. Table 3 lines them up:








Dimension
Claude Code
OpenClaw




System scope
CLI/IDE coding harness; ephemeral per-session process
Persistent WebSocket gateway daemon; multi-channel control plane


Trust model
Deny-first per-action rule evaluation with hooks and an optional ML classifier; seven permission modes; graduated trust spectrum
Single trusted operator per gateway; DM pairing and allowlists for inbound channels; opt-in sandboxing with configurable scope and multiple backends


Agent runtime
Iterative async generator (queryLoop()) as the system center
Agent runner embedded inside the gateway’s RPC dispatch; per-session queue serialization


Extension architecture
Four mechanisms at graduated context costs: MCP, plugins, skills, hooks
Manifest-first plugin system with twelve capability types and a central registry; separate skills layer; built-in MCP


Memory and context
CLAUDE.md four-level hierarchy; five-layer compaction pipeline; LLM-based memory scan
Workspace bootstrap files; a separate memory system (daily notes, optional “dreaming” for long-term promotion); auto-compaction with pluggable providers; optional hybrid vector + keyword search


Multi-agent and routing
Task-delegating subagents (Explore, Plan, general-purpose); worktree isolation; only the final response returns to the parent
Multi-agent routing with isolated agents and channel dispatch, plus sub-agent delegation with configurable nesting depth



The trust boundary is in different places. Claude Code puts it between the model and the execution environment, while OpenClaw puts it at the gateway perimeter, assuming a single trusted operator and explicitly not supporting hostile multi-tenant isolation. Claude Code’s extensions change what one agent can do, while OpenClaw’s plugins add capabilities across every agent on the gateway. The two are not purely alternatives: OpenClaw can host Claude Code (and OpenAI Codex, and Gemini CLI) as an external coding harness through its Agent Client Protocol integration, so they stack.

title: Dive into Claude Code: The Design Space of Today’s and Future AI Agent Systems
text:
What the analysis concludes
The discussion reads the architecture as a set of consistent choices rather than a grab-bag:

Minimal scaffolding, rich harness: the system invests in deterministic infrastructure (context management, tool routing, recovery) instead of decision scaffolding like explicit planners or state graphs, on the premise that a more capable model gains more from a rich operating environment than from a framework that constrains its choices.
Graduated layering over single switches: permission modes, compaction layers, and extension points are all spectrums rather than one-shot mechanisms.
Append-only over queryable: state favors an auditable log over a mutable store that would be easier to query.
Model judgment inside a deterministic harness: probabilistic guidance (CLAUDE.md) is kept on a separate code path from deterministic enforcement (permission rules).
A trust trajectory, not a fixed state: autonomy is “co-constructed” over time, with auto-approve rates rising from about 20% under 50 sessions to over 40% by 750, so the design targets a relationship that loosens as trust builds.
What it deliberately does not do: no planning graph imposed on the model, no single unified extension mechanism, and no full restore of session-scoped trust state on resume.

The paper also names four standing tensions it does not claim to resolve: safety versus autonomy, the permission model under adversarial conditions, context efficiency versus transparency, and simplicity versus extensibility.

title: Dive into Claude Code: The Design Space of Today’s and Future AI Agent Systems
text:
Six open directions
The paper closes with six open directions for future agent systems: the observability and silent-failure gap, cross-session persistence and longer-term memory, evolution of the harness boundary (where, when, and what the agent acts on), horizon scaling from a single session to a longer program of work, governance and oversight at scale, and a long-term-human-capability lens for judging these systems.

title: Dive into Claude Code: The Design Space of Today’s and Future AI Agent Systems
text:
References

Liu, Jiacheng, Zhao, Xiaohan, Shang, Xinyi, Shen, Zhiqiang. “Dive into Claude Code: The Design Space of Today’s and Future AI Agent Systems.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2604.14228), April 14, 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.14228

title: Dive into Claude Code: The Design Space of Today’s and Future AI Agent Systems
text:
Related Posts

APIs, Tools, Skills, and Where MCP Fits: an earlier take on the same extensibility taxonomy this paper formalizes, drawing the MCP boundary differently.
Where Claude Code Tokens Go: the outside-the-tool measurement of the context cost that the paper’s compaction pipeline is built to manage.
A Cursor Agent Erased a Company’s Production Data in 9 Seconds: a real instance of the single-destructive-call failure mode the per-action permission gate is meant to catch.
Snowflake Cortex AI Escapes Sandbox and Executes Malware: another agent-safety boundary failure, a counterpoint to the deny-first “untrusted model on a trusted machine” posture.
How Anthropic Teams Use Claude Code: an earlier look at Claude Code as a product, against this source-level architectural read.

title: Conformal Thinking: Risk Control for Reasoning on a Compute Budget
text:
The threshold needed to hit a target test risk varies a lot across early-stopping signals (left), and no single signal is the most efficient at every risk level (right), which is what motivates choosing thresholds by risk control rather than by hand. Figure 1 from the paper [1].
In Conformal Thinking: Risk Control for Reasoning on a Compute Budget [1] (ICML 2026), Xi Wang, Anushri Suresh, Alvin Zhang, Rishi More, William Jurayj, Benjamin Van Durme, Mehrdad Farajtabar, Daniel Khashabi, and Eric Nalisnick (Johns Hopkins University and Apple) recast the question of when to stop a reasoning chain as distribution-free risk control, and add a lower threshold that gives up early on problems the model is unlikely to solve.

title: Conformal Thinking: Risk Control for Reasoning on a Compute Budget
text:
Methods

Signals and the two thresholds
Conformal Thinking treats a reasoning chain as a sequence of chunks (the text between consecutive \n\n breaks) and, at the end of each growing chunk, reads a scalar signal \(s_t\) off the model — oriented so that a larger \(s_t\) means the model looks more confident it has converged. The signal is itself a choice: \(s\) denotes which signal (a function of the trace so far) and \(s_t\) its value at chunk \(t\), and the choice of \(s\) is one more thing to calibrate. The paper compares four:

Confidence [2] — force the model to begin its final answer, greedily roll it out, and score that rollout by its length-normalized log-likelihood (higher = more confident).
EAT (Entropy After /think) [3] — at that same forced-answer point, read the entropy of the next-token distribution instead of rolling an answer out; low entropy means the model is peaked on what to answer.
Trained probe [4] — a probe trained on AIME (a hard math-competition benchmark) to predict convergence (Qwen3-8B only).
Token count — the raw number of tokens generated so far, a length-only baseline.

Both thresholds operate on \(s_t\) — one on its current value, one on its trajectory — and both are chosen to respect a user-specified error tolerance \(\epsilon\) rather than tuned by hand:

Upper threshold \(\lambda_+\): a level on the current value of \(s_t\) — stop once \(s_t\) clears \(\lambda_+\), on the assumption that the model has converged on its answer. This is the standard confidence-based early-exit rule, and it controls the false positive risk of stopping with a wrong answer.
Lower threshold \(\lambda_-\): the paper’s new mechanism, and the reason it is not a fixed floor. \(\lambda_-(t)\) is a rising schedule — a logistic (sigmoid) curve in \(\omega_t\), the tokens spent by chunk \(t\), climbing from a low asymptote \(l\) toward a high one \(u\) (typically \(\lambda_+\)) as the budget \(B\) is consumed:
\[\lambda_-(t) = \sigma\big(c(\omega_t - mB)\big), \qquad \sigma(z) = \frac{u - l}{1 + e^{-z}} + l \tag{12,13}\]
with slope \(c\) and its midpoint at a fraction \(m\) of the budget. The chain gives up at the first chunk where confidence falls to or below the floor, \(s_t \le \lambda_-(t)\). Because the floor keeps rising, the model must raise its confidence to stay above it; if confidence stalls — the signature of an instance it is unlikely to solve — the floor overtakes it and reasoning halts before the full budget is spent. This is what makes the rule a constraint on the trajectory of \(s_t\) rather than its current value, and it controls the false negative risk of giving up on an instance more reasoning would have solved. Of these symbols, \(\omega_t\) is the running token count and \(B\) the fixed budget; the schedule’s shape — slope \(c\), midpoint \(m\), and low asymptote \(l\) — is what risk control calibrates.

The two thresholds save tokens in complementary places: the upper one trims wasted reasoning after the model has effectively converged, while the lower one avoids spending tokens on instances where further reasoning is unlikely to pay off. The next figure plots a confidence trajectory against token usage for Qwen3-8B on AIME. On an unsolvable instance (left), confidence fluctuates and never reaches the upper threshold, so the lower threshold halts the run before it consumes the full budget. On a solvable instance (right), confidence climbs steadily and crosses the upper threshold, ending the chain once the model is confident enough.



Dual-threshold early exit on Qwen3-8B. Left: an unsolvable instance, halted by the lower threshold. Right: a solvable instance, ended by the upper threshold. Figure 2 from the paper [1].




Calibrating the thresholds (risk control)
Given the target \(\epsilon\) and a validation set \(\mathcal{V}\) of \(N\) examples, the two thresholds are selected by distribution-free risk control so the true error rate on unseen data stays at or below \(\epsilon\) with high probability. That error rate is not raw accuracy but the validation mean of a per-instance loss \(\ell\) in \([0,1]\). Writing \(f_t(x)\) for the model’s answer at step \(t\) and \(y^*\) for the correct one, with \(\tau_n\) the exit step that \(\lambda\) induces on example \(n\), the risk is
\[\widehat{\mathrm{Risk}}(\lambda;\mathcal{V}) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\ell\big(y^*_n,\, f_{\tau_n}(x_n),\, s_{\tau_n}(x_n);\, \lambda\big). \tag{15}\]
The two thresholds plug in different losses. The upper one fires only when confidence has cleared \(\lambda_+\) (so the rule stops) and the answer is wrong — a false positive:
\[\ell^{+} = \mathbb{I}[s_t \ge \lambda_+]\cdot\mathbb{I}[f_t(x) \ne y^*]. \tag{8}\]
The lower one is its opposite, a false negative that fires when the rule gives up (\(s_t \le \lambda_-\)) on an instance some later step, up to the budget horizon \(T\), would have answered correctly:
\[\ell^{-} = \frac{\mathbb{I}[s_t \le \lambda_-]}{T - t + 1}\sum_{t \le k \le T}\mathbb{I}[f_k(x) = y^*]. \tag{9}\]
Both losses need the full reasoning trace and the gold answer, so calibration runs offline on labeled data. How that error rate is estimated from a finite validation set is what decides whether the guarantee actually holds:

Naive plug-in (the paper’s “no finite-sample correction”) keeps every threshold whose empirical validation risk \(\widehat{\mathrm{Risk}}(\lambda;\mathcal{V})\) — computed in a single pass over \(\mathcal{V}\) — is at or below the user’s target \(\epsilon\). On a finite, and here deliberately small (\(N = 50\)), validation set that empirical risk is an optimistic estimate of the true risk, so the selected thresholds overfit \(\mathcal{V}\). Across the 40 random validation/test resamples the mean test risk stays controlled, but its per-resample spread crosses \(\epsilon\) often enough that an individual run violates the target.
UCB (concentration-based upper confidence bound) thresholds an upper bound on the risk rather than the point estimate. For a loss bounded in \([0,1]\) and a chosen failure probability \(\delta\), Hoeffding’s inequality gives, for a fixed signal-threshold pair,
\[\mathrm{Risk}(s,\lambda) \;\le\; \widehat{\mathrm{Risk}}(\mathcal{V},s,\lambda) + \sqrt{\frac{\log(1/\delta)}{2N}} \quad\text{with probability } \ge 1-\delta,\]
so \(1-\delta\) is the confidence level; calibration keeps only thresholds whose bounded risk clears \(\epsilon\). The correction term inflates when the validation size \(N\) is small and vanishes as \(N\) grows, so the conservativeness adapts to how much data backs the estimate.
Scanning many candidates is not a separate method but an additional correction to UCB: the Hoeffding bound holds for one fixed \((s,\lambda)\), so sweeping many signals and thresholds invites multiple-comparison inflation. A union bound over the candidate grid \(\mathcal{G}\) — the set of all \((s,\lambda)\) pairs being searched — would correct it, replacing \(\delta\) with \(\delta/|\mathcal{G}|\). The paper flags this but uses the plain single-candidate correction and reports realized risk on a held-out test set.

In the two-threshold setting the single target splits in two, and the thresholds are calibrated in two decoupled steps rather than one joint search over \((\lambda_+, c)\) pairs: UCB first selects \(\lambda_+\) against an upper target \(\epsilon^+\), then — with \(\lambda_+\) fixed — the lower-threshold shape \(c\) is selected against a lower target \(\epsilon^-\). The second step still controls risk because \(\lambda_+\) is already locked. A fully joint search (via learn-then-test) is possible, but the authors found the decoupled procedure works as well in practice, at some loss of theoretical rigor.


Choosing a signal (efficiency loss)
Risk control rarely returns a single answer — for a given \(\epsilon\), every signal-and-threshold pair \((s,\lambda)\) whose UCB-corrected risk clears the budget is feasible, and usually several do. The efficiency loss is the tie-breaking objective: it scores how many tokens a configuration wastes, normalized by the total budget \(T\), and does not itself depend on the calibration. Two forms target the two thresholds:

Upper-threshold loss is normalized regret — the fraction of the budget spent reasoning after the answer was already right:
\[\mathcal{J}^{+}(t) = \frac{1}{T}\max(0,\, t - t'), \qquad t' = \min\{t \le T : f_t(x) = y^*\}, \tag{10}\]
where \(t'\) is the oracle stopping step, the first one whose answer is correct.
Lower-threshold loss counts wasted deliberation instead — the fraction of steps so far whose answer was still wrong, which approaches \(1\) when a long run never makes progress:
\[\mathcal{J}^{-}(t) = \frac{1}{T}\sum_{k \le t}\mathbb{I}[\,y^* \ne f_k(x)\,]. \tag{11}\]
Selection averages the per-instance loss over the validation set and keeps the feasible candidate that minimizes it:
\[\widehat{\mathcal{J}}(s,\lambda;\mathcal{V}) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\mathcal{J}\big(\tau_n(s,\lambda)\big), \tag{16}\]
with \(\tau_n\) the exit step of the \(n\)th sample. Across the candidate signals this yields an ensemble that selects the cheapest signal-and-threshold for each target risk and dataset.

title: Conformal Thinking: Risk Control for Reasoning on a Compute Budget
text:
Results
The authors evaluate on four reasoning models — Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-30B-A3B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B, and the vision-language model Qwen3-VL-8B — across AIME (1983–2025), a subset of DeepScaleR with AIME removed, GPQA-Diamond, and the vision benchmark MathVision. Generation uses each model card’s recommended decoding settings under vLLM. The four stopping signals from Methods are compared. Thresholds are calibrated over 40 random validation-test splits with a validation set of 50 samples (5 percent), sweeping \(\epsilon\) from 0 to 1 in steps of 0.01. Two things are measured: whether the achieved test risk stays under \(\epsilon\) (control), and how many questions the model answers correctly against the total tokens spent (efficiency).

Finite-sample correction keeps risk on target (Figure 4): with the UCB correction, the achieved risk on the held-out test set stays at or below the user-specified \(\epsilon\) across the 40 splits. The naive plug-in keeps the mean risk controlled, but its variance bands routinely cross the \(y=x\) line, so individual runs exceed the target.
The ensemble picks the most efficient signal per risk level (Figure 5): selecting the signal-threshold pair with the lowest efficiency loss on validation transfers to a better accuracy-versus-token trade-off on test than any single fixed signal. On Qwen3-8B, where the trained probe is one of the four candidate signals, the ensemble selects it over the other three (confidence, EAT, token count) at essentially every risk level — the probe is simply the most efficient signal there.
The lower threshold pays off when unsolvable instances are common (Figure 6): on pooled AIME and GPQA-Diamond sets with controlled solvable-to-unsolvable ratios, the upper-only rule clusters at the high-token end because many runs never reach the confidence cutoff and run to the budget limit. Adding the lower threshold shifts the accuracy-versus-token curve toward fewer tokens at similar accuracy, and the gain grows as the solvable-to-unsolvable ratio shifts from 3:1 to 1:3. At a representative operating point, solvable instances tend to exit via the upper threshold and unsolvable ones via the lower threshold, matching the design intent.




Empirical verification of risk control across the 40 validation/test resamples (shaded regions are mean ± one standard deviation); the dashed line is \(y=x\), the target. Top row: false-positive risk; bottom row: false-negative risk (Eq. 9). Left column: Naive plug-in; right column: UCB. Naive’s bands routinely cross above \(y=x\), so individual runs exceed the target \(\epsilon\), while UCB’s finite-sample correction keeps the achieved test risk at or below \(\epsilon\). Figure 4 from the paper [1].





Across four models, picking the lowest-efficiency-loss signal per risk level (the ensemble) transfers from validation to a better accuracy-versus-token trade-off on the test set than any single fixed signal. Figure 5 from the paper [1].





Lower-threshold gains grow as unsolvable instances become more prevalent. Qwen3-8B with the confidence signal on pooled AIME+GPQA at solvable:unsolvable ratios of 3:1, 1:1, and 1:3. Top: accuracy versus total tokens — the upper-only rule (blue) clusters at the high-token end because many runs never reach the confidence cutoff and run to the budget limit, while adding the lower threshold (lower+upper, orange) shifts the curve left at similar accuracy, with the gap widening as unsolvable instances dominate. Bottom: at a representative operating point, solvable instances tend to exit via the upper threshold and unsolvable ones via the lower threshold. Figure 6 from the paper [1].

title: Conformal Thinking: Risk Control for Reasoning on a Compute Budget
text:
My Notes

Standard risk control applied to a new quantity: the machinery is the usual distribution-free risk control [5] (Learn-then-Test and risk-controlling prediction sets), which turns any black-box score into one with a finite-sample guarantee. The closest LLM precedent, Conformal Language Modeling [6], calibrated a stopping rule over a set of sampled candidates so the returned set provably contains an acceptable answer. This paper instead calibrates when to stop a single reasoning chain, trading error rate against compute.
A rising floor turns the stop test into a rate-of-progress check: a static lower threshold would fire only when confidence drops, which rarely happens on a stuck run, where confidence tends to sit flat and low. Because the floor instead climbs with the budget, the question becomes whether confidence is rising fast enough rather than whether it is high enough right now — that is what lets the rule abandon instances whose confidence never improves. It is calibrated giving-up that sidesteps metacognition: it reads the trajectory from outside and imposes a schedule, never judging whether the question is answerable, which is exactly the judgment AbstentionBench [7] finds reasoning models make poorly.
CROP applies the same risk control to a finished trace: CROP [8] runs after the trace is generated, certifying the longest leading prefix whose step-risk proxies all stay below a calibrated threshold and routing the uncertified suffix to repair. Conformal Thinking instead runs during generation, calibrating stop/continue thresholds against a compute budget. Both fix a single threshold off a step-level signal under exchangeability.
The guarantee rests on exchangeability: the framework inherits conformal prediction’s core assumption that calibration and test data are exchangeable, and the paper’s own ablations show that is where it strains. False-negative control from the lower threshold degrades under a shift from short to long reasoning horizons, and the size of the efficiency gain depends on the solvable-to-unsolvable mix of the test set. A production query stream that drifts away from the calibration set would weaken the risk guarantee with no visible signal that the target \(\epsilon\) is no longer being met.

title: ResearchQA: Evaluating Scholarly Question Answering at Scale Across 75 Fields with Survey-Mined Questions and Rubrics
text:
ResearchQA’s generation pipeline (left) and the field distribution of its test split (right): top venues per field feed survey-article retrieval, and aligned query/rubric pairs are mined from survey sections, yielding 21K queries across 75 fields skewed toward health sciences and medicine. The diagram labels the downloadable-article pool 135K, but the paper’s text gives 134K (§2.1). We use 134K throughout. Figure 2 from the paper [1].
In ResearchQA [1], Li S. Yifei, Allen Chang, Chaitanya Malaviya, and Mark Yatskar (University of Pennsylvania), the team behind ExpertQA [2], scale expert-style scholarly QA evaluation from 32 fields to 75 by mining queries and grading rubrics from survey articles instead of paying domain experts to author them.

title: ResearchQA: Evaluating Scholarly Question Answering at Scale Across 75 Fields with Survey-Mined Questions and Rubrics
text:
Methods
The core idea is that a survey article is pre-distilled expert knowledge: its section structure already encodes what questions a field cares about and what a complete answer must contain. ResearchQA turns that structure into an evaluation set through a four-stage pipeline, with quality filters at each step:

Extract top venues per field. Pull each field’s top-20 venues by h5-index from Google Scholar Metrics, then manually redistribute Google Scholar’s 257 fields into 94 cleaner ones (660 venues total), since its categories are alternately too granular and too broad. The final test split spans the 75 fields that yield enough qualifying surveys downstream.
Retrieve survey articles. Fetch candidate survey articles from those venues via Crossref, Semantic Scholar, and S2ORC, then filter to genuine literature reviews (134K downloadable articles → 54K surveys).
Generate queries from survey sections. Turn each qualifying survey section into a self-contained research query plus a reference answer, filtered for self-containment, low answer variability, and citation content.
Generate rubrics. For each query, build a hybrid rubric of up to 8 items naming query-specific criteria a good answer should meet. The rubric is fixed once per query, built from the survey’s own reference answer rather than from any candidate response, and the same rubric then scores every system’s answer to that query. Two rubrics are drafted and merged: a survey rubric conditioned on the query plus the survey’s reference answer, and a parametric rubric conditioned on the query alone. The union is deduplicated, reranked by importance, and stripped of items that cite papers unmatchable on Google Scholar, keeping the top 8 (about 7.5 on average, ~61% from the survey rubric). Each item comes from one of three prompt types, sampled for topic diversity:

Information-based items ask for a specific statement, finding, opinion, or comparison.
Depth-based items ask for elaboration or explanation.
Citation-based items ask whether the answer cites a specific article.


The result is 21K queries and 160K rubric items spanning 75 fields across 7 domains, weighted toward health sciences and medicine. Thirty-one Ph.D. annotators across 8 fields then validate the artifact: they judge that 90% of queries reflect genuine Ph.D. information needs and that 87% of rubric items are worth a sentence or more in a complete answer.



An example ResearchQA query mined from a survey, with its evaluation rubric: an automatic judge scores a system’s long-form answer from 0 to 4 on each of up to 8 query-specific rubric items, the first of which asks whether the answer cites a specific paper. Figure 1 from the paper [1].

title: ResearchQA: Evaluating Scholarly Question Answering at Scale Across 75 Fields with Survey-Mined Questions and Rubrics
text:
Results
ResearchQA evaluates 18 systems in four classes (parametric LLMs, naive retrieval, production retrieval, and deep-research agents) across 7.6K head-to-head battles. Each answer is scored on two expert-validated metrics: average rubric coverage % (an absolute 0–4 score per rubric item, validated to agree with plurality Ph.D. labels 74% of the time when coverage and direct judgments are ensembled) and an Elo leaderboard score from pairwise preferences. Rubric items map to dimensions sampled from ScholarQABench and SciArena, including correctness, citations, coverage, relevance, organization, and attribution.
The headline is a ceiling, not a ranking:

No parametric or retrieval-augmented system clears 70% coverage. The top system overall, Perplexity’s deep-research agent, reaches 75.29%, leaving a quarter of rubric items uncovered even at the frontier.
The gap is worst exactly where it matters for scholarship. The highest-ranking system fully addresses fewer than 11% of citation rubric items, 48% of limitation items, and 49% of comparison items: it answers the question but rarely cites the right work, names the caveats, or contrasts alternatives.
Naive retrieval barely helps. Bolting a simple retriever onto a parametric model often fails to lift coverage, and on average the same model differs by only 7.6% coverage between naive and production retrieval.
The ceiling isn’t a verbosity artifact. Because coverage is recall-based, longer answers mechanically tend to cover more, so the obvious worry is that the metric just rewards length. Figure 6 bounds that: coverage rises with answer length but plateaus around 85% past ~2,000 words (about four pages), even though deep-research systems write up to 3,000 words while human-written answers on similar topics average under 300 words. The ceiling holds at the longest answers, so the uncovered rubric items are genuine omissions, not a side effect of short responses.




Rubric coverage versus answer length for the top deep-research systems, with and without length-guidance prompting. Figure 6 from the paper [1].

title: ResearchQA: Evaluating Scholarly Question Answering at Scale Across 75 Fields with Survey-Mined Questions and Rubrics
text:
My Notes

Survey-mining swaps the expensive ingredient in ExpertQA for a scalable one. ExpertQA [2] paid 484 experts to author 2,177 questions in 32 fields, and that human-authoring step is exactly what capped its size and breadth. ResearchQA, from the same group, treats published surveys as compiled expertise and mines 21K queries across 75 fields from them, a roughly 10× scale-up that trades direct expert authoring for the assumption that survey sections already encode what experts would ask. The 90% Ph.D.-endorsement rate is the evidence that the proxy mostly holds.
The evaluation target moved from per-claim attribution to rubric coverage, which measures a different failure. ExpertQA asked whether each emitted claim was supported by its cited evidence (a precision-style check on what the model said). ResearchQA’s rubric coverage asks whether the answer contains what a good answer should (a recall-style check on what the model omitted). The two are complementary, and ResearchQA’s low citation-coverage number (under 11% of citation items fully addressed) shows the recall view exposes a failure the precision view can miss: a system can avoid unsupported claims simply by never attempting the citations a complete answer needs.
Rubric coverage inherits the LLM-as-judge grounding problem it is trying to escape. The metric is only as trustworthy as the automatic judge scoring each rubric item, and the paper reports 74% coverage agreement and 69% pairwise agreement with Ph.D. humans, only reached after ensembling. That is squarely the contested LLM-as-judge reliability question, where prior work has shown LLM evaluators can be pushed to misrank answers outright [3].
A reusable recipe for any field with a survey literature. The pipeline needs only Google Scholar venue rankings and survey-article databases, so the same machinery could generate domain-specific evaluation sets wherever review articles exist, without recruiting a single expert. The bottleneck for trustworthy domain evaluation then shifts from expert availability to survey availability, which is far less scarce.

title: An Expert Schema for Evaluating Large Language Model Errors in Scholarly Question-Answering Systems
text:
Distribution of error types across question categories: each row is a question type normalized to sum to 1, each column an error type, with darker shading marking error types that dominate a given question category. The heatmap shows that error profiles differ sharply by question type. Figure 2 from the paper [1].
In An Expert Schema for Evaluating Large Language Model Errors in Scholarly Question-Answering Systems [1] (CHI 2026), Anna Martin-Boyle and Harmanpreet Kaur (University of Minnesota), with William Humphreys, Martha Brown, and Cara Leckey at NASA Langley Research Center, build a schema of how working scientists actually judge LLM answers about their own field, arguing that automated metrics miss how they assess those answers.

title: An Expert Schema for Evaluating Large Language Model Errors in Scholarly Question-Answering Systems
text:
Methods
The study runs a retrieval-augmented QA system over scientific papers (documents are chunked, vectorized, retrieved per question, and fed to an LLM that generates a long-form answer), then examines how domain experts evaluate its output in two phases. The LLM-generated answers are the object of evaluation throughout, and the two phases use different sets of them: the Phase 1 answers became the coded data that built the schema, while in Phase 2 a fresh batch was the material experts evaluated to validate it.

Phase 1, schema development. Three NASA Langley scientists took part. Two posed questions about papers they had authored (28 in aeroacoustics, 40 in non-destructive evaluation) and the QA system generated an LLM answer to each, so the ground truth was known to the evaluator. The third wrote no questions and was kept aside to label those answers for errors independently, a perspective the authors kept unbiased by not having that expert author any of the questions. Thematic analysis of the resulting 68 question-answer pairs yielded 20 recurring error patterns, organized into seven categories. The complete schema is in The Schema below.
Phase 2, schema validation. Ten additional scientists each wrote questions about their own papers, and the system generated LLM answers that the experts evaluated in think-aloud contextual inquiries. They evaluated unaided first, then with the schema (the Phase 1 list of 20 error patterns grouped into seven categories) in hand, to test whether it helped them catch errors they had missed.

Across both phases the authors collected 188 expert-posed questions and sorted them into 11 question types (a separate classification from the error schema, grouping the questions rather than the errors):

Methodological Inquiry and Improvement: compares approaches and asks how methods could be transferred or refined.
Meta-Analysis and Contextualization: asks about institutional motivations and synthesizes insights across multiple papers.
Critical Evaluation and Validation: probes assumptions and biases, and whether research choices were adequately justified.
Application and Practical Implications: asks how findings translate to real-world use and what tradeoffs implementation brings.
Technical Details and Specifications: asks for the parameters, equations, or configurations needed to replicate the work.
Definitions and Concepts: asks to clarify core ideas and key terms.
Future Directions and Extrapolation: looks past current findings to next steps and where the research is heading.
Binary / Factual Verification: asks to confirm or deny a discrete fact, without interpretation.
External Context: asks for knowledge beyond the paper, such as external standards or developments since publication.
Numerical Analysis and Derivation: asks the system to calculate or reason mathematically with data from the paper.
Procedural Information: asks how a study was conducted, focusing on the sequence of steps.

They then mapped the error patterns against each question type (Figure 2, the cover heatmap).



An error one domain expert caught that a model developer missed: a chronological mistake about test sequences that only someone who knew the underlying work would flag. Figure 1 from the paper [1].

title: An Expert Schema for Evaluating Large Language Model Errors in Scholarly Question-Answering Systems
text:
The Schema
The full taxonomy, for reference: 20 error patterns under seven categories, paraphrased from the paper’s Tables 1 and 2 [1]. Hallucinations are a single pattern broken out into seven sub-types.

Incorrect answer

Completely incorrect: the answer is entirely wrong.
Partially incorrect: a mix of right and wrong, covering basic accuracy slips, misinterpreting paper content, self-contradiction, reference confusion, and misread tables or equations.
Superfluous content: irrelevant or unnecessary information.

Hallucinations (plausible-looking content that is fabricated or false)

Terminology: invented or wrongly defined terms and acronyms.
Numerical data: made-up statistics, measurements, or metrics.
Mathematical constructs: invented equations, formulae, or relationships.
Technical content: false technical characteristics, properties, limitations, or capabilities.
External context and world knowledge: wrong general science or related-literature claims.
Document structure: invented page, section, table, or figure numbers.
Citation information: fabricated citations or parts of them (authors, dates, titles, venues, DOIs, page numbers).

Incomplete answer

Major omissions: important content left out: an ignored section, a missed main point, an ignored paper in a multi-document question, an incomplete definition, missing references, or chronological gaps.
Lacking details: high-level concepts present but lower-level detail missing.
Multimedia comprehension: fails to connect formats, for example not linking a table to its caption or in-text reference.

Question interpretation

Question misinterpretation: a wrong reading that leads to a wrong answer.
Question redirection: answers a different question than the one asked.

Synthesis issues

Document linking failure: can’t tie information to the right document across multiple papers.
Chronological confusion: misreads temporal relationships.
Disjointed response: fragmented or poorly integrated, for example discussing each paper in isolation.
Source confusion: misattributes information across papers.

Formatting issues

Verbosity: unnecessarily wordy or repetitive.
Notation errors: incorrect technical notation.
Language issues: improper wording, spelling, grammar, or syntax.
Inconsistent referencing: inconsistent in how it references content.

System failures

LLM limitations: model-inherent issues such as limited context length, no multi-modal understanding, and no access to external libraries.
Retrieval failures: the retriever did not supply the needed context.
Data structure issues: internal data-organization problems leaking into outputs.

title: An Expert Schema for Evaluating Large Language Model Errors in Scholarly Question-Answering Systems
text:
Results
Because this is a qualitative HCI study rather than a leaderboard, the results are the schema itself and the evaluation behavior it exposes, validated through the two-phase design (3 experts in development, 10 in validation, all recruited through NASA Langley’s internal networks).

The schema generalizes to a second expert group. All seven categories reappeared in Phase 2’s independent coding of the 10 new experts’ unprompted feedback, which suggests expert error-spotting is consistent across people rather than an artifact of the development team.
Experts evaluate with structured strategies, not gut reaction. They apply technical precision testing, value-based assessment tied to research use, and meta-evaluation of their own checking process, behavior that automated metrics do not model.
The schema is also a scaffold. Giving experts the schema during contextual inquiries turned up errors they had overlooked when evaluating unaided. The most common were hallucinated or misattributed citations, but experts also caught missing tables and figures, chronological gaps, disjointed responses, and missed main points once the inventory prompted them to look. The taxonomy does double duty as a checklist for human review.
Error profiles differ by question type (Figure 2). The 11 question types do not fail the same way, which suggests evaluation and mitigation should be differentiated by question type rather than applied uniformly.

title: An Expert Schema for Evaluating Large Language Model Errors in Scholarly Question-Answering Systems
text:
My Notes

This is the human-process complement to the automated-benchmark line, and it is openly skeptical of it. Benchmarks like ExpertQA [2] and ResearchQA [3] push toward scalable automated scoring, while this paper argues those metrics are too coarse to capture how experts judge, and studies the assessment process itself. The two programs answer different questions, what a good answer should contain versus how a scientist decides whether it does, and the schema is the missing description of the second.
Evaluators grading answers about their own papers provides strong but narrow ground truth. Recruiting scientists to assess QA output on work they authored removes the usual annotator-knowledge gap, since they know what the correct answer is. The cost is scale and breadth: 3 experts in development and 10 in validation, all from one research center, which makes the schema’s categories credible but their relative frequencies hard to generalize.
The schema-as-scaffold result is the practically useful finding. That structured prompts help experts catch overlooked errors matches a long line of checklist research in medicine and aviation, where externalizing tacit criteria improves detection. It points at the paper’s own proposed direction: schema-driven review tools.
Error-by-question-type echoes the cross-benchmark pattern that difficulty is not uniform. ExpertQA found list, advice, and opinion questions hardest [2], and this paper independently finds error profiles vary by question type. The convergence across an automated benchmark and a qualitative study is the stronger signal: question type, not just domain, is a primary driver of LLM-QA difficulty.
